title: Vercel Flags starts 7x faster and no longer extends function duration
description:
On Vercel, the Vercel Flags SDK now initializes faster on cold starts, and usage reporting no longer keeps functions running after the response.

Faster cold starts

Two changes speed up SDK initialization on cold starts:

  • The SDK loads and parses the flags datafile bundled with your deployment as soon as the client is created, so it’s ready before your code evaluates its first flag.

  • Every function invocation now includes the current datafile revision, so the SDK can check whether the bundled datafile is up to date without a network request.

In internal testing, eliminating the network wait reduced p75 cold-start SDK initialization time from over 70 ms to 10 ms, roughly 7x faster.

After initialization, flag reads are effectively instant. Across cold and warm invocations, p99 flag-read latency is under 1 ms.

Usage reporting no longer extends function duration

The SDK previously used waitUntil for usage reporting, keeping functions running after the response was sent. It now passes usage events to the Vercel runtime, so reporting no longer adds to function duration.

Update @flags-sdk/vercel to version 1.5.3 or later and redeploy your application:

Learn more in the Flags SDK documentation.

Read more

title: Node.js 26 LTS is now Generally Available on Vercel
description:
Node.js 26 LTS is now Generally Available for builds and Vercel Functions.

This release includes:

  • HTTP/2 by default for built-in fetch (Undici 8) lets multiple requests share a connection with servers that support it. This can reduce latency when your functions call APIs or databases over HTTP.

  • Temporal API offers an alternative to Date with immutable values and built-in time zone and calendar support.

  • V8 version 14.6, the updated JavaScript engine, adds features such as Map.prototype.getOrInsert() to retrieve an existing value or insert a default when a key is missing.

Using Node.js 26

Node.js 26 is the default for all new projects.

  • Automatic upgrades: If engines.node in your existing project’s package.json allows 26, such as >=20, your Node.js builds on Vercel will use 26 on the next deployment.

  • Manual upgrades: Set engines.node to 26.x in your project's package.json and redeploy.

  • Prebuilt deployments: Use Vercel CLI version 65.8.0 or later to deploy Node.js 26 Functions.

  • HTTP/1.1 in Functions: To keep HTTP/1.1, set the VERCEL_FETCH_DISABLE_H2 environment variable to 1 and redeploy.

Minor and patch updates to Node.js 26 roll out automatically for builds and Vercel Functions.

Read the Node.js version documentation to learn more.

Read more

title: Vercel Connect adds webhook triggers for more providers
description:
Vercel Connect now supports webhook triggers for Resend, X, Twilio, Notion, and Telegram.

Connect receives webhook events, such as Telegram bot messages or emails received by your Resend domain, and forwards them to an endpoint in your Vercel project. It verifies incoming requests and handles provider heartbeats and verification challenges for you.

To get started:

  1. Open Vercel Connect in the dashboard. Enable triggers when creating a connector for your provider or in an existing connector’s settings. Connect registers webhooks automatically for Resend and Telegram.

  2. For Twilio, Notion, and X, use the webhook URL from Connect and follow its instructions to complete setup in the provider’s settings.

  3. Add a trigger destination to choose the project and endpoint that should receive events.

You can turn triggers on or off later in the connector’s settings.

In the connector’s Observability tab, select Live to watch incoming trigger events.

These connectors join existing trigger support for Slack, Discord, Microsoft Teams, GitHub, and Linear.

Learn more in the Connect triggers documentation.

Read more

title: Vercel Agent can now validate alerts before paging
description:
Vercel Agent can now investigate alerts from Vercel monitors before they reach your paging system. With validation enabled for a webhook destination, only alerts Agent classifies as Critical are sent to it.

To enable validation:

  1. Open a monitor’s notification settings and create or link a webhook destination for your paging system, such as incident.io.

  2. Select Critical Only next to that destination.

You can also configure notification destinations with the Vercel CLI using vercel monitors notifications. Add --critical-only when linking or updating a webhook destination.

Agent checks logs and metrics to assess impact. For example, it can identify health-check errors that don’t affect customers or confirm sustained 5xx errors affecting checkout requests. You can also add context to each monitor to guide Agent’s investigation.

Alert validation is available on Pro and Enterprise plans with Observability Plus. Observability Plus includes ten Agent investigations per billing cycle, with additional investigations billed separately. Custom monitors cost $0.0035 per GB of data scanned. Built-in alerts remain included with Observability Plus.

Learn more in the alert webhook documentation.

Read more

title: HarnessAgent now supports image inputs for all harness adapters
description:
The AI SDK HarnessAgent layer now accepts image inputs across every harness adapter.

Pass images alongside text in the standard AI SDK message format: a content array mixing { type: 'text' } and { type: 'file' } parts.

Image input is processed by the harnesses' underlying vision models and supported across all available adapters: Claude Code, Cline, Codex, Cursor, Deep Agents, fx, GitHub Copilot, Grok Build, OpenCode, Pi.

Read the HarnessAgent image inputs documentation to get started.

Read more

title: Create custom monitors in Vercel Observability
description:
You can now create custom monitors to get alerts based on your Vercel Observability query results.

For example, you can track signals such as AI Gateway costs, Core Web Vitals and other performance metrics, Workflow and external API failure rates, or Vercel Sandbox CPU time.

Each monitor tracks a single metric, such as response time, or a ratio of two metrics, such as errors divided by total requests. Choose statistical anomaly detection or a fixed threshold, then configure the detection window, filters, and grouping.

To create a monitor, inspect a chart’s query in Observability, start from a preset, or open Settings > Alerts for your team.

You can also define a custom monitor in a JSON file and create it with vercel monitors add in the Vercel CLI. Run vercel monitors schema --type custom for the schema and examples.

Receive alerts through email, Slack, Vercel Inbox, push notifications, or team-level webhooks. You can also add context for Vercel Agent to use when investigating an alert.

Custom monitors are available on Pro and Enterprise plans with Observability Plus, at $0.0035 per GB of data scanned. Built-in alerts remain included with Observability Plus.

Create a custom monitor or learn more in the configuration documentation.

Read more

title: Customizable widgets for project cards
description:
The Overview tab in the dashboard now lets you choose which metric appears on each project card.

Project cards used to show a fixed Real Experience Score in the top right, but not everyone on your team watches the same signal. You can now swap that slot for whichever metric matters for that project. A security-sensitive project can show firewall activity, while a marketing site project shows traffic.

Available widgets

  • Firewall: allowed requests, denied requests

  • Observability: alerts, edge requests, function invocations, error rate

  • Speed Insights: Real Experience Score, LCP, CLS

  • Web Analytics: visitors online, visitors, page views

Pick per project

Open the switcher in the top right of any project card. The menu shows the current value for each available metric. When you select one, your choice is saved for that project and follows your account across refreshes and devices.

Enable features from the card

If a project does not have a feature enabled, you can start the enable flow from the widget menu without leaving the Overview tab. This is available for Speed Insights Plus, Web Analytics, and alerts.

Get started

Open your team’s Overview tab and use the switcher on any project card.

Read more

title: Vercel CLI adds Spend Management
description:
You can now view and manage your team's Spend Management budget from the Vercel CLI. Run vercel budgets and you, or the scripts and agents you run, get back your current spend and the active budget.

View, set, and remove a budget

This is the same On-Demand Budget shown in your team's billing settings. Setting a budget does not stop usage on its own. The --pause flag pauses production deployments of all projects when spend reaches 100%.

List budget alert history

You can now see your budget alert history. Run vercel budgets alerts for the full log, filtered with --since, --until, --limit, and --json. A bare vercel budgets prints the three most recent alerts.

Managing budgets requires the Owner or Billing role. Spend Management is available at no additional cost to Pro teams and to Enterprise teams on the Flexible Commitment plan.

Full reference now available in the vercel budgets CLI reference. Read more about Spend Management.

Read more

title: I built a self-hosted app to see all my Steam, PlayStation and Xbox games in one place
description:
I play on PC, PS5 and Xbox, plus a Switch that sits next to the TV. Every platform has its own library, its own stats and its own idea of what "played" means. I wanted one page where I could see everything: what I own, what I actually played, and the pile of games I keep buying and never start.

The existing tools didn't fit what I wanted. Some are desktop-only, some are hosted services where my data lives on someone else's server. I run a small homelab anyway, so I built Playroom, a self-hosted web app for your whole game collection.

Live demo (fake collection, read-only): https://hexguardsec.github.io/playroom-selfhosted/
Source: https://github.com/HexGuardSec/playroom-selfhosted

What it does

  • Syncs Steam, PlayStation (PS3 to PS5 trophies) and Xbox automatically. Nintendo games are added by hand, since there is no public API.
  • Covers, playtime, achievements and trophies, ratings and notes for every game.
  • An activity calendar built from each sync, so you can see when you actually played.
  • A backlog view with estimated time to beat, to face the pile of shame.
  • Public or private collection, 15 interface languages.

Things that were harder than expected

PlayStation has no public API. Playroom uses the same endpoints as the official PlayStation website, with an NPSSO token you get from your own account. It works, but it can break if Sony changes something, and the docs say so clearly.

Xbox history is noisy. On Windows, the Xbox app records PC games launched through Game Bar, even games that have nothing to do with Xbox. My first sync showed almost 200 "Xbox" games. Playroom now keeps a title only if it ran on a console or has Xbox achievements, and my list went down to the 95 games I really played.

PS4 and PS5 versions of the same game show up as two trophy lists. Playroom merges them into a single entry.

Built for people who self-host

  • One Docker container, no database to run. Data stays in a single folder you can back up.
  • No runtime dependencies: Node.js 22 and plain browser JavaScript, nothing from npm.
  • Security first: scrypt password hashing, strict Content Security Policy, CSRF protection, a non-root container with a read-only file system and no Linux capabilities. API keys never appear in logs or URLs.
  • No telemetry. Playroom never phones home.

Running it takes one command:

docker run -d --name playroom -p 8080:8080 \
  -v ./data:/app/data \
  ghcr.io/hexguardsec/playroom-selfhosted:latest

On first launch, the container logs print a one-time setup code, and the web page walks you through creating your account and adding your API keys.

A note on how it was built

I built Playroom with a lot of help from an AI assistant (Claude). I designed it, tested it on my own setup and reviewed the code, and the repository has an AI-DECLARATION.md file that explains what was AI-generated and what wasn't. I'd rather be upfront about it.

What's next

The next version (planned for mid-December) adds notifications (Discord, ntfy), JSON/CSV export, backup and restore, and an import from Playnite. The full roadmap is in ROADMAP.md.

If you try it, I'd love your feedback: issues and ideas are welcome on GitHub, and there's a Discord server for questions: https://discord.gg/xy9nYXxRvW

And if you also have a backlog that scares you a little, tell me how many unplayed games you have. Mine is not a number I'm proud of.

title: Put These Two Features to Work in Quant Trading: Let AI Write Strategies, Run Tests, and Close the Loop
description:
Recently, a user in the community raised a very practical question: when you use a browser-based AI to modify a strategy, you have to keep copying code between the chat window and the FMZ editor. Once the conversation gets long, you have to explain the background all over again. Switching to a coding tool such as Codex does let you edit a local project directly, but can you still make use of FMZ's candlestick annotations, logs, and profit curves at the same time?

Yes. Connect your local project, FMZ remote synchronization, and the Extended API, and after changing the code, the AI can go on to read the strategy's runtime records, check its actual behavior, and make the next round of adjustments. The platform's charts remain available, while source code, tests, and review materials accumulate locally.

Using Codex and a JavaScript strategy as examples, this article introduces the way we actually collaborate with AI in our strategy research. Other AI coding tools that can read and write project files and execute scripts can follow the same workflow.

It seems that quite a few people don't know these tools can be used together this way, so this article was clearly needed! The examples below use GPT6. A model that is too weak may not be up to the task, so try to use a leading model. Let's get started.

Quick tip: >_<! If the article feels too long and you don't want to read it all, you can simply hand it to AI. It will explain it clearly and tell you what you need to do.

1. First, Define the Roles of Development and Execution

The overall workflow can be organized like this:

Propose a strategy idea, constraints, and acceptance criteria
              ↓
AI reads the local project → Modifies code → Runs tests
              ↓
FMZ remote synchronization → Verify platform source code and parameters → Load the new version
              ↓
FMZ Docker runs the strategy, producing status information, order records, and profit data
              ↓
Retrieve data through the Extended API → Review locally → Make the next round of changes

The local project preserves the development process, FMZ Docker executes the strategy, and the FMZ interface continues to provide monitoring and charts. AI performs specific tasks based on the files, tool permissions, and runtime data made available to it.

Day-to-day trading should still follow explicit rules in the strategy code. The AI in this article is used for development and review. There is no need to call a large language model before every order, nor do you need to put exchange API keys into the chat history.

There is an important prerequisite here: what AI can analyze depends on which data sources and tools we have actually connected. With only local source code, it cannot know what happened last night. With only a screenshot of the status panel, it cannot reconstruct an entire night's order changes, either.

2. Create a Local Project That AI Can Pick Up and Continue

In plain English: create a local strategy development directory (folder), set up a series of project directories and files inside it, and then let your installed Codex application work in that strategy development directory.

If you are not comfortable setting up Codex CLI, you can also use the Codex desktop app for your operating system, which is quite convenient. The instructions below use Codex CLI.

If you already have Node.js and npm installed, you can install Codex CLI in a terminal and then enter your strategy directory:

npm install -g @openai/codex
cd "your-strategy-project-directory"
codex

Follow the prompts to sign in on your first run. Codex can read project files, modify code, and execute local commands, subject to the current permission settings. Refer to the official Codex CLI documentation for installation and sign-in instructions.

Start by downloading the existing source code from FMZ and exporting the complete strategy configuration as well. A .js file contains only code, whereas the .xml file from a complete strategy export also contains configuration such as parameters. The two are not interchangeable. For the differences, see FMZ's guide to importing and exporting complete strategies.

A small project can use the following structure:

my-strategy/
├── AGENTS.md                   # Project rules for AI
├── README.md                   # Current version, how to run it, and outstanding issues
├── strategy-design.md          # Signals, positions, exits, and profit accounting definitions
├── quant.js                    # Source code to synchronize to FMZ
├── complete-strategy-export.xml # Backup of platform configuration: parameters, interactive controls, etc.
├── tests/                      # Tests for key calculations and order scenarios
└── reports/                    # Runtime snapshots, reviews, and version verification records

A complex strategy can be split into multiple modules and then built into a single release file. In that case, establish a fixed build entry point so that local modules, the release file, and the source code in the web editor do not each end up being edited separately.

Codex supports reading project guidance from AGENTS.md. We can put frequently repeated requirements in this file, for example:

# Project Rules

- Before making changes, read README.md, strategy-design.md, and the latest review report.
- Use the local source code as the basis for development; if someone edits the code manually in the web interface, pull it back and compare it first.
- When changing order logic, check partial fills, fills during cancellation, and duplicate updates.
- Preserve profit accounting, recording realized P&L, unrealized P&L, trading fees, and funding fees separately.
- Record test results before release; after release, verify the source code and the version running in live trading.
- Read keys from local environment variables or a separate credentials file; do not put them in source code or reports.

For how project rules are loaded, see Codex's AGENTS.md documentation. This file guides collaboration; actual permissions are still controlled by the tools and API permissions.

At the end of each round, also ask AI to update the README: which version is local, which version is stored on the platform, which version is running live, and what evidence is still needed next. Even if you switch to a new conversation, work can resume from these files without retelling the entire chat history. Use Git alongside the source code to save checkpoints for comparison and rollback.

3. Connect FMZ's Two Channels

Essential reading: before putting the following into practice, have your Codex Agent thoroughly read the FMZ platform's API documentation. Simply tell the AI to read the FMZ platform documentation first.

There are two channels to connect: one for uploading code and one for reading runtime data. First, distinguish between the credentials involved:

  • Strategy synchronization token (strategy synchronization code): open the page for the strategy you want AI to design and work on:


Once you have the synchronization code, you can give it directly to AI. You can delete the code when you are finished using it, so there will be no security issues.

  • FMZ Extended API, on this page: https://www.fmz.com/m/account#apikey.


Once you have the Extended API KEY, you can give it directly to AI. You can also delete it after use, or save it in a file for AI to read when needed.

1. Upload Source Code with Remote Synchronization (AI Can Do This; You Only Need to Understand the Basics Here)
Find the remote synchronization option on the target strategy's editing page and obtain the synchronization command provided for that strategy. Using the endpoint employed in our current project as an example, the core operation is to upload source code to https://www.fmz.com/rsync with the strategy's Bearer token.

Here is the Bash version. First, set the FMZ_SYNC_TOKEN environment variable through your local credentials configuration. The file to upload is quant.js in the current directory:

# Exit immediately if the token is missing; do not put the real token in this script.
: "${FMZ_SYNC_TOKEN:?Please configure FMZ_SYNC_TOKEN first}"

printf 'Authorization: Bearer %s\n' "$FMZ_SYNC_TOKEN" |
  curl --fail-with-body --silent --show-error \
    --header @- \
    --upload-file quant.js \
    https://www.fmz.com/rsync

Use the path and token in the command generated by your own strategy editor. After synchronization, check the response and the target strategy, then read the source code back for comparison. An HTTP 200 response alone does not mean the entire release is complete.

Successfully synchronizing the source code does not mean the running live trading instance has loaded the new code. In this project's actual synchronization process, after the platform's source code was updated, the original process continued running the old version. The new version would only load on the next start. Release records therefore need to keep both the "synchronized version" and the "currently running version." Use the new startup logs and the version shown in the status panel to establish the latter.

Source code synchronization is no substitute for parameter migration, either. When code adds or changes parameters, interactive controls, or template references, also verify the platform configuration and the parameter values saved in existing live trading instances. The update plan should explain how existing positions, pending orders, and the persistent ledger will be carried forward.

2. Read Live Trading Data with the Extended API (AI Can Do This; You Only Need to Understand the Basics Here)
Open "API Interface" in your FMZ account settings and create an Extended API Key. For the initial connection, you can enable only GetRobotDetail,GetRobotLogs, which read live trading instance details and runtime records, respectively. FMZ supports configuring permissions by API method name; see the Create ApiKey documentation.

The following Python 3 example only queries live trading instance details; it does not modify a strategy or start a live trading instance. Before running it, set three environment variables locally: FMZ_ACCESS_KEY, FMZ_SECRET_KEY, and FMZ_ROBOT_ID. The live trading instance ID is not the strategy ID.

import hashlib
import json
import os
import time
from urllib.parse import urlencode
from urllib.request import Request, urlopen

params = {
    "version": "1.0",
    "access_key": os.environ["FMZ_ACCESS_KEY"],
    "method": "GetRobotDetail",
    "args": json.dumps([int(os.environ["FMZ_ROBOT_ID"])]),
    "nonce": str(time.time_ns() // 1_000_000),
}
message = "|".join([
    params["version"], params["method"], params["args"],
    params["nonce"], os.environ["FMZ_SECRET_KEY"],
])
params["sign"] = hashlib.md5(message.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()

request = Request(
    "https://www.fmz.com/api/v1",
    data=urlencode(params).encode("utf-8"),
    headers={"Content-Type": "application/x-www-form-urlencoded"},
    method="POST",
)
with urlopen(request, timeout=20) as response:
    payload = json.load(response)

data = payload.get("data") or {}
if payload.get("code") != 0 or data.get("error") or not data.get("result"):
    raise RuntimeError("FMZ query failed; check code and data.error in the response")

robot = data["result"]["robot"]
fields = ("id", "status", "strategy_id", "start_time", "refresh", "profit")
print(json.dumps({k: robot.get(k) for k in fields}, ensure_ascii=False, indent=2))

The signature concatenation follows the FMZ Extended API authentication documentation, and the response structure follows the GetRobotDetail documentation. The example retains HTTPS certificate verification and checks for application-level errors returned by the platform.

This is only a single-query example. When turning it into a reusable tool, also handle timeouts, rate limits, and error logging. Requests using the same Key should centrally manage an increasing nonce to avoid conflicts between concurrently running scripts. See the Extended API interface details for the relevant requirements.

It is fine if you are unfamiliar with the API. You can give AI the official documentation and the structure above and ask it to generate a query script in your project. Inject credentials through local input or a separate configuration, and let AI call the script. Do not copy real keys into public articles, strategy source code, or version-control repositories.

4. How to Keep Using FMZ's Charts and Profit Curves

Editing locally changes where the code is maintained. The strategy still runs on FMZ Docker, and its existing Log, LogStatus, LogProfit, Chart, and other outputs remain available. These display runtime logs, the status panel, the profit curve, and custom charts, respectively. See FMZ's logging and charting function documentation.

For AI-assisted review, you can retrieve the data behind these displays locally:


The GetRobotLogs documentation describes the three groups of records—logs, profit, and charts—as well as the status panel field. Set the number of records requested according to your actual needs, read them in batches, and deduplicate them by record ID. Follow the official GetRobotLogs documentation and the actual responses for the API's response structure and parameters.

The API returns data stored by the platform, not a screenshot of the entire web page. If existing candlestick annotations are recorded in chart data, they can be parsed alongside the series definitions. If the output consists only of images, those images need to be provided separately. Nor can tick-by-tick order book data that the strategy never saved be reconstructed from a profit curve.

So, beyond charts, it is best to leave structured records of key actions. For example, for a single order, you should at least be able to trace:

SUBMIT: What side, price, and quantity were submitted?
ACK: Did the exchange accept the order, and what order ID did it return?
FILL: What quantity actually filled, at what price, and with what fees?
CANCEL: Why was the order canceled, and what was the cancellation result?
SETTLED: Have the final filled quantity and position been reconciled?

Only then can AI distinguish between "a signal occurred," "an order was submitted," and "an order actually filled." A buy log or an order ACK does not mean a purchase has completed. Partial fills may also continue to arrive after a cancellation request has been sent.

Keep the status panel concise, showing the version, freshness of market and account data, positions, current orders, main reasons preventing action, and net profit. Detailed diagnostics can be output on demand. The following illustrative snippet is intended to be embedded in an existing main loop; diag is maintained by the strategy's own statistics module:

// Place this in the existing command dispatch logic; if GetCommand is already called, do not consume commands again.
var command = GetCommand();
if (command === "diagnostics") {
    Log("DIAGNOSTICS", JSON.stringify({
        version: diag.version,
        observedAt: Date.now(),
        decisions: diag.decisions,
        signalPassed: diag.signalPassed,
        orderAttempts: diag.orderAttempts,
        blockers: diag.blockers
    }));
}

Here, diagnostics is a command implemented by the strategy itself, not a built-in FMZ diagnostics feature. You can configure an interactive button, or trigger it through the API after separately enabling CommandRobot permission. For the command-receiving mechanism, see FMZ's GetCommand documentation.

Profit accounting also needs clear definitions. Our project breaks strategy net profit down into realized P&L, unrealized P&L, trading fees, and signed funding fees, with account equity displayed separately. LogProfit only records the value passed to it. It does not automatically account for all costs, nor does it distinguish deposits, other strategies' P&L, and the strategy's own returns on the strategy's behalf.

To avoid flooding the logs, you can record profit after events such as fills, reconciled position changes, or fees being posted, while continuously updating valuations in the status panel. When reviewing a run, save both the accounting period and the valuation time so that an event-sampled curve is not mistaken for an account equity curve updated every second.

5. A Practical Case: Why a Strategy Ran All Night Without Trading

During one iteration of Flow Efficiency Maker, the live trading instance ran for about 15 hours without making a new trade. The status panel at that moment showed the strategy waiting for a signal, but it could not tell us whether that had been the case all night.

We examined the runtime records, diagnostic snapshots, and the corresponding version of the source code together and established several specific facts:

  • Of about 209,000 decision samples, roughly 189,000 had valid model data. The market data inputs had not been invalid throughout the night.
  • Only one sample reached recovery confirmation. That candidate had about 3.35 bp of remaining room to its target, below the strategy's required 5 bp cost buffer.
  • The account, limits, and stopping mechanisms were not the main reasons for the lack of trades in this instance.

Further code inspection revealed a conflict between the recovery conditions and cost requirements: the strategy was designed to capture price shocks starting at about 8 bp, but required at least 20% recovery before entering confirmation, with the target set at 80% recovery. Ignoring small differences from the price denominator and rounding, the maximum available room was approximately:

8bp × (80% − 20%) = 4.8bp

That was already below the 5 bp cost buffer, and subsequent confirmation could consume still more of the available room. This explained why, even with apparently normal market data and the strategy continuously computing, it struggled to produce executable orders. Decision samples were highly correlated, so the counts above cannot be treated as the number of independent trading opportunities, either.

Subsequent adjustments used this finding to align recovery timing with the room available to cover costs. We also added event-stage statistics to record whether opportunities disappeared at the identification, confirmation, cost, or execution stage. For validation, we used the same synthetic market data to compare behavior before and after the changes, then checked compatibility with the platform's runtime environment.

This case illustrates the value of the collaboration workflow: use live trading evidence to locate specific conditions in the code, then use tests to validate the changes. It does not prove that the new version has acquired a profitable edge. Preset fills in synthetic scenarios cannot be treated as a market backtest. Ultimately, we still need to observe price movements after real fills, exit costs, and net profit.

6. Organize Each Round of Changes as a Verifiable Experiment

After connecting the tools, it is not enough to tell AI simply to "keep optimizing." Each iteration should have a goal whose outcome can be assessed, such as "identify the main reason there have been no trades in the last 12 hours" or "check whether partial fills during cancellation are being counted twice."

You can describe a task like this:

First, read the project rules, strategy design, and latest validation report, and establish which versions are present locally, in the platform source code, and in the current live trading instance. Use the Extended API to retrieve the last 12 hours of logs, profit records, and diagnostic information, and save them in reports by time and record ID. Distinguish between signals not triggering, insufficient order amount, insufficient room to cover costs, failed order submissions, and orders canceled without fills, and provide supporting data. Once the cause is confirmed, modify the local code and run the relevant tests, recording the differences in behavior before and after the changes. Carry out source code synchronization and the live trading restart separately, as agreed for this round, and state in the report exactly which steps have actually been completed.

This task description connects the subject of the investigation, the evidence, the changes, and the release status. When first connecting the tools, you can limit the work to queries, then gradually add authorized synchronization and testing operations as you become familiar with the workflow. The Extended API includes both query and control endpoints; there is no need to enable every permission just to read logs.

Validation should also be separated into levels, so that a single statement such as "tests passed" does not stand in for answers to every question:


For example, for a market-making strategy that relies on individual trades and order book queues, an ordinary candlestick backtest cannot adequately test queue-based fills and adverse selection. The test report needs to describe the data granularity, matching assumptions, sample period, and scenarios not covered. Any uncovered questions should remain on the list of items to validate.

It is useful for each round to leave four deliverables: the modified source code, test results addressing that round's issue, runtime data and review conclusions, and a clear release status. In the next round, AI can read these files and continue researching the unresolved issues.

With this approach, developers can devote more attention to strategy hypotheses, trading constraints, and evaluating the evidence: let AI perform repeatable queries, changes, and checks, while FMZ handles strategy execution and result recording. Only when each change has a corresponding version and validation record can we later determine what it actually solved.

While we're here, let me also share a strategy used in the hands-on work discussed in this article

title: I ran the most hyped AI agent catalog on GitHub through three subagents and installed exactly zero agents from it. This post is
description:
The setup

The catalog: 273 agent files across 22 divisions, 169k stars, MIT license. Each file is a role with rules, deliverable templates and success metrics. Solid work, and mostly noise for any specific business: divisions for Douyin, WeChat, Unity, carousel generators for platforms you may not even be able to reach. The useful fraction is maybe 10 percent, but that fraction contains methodologies it'd take you months to polish yourself.
Our side: a CRM where an Obsidian vault is the single database and agents run the operations layer. Five scheduled roles (commercial director, finance director, CEO, marketer, on-call SRE), an hourly inbound cycle over email and messengers, and a company charter with hard gates. An agent physically cannot send an invoice below the price floor or promise a client a deadline without owner confirmation.
That context matters. A prompt is a personality without memory. What turns it into an employee's the bundle: skill plus schedule plus gates plus access to live company data.

The extraction run

Three subagents in parallel, each with a zone: marketing, sales and paid media (53 files), finance, PM, support, product and strategy (40 files), testing, engineering and specialized roles (about 70).
My instruction to each subagent: read everything, return a verdict per file in the context of our system. Steal, skip, or reference. Not a summary, a decision: what exactly to take and where exactly to put it.
By midday I had verdict tables for 160+ files, deep breakdowns of the top five per zone, and an implementation plan. Then the surgery: edits went into concrete role skills, and since our automation prompts reference those skills, every scheduled ritual picked up the new rules on its next run. Nothing was redeployed. Nothing restarted.
If you want to replicate this, the load-bearing detail we found is the verdict format. 'Interesting' is not a verdict. 'Steal the dunning ladder into the commercial director skill, replace our D+7 single reminder with a five step sequence' is.

What came out of it

The dunning ladder. Receivables now walk a fixed sequence: D-3 heads-up, D+1 reminder with the PDF, D+7 serious reminder with the acceptance act, D+14 formal demand plus a pause-work question, D+30 pre-legal. The first three steps send themselves.
Decisions with defaults. The behavioral design principle that tied it all together: every question to the owner arrives with a drafted answer. Not 'what do we do about this debtor' but 'letter drafted, send or edit'. One click beats an hour of deliberation, and default consent beats both.
The evidence protocol. This one targets the real disease of agent-run companies, fantasy reports. The rules we adopted:

  • Every 'it works' claim requires proof: screenshot, curl output, log, green run. Otherwise the status is NOT TESTED.
  • Four statuses: PASS, FAIL, NOT TESTED, NOT DETERMINED. NOT TESTED means the hole is in the testing, not a hidden all-clear.
  • Automatic fail for 'no issues found' without a documented scope.
  • Default verdict for fresh work: NEEDS WORK. First implementations take two or three revision cycles, that's normal.
  • Perfect scores from a previous agent are a red flag. Reproduce two or three claims at random. The citation audit loop. Once a month, 20 to 40 live buyer prompts run through ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini and Yandex Neuro. The table records who gets cited. Lost prompts, the ones where a competitor wins, get a root cause check (comparison page, FAQ schema, freshness), a fix pack, and a re-check with the same prompt set 14 days later. Benchmark before fixes, always. Sales qualification. Six questions we now ask on every lead, no exceptions: what is broken, why, what does it cost, who else cares, why now, what happens if nothing is done. Plus the value equation as an offer auditor: value = (dream outcome x perceived likelihood) / (time delay x effort). Cut the price only after squeezing the other three levers. ## Why zero agents got installed Three reasons worth stating plainly:
  • A personality without memory is not an employee. Those 273 prompts do not know our clients or our price floor.
  • Idle agents burn attention and budget. Our roles wake in their slot, do the work, write the journal, sleep.
  • Of the file format itself, only three sections survived contact with reality: hard rules (numbered Never/Always), a ready deliverable template, and verifiable metrics. Identity and vibe are cosmetics. ## Takeaways The competitive edge of 2026 isn't access to AI. Everyone has that. The edge is the speed of absorbing methodologies, because the world produces them faster than any human reads. A company with reading and adoption on a conveyor upgrades weekly. A company without one reads about upgrades on LinkedIn. Second: agents don't replace the owner, they prepare decisions. Approval mode instead of decision production. Third: honest systems beat pompous ones. We rejected dozens of prompts with '+300% leads' claims, numbers out of thin air. Verifiable rules went to production the same day. Apply the same filter to everything sold to you as a miracle. Originally published at https://automata.sale/en/blog/ai-automation/273-agenta-v-odin-den/

title: pandas crosstab normalize: Row, Column and Total Percentages (Plus the margins, NaN and Multi-Label Traps)
description:
pd.crosstab builds a frequency table from two columns in one line, and the normalize argument turns those counts into shares. The catch is that there are three different percentages hiding behind normalize, and they answer three different questions. Add margins=True, missing values, empty categories or rows that belong to several groups at once, and it gets easy to publish a percentage that does not mean what the chart title says.

This guide covers pandas crosstab normalize end to end: normalize="index", "columns" and "all", what margins does to each, weighted shares with values and aggfunc, how NaN keys and unused categories quietly change the table, the right denominator for multi-label data after explode, and a quick chi-square check of whether two categories are related at all.

Tested on pandas 3.1, NumPy 2.5 and SciPy 1.18. The data is synthetic and seeded: 400 made-up tickers, each with a listing board and one theme tag. Every table below is real output.

Sample data: one row per item, two categorical columns 

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

rng = np.random.default_rng(11)
tags = ["AI chips", "Robotics", "EV battery", "Cloud", "Biotech"]
boards = ["Main", "ChiNext", "STAR"]
n = 400
df = pd.DataFrame({
    "ticker": [f"T{i:03d}" for i in range(n)],
    "board": rng.choice(boards, n, p=[0.55, 0.25, 0.20]),
    "tag": rng.choice(tags, n, p=[0.25, 0.2, 0.2, 0.2, 0.15]),
    "mentions": rng.poisson(20, n),
})
# make one cell empty on purpose
df.loc[df.board.eq("STAR") & df.tag.eq("Biotech"), "tag"] = "AI chips"
print(df.head())
print(pd.crosstab(df.tag, df.board))

  ticker    board         tag  mentions
0   T000     Main  EV battery        16
1   T001     Main       Cloud        16
2   T002  ChiNext    Robotics        18
3   T003     Main    Robotics        20
4   T004     Main  EV battery        21
board       ChiNext  Main  STAR
tag                            
AI chips         24    59    22
Biotech          14    38     0
Cloud            17    40    12
EV battery       23    46    21
Robotics         19    51    14

The first argument becomes the rows (index), the second the columns. Without normalize you get counts.

normalize="index": each row sums to 1

Use this when the question is "within each tag, how are items split across boards?"

print(pd.crosstab(df.tag, df.board, normalize="index").round(3))

board       ChiNext   Main   STAR
tag                              
AI chips      0.229  0.562  0.210
Biotech       0.269  0.731  0.000
Cloud         0.246  0.580  0.174
EV battery    0.256  0.511  0.233
Robotics      0.226  0.607  0.167

Read across a row: 73.1% of Biotech items are on Main, and none are on STAR. Each row adds up to 1.0. normalize=1 does not mean this; integer values follow the axis convention, so 0 is "index" and 1 is "columns". Use the strings to avoid mixing them up.

normalize="columns": each column sums to 1

Use this when the question is "what is the tag mix of each board?"

print(pd.crosstab(df.tag, df.board, normalize="columns").round(3))

board       ChiNext   Main   STAR
tag                              
AI chips      0.247  0.252  0.319
Biotech       0.144  0.162  0.000
Cloud         0.175  0.171  0.174
EV battery    0.237  0.197  0.304
Robotics      0.196  0.218  0.203

Now read down a column: 31.9% of STAR items are AI chips, compared with 25.2% on Main. This is the table you want for a stacked bar chart with one bar per board.

normalize="all" (or True): the whole table sums to 1 

print(pd.crosstab(df.tag, df.board, normalize="all").round(3))

board       ChiNext   Main   STAR
tag                              
AI chips      0.060  0.148  0.055
Biotech       0.035  0.095  0.000
Cloud         0.042  0.100  0.030
EV battery    0.058  0.115  0.052
Robotics      0.048  0.128  0.035

Each cell is a share of all 400 rows. Main × AI chips holds 14.8% of everything. This view suits a heatmap of joint frequencies but is rarely the right number for a sentence like "X% of AI chip names are on Main".

What margins=True adds with each normalize option

margins=True adds an All row and/or column, but which one you get depends on normalize:

for how in ["index", "columns", "all"]:
    t = pd.crosstab(df.tag, df.board, margins=True, normalize=how)
    print(f"normalize={how!r}: rows={t.index.tolist()[-1]!r}, cols={t.columns.tolist()}")
print(pd.crosstab(df.tag, df.board, margins=True, normalize="columns").round(3))

normalize='index': rows='All', cols=['ChiNext', 'Main', 'STAR']
normalize='columns': rows='Robotics', cols=['ChiNext', 'Main', 'STAR', 'All']
normalize='all': rows='All', cols=['ChiNext', 'Main', 'STAR', 'All']
board       ChiNext   Main   STAR    All
tag                                     
AI chips      0.247  0.252  0.319  0.262
Biotech       0.144  0.162  0.000  0.130
Cloud         0.175  0.171  0.174  0.172
EV battery    0.237  0.197  0.304  0.225
Robotics      0.196  0.218  0.203  0.210
  • normalize="index" adds only an All row: the board split across the full sample (58.5% Main). A row-total column would be all ones, so pandas leaves it out.
  • normalize="columns" adds only an All column: the tag mix across all boards. This is the baseline to compare each board against. STAR's 31.9% AI chips versus 26.2% overall is the kind of difference worth reporting.
  • normalize="all" adds both, and the bottom-right corner is 1.0.

Use margins_name="Total" to rename the All label.

Weighted shares with values and aggfunc

Counting rows treats every item equally. To get shares of a numeric column (mentions, revenue, volume), pass values and aggfunc. normalize then applies to the aggregated values:

w = pd.crosstab(df.tag, df.board, values=df.mentions, aggfunc="sum",
                normalize="columns")
print(w.round(3))

board       ChiNext   Main   STAR
tag                              
AI chips      0.265  0.270  0.303
Biotech       0.137  0.164  0.000
Cloud         0.163  0.161  0.179
EV battery    0.228  0.190  0.313
Robotics      0.207  0.214  0.204

This is "share of mentions", not "share of tickers". The two can differ a lot when a few items dominate the numeric column. normalize with values only makes sense for additive aggregates like sum or count. Normalizing a mean produces numbers that are hard to interpret.

NaN keys are dropped silently

Rows whose row or column key is NaN do not appear anywhere in the table, and the percentages are then computed without them:

d2 = df.copy()
d2.loc[[0, 1, 2], "board"] = np.nan
print("rows in table:", pd.crosstab(d2.tag, d2.board).to_numpy().sum(), "of", len(d2))
print("after fillna:", pd.crosstab(d2.tag, d2.board.fillna("Unknown")).to_numpy().sum())

rows in table: 397 of 400
after fillna: 400

Three rows vanished without a warning. If missing values matter for your denominator, fill them with an explicit label like "Unknown" first.

Keeping empty categories (and their order)

A tag that never appears gets no row. If the column is a Categorical, dropna=False keeps unused categories, and the row order follows the category order instead of alphabetical order:

d3 = df.copy()
d3["tag"] = pd.Categorical(d3.tag, categories=tags + ["Fintech"])
print(pd.crosstab(d3.tag, d3.board).index.tolist())
print(pd.crosstab(d3.tag, d3.board, dropna=False).index.tolist())
print(pd.crosstab(df.tag, df.board).reindex(tags + ["Fintech"], fill_value=0).tail(2))

['AI chips', 'Robotics', 'EV battery', 'Cloud', 'Biotech']
['AI chips', 'Robotics', 'EV battery', 'Cloud', 'Biotech', 'Fintech']
board    ChiNext  Main  STAR
tag                         
Biotech       14    38     0
Fintech        0     0     0

For plain string columns, reindex(..., fill_value=0) on the counts is the simplest way to force a fixed set of rows. Do it before normalizing. An all-zero row cannot be row-normalized (0/0 gives NaN).

Multi-label data: the denominator after explode

When an item can carry several tags, the usual approach is a list column plus explode. The table still works, but the denominator changes:

ml = df[["ticker", "board"]].copy()
ml["tags"] = [list(rng.choice(tags, size=rng.integers(1, 4), replace=False))
              for _ in range(len(ml))]
ex = ml.explode("tags")
print(len(ml), "items ->", len(ex), "item-tag rows")
print(pd.crosstab(ex.tags, ex.board, normalize="columns").sum().round(3).tolist())

share = pd.crosstab(ex.tags, ex.board).div(ml.board.value_counts(), axis=1)
print(share.round(3))

400 items -> 837 item-tag rows
[1.0, 1.0, 1.0]
board       ChiNext   Main   STAR
tags                             
AI chips      0.412  0.440  0.464
Biotech       0.485  0.466  0.536
Cloud         0.381  0.410  0.377
EV battery    0.433  0.376  0.333
Robotics      0.402  0.385  0.406

normalize="columns" on the exploded table still sums to 1. That gives you the share of tag assignments, not the share of items. If the question is "what fraction of STAR items carry the AI chips tag?", divide the counts by the number of items per board, as share does. Those columns add up to more than 1, which is correct for multi-label data.

Same result with groupby, and a chi-square check

crosstab is a convenience wrapper. The groupby version gives the same row shares and slots into longer chains more easily:

alt = (df.groupby("tag")["board"]
         .value_counts(normalize=True)
         .unstack(fill_value=0))
print(np.allclose(alt, pd.crosstab(df.tag, df.board, normalize="index")))

from scipy.stats import chi2_contingency
res = chi2_contingency(pd.crosstab(df.tag, df.board))
print(f"chi2={res.statistic:.2f}  dof={res.dof}  p={res.pvalue:.4f}")

True
chi2=15.05  dof=8  p=0.0582

Pass raw counts to chi2_contingency, never a normalized table, because the test depends on sample size. Here p ≈ 0.058. Even with a completely empty STAR × Biotech cell, 400 rows are not quite enough to reject independence at the 5% level. That is a useful reminder not to over-read one striking cell in a percentage table.

FAQ

How do I show crosstab percentages as 0–100 with a % sign?
Multiply by 100 and format at the end, for example (t * 100).round(1).astype(str) + "%", or use t.style.format("{:.1%}") in a notebook. Keep the numeric table for further calculations.

Why don't my row percentages add up to exactly 100?
Rounding. Each cell is rounded separately. Round only for display, or use a largest-remainder method if the displayed numbers must add up.

crosstab or pivot_table?
Same machinery. crosstab takes arrays or Series and has normalize; pivot_table takes a DataFrame and column names and has no normalize, so you divide yourself.

Conclusion

Pick the denominator before you pick the function. normalize="index" answers "how is each row group split?", "columns" answers "what is each column group made of?", and "all" gives joint shares. margins=True adds the matching baseline row or column. Fill NaN keys you want counted, reindex empty categories before normalizing, divide by item counts instead of tag counts for multi-label data, and run significance tests on raw counts.

Stock-to-theme tables are a typical multi-label case: one stock belongs to several concepts, and "share of stocks" and "share of tag assignments" give different answers. Lava's concept stock lookup shows a real version of such a mapping for A-share concept themes.

中文简介：本文用 400 条固定种子的合成数据（虚构代码、上市板块、主题标签）讲解 pandas crosstab 的 normalize 参数：normalize="index" 每行合计为 1，"columns" 每列合计为 1，"all" 全表合计为 1；margins=True 在不同 normalize 下分别只加 All 行、只加 All 列或两者都加；用 values+aggfunc="sum" 计算加权占比；键为 NaN 的行会被静默丢弃，需先 fillna；Categorical 配合 dropna=False 或 reindex 保留空类别；多标签数据 explode 后按列归一化得到的是「标签分配占比」，若要「条目占比」需除以每列条目数；最后给出 groupby 等价写法，并说明卡方检验应使用原始计数。

title: The site he wants redone was redone to do the opposite
description:
"I need to finally redo the Palo Alto AI Lab site." It was redone four months ago, deliberately, to do the opposite

Anton wants to get into SEO and GEO to promote the lab and the community. He spoke to someone from HeroicRankings.com and wants to study their approach. He positions the lab as a community of AI engineers, AI-native builders and power users; lists the themes to build visibility around; wants to understand what SEO and GEO consist of, which routines to build, how to tie it to articles, GitHub, events and social, and how to earn backlinks. Then: "I need to finally redo the Palo Alto AI Lab site. It should look like a modern, full community" - with five offers stated on the site: build tools and we have an audience to test them; have a product and we will present it; strong engineer, become a speaker; want to be a power user, come to the calls.

The agency is real and does exactly what he described. Everything else here has history.

The site already exists, and it sells something else. Read live today:

element what is there now
title Palo Alto AI Lab | Independent multi-agent orchestration and agent governance research
description Independent research lab working on multi-agent orchestration, agent governance, and zero-knowledge methods. Open artifacts, published evals, named authors.
h1 Palo Alto AI Lab: the fleet experiment
structure 8 h2, 11 h3, 43 links, JSON-LD present, canonical present

And the words he wants to rank for are not on the front page at all. Counted in the served HTML: "meetup" 0, "community" 0, "speaker" 0, "MCP" 0, "harness" 0, "AI-native" 0, "power user" 0. "Engineer" twice, "builder" once.

So the gap is not that the site looks dated. It is that the site sells an independent research lab - orchestration, governance, zero-knowledge, published evals - and he wants it to sell a community.

And that positioning was a decision, not an accident. A Decision Memo from 23 July, still active, titled "palo-alto.ai → text-only research-lab site as hiring/acqui-hire magnet". Built on a deep research with 467 sources, with its target reader named outright: a recruiter, research lead or acqui-hire scout at a frontier lab, Anthropic first.

That memo cut, by name, four of his five new offers:

he wants now the memo's verdict in July
"we have an audience that will test your tools" hero "I want you AI BUILDER" + book-a-call → CUT, "a sales funnel, wrong audience"
"have an AI product - we can present it" "We enable Founders/VCs/Angels" → CUT, "sales"
"come to the calls, tell us your tasks" "book a call" named a genre violation that cheapens the page
"strong engineer - become a speaker" "we are looking for co-founders" → rewrite into a real Team page with bios and links

The memo's thesis was that trust on such a page comes from traceability and restraint - verifiable anchors, dated activity, named authors - and that partner logo strips, "trusted by" and "book a call" read as hype to the exact insider he is trying to attract.

None of which means he is wrong now. Goals move, and a community funnel is a legitimate thing to want. But the site is not un-redone: it was rebuilt four months ago on purpose to be the opposite of what this post describes, and both cannot live on one front page. That is a decision to make, not a redesign to order.

"I want to understand what SEO and GEO consist of" has four applied studies behind it. From the registry:

  • DR26-06-30-HUB-01 - Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) and Content Strategy 2025-2026, applied, closed by its own Decision Memo
  • DR26-07-27-ZB-03-2306 - SEO+GEO per-platform strategy: what to write where so humans find it and LLMs cite it; platform map, canonical and duplicates, applied, with its own memo
  • DR26-08-04-ZB-09-1803 - a step-by-step protocol for entering AI-engine answers for a small independent lab with zero backlink mass, applied
  • DR26-08-04-ZB-08-1744 - GEO analytics from origin logs, and whether an open tool exists, applied

The third is almost verbatim the closing sentence of his post. Plus four distilled insight notes and two Decision Memos, including a platform map from 27 July.

And the pipeline is already on the shelf. Thirteen skills, by name: /geo, /audit-website-aeo, /improve-aeo-geo, /geo-content-research, /geo-content-planning, /write-seo-geo-content, /create-geo-charts, /build-backlinks, /build-resource-pages, /research-brand, /research-keywords, /audit-content, /reddit-opportunity-research.

Audit the site, research the brand, research the keywords, plan the content, write it, build the resource pages, hunt backlinks, chart the result. Every stage he describes as "which routines do I need" has a skill named after that stage.

⚠️ Which makes the honest shape of this commission not "learn SEO and GEO" but: four studies and thirteen skills exist, and the lab's visibility is where it is. So the open question is whether the pipeline has ever been run end to end, not whether it exists.

⚠️ One claim I could not verify, one I can measure. The meetups "several times a week" are unreadable from this machine - the public Luma addresses answer with redirects and need a logged-in session. The "grateful audience" was measured three days ago for another post: 176,992 subscriptions across Telegram and X delivering about 300 readers per post, with the 144,878-subscriber English channel reaching 64. An SEO strategy aimed at growing that audience starts from a reach failure, not a traffic shortage.

⚠️ And the agency checks out. HeroicRankings.com is live, calls itself "SEO, GEO & Link Building Agency", leads with "B2B SEO Agency for Google and AI Search", and claims citation work across 30+ languages. Nothing in his account of the conversation is off.

⚠️ Caveats. Site and agency figures are single unauthenticated GETs today from one machine, parsed from served HTML; term counts run against that HTML, so they include markup and miss client-rendered content. The registry check is a case-insensitive scan of 703 lines. The Decision Memo was read in full, including its KEEP/CUT table. Skill names come from a listing of 280 directories; I did not open each file to confirm scope, and I did not check their run counters - that is the obvious next measurement and it was not taken. Luma could not be read. The audience numbers are carried over from the 17 November measurement, not re-taken.

The full story, in two versions:
📖 For humans, the longread: https://github.com/tonydzi/clawrush/blob/main/longreads/20261116.md
🤖 For machines, the devlog: https://github.com/tonydzi/clawrush/blob/main/devlog/20261116.md. Just hand this link to your coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor) and it will figure everything out: it is written for machines.

🔗 All our channels and contacts in one place: https://linktr.ee/PaloAltoAI

Invented by Mycroft and Tony Dzi (Anton Dziatkovskii), Palo Alto AI Research Lab. Proudly made in Silicon Valley.

title: Dovod: a compiled language where a function without evidence does not compile
description:
AI agents now write code faster than anyone can review it. The bottleneck has moved from writing to checking. Dovod is a small compiled language built around that fact: checking is not an optional step after the code is written, it is part of what makes the code valid.

Dovod (Russian довод) means "an argument, a piece of evidence". Code in it carries its own evidence.

Repo: https://github.com/helgard-orlm/dovod (MIT). The whole language is one spec file of about 9 KB, meant to be read once in a single context window.

A first look 

fn clamp(x: Int, lo: Int, hi: Int) -> Int
  need lo <= hi                        // precondition, checked on every call
  give out >= lo and out <= hi         // postcondition on the result
  ex clamp(5, 0, 3) == 3               // examples: run at every check / build
  ex clamp(-1, 0, 3) == 0
  ex clamp(2, 0, 3) == 2
{
  if x < lo { return lo } else if x > hi { return hi }
  return x
}

fn main() uses io {
  print("clamp(15, 0, 10) = " + show(clamp(15, 0, 10)))
}

It compiles to C: no garbage collector, single-owner value semantics, no references, no null, no globals. Integer overflow, out-of-bounds access and failed contracts trap instead of silently continuing.

Rule 1: no examples, no compile

A pure function with no ex lines is a compile error. Examples run on every check and every build. The only way out is an explicit excuse:

fn fast_inv_sqrt(x: Float) -> Float
  assume "accurate to 1e-6 for x in 0.01..100; checked by hand against a table"
{ ... }

An assume is allowed, but it is not hidden: it shows up in the trust report together with every function that depends on it.

Rule 2: an example must be able to fail

The easy way to satisfy "every function needs an example" is an example that tests nothing. The compiler rejects that:

fn double(x: Int) -> Int
  ex double(2) == double(2)
{
  return x * 2
}

vac.dv:2:16: E-VACUOUS: both sides of this comparison are the same expression, so it pins down nothing
    fix: compare with a concrete expected value: `ex double(...) == <value>`

Beyond the obvious cases, every example is also re-run against two mutants of its function's result. An example that passes either way pins down nothing and is rejected.

Rule 3: the compiler tells you how strong your examples are

After the examples pass, the compiler mutates each function body one small change at a time — a number +1, < to <=, == to !=, + to -, and to or, a removed assignment — and re-runs the examples. Every change that no example notices is a place where the code could be wrong while all tests stay green.

// is the shop open at this hour? (opens 9, closes 18)
fn open_at(hour: Int) -> Bool
  ex open_at(12) == true
  ex open_at(3) == false
{
  return hour >= 9 and hour < 18
}

$ dovod weak shop.dv
shop.dv:6:18: W-WEAK: in `open_at` no example notices if `9` becomes `10`
shop.dv:6:15: W-WEAK: in `open_at` no example notices if `>=` becomes `>`
shop.dv:6:31: W-WEAK: in `open_at` no example notices if `18` becomes `19`
shop.dv:6:29: W-WEAK: in `open_at` no example notices if `<` becomes `<=`
1 of 5 small changes are noticed by the examples; 4 are not.

Two examples, both passing, and neither boundary is actually checked. Add ex open_at(9) == true and ex open_at(18) == false and the score becomes 5/5. dovod check prints the score for the whole file; dovod weak lists every surviving change with its line and column.

The compiler also reports every block that no example ever reached.

Rule 4: effects are declared — exactly 

fn main() uses io, fs_read { ... }

A function that touches the console, files, the clock, randomness, command-line arguments or a module's device must declare it. An undeclared effect is an error, and so is a declared effect the function never uses. There is no other way to reach the outside world, so the effect list on main is the complete answer to "what can this program touch?".

Small slips are errors

Things that are a warning or a lint elsewhere are errors here: shadowing, unused names, an ignored result, a non-exhaustive match, implicit conversions. Labelled arguments (f(x, lo: 0)) are checked against the parameter name at that position. There is one way to do each thing.

The trust ledger

dovod trust prints a report meant for someone who will not read the code. A real one, for a small window program that compares grocery prices per kilo (trimmed):

$ dovod trust examples/prices.dv
  can:    read/write the console (io); show a window or page in a web browser and
          read what the user does there (opens a network port) (ui)
  cannot: read files; write files; read command-line arguments; read the clock;
          use randomness; network; run other programs

  function   status          examples  blocks  strength
  per_kilo   self-checked    8/8       6/6     7/7
  best       self-checked    5/5       5/5     6/7
  view       self-checked    4/4       5/5     7/7
  update     self-checked    16/16     12/12   14/14
  main       shell           -         -       -        effects: io, ui

  summary: 9 self-checked, 1 shell. Unchecked shell = 18 of 266 function lines (6%).
  taken on faith: nothing.
  outside this ledger (no example reaches it):
    - Dovod's C runtime under every program (text, lists, traps): 276 lines of C
    - module `ui`: 4 native function(s), 326 lines of C
    - the shell functions themselves (main): they run only in the real program
    - whether the task was understood: examples by the code's author share the author's reading of it

Statuses: self-checked (all examples pass and reach every block), partial (some block never ran — the line is named), assumed, shell (the effectful outer layer), witnessed / witness-failed.

Two design choices are deliberate:

  • self-checked, not "correct". Examples written by the code's author catch slips and forgotten cases, but not a misunderstood task: the same misunderstanding goes into both. For an independent check, someone else (a person or another model) writes a witness file that uses the code, and dovod trust FILE --witness W.dv upgrades a function to witnessed or reports witness-failed.
  • The ledger says what it cannot see. Native code in the runtime and in modules is listed with its size, so "taken on faith: nothing" is never read as "everything is verified".

Built for an agent's loop

  • Every diagnostic has file:line:col, a stable code (E-NAME, E-EFFECT, E-EXAMPLE, E-VACUOUS, W-WEAK…) and usually a concrete fix: line. --json gives the same to a machine.
  • dovod card FILE prints only signatures, contracts and two examples per function — the interface to hand to another agent without the bodies.
  • dovod spec prints the whole language; dovod spec NAME prints a module's page. 
slips.dv:18:5: E-NAME: unknown name `totl`
    fix: did you mean `total`?
slips.dv:24:3: E-EFFECT: `loud` does `io` (read/write the console) but does not declare it
    fix: add `uses io` to `fn loud` — or move this out of a pure function

Modules

The core stays one page; everything task-specific is a module enabled with use NAME. A module cannot add syntax, its exports carry its prefix, and only simple values cross the boundary to native code. Current modules:

  • ui — a window (or a page on the local network) with buttons, fields, sliders and tables, drawn by the user's browser and served by the program itself. The screen is a value: fn view(model) -> UiNode and fn update(model, ev) -> Model are pure functions with examples; the browser only renders.
  • video — play media files in a window on Windows (Media Foundation). dovod build --target win64 produces a single .exe with no DLLs.
  • ble — listen to Bluetooth LE advertisements on Windows: address, name, signal strength, services, manufacturer.
  • mcu — Arduino-family boards. dovod build FILE --target arduino --fqbn arduino:avr:leonardo writes a sketch folder and compiles it with arduino-cli. Debounce, long-press and timer-wrap logic is pure code whose examples run on the PC before anything is flashed. The lamp.dv example (button + light, 26 examples) is 6.9 KB of flash and 337 bytes of RAM on an ATmega32U4.

The program always owns its event loop: modules expose a pull function (video_next(), ble_next(timeout)), so the effects of main stay the whole truth.

Speed

Same code in Dovod and Python 3.13, Intel N100, one run each, with all Dovod checks (overflow, bounds, contracts) on:

task Dovod Python
prime sieve to 5,000,000 25 ms 590 ms
longest Collatz below 1e6 298 ms 10,061 ms
building 2M number strings 113 ms 145 ms

A single run on a low-power CPU: read it as "native code, as expected", not as a benchmark.

Try it

Needs Python 3.10+ and a C compiler (gcc or clang).

git clone https://github.com/helgard-orlm/dovod && cd dovod
bin/dovod check examples/shapes.dv          # static checks + run all examples
bin/dovod weak  examples/shapes.dv          # which small code changes no example notices
bin/dovod run   examples/wordfreq.dv README.md
bin/dovod build examples/bench.dv -o bench  # native binary
bin/dovod trust examples/prices.dv          # the ledger
bin/dovod card  examples/wordfreq.dv        # interface only
bin/dovod spec                              # the whole language
tests/run.sh                                # compiler self-test (incl. ASan/UBSan/leak check)

Status and limits

Version 0.3, experimental. Not there yet: maps, generics, closures, namespaces, network and process effects, Unicode-aware text indexing (Text is indexed by bytes). Examples are not proofs: an example can be refutable and still weak (ex f(1) != 0) — the strength score and witnesses exist to expose exactly that.

Related work that shares ideas: Vera (contracts and Z3 for LLM-written code), Hylo (mutable value semantics), Koka (effect types), and mutation testing in general. Dovod's own combination is mandatory examples, mutation strength reported by the compiler, a ledger of what is taken on faith and what is invisible, and exact effects — aimed at the case where a model writes the code and a person has to decide whether to trust it.

If you give SPEC.md to a model and let it write something, I'd like to hear how it went.

title: Tracing AI Agents: How Managed Tracing Helps Security Teams
description:
Your agent called a payments tool at 2:14 a.m. The log says “200 OK.” Nothing looks wrong. Yet the agent pulled the wrong customer record two steps earlier, and every action after that rested on it. Security teams hit this wall daily. Application logs record what happened, not why. AI agent tracing closes that gap by recording each decision, tool call, and piece of retrieved context as one connected chain. This post covers what to capture, why managed tracing beats a DIY pipeline, and how to turn traces into detections.

Why Do Standard Logs Fail for AI Agent Security?

Standard logs answer one question: did the call succeed? Security teams need a different one: was the call justified?

An agent run where five log lines show success while a stale retrieval at step two corrupts every later step.

What a Silent Failure Looks Like in a Multi-Step Workflow

A multi-step agent plans, retrieves context, calls tools, and drafts an answer.

Each step can succeed technically while failing logically. Suppose retrieval returns a stale record at step two. The agent treats it as ground truth and passes it to a billing tool at step three.

Every log line shows success. No exception fires. The error surfaces only when a customer complains.

Meanwhile, the evidence you need sits scattered across model logs, API gateways, and vector store queries, with no shared identifier tying them together.

Where Security Teams Lose the Trail

Fragmentation is the real problem. Different services timestamp events differently and name sessions differently. During an incident, analysts stitch records together by hand. That work takes hours, and it often fails.

Moreover, agents act with real permissions, so one unexplained action can mean data exposure. Without a causal chain, you cannot tell a prompt injection from a model quirk, and you cannot prove either to an auditor.

What Does AI Agent Tracing Actually Capture?

AI agent tracing records one agent run as a tree of timed spans. Each span represents a step: a model call, a retrieval, or a tool invocation. A shared trace ID binds them together.

As a result, analysts replay the full decision path instead of guessing. The OpenTelemetry community also publishes semantic conventions for generative AI, which gives teams a vendor-neutral way to name these fields.

Spans, Tool Calls and Retrieved Context

A useful span carries the inputs, the outputs, the tool name, the caller identity, and the source of any retrieved context. Here is a trimmed example:

Notice the input_source and permission_scope fields. They let a reviewer ask two questions fast: where did this data come from, and was this agent allowed to act on it?

Table of trace fields, what each records, and the security question each answers.

How Does Managed Tracing Differ From Building It In-House?

Managed tracing means a provider runs the collection, storage, and query layers for you. Self-built pipelines look cheap at first. However, the hidden work arrives quickly. Schemas drift as frameworks change.

Retention rules differ per regulation. Raw prompts need their own access controls, since traces often contain sensitive data. Consider the trade-offs:

Schema upkeep: in-house teams patch parsers whenever an agent framework changes, while managed tracing absorbs those changes.
Retention and immutability: managed setups enforce retention windows and tamper-evident storage by default.
Redaction: managed pipelines mask secrets and personal data before anything is stored.
Ownership: security teams keep policy control, and engineers keep their sprint capacity.

Therefore, the real question is rarely whether to trace. It is who maintains the pipeline when the third framework migration lands.

Comparison of in-house tracing and managed tracing across schema upkeep, retention, sensitive data and maintenance.

How Can Security Teams Use Traces to Catch Prompt Injection and Permission Abuse?

Traces turn agent security monitoring from guesswork into querying. Start with three detections:

Untrusted input reaching a privileged tool. Flag any span where retrieved web or email content feeds a tool with write permissions.
Scope drift. Alert when an agent calls a tool outside its declared permission scope.

Instruction shifts. Compare the plan span before and after retrieval. A sudden goal change often signals injection.

Each rule works because the trace preserves ordering. A flat log cannot show that retrieval preceded the odd tool call. A trace can.

Furthermore, these checks line up with the risks OWASP lists for agentic applications. Teams validating every AI output before production use traces as the evidence behind each block or approve decision.

Over time, the same traces feed regression tests. Replay a flagged run against a patched agent, then confirm the behavior no longer reproduces.

Flow of three trace detections from untrusted retrieval to alert and review.

How Does Xccelera Support Trustworthy Agent Operations?

Xccelera builds enterprise agentic systems where governance ships with the agents, not after them.

Its approach places a monitoring layer above the execution infrastructure, so every agent output faces policy checks before it reaches a downstream system.

An evidence layer runs alongside and records inputs, tool calls, retrieved context, and final outputs inside the customer’s own environment.

Security teams therefore get a complete, timestamped record without forensic reconstruction.

Human reviewers stay in the loop where risk demands approval, and engineers keep delivery speed because the checks run in parallel with the work. This lets enterprises scale autonomous agents with proof instead of assumptions.

title: How to stop AI coding agents from pushing API keys to GitHub
description:
An AI coding agent needs a key to test something, finds one in your environment (an OpenAI, Claude or GitHub token), writes it into a config file to make the test pass, commits, and pushes. It did exactly what you asked. The key is now in your git history.

Once a secret reaches a remote, deleting it is not enough: forks, clones, mirrors and caches may already have it. The only real fix is rotating the key, and the only cheap fix is never letting it leave your machine.

This guide sets that up so it holds even when the agent is the one pushing.

Why the usual safeguards don't hold

.gitignore keeps .env out of git, but the agent didn't put the key in .env. It put it in config.go, a test fixture, or a README example.

A pre-commit hook scans for keys, but it runs on the same machine as the agent, as the same user. One git commit --no-verify and it's skipped. Hooks also aren't versioned by git, so a fresh clone or a new worktree has none.

GitHub push protection does block many key types before they land, and on public repositories it's on by default. But anyone with write access can bypass it by picking a reason like "used in tests", on private repositories it's part of the paid GitHub Secret Protection add-on, and it only exists on GitHub - not on Gitea, a self-hosted GitLab or anything else.

The common problem: every one of these either sits where the agent can switch it off, can be waved through, or doesn't cover the repo you care about.

Already covered? If your repo is public on GitHub and nobody would bypass a warning, push protection already does much of this. The rest of this guide is for private repos without the add-on, other git hosts, and anyone who wants a check with no bypass option.

A newer leak: the agent's own settings file

Agents keep their own config inside the repo, and that config can hold secrets too. When you approve a command in Claude Code with "Yes, and don't ask again", it saves that exact command to .claude/settings.local.json so it can match it next time. If the command had a password or token in it, the secret is now in that file. Claude Code sets git to ignore the file when it creates it, but that doesn't help once the file is already tracked. Apiiro scanned 104,185 public copies of the file on GitHub and found 1,122 with at least one real secret. Two widely used secret scanners, Gitleaks and TruffleHog, each missed hundreds of those files, and 215 slipped past both. Most of the misses were passwords typed into commands (PGPASSWORD=, sshpass -p, mysql -p), which carry no prefix for a scanner to recognise.

Check yours:

git ls-files .claude/settings.local.json   # prints the path if git tracks it

If it prints the path, untrack it and keep it ignored:

git rm --cached .claude/settings.local.json
echo '.claude/settings.local.json' >> .gitignore

Any secret in it that was ever pushed is leaked: rotate it (see "Already leaked?" below). To keep new ones out, pass secrets through environment variables rather than typing them into commands you approve.

The fix: a check the agent can't route around

Put the check on a separate machine between the agent and GitHub, and take away the agent's direct route to GitHub.

  YOUR COMPUTER            THE GATEWAY                 GITHUB
  (you + the agent)        (checks every push)         (your real repo)

  git push ──────────────► checks against rules ────► forwarded if clean
                           rejected if not

Two rules make this a real boundary:

  1. Your computer only pushes to the gateway. Your origin points at the gateway, not at GitHub.
  2. Only the gateway can write to GitHub. It holds the GitHub token. Your computer, and so the agent, doesn't have one.

Now --no-verify changes nothing: the check runs on the gateway, on the server side of the push, where the agent can't reach it.

This is what nimblegate does. It's self-hosted, runs as one Docker container, and nothing in it phones home. The steps below use it; the ten-minute version is the quick start.

Prefer to watch? The whole setup, start to finish, in 6 minutes:

Step 1: Run the gateway

On any small server, VM or home-lab box with Docker (not your laptop):

curl -O https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nimblegate/nimblegate/main/compose.yaml
docker compose up -d

The admin dashboard is on port 7900 (bound to localhost) and git pushes go to port 2222. Claim your admin login with the setup token from the logs, add your SSH public key, and register the repo with its GitHub URL and a GitHub token. The token is stored on the gateway only.

Step 2: Point your repo at the gateway

On your computer, add a shortcut to ~/.ssh/config:

Host nimblegate
  Hostname  192.0.2.10        # your gateway's address
