title: Technical Writers Should Be the Ones Writing AI Skill Files
description:
If you use AI to write documentation, you’ve probably seen this happen more than once. One prompt gives you a page that follows your style guide perfectly. The next prompt forgets your heading style, renames your product, and writes the release notes in a format your team stopped using a year ago, so you end up pasting the same instructions into every conversation and fixing the same mistakes in every draft. For a while I thought this was just the price of working with AI. Then I started writing skill files, and I realised that the fix for this problem looks a lot like the work technical writers already do every day.

What a skill file actually is

A skill file is a set of instructions that teaches an AI tool how to do one specific task the way you want it done. In practice, a skill is a folder containing a SKILL.md file.

It includes a name and a description at minimum, along with instructions that tell the agent how to perform the task. It can also bundle scripts, reference materials and templates. The name and description sit at the top of the file and tell the AI when the skill is useful, while the rest of the file is plain Markdown that explains how to do the work.

Looking for a SKILL file sample that turns your PRD into an actionable, ready-to-review draft? Check out PRD TO DOCS AI SKILL

The clever part is how the AI reads it. The agent scans the descriptions, and when one matches the current task, the whole skill, including its instructions and supporting files, enters the agent’s context. That means you can keep many skills ready without filling every conversation with instructions the AI doesn’t need yet, and the right one loads only when you ask for that kind of work.

Skill files also aren’t tied to one tool anymore. Anthropic shipped skills in October 2025 and published the format as an open standard on December 18, 2025, and the official showcase now lists more than 40 tools that support it, including GitHub Copilot, VS Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI and OpenAI’s Codex. So a skill you write once can work in whichever AI tool your team happens to use.

The easiest way I’ve found to explain the difference between a prompt and a skill file is to think about onboarding.

  • A prompt is like explaining a task to a new teammate in a quick chat, which works once but is gone the next day.

  • A skill file is the onboarding document you hand them on day one, with your style rules, your templates and a checklist for what good work looks like, so every task they do after that starts from the same place.

Why technical writers are the right people to write them

When you look closely at a skill file, it’s really documentation, except the reader is an AI that follows every word it has.

Most of the skills of a good skill file are skills we already use at work:

  • Structure: We know how to turn messy information into a clear structure, which is exactly what a skill needs. Style guides, templates and information architecture are part of our daily work, and frameworks like Diátaxis already teach us that a how-to guide and a feature overview need different structures.
  • Clear language: We’re trained to remove ambiguity, because ambiguous instructions confuse AI in the same way they confuse users. A rule like “keep it consistent” means nothing to an AI. A rule like “use sentence case for headings and bold only UI labels” produces the same result every time.
  • Defined terms: We define terms before we use them, which stops the AI from inventing its own names for your features.
  • Knowing what good output looks like: We already review docs every day, so we know how to tell when a draft is right. A skill without a final checklist will happily produce confident drafts that are wrong, and writing that checklist comes naturally to someone who reviews documentation for a living.
  • Knowing the workflow: We sit between product, engineering and support, so we know the full path a feature takes from a PRD to release notes. Engineers are writing excellent skills for coding tasks, but a skill for documentation needs someone who understands what users need from the docs and where they usually get stuck.

What a good skill file changes in your day

The biggest change for me was how much repeated manual work disappeared. Before I used skills, a lot of my time went into pasting the same style rules, correcting product names, rebuilding page structures and reformatting release notes into our five standard sections. Once those rules lived in one skill file, I stopped fixing them by hand, because every draft started from the same instructions.

The second change was consistency across the team. When every writer uses the same skill, drafts from different people come back with the same structure, the same terms and the same tone. Reviews get faster as a result, because the reviewer is checking facts instead of formatting.

I want to be honest about what a skill file doesn’t change, though. The AI still writes the first draft, and you still have to check every field, every default and every step against the real product before anything ships. A good skill makes that checking easier, because the drafts are predictable and the open questions are listed up front, but it doesn’t remove the need for a writer who knows the product.

From one PRD to five consistent drafts

The task where a skill file has saved me the most time is turning a product requirements document into docs. When a PRD lands, the usual routine is to read it a few times, list the questions for the product manager, wait for answers, and then write the feature overview, the how-to guide and the release notes one by one. Each of those pages follows rules your team has agreed on, and every one of those rules is something the AI has to be told.

So I packaged the skill I use for this into a product called the PRD to Docs AI Skill You give the AI a PRD, and the skill produces five drafts that follow the same structure every time:

  1. A questions log: This lists the few questions that decide whether the docs are correct, with the assumption taken for each one, so you can start writing before the PM replies.
  2. A glossary: It gives one plain definition for every new term.
  3. A feature overview: It explains what the feature does and who can use it.
  4. A how-to guide: It covers the main task from start to finish.
  5. Release notes: These are split into What’s new, What’s enhanced, What’s changed, Deprecated and Removed.

The questions log is my favourite part. In my experience, a wrong assumption costs more time than a slow draft, and seeing the risky assumptions listed before any writing starts changes how the whole review goes.

To make the skill yours, you fill in a few settings and a short profile of your company, such as your product names and your voice. From then on, every draft reads like your docs instead of generic AI output. The package includes the full SKILL.md file, a finished example company profile, a ZIP ready to upload to Claude and a 24-page setup guide. It works best in Claude and Claude Code, and you can paste the same instructions into other AI tools too.

How to start writing your own skill file

You don’t need my skill to get started, and I’d encourage every technical writer to try writing one, because it’s quickly becoming part of the job. These steps are a good place to begin:

  1. Pick one recurring task: Release notes work well, because they follow the same format every time and take more time than they should.
  2. Write down what good looks like: Add one real example your team approved, so the AI has a model to match instead of guessing.
  3. Turn every preference into a specific rule: Replace adjectives like “clear” or “consistent” with instructions the AI can follow exactly.
  4. Add a final checklist: List what the AI must confirm before it hands you the draft, such as product names, headings and section order.
  5. Test it on two or three real inputs: When a draft comes back wrong, fix the skill instead of the draft, so the same mistake doesn’t come back next time.

Conclusion

AI can write first drafts faster than any of us, but it still needs someone to tell it what good documentation looks like. That person should be the technical writer. We already know the structure, the rules, the terms and the checks, and a skill file is just the place where all of that finally gets written down for a new kind of reader.

If you’d like a working example to learn from or build on, the PRD to Docs AI Skill is a good starting point. Either way, I’d love to know whether you’ve written a skill file for your docs work yet, and which task you would automate first. Tell me in the comments.

title: 90% of Claude Code Is Written by Claude — Here's How the Team Verifies Every Change
description:
On the Claude Code team, the vast majority of the code — around 90% — is written and reviewed by Claude itself. At that scale, the question is no longer whether an agent can write code. It's whether an agent can prove its code works.

That's the subject of a new post from Anthropic's Claude.dev blog, "How the Claude Code team thinks about verification," written by Addy Osmani and published on November 16. The core argument is simple: verification loops are what let you delegate more work to agents. Without them, you can really only run one or two Claudes at a time, because you have to check everything yourself. With them, you can run dozens or hundreds in parallel.

Why verification beats better prompting

In internal testing around structured file generation, having a separate grader check Claude's work against a rubric improved task success by up to 10 points over a standard prompting loop — with the largest gains on the hardest problems.

The reason is economic. Things that used to be expensive to verify — tests, benchmarks, specs, real end-to-end runs — are now cheap to ask an agent to produce. And once generated, those tests run as software, so they can be executed frequently without burning many additional tokens.

The loop closes when results feed back into the agent's behavior. If an agent repeatedly fails a test that checks logs for user data, the team adds a hook or a more explicit rule in CLAUDE.md to stop it happening again. Verification isn't just a gate; it's how the agent gets better at the task.

The three tests worth investing in

Not all tests are equal, and the post is blunt about the failure modes: flaky tests train the agent to re-run tests instead of fixing code, and slow tests mean fewer tests per batch, which makes bugs harder to pinpoint. Heavier tests belong before the change is committed. Within that frame, three types earn their keep.

End-to-end tests. If you focus on one type, pick this one. E2E tests describe real user flows — add an item to a cart, check out, reach the confirmation page. They are hard to fool: either the whole feature works or it doesn't. And unlike a unit test that just says "timeout after 30 seconds," an E2E failure gives you a step trace, a screenshot, and a description of what broke. Unit tests are faster and less flaky, but you can pass them all and still ship a broken feature, because neither the agent nor the test understood the full task.

Property tests. Most tests are written around what you thought might go wrong. Property tests hunt the edge cases people tend to miss — exactly where agents often fail. You write a statement you think can't fail (round-trip encoding, an invariant like "account balance can never become negative," idempotency, equivalence with a naive implementation), then let a library — fast-check for JS/TS, Hypothesis for Python, proptest for Rust — generate thousands of inputs trying to prove it wrong. The edge cases come from the library, not from the agent that wrote the original code, so they don't share its blind spots. They're especially useful in rewrites, where the spec has drifted from production behavior and is no longer a reliable source of truth.

Differential tests. When functionality is expected to stay the same — a large-scale migration, for example — run the old system and the new system on the same inputs and compare. Any difference is a bug or a breaking change. The trick is using randomly generated inputs or a sample of production traffic, normalizing irrelevant differences like whitespace, and keeping a list of approved changes for places where the new environment is supposed to differ.

How the team applies verification in practice

The post then gets specific about how the Claude Code team runs its own workflow:

Verification means running the change. Running the app end to end matters more than tests. Claude tests the whole app the way a human or QA engineer would — the Claude Chrome extension for web changes, an iOS or Android MCP for mobile, computer use for desktop, or a locally running service for backend work. The team codifies how to boot the simulator or run the app in a skill called verify, stored in the repo's .claude/skills/ folder, close to the relevant code. Claude knows to use it before committing. Then they invest in making that skill fast and reliable, iterating and stress-testing it, because it's the smoke test harness for everything.

Failing tests escalate to a human. Nobody can read every change, so failures are the signal for what needs a person. Claude runs the checks and tries to fix anything that fails. If a check is still failing after three rounds, Claude stops and brings in a human.

Code owners write their own checks. The people who own the code write and refine the checks for it, until they flag what the owner would flag. When a check pulls in a reviewer, it should say why, so the reviewer doesn't have to work it out from the diff.

Reliability checks trigger on the diff. The team maintains a 39-item reliability checklist, each item with a trigger readable from a diff, a check, and the incident or PR behind it. One example: "--resume loads old transcripts" — when session storage or message types change, the team asks whether a new field loads safely, since older transcripts won't have it. Claude reads the diff and checks only the items whose trigger matches, usually 3 to 10, so nobody has to memorize past outages.

One reviewer, multiple rounds. The team doesn't improve reviews by stacking on more reviewers; tuning the primary reviewer beats adding a second, more expensive one. Instead they keep a REVIEW.md file describing what the reviewer should pay attention to for that code. Review rounds build on each other, each pass pointing at context from earlier rounds and past failures rather than re-checking everything from scratch. It's cheaper, and it finds more.

Changes can't modify their own checks. If a change can modify the check that judges it, the check is broken. Code Review reads REVIEW.md from the base or default branch — never from the pull request's changes. The rules that gate changes live on a branch the change can't touch. Reviews are also reserved for commits: a passing review on an out-of-date commit means nothing. And cheap checks run first — Claude runs tests, build, and linter before opening a pull request, so it doesn't spend shared review and CI time on a bug it could have caught itself.

New gates start in observe mode. Every commit is stamped with how it was verified — the stamp even includes "none," so unverified commits can be queried. A commit gate can block a commit if the session didn't include /code-review or /verify, with off, observe, and enforce modes. Observe mode logs what would have been blocked, so false positives can be reviewed before anyone is affected. Enforce mode blocks the commit, though any commit can explain in its message why it wasn't verified, and if commits have been blocked twice in a session, the next one is allowed through so Claude doesn't get stuck.

Test your checks on what actually matters. The team regularly reviews the reviewers, tracking how many merged changes were reverted, how many changes a maintainer rejected before merging, and a size-matched subset of changes that stayed clean. The Code Review team built a formal evaluation from past incidents and reverts: each example recreates the repo at the time of review with a one-sentence answer key for the bug, and only findings that correctly describe that bug score. Merged, stable changes serve as a control against over-flagging, and the tuning set is kept separate from the fixed test set. Recall is measured separately for raw findings, post-verification, and final review, so the team can see whether the system is losing bugs it already found. Importance is graded too — findings are tagged Important, Nit, or Pre-existing, so a reviewer doesn't hold an author responsible for a bug that was already there. Finally, recall is tuned up only to the point where the next improvement would be overfitting to the eval rather than actually catching bugs.

Turn misses into rules. The repo has two ways of converting a missed case into a rule. First, patterns are extracted from human code review comments and PR reverts: a candidate must occur in at least two PRs and be identifiable from a diff, then three agents try to disprove it, and a human reviews and approves it in a PR. Second, three bug finders replay a PR associated with a known incident — if at least two find the bug, it's a detectable bug, and missing it on a small diff is a gap worth writing into REVIEW.md. Flaky tests get the same treatment: Claude can't skip them, add sleeps, or retry until they pass. If it can't find the root cause, it deletes the test and writes down why. And rules need pruning — test suites, verification steps, and .md files only grow, so the team tidies them on a routine.

The shift that matters

The post's closing line reframes the whole job: once verification works, your work shifts from reading every diff to defining what "done" looks like and reviewing the evidence. That's what lets you run many Claudes at once.

For teams adopting coding agents, the takeaway isn't "write more tests." It's that the verification layer is a system of its own — one that needs to be fast, honest, and out of reach of the changes it judges. Keep it close to the code it protects, grade it against the bugs that actually hurt, and write down the lesson every time it misses something, so it never misses the same thing twice.

Source: Anthropic, "How the Claude Code team thinks about verification" (claude.dev, November 16, 2026).

title: FaceScored: an AI face score you can audit, computed entirely in your browser
description:
FaceScored is a free AI face rating tool that performs the whole analysis inside your browser tab.

What happens to the photo

Nothing is uploaded. The app reads the photo locally, runs MediaPipe face landmark detection, measures facial symmetry and proportion ratios, then renders a score next to the formula that produced it. No account, no server-side copy of the image.

How the symmetry number is built

The symmetry test averages the horizontal imbalance across six landmark pairs, normalises it by face width, and applies the same formula the homepage rating uses. Two of the pairs are the inner and outer eye corners, measured against the vertical reference line through the face. The result also surfaces the two largest measured deviations, so the score can be read against the measurements behind it.

  • Face rater: https://facescored.com
  • Symmetry breakdown: https://facescored.com/face-symmetry/

Why two photos of the same face score differently

The calculation works on landmark positions in a 2D image, so camera perspective, head rotation, expression and landmark-detection noise all move those positions. The site states this itself and does not present the output as a medical assessment.

Free vs paid

Free: overall symmetry score, left and right mirrored comparisons, deviation list, browser-local processing.

Optional full report (currently listed at $16.99, one-time): six dimensions - symmetry, proportions, jawline, eye-angle balance, face shape, skin clarity - written feature notes, heuristic percentile estimates and a printable PDF. Percentiles are model heuristics, not measured population rankings.

title: From Plain HTML to a Real Website: A Step-by-Step CSS Story for Beginners
description:
Have you ever written your first HTML code, opened it in a browser, and wondered why your webpage looked so plain?

You created a heading. You added a paragraph. You included a button. Everything appeared on the screen, just as you expected.

But something was missing.

The webpage had structure, but it lacked the visual presentation you imagined. The elements felt disconnected, the spacing was basic, and the page didn't yet look like the polished websites you visited every day.

Then you discovered CSS.

Suddenly, you could change colours, improve typography, organize content, create layouts, and adapt your webpage to different screen sizes.

What started as a few lines of HTML could gradually become a complete, visually engaging web experience.

This is the story of how a plain HTML page evolves into a polished website through the power of CSS.

Whether you're learning frontend development for the first time or refreshing your CSS fundamentals, let's walk through the transformation step by step.

Stage 1: HTML — Building the Foundation

Every great webpage needs a structure.

Before thinking about colours, animations, or layouts, developers need to define the content that will appear on the page.

This is where HTML comes in.

HTML stands for HyperText Markup Language. It provides the structure and meaning of webpage content through elements such as headings, paragraphs, links, buttons, and images.

Imagine you're building a simple personal website.

You might begin with this HTML:

<!DOCTYPE html>




My First Website


Welcome to My Website


I'm learning web development
and building my first webpage.

Learn More

Save the file as index.html and open it in your browser.

You'll see a heading, a paragraph, and a button.

Congratulations! You have created a webpage.

However, the browser's default styling determines much of its initial appearance. You haven't yet established a specific visual style or custom layout.

That's perfectly fine.

The first stage isn't about making the page beautiful. It's about giving it a meaningful structure.

Once the foundation is in place, you can begin shaping how the content appears.

Stage 2: Add CSS — Give the Page Its First Visual Identity

Now imagine looking at your HTML page and deciding that it needs more personality.

You want a better background, a more distinctive heading, and a button that looks intentional rather than ordinary.

CSS makes these changes possible.

CSS stands for Cascading Style Sheets. It controls how HTML elements are presented, including their colours, typography, spacing, borders, and layout.

First, create a file called style.css.

Next, connect it to your HTML document by adding this line inside the head element:

Your HTML document can now load the styles defined in the CSS file.

Let's start with a few simple rules:

body {
background-color: #F5F5F5;
color: #2E2E2E;
}

h1 {
color: #800020;
}

button {
background-color: #800020;
color: white;
border: none;
padding: 12px 20px;
}

What has changed?

The page now has a light background.

The text has a dark colour.

The heading uses a deep burgundy.

The button has a coloured background, white text, and internal spacing.

The content is still the same, but the visual presentation has started to change.

This is one of the exciting moments in learning CSS: you change a few properties, refresh the browser, and immediately see the difference.

But colour is only the beginning.

A professional interface also needs readable typography, thoughtful spacing, and a layout that makes sense.

Stage 3: Typography — Make the Content Easier to Read

Imagine visiting a website where every heading is the same size as the body text.

Even if the information is useful, it may be difficult to scan.

Typography helps establish visual hierarchy. It guides readers towards important information and makes content easier to understand.

With CSS, developers can control properties such as:

font-family — the typeface used for text.

font-size — the size of the text.

font-weight — the weight or thickness of the characters.

line-height — the height of each line box.

letter-spacing — the spacing between characters.

text-align — how inline content is aligned within its containing block.

Let's improve the typography of our webpage:

body {
font-family: Arial, sans-serif;
font-size: 16px;
line-height: 1.6;
}

h1 {
font-size: 36px;
font-weight: 700;
line-height: 1.2;
}

The body text now has a defined font family, size, and line height. The heading is larger and heavier, making it easier to distinguish from the paragraph.

Notice that we haven't changed the actual words on the page.

We've improved how those words are presented.

That distinction matters because good typography isn't simply decorative. It helps people scan information, recognize headings, and read comfortably.

A webpage should not only contain useful information; it should present that information clearly.

Stage 4: Spacing — Give Every Element Room to Breathe

Now let's address another common problem beginners encounter: crowded content.

Imagine a heading sitting directly above a paragraph, followed immediately by a button. Everything appears tightly packed together.

The page may technically work, but the experience feels uncomfortable.

CSS spacing properties help solve this problem.

Two particularly important properties are margin and padding.

Margin controls the space outside an element's border.

Padding controls the space between an element's content and its border.

For example:

h1 {
margin-bottom: 16px;
}

p {
margin-bottom: 24px;
}

button {
padding: 12px 20px;
}

These rules create space below the heading and paragraph while giving the button more internal room.

You can also use the gap property when arranging elements with Flexbox or Grid.

Why does this matter?

Spacing helps separate related sections, establish visual rhythm, and make interfaces easier to scan.

However, more spacing isn't always better. The goal is to create a balanced relationship between elements.

A heading should feel connected to its content, while separate sections should have enough space to distinguish them.

As you practise CSS, pay attention to how even small spacing changes can influence the overall appearance of a page.

Stage 5: Layout — Arrange the Content Intentionally

At this stage, your webpage has colours, readable text, and improved spacing.

But what if you want to create a more complete layout?

Perhaps you want a navigation bar at the top, a main content area in the centre, or several service cards arranged side by side.

This is where CSS layout techniques become especially useful.

Two essential tools are Flexbox and CSS Grid.

Using Flexbox

Flexbox is useful for arranging items along a row or column.

For example, suppose you want to position a logo on the left and navigation links on the right.

You can use Flexbox to align these elements and distribute available space.

.navbar {
display: flex;
justify-content: space-between;
align-items: center;
}

Here, display: flex establishes a flex container. justify-content distributes items along the main axis, while align-items aligns them along the cross axis.

Using CSS Grid

Grid is useful for layouts that involve rows and columns.

Suppose your website contains three service cards.

You could arrange them using:

.services {
display: grid;
grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr);
gap: 20px;
}

This creates three equal-width columns with space between them.

Flexbox and Grid are not competing technologies. They solve different layout problems and can work together within the same webpage.

The important lesson is that developers don't need to position every element manually.

Instead, they can use CSS layout systems to create organized, adaptable structures.

Good layout transforms a collection of elements into a coherent interface.

Stage 6: Responsive Design — Make the Website Adapt

Your webpage looks great on your laptop or desktop screen.

But then you open it on a mobile phone.

The three service cards are squeezed together. The heading takes up too much space. The content extends beyond the screen.

Suddenly, the layout doesn't look so good.

This is why responsive design matters.

Responsive design is an approach to building interfaces that adapt to different screen sizes and viewing conditions.

CSS supports responsive design through flexible layouts, relative sizing, media queries, and other techniques.

Let's return to our three-column service layout:

.services {
display: grid;
grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr);
gap: 20px;
}

@media (max-width: 600px) {
.services {
grid-template-columns: 1fr;
}
}

On wider screens, the layout displays three columns.

When the viewport is 600 pixels wide or narrower, it switches to one column.

This is a basic example. Depending on the design, a developer might also adjust typography, padding, navigation, image sizing, and other layout details.

Responsive design isn't simply about shrinking a desktop website.

It's about making deliberate adjustments so the content remains usable within the available space.

And here's an important point: you shouldn't wait until the very end to think about responsiveness.

Testing different screen sizes throughout development helps you identify layout problems earlier and make better design decisions.

Stage 7: Final Polish — Turn a Good Start into a Better Experience

Your webpage now has structure, colours, typography, spacing, layout, and responsive behaviour.

Is it finished?

Not necessarily.

The final stage involves reviewing the details and checking whether the page works as intended.

Developers might ask questions such as:

Are the headings and paragraphs easy to read?

Are the elements aligned consistently?

Is the spacing balanced?

Are the buttons easy to identify?

Do interactive elements have visible focus states?

Does the layout work on different screen sizes?

Are there unexpected horizontal scrollbars?

Are the colours sufficiently distinguishable?

Do animations respect users who prefer reduced motion?

For example, you could add a subtle transition to your button:

button {
transition: background-color 0.3s ease;
}

button:hover {
background-color: #5C0017;
}

The background colour changes smoothly when the pointer hovers over the button.

You would also want to check that keyboard users can identify the focused button and that the hover effect isn't the only indication of interactivity.

The final polish isn't about adding as many effects as possible.

It's about checking the details, improving consistency, and removing unnecessary friction from the experience.

Sometimes, the best improvement is a small spacing adjustment. Other times, it means simplifying a layout or removing an effect that distracts from the content.

Polish is about making deliberate decisions, not adding decoration for its own sake.

The Transformation: What Did CSS Actually Change?

Let's step back and look at the complete journey.

Stage
HTML structure

What changes?
The content and meaning are defined.

Stage
Add CSS

What changes?
Colours, backgrounds, and basic styles establish a visual foundation.

Stage
Typography

What changes?
Text becomes easier to scan, with clearer hierarchy.

Stage
Spacing

What changes?
Elements gain room and visual separation.

Stage
Layout

What changes?
Content is arranged into meaningful sections.

Stage
Responsive design

What changes?
The layout adapts to different screen sizes.

Stage
Final polish

What changes?
Consistency, usability, and remaining issues are reviewed.

Notice something important: the content itself hasn't necessarily changed much.

The heading is still a heading. The paragraph is still a paragraph. The button still represents an action.

What changes is how the content is presented and how the different elements work together visually.

This is the role CSS plays in frontend development.

It provides the tools developers need to shape the presentation of HTML content into an interface that is easier to understand and use.

HTML, CSS, and JavaScript: How Do They Work Together?

To understand this transformation fully, it's helpful to remember the different responsibilities of the core frontend technologies.

HTML provides structure and meaning.

It defines elements such as headings, paragraphs, links, forms, and buttons.

CSS controls presentation and layout.

It determines colours, typography, spacing, positioning, responsive behaviour, and other visual characteristics.

JavaScript adds behaviour and interaction.

It can respond to events, update content, manage interactive components, and communicate with APIs.

Consider a navigation menu.

HTML provides the navigation links and their structure. CSS determines their appearance and layout. JavaScript may control opening and closing a menu on mobile devices.

The exact implementation depends on the project, and not every interaction requires JavaScript.

The key is understanding that these technologies work together while serving different purposes.

When you understand those responsibilities, debugging becomes easier because you have a clearer idea of where a particular problem belongs.

How Beginners Can Practise This Transformation

You don't need to build a complete business website to begin learning CSS.

Start with a small page and improve it gradually.

Here is a simple practice plan:

Exercise 1: Build the structure. Create a heading, paragraph, button, and a few sections using HTML.

Exercise 2: Introduce styling. Choose a background colour, text colour, and button style.

Exercise 3: Improve typography. Experiment with font size, weight, family, and line height.

Exercise 4: Adjust spacing. Use margins, padding, and gaps to improve the relationship between elements.

Exercise 5: Practise layout. Create a navigation bar or a group of cards using Flexbox or Grid.

Exercise 6: Make it responsive. Resize your browser and adjust the layout where necessary.

Exercise 7: Review and refine. Check alignment, contrast, keyboard focus, and any layout problems.

After every change, save your files and refresh the browser.

Observe the result.

If something doesn't look right, investigate the relevant CSS rules and experiment with one change at a time.

You can also use your browser's Developer Tools to inspect elements and test styles.

This process teaches you more than memorizing CSS properties. It helps you understand how individual rules influence the overall page.

And don't worry if your first attempt doesn't look professional.

The purpose of practice is to learn how to improve it.

Final Thoughts: Every Polished Website Starts Somewhere

The journey from plain HTML to a polished website isn't a single dramatic transformation.

It's a series of decisions.

You define the structure. You introduce styling. You improve typography. You adjust spacing. You organize the layout. You make it responsive. Then you review the details.

Each step contributes to the final experience.

That is why CSS deserves more attention than simply being described as the language that makes websites beautiful.

It helps developers organize information, establish visual hierarchy, create adaptable layouts, and present content in ways that support usability.

If you're learning frontend development, remember this: you don't have to master everything before you start building.

Create something small. Improve one part. Test it. Learn from what happens. Then move to the next step.

Over time, those small improvements will help you develop a stronger understanding of CSS and how real websites are built.

Your first plain HTML page is not the final destination. It's the starting point.

Let's Discuss

If you were transforming a plain HTML page into a polished website today, which stage would you be most excited to work on: typography, spacing, layout, responsive design, or final polish?

Share your thoughts in the comments!

title: How Yoast SEO Actually Works Under the Hood: A Technical Breakdown for WordPress Developers
description:
Yoast SEO from a Systems Perspective

Hầu hết tài liệu về Yoast SEO mô tả nó từ góc độ người dùng cuối: điền focus keyphrase, chờ đèn xanh, đăng bài. Nhưng với người xây dựng hoặc quản lý WordPress từ góc độ kỹ thuật, câu hỏi thực sự là: Yoast SEO làm gì với database, với DOM và với HTTP response — và làm thế nào nó có thể tích hợp hoặc xung đột với các hệ thống khác trong stack?

Bài này phân tích cơ chế hoạt động thực tế của Yoast SEO: cách nó ghi metadata, tạo sitemap, inject schema, và những điểm cần chú ý khi triển khai trong môi trường có nhiều plugin hoặc automation pipeline.

Lớp metadata: Yoast ghi dữ liệu đi đâu?

Khi người dùng điền Tiêu đề SEO và Thẻ mô tả trong editor, Yoast không ghi vào bảng wp_posts. Toàn bộ metadata của Yoast lưu trong wp_postmeta với các key có prefix _yoast_wpseo_:

  • _yoast_wpseo_title — tiêu đề SEO tùy chỉnh (nếu khác template mặc định)
  • _yoast_wpseo_metadesc — thẻ mô tả
  • _yoast_wpseo_focuskw — focus keyphrase
  • _yoast_wpseo_linkdex — điểm SEO (0–100) được tính toán và cache lại
  • _yoast_wpseo_content_score — điểm khả năng đọc
  • _yoast_wpseo_canonical — canonical URL tùy chỉnh nếu có
  • _yoast_wpseo_meta-robots-noindex — chỉ thị noindex cụ thể cho bài

Đây là điểm quan trọng khi xây dựng automation pipeline: nếu muốn ghi metadata hàng loạt qua code (ví dụ từ một AI content pipeline), anh em cần update_post_meta() vào đúng các key này, không phải ghi vào post title hay excerpt thông thường.

Lưu ý khi dùng Yoast với WP-CLI hoặc REST API: Yoast có REST API endpoint riêng (/wp/v2/yoast_head) trả về rendered head HTML. Nhưng để ghi ngược lại metadata qua REST, cần đảm bảo schema của Yoast đã đăng ký field trong register_rest_field() — không phải mặc định của WordPress core.

XML Sitemap: cơ chế tạo và cập nhật

Yoast không tạo sitemap bằng cách generate file tĩnh vào filesystem. Thay vào đó, sitemap được serve động qua WordPress rewrite rules. Khi truy cập ten-website.com/sitemap_index.xml, WordPress xử lý request qua query var sitemap=1 và Yoast intercept để render XML output.

Cấu trúc sitemap index phân cấp như sau:

  • sitemap_index.xml — file index chứa danh sách sitemap con
  • post-sitemap.xml — tất cả bài viết (post_type=post)
  • page-sitemap.xml — tất cả trang (post_type=page)
  • product-sitemap.xml — sản phẩm WooCommerce nếu có
  • category-sitemap.xml, post_tag-sitemap.xml — taxonomy nếu được bật

Sitemap được cache trong wp_options với key wpseo_sitemap_cache_validator. Cache bị invalidate mỗi khi post được publish, update hoặc delete — trigger qua WordPress hooks publish_post, save_post, delete_post.

Ngoài ra, Yoast gửi XML-RPC ping đến Google và Bing mỗi khi sitemap được cập nhật — hành vi này có thể tắt bằng filter wpseo_allow_xml_sitemap_ping nếu không muốn.

Schema injection: Yoast xây dựng JSON-LD thế nào?

Yoast inject schema markup dưới dạng JSON-LD vào <head> của mỗi trang. Thay vì schema phẳng, Yoast dùng Graph approach — một JSON-LD object duy nhất chứa nhiều entity liên kết nhau qua @id:

{
  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@graph": [
    { "@type": "WebPage", "@id": "https://example.com/post/#webpage" },
    { "@type": "Article", "@id": "https://example.com/post/#article" },
    { "@type": "Person", "@id": "https://example.com/#/schema/person/xxx" },
    { "@type": "Organization", "@id": "https://example.com/#organization" },
    { "@type": "WebSite", "@id": "https://example.com/#website" }
  ]
}

Graph approach này có ưu điểm là tránh khai báo entity trùng lặp và cho phép extend schema bằng cách thêm node mới vào graph thay vì sửa vào JSON đã có. Developer có thể hook vào wpseo_schema_graph_pieces để thêm custom schema piece hoặc modify piece đã có.

Focus keyphrase analysis: scoring engine hoạt động ra sao?

Hệ thống đèn màu của Yoast không phải heuristic đơn giản. Scoring engine chạy phía client (JavaScript) và phía server:

  • Client-side analysis: Chạy trong browser khi người dùng đang soạn thảo. Yoast dùng thư viện JavaScript yoastseo (open source, có trên npm) để parse nội dung bài, tách câu, tính mật độ từ khóa và score từng assessment.
  • Server-side scoring: Điểm cuối cùng được lưu vào _yoast_wpseo_linkdex và _yoast_wpseo_content_score khi save post.

Mỗi assessment (keyword in title, keyword density, text length, image alt tags...) trả về một trong ba trạng thái: GOOD, OK, BAD — ánh xạ ra đèn xanh, cam, đỏ. Điểm tổng là weighted average của tất cả assessments.

Điều quan trọng cần hiểu: scoring engine của Yoast là rule-based checklist, không phải mô hình ML. Nó không dự đoán khả năng xếp hạng — nó kiểm tra danh sách tiêu chí kỹ thuật xác định trước. Đèn xanh chỉ có nghĩa là bài pass checklist, không có nghĩa gì hơn.

Khi nhìn vào hệ sinh thái plugin SEO WordPress rộng hơn — không chỉ Yoast — và cách các plugin như Rank Math hay Yoast so sánh với nhau ở tầng kiến trúc, bài viết phân tích toàn diện về Yoast SEO cung cấp bức tranh rõ hơn từ góc độ người triển khai.

Xung đột plugin: vấn đề meta duplication

Vấn đề phổ biến nhất khi Yoast xung đột với plugin khác là meta duplication: hai plugin cùng output <title> tag hoặc cùng ghi og:title vào head, dẫn đến Google và Facebook đọc giá trị khác nhau.

Yoast handle việc này bằng cách:

  • Remove WordPress default title output: remove_action('wp_head', '_wp_render_title_tag', 1)
  • Remove theme title nếu theme dùng wp_title()

Rank Math và AIOSEO làm tương tự — đây là lý do không thể chạy song song hai plugin SEO: cả hai đều cố remove title của nhau và inject title của mình, kết quả là race condition không đoán được.

Cách kiểm tra xung đột: Inspect source HTML của bất kỳ trang nào, tìm trong <head> xem có nhiều hơn một <title> tag hoặc nhiều og:title không. Nếu có, đang có plugin conflict.

Tích hợp Yoast với AI automation pipeline

Khi xây dựng pipeline tự động hóa nội dung trên WordPress — ví dụ AI viết bài và điền metadata hàng loạt — cần hiểu cách Yoast expect data được ghi vào.

Có hai cách tiếp cận:

Cách 1: Ghi trực tiếp vào wp_postmeta

Dùng update_post_meta($post_id, '_yoast_wpseo_title', $seo_title) và update_post_meta($post_id, '_yoast_wpseo_metadesc', $meta_desc). Cách này nhanh và không phụ thuộc vào Yoast API, nhưng cần đảm bảo format đúng (plain string, không có HTML tags).

Cách 2: Dùng Yoast REST API hoặc plugin-specific hooks

Yoast expose một số filter cho phép can thiệp vào quá trình render: wpseo_title, wpseo_metadesc, wpseo_canonical. Dùng các filter này nếu muốn dynamic override mà không lưu vào database.

Onic AI SEO Automation xử lý vấn đề này bằng cách nhận diện Yoast tự động và ghi tiêu đề SEO, thẻ mô tả trực tiếp vào đúng trường của Yoast khi tối ưu hàng loạt — không cần can thiệp thủ công từng bài. Đây là ví dụ về cách một automation layer cần "biết" cấu trúc lưu trữ của từng plugin SEO để ghi đúng chỗ, thay vì ghi vào post title thông thường rồi bị Yoast override.

Sitemap và crawl budget: điểm cần lưu ý cho large-scale site

Với website có hàng trăm nghìn URL (WooCommerce lớn, news site), cần chú ý đến cách Yoast handle sitemap size:

  • Yoast tự động split sitemap khi vượt quá 1,000 URLs mỗi file (configurable qua filter wpseo_sitemap_entries_per_page)
  • Với large catalog, sitemap generation có thể gây timeout nếu chạy on-request. Nên pre-generate bằng WP-CLI: wp yoast index --reindex
  • Cân nhắc exclude post types không cần index (custom post type nội bộ, revision logs) khỏi sitemap qua Yoast Settings để giảm crawl budget lãng phí

Kết luận: Yoast SEO trong kiến trúc WordPress

Yoast SEO là một metadata management layer đặt trên WordPress core — không phải một công cụ "magic SEO". Hiểu cơ chế lưu trữ trong wp_postmeta, cách sitemap được serve động qua rewrite rules, Graph schema approach và scoring engine rule-based giúp developer tích hợp đúng, debug nhanh hơn và xây dựng automation pipeline không phá vỡ dữ liệu hiện có.

Khi kết hợp Yoast với AI automation pipeline, điểm mấu chốt là pipeline cần biết Yoast lưu metadata đi đâu (_yoast_wpseo_* keys trong wp_postmeta) và ghi vào đúng chỗ — đây là sự khác biệt giữa automation hoạt động đúng và automation tạo ra dữ liệu không nhất quán.

Bài gốc: https://onic.vn/kien-thuc/yoast-seo/

title: Preparing Website Content for Query Fan-Out in Google AI Search
description:
Originally published on We0 on November 17, 2026. This English edition was adapted with AI assistance.

Google’s November 12, 2026 Search announcement describes Gemini 4 Hydrogen and improved query fan-out. For website teams, the practical work is familiar: answer concrete sub-questions, state evidence and constraints, and keep important information crawlable.

What Changed in This Upgrade: From Matching Words to Understanding Constraints

Search's underlying logic has changed several times. Moz breaks the past decade into three stages: lexical retrieval looks at where and how often words appear; semantic retrieval uses machine learning to understand meaning; hybrid retrieval fuses the two result sets and reranks them. AI search no longer looks only for 'a page that can rank,' but for 'the most relevant, extractable, and comparable information fragments' (Moz).

Stage What the system mainly looks at Focus of page optimization
Lexical retrieval Whether words appear, where they appear, and how often Keyword coverage and density
Semantic retrieval Meaning behind words and synonymous expressions Topical relevance and semantic completeness
Hybrid retrieval Reranking after fusing the two result sets Both structure and content quality
AI retrieval Whether a passage can answer a specific sub-question Extractability, atomicity, verifiability

Google’s November 12 announcement describes improved handling of complex questions and query fan-out. This pushes the 'sourcing by fragment' trend one step further. Rules such as how many characters a title should have or how many times a keyword should appear cover an increasingly narrow range of intent.

What Is Query Fan-out

Query Fan-out means the system splits a prompt into multiple related retrievals, extracts the most relevant passages from each result set, and combines relevant information for the response; the exact selection and ranking process is not fully public (Moz).

It changes the evaluation standard: no longer 'whether this page as a whole is well written,' but 'whether a certain passage on this page can independently answer a specific sub-question.' If a passage discusses pricing, features, deployment, and after-sales support at the same time, its match on each sub-question is diluted. Moz uses cosine similarity to explain this phenomenon: the more focused the topic, the closer the passage and the question are in vector space.

Why One Complex Question Maps to Multiple Sub-Questions

Take 'Which AI website builder is suitable for small and medium-sized businesses without a development team?' as an example. This sentence contains four layers of constraints: type of tool, scope of capabilities, team conditions, and company size. If any layer is missing, the user cannot make a decision based on it. A retrieval system may explore related subtopics such as pricing, features, maintenance, SEO, and deployment. This is a useful content-planning model, rather than a guarantee about the exact queries issued.

What the user is really judging Sub-question that needs to be answered Page recommended to carry it
Can the budget bear it Pricing model, whether there is a free tier, subsequent hidden costs Pricing and plan explanation page
Can it create the pages needed Which page types are supported, whether forms and CMS are included Features overview page
Who maintains it after launch Whether changing copy or images requires developer involvement Operations and maintenance explanation
Can it be found in search Structured data, speed, multilingual support, indexing foundation SEO and GEO capabilities page
How to put it on your own domain Domain binding, certificates, deployment process Deployment explanation page

This table is also a content schedule: each sub-question corresponds to a placement that can be cited on its own, and these placements are connected with internal links. This is easier to maintain than cramming all answers into one long page, and it is also easier to add data later.

How Should a Product Page Organize Information?

The most common problem with product pages is 'context first, conclusion later': a long stretch of brand philosophy, with the real answer on the third screen. This is unfriendly to both people and retrieval systems.

Moz's approach is: use clear subheadings, place the answer near the heading, discuss only one point per paragraph, include useful data points, and express facts with clear semantic relationships (Moz).

A product page skeleton you can apply directly:

  1. Explain in one sentence for whom it solves what problem;
  2. Capability boundaries: what it can and cannot do, three to five items each;
  3. Key parameter table: page types, language support, backend, deployment method;
  4. Suitable and unsuitable scenarios;
  5. Pricing structure and billing basis;
  6. How common objections are addressed;
  7. Next step and contact information.

Why Comparison Content Deserves Attention

Questions phrased as 'which type,' 'which is better,' or 'A or B' naturally require multi-constraint comparison and are most likely to be split into sub-queries. The value of this type of content is not in taking a position, but in providing comparable dimensions.

Effective practices include: comparing similar solutions in the same table; stating the basis and date of each piece of information; and clearly writing 'when it is not suitable to choose it.' A comparison page is more useful when it states limitations as well as advantages. When discussing brand narratives, Moz also notes that when AI systems judge credibility, they look at whether multiple sources corroborate one another. The same answer appearing repeatedly on the official website, in media, and in partner content carries more weight than a single point of self-praise.

How Should Data, Images, and Tables Be Organized?

Tables and structured data are themselves 'answers that have already been organized.' When a results page needs to present a comparison relationship, a clearly structured table is easier to adopt than ten paragraphs of prose.

  • Tables should have headers and units, one dimension per column, and should not merge information with different meanings;
  • Images should have captions that clearly state what question the image answers, rather than a generic label like 'product screenshot';
  • Numbers in the body text should indicate source and date, with priority given to those that can be clicked through and verified;
  • Terminology should be consistent across the same site; do not use three different names for the same capability;
  • Add structured markup for common Q&A to help systems identify the correspondence between questions and answers.

How Can a Website Cover the Different Needs in User Questions?

Covering all sub-questions on a single page is neither realistic nor good for maintenance. A more stable approach is a topic cluster: one core page answers 'what it is and who it is for,' while several sub-pages answer pricing, features, deployment, migration, and industry scenarios, connected with two-way internal links.

Coverage can be checked with a question list: list the questions sales and customer support have been asked most often in the last three months, and confirm one by one whether the site has a corresponding page that can be cited on its own. The missing items are the content to add next. This list is often closer to real questions than keyword tools.

Technical Foundation: Crawling, Rendering, and Speed

No matter how well the content is written, it is meaningless if it cannot be retrieved. Moz points out that many AI crawlers only fetch raw HTML and do not execute JavaScript, so product details, descriptions, and answers rendered on the client side may not be visible at all. Slow responses can cause some clients to abandon a request. A 499 log entry generally means the client closed the connection; it does not by itself identify an AI crawler or establish why it left. Test caching alongside the actual bottleneck (Moz).

The corresponding checks are straightforward: whether core information is written in the HTML source; whether first-screen loading is fast enough; whether important pages have stable URLs; whether there is a clear correspondence between multilingual versions. These are engineering-side actions, but they directly determine whether content can enter the candidate pool.

How to Measure Whether the Adjustments Are Effective

Don't look only at total traffic. Moz breaks the effectiveness of AI search into three layers: the input layer looks at sub-query rankings, passage relevance, and crawl activity; the channel layer looks at the brand's appearance rate in AI answers, citation rate, and citation accuracy; the performance layer looks at conversion and lead quality after this traffic reaches the site (Moz). The three layers flow in sequence. Looking only at the last layer makes it impossible to tell whether the problem is content or handoff.

A Practical Content Checklist for Query Fan-Out

Turning the previous sections into actions, here are five things in priority order from high to low:

  1. Change the product page to an answer-first structure, with each paragraph carrying only one sub-question;
  2. Add a parameter comparison table for the core product, and state the basis and update date;
  3. Use a list of real questions to take stock of coverage and fill in missing pages;
  4. Check the HTML readability and loading speed of key pages;
  5. Set up a monthly review to record changes in citation status.

To judge whether an adjustment is worth doing, filter it with three questions: Does it answer a sub-question a user would really ask? Can this answer be extracted and used on its own? Are the numbers and boundaries in it supported by evidence? If all three are 'yes,' then act.

Where we0 Fits in This Chain

Structural adjustments often get stuck on execution cost: changing page structure, adding content modules, connecting a CMS, handling multilingual support, and deployment. we0 is an AI workspace from website building to lead generation, covering natural language website building, multi-agent collaboration, CMS backend, multi-style design, domain deployment, and SEO and GEO optimization (we0.ai). These capabilities solve the engineering part of 'landing the structural adjustments'; which sub-questions are worth answering and which data can be made public still need to be judged by the business side.

FAQ

Will Query Fan-out replace traditional SEO?

It will not replace it, but it will change the focus. Traditional SEO addresses whether a page can be indexed and ranked, while Query Fan-out cares about whether a certain passage on a page can answer a specific sub-question. The two are additive, not alternatives.

Are longer pages more likely to be cited?

No. Focus can make a passage easier to interpret, but length and topic count are not a published citation formula. Provide enough context and evidence for a complete answer.

Is it necessary to make a comparison table into a separate page?

If this type of comparison is a key part of the user's decision, it is worth making into a separate page. Unified dimensions, clear basis, and update dates are more practical than scattering the information across several articles.

Is it okay to have only a Chinese-language site?

It depends on where the customers are. When targeting foreign trade or multilingual markets, there should be a clear correspondence between language versions to avoid the same capability being described inconsistently across different language versions.

How long does it take to see changes?

There is no uniform answer. Structural adjustments, content completion, and crawling and speed optimization usually need to be advanced in parallel. The effect shows up in citation rate and lead quality, not in a traffic peak on a certain day. Quarterly evaluation is more reasonable than weekly evaluation.

Related Tools

  • Google Search Console: check indexing, queries, and page performance
  • Structured data testing tool: check whether Q&A and product markup are correctly recognized
  • Page speed testing tool: locate loading bottlenecks and caching issues

Related Links

  • Google official announcement: Search upgrade with Gemini 4 Hydrogen
  • The Verge: Google's new Gemini model is better at understanding complicated questions
  • Moz: Stop Calling It SEO: 12 Strategies To Dominate AI Search in 2026
  • we0.ai official website

Summary

Gemini 4 Hydrogen entering Google Search strengthens the understanding of complex questions and the decomposition of sub-queries. The adjustment that website content needs to make is essentially a shift from 'writing pages around keywords' to 'organizing extractable answers around sub-questions': conclusions first, atomic paragraphs, comparable dimensions, verifiable data, and a crawlable foundation. Product pages, comparison pages, tables, and topic clusters are the four most direct landing points, while measurement should be viewed across the input, channel, and performance layers. Structural adjustment is not hard to think through; what is hard is sustained execution. Turning the page skeleton, content modules, and deployment process into reusable capabilities is more valuable than a one-time redesign.
