title: A Viewing Window, Not A Key To The Cage
description:
An admin screen may look at any table of any service - through glass. Read only, a timeout, caps, a log line, one at a time, and the glass is shut until someone opens it on purpose.

👋 Hi, I'm Anton - a software engineer. These days I work on a platform: contracts, generated code, data paths and the tooling around them. Running notes live on my GitHub: github.com/brilliant-almazov.

The guarded query is built into the shared library and is off by default. No service imports it directly yet; everything below describes what is built, not how much it is used.

This is part 2 of the series on what a shared platform does for every service, told as a zoo. Maybe you already do it better, maybe you'd do it another way - this is how it is going, and where it stops.

In real life

Ember, the small dragon of our zoo, guards the gold. That is what dragons do, and in our zoo the gold is the data: every resident keeps its own pile in its own cave, and nobody else is supposed to touch it.

Nora, the keeper, wants to count the coins. Not take them - just count. "Give me a key, I'll just count." Ember's answer is the answer every database owner has given: "Nobody touches my gold." And Ember is right. A key does not know the difference between counting and carrying.

So the zoo puts a viewing window into the cave wall. Pickle presses a nose to the glass and is delighted: "I can see every coin!" Biscuit tries to pass a bone through - "can I feed it?" - and learns what glass is for: look only. And when too many faces press against the window at once, Pip does the one thing that keeps the dragon calm: "Full. No waiting. Come back later."

That is the whole part in four panels. The admin screen can look at any table - through the service, through glass, one look at a time.

The key nobody should have

Admin screens want data. A list of records, a count, a join to check one thing on a Tuesday. The easy answer is a database address per service in the admin's configuration, and from then on the admin holds a key to every cave. A key does not know the difference between a SELECT and an UPDATE, does not know when to stop, and leaves no trace in the service that owns the data.

The library's answer is a guarded query that lives inside the service. The admin screen asks the service; the service runs the query on its own terms; the database address never leaves the resident. The line in the library's description says it plainly: the admin gets the schema and any selection through the service, not through a direct database address.

Six panes of glass

Every query that comes through the window passes the same guards.

Guard What it stops
a read-only transaction any write, however it is spelled
a statement timeout a query that would run all afternoon
a row cap a result that would not fit on any screen
a byte cap a few rows with huge values
its own small pool, or a replica the window starving the service's real work
one log line per query a look nobody can account for later

The settings, as a form - the names here are illustrative, the shape is what the library takes:

data_query:
  enabled: false              # off by default
  concurrency: <n>            # over it: busy at once, no waiting
  pool: <small own pool | replica>
  statement_timeout: <duration>
  max_rows: <n>
  max_bytes: <n>
# every query: a read-only transaction, the timeout, one log line

Two choices in that form matter more than the rest.

Off by default. The window is a wall until someone turns it into glass on purpose, for one service, with a switch in that service's environment. A new service does not get an open window because it was born.

Busy means no. When the number of running queries reaches the concurrency limit, the next one is refused at once - not queued, not made to wait. A queue in front of a database is a queue that grows exactly when the database is slow. Refusing at once keeps the cost of a look bounded and moves the waiting to the person who can decide whether to come back.

A key versus a window

The difference is not only safety. A key spreads knowledge of a service's database into every tool that holds it: the address, the credentials, the shape of the tables. A window keeps that knowledge in the service, which already describes its own tables through the sign from the previous part. The admin screen asks "what do you have" and "show me" - and both answers come from the resident.

Who looks through it yet

The window is new. The package is small - around forty files - and it reached the library late in October. No service imports it directly, and on every server it is off unless switched on. That is the state I can describe: the glass is installed, the switch is in the off position, and the first visitor is the admin screen it was built for.

What went wrong

The thing this part answers is a habit rather than an incident: when a screen needs data from a service, the fastest path is always a direct database address, and every such shortcut is a key handed out for good. The window exists because "just give the admin read access" kept being the easiest answer, and easy answers are the ones that stay.

The second lesson is in the busy refusal. A first instinct for "too many queries" is a queue. A queue in front of a struggling database makes everything slower at the worst moment, so the library refuses instead and lets the caller decide.

What I do not claim

  • Not that any service runs with the window open today. It is off by default and imported by none directly.
  • Not that the guards are measured under load. They are built.
  • Not that read only is enough on its own. It is one guard of six, on purpose.
  • Not the exact names of the settings. The form above shows the shape.

What of this is method

  • Look through the owner, not around it. The service holds its database address; tools ask the service.
  • Every look is bounded and written down. Read only, a timeout, caps, a log line.
  • Shut until opened, busy means no. Off by default; over the limit, refuse at once.

Zoo keeping, built in - Part 2. Next: The Error That Escaped Without A Collar.

If your admin tools hold database addresses, how many caves do they have keys to? If you route queries through the service, what guards did you put on the glass? If you queue queries when busy, what happens to the queue when the database is slow? Who in your zoo has a key that should be a window?

title: Every deploy gave a full share of traffic to JVMs that had not compiled anything yet
description:
Our stock lookup service answers in about twelve milliseconds at the ninety ninth percentile, and the shop calls it with a timeout of two hundred and fifty. It runs as eight pods behind an Application Load Balancer that sends traffic straight to the pods. For a year, every deploy produced a small burst of timeouts in the shop: a few hundred failed lookups, products shown as unavailable for a minute, then nothing. We had filed it under deploys being a bit noisy.

In October we started deploying several times a day, and the bursts became a visible share of the shop's errors, so I looked properly. Every timeout came from a new pod, in its first forty to sixty seconds.

A JVM starts by interpreting bytecode. Methods that run often get compiled, quickly by the C1 compiler first and later, after many more invocations, into optimised code by C2. Until the hot paths are compiled, a request costs many times what it will cost a minute later, and class loading and the first database connections add to it. Our readiness probe said ready as soon as Spring had started, so the load balancer gave each new pod its full share of traffic immediately. The pod was correct, only slow, and slow was enough to cross the shop's timeout.

The rollout replaced pods two at a time, so at every step a quarter of the traffic was going to cold code.

The service now warms itself before it reports ready. At start it replays a few thousand recorded stock lookups through the real code path against the real database, and readiness turns true only when that is done and the last batch has a p99 within twice the normal figure. The target group has slow start set to ninety seconds, so the load balancer ramps a new pod's share of requests up over that time instead of handing it everything at once. The deploy bursts have gone, and each rollout takes two minutes longer, which nobody has noticed.

Ready meant the process was up. It needed to mean the process was fast.

– Sergey Shinder

title: Self-Healing Data Pipelines: Detecting and Recovering From Failures With AI
description:
How AI-powered monitoring, data observability, and controlled automation can make production data pipelines more reliable.

A data pipeline can finish successfully and still deliver incorrect information.

Imagine an ETL job completes on schedule, but a source API returns only half the expected records.

The dashboard loads. No job failure appears. Yet the business is making decisions using incomplete data.

This is why pipeline health and data quality aren't the same thing.

Self-healing data pipelines address this problem by combining monitoring, anomaly detection, root-cause analysis, and automated recovery.

But how does this work in practice?

1. What Is a Self-Healing Data Pipeline?

A self-healing data pipeline detects abnormal conditions, investigates likely causes, and performs approved recovery actions with minimal manual intervention.

A typical architecture includes four stages:

The objective isn't to give AI unrestricted access to production systems.

It's to detect problems earlier and automate routine, low-risk responses.

2. Common Pipeline Failures AI Can Detect

Traditional monitoring often focuses on failed jobs and infrastructure errors.

However, data quality problems can occur even when pipelines continue running.

AI-assisted monitoring can identify:

  • Schema drift: Unexpected changes to field names, types, or structures.

  • Missing records: Data volumes falling below expected levels.

  • Duplicate records: Repeated transactions or customer information.

  • Data drift: Significant changes in data distributions.

  • Delayed feeds: Data arriving later than expected.

  • Performance degradation: Unusual increases in processing time.

These problems can affect reporting, analytics, and machine learning.

As Deep Data Insight explains in its article on why AI projects fail because of poor business data, AI systems depend on complete, consistent, and connected information.

3. How AI-Powered Pipeline Recovery Works

Detecting an anomaly is only the beginning.

The next step is determining whether the system can safely recover.

For example, a temporary API timeout may be resolved by retrying the request.

However, an unexpected change to financial transaction fields should not be automatically accepted without validation.

Recovery decisions should depend on the risk and business impact of the failure.

4. Example: A Simple Data Quality Check

Before introducing advanced anomaly detection, developers can begin with straightforward validation rules.

Here's an illustrative Python example:

This is a basic rule-based validation example, not a complete AI-powered self-healing implementation.

In a production environment, monitoring could combine these checks with historical patterns, anomaly detection models, metadata, and data lineage.

For example, instead of relying only on a fixed minimum, an anomaly detection system could identify unusual record volumes based on normal weekday, seasonal, or business patterns.

The important principle is to establish reliable data quality checks before automating recovery.

5. Why Data Observability Matters

Monitoring whether a pipeline runs isn't enough.

Developers also need visibility into the information moving through it.

A reliable data observability strategy should include:

Infrastructure monitoring: CPU, memory, storage, and network availability.

Pipeline monitoring: Job execution, processing times, retries, and dependencies.

Data quality monitoring: Completeness, accuracy, validity, consistency, and duplication.

Data lineage: Understanding where data originates and which downstream systems depend on it.

Business impact monitoring: Identifying how technical problems affect reports, customers, and operations.

These capabilities form part of the data engineering foundation discussed in Deep Data Insight's article on data engineering vs. data science.

6. When Should Automated Recovery Stop?

Not every pipeline failure should be fixed automatically.

Some changes require human judgment because they affect business rules, sensitive information, or regulated processes.

Human approval should normally be required before:

  • Modifying or deleting production records.

  • Accepting unknown schemas.

  • Changing access permissions.

  • Replacing authoritative data sources.

  • Modifying financial or healthcare calculations.

  • Redeploying production AI models.

Automated recovery should follow predefined rules, maintain audit logs, and support rollback where possible.

Self-healing means controlled automation, not unlimited AI autonomy.

7. Building a Self-Healing Pipeline Strategy

You don't need to rebuild every pipeline to introduce self-healing capabilities.

Start with the existing architecture.

Step 1: Identify critical pipelines

Prioritize workflows supporting reporting, customer operations, compliance, and AI applications.

Step 2: Define quality requirements

Establish acceptable standards for completeness, timeliness, accuracy, and consistency.

Step 3: Map dependencies

Document data sources, transformations, destinations, and responsible owners.

Step 4: Establish normal behavior

Measure expected data volumes, processing times, and error rates.

Step 5: Automate low-risk recovery

Start with controlled retries, alerts, and record quarantine.

Step 6: Review recovery results

Use incident feedback to improve detection rules, automation, and escalation procedures.

For pipelines that process documents and other unstructured information, intelligent document processing can support data extraction and validation before information enters downstream systems.

8. How Deep Data Insight Supports Reliable Data Pipelines

Deep Data Insight helps organizations assess, design, and improve data pipelines supporting analytics and enterprise AI.

Its work includes:

  • Data pipeline assessment.

  • Batch and real-time data integration.

  • AI-powered data quality monitoring.

  • Data observability and dependency analysis.

  • Controlled automated recovery.

  • Custom enterprise AI solutions.

Deep Data Insight's Artificial Intelligence services support organizations implementing AI within their existing data environments.

Its data science implementation and support services help organizations develop and maintain data-driven solutions.

The objective is to create reliable, observable, and maintainable systems rather than relying on reactive troubleshooting.

Final Thoughts

Data pipeline failures are inevitable.

APIs become unavailable, schemas change, records arrive late, and processing volumes increase.

The important question is how quickly teams can detect, investigate, and recover from these problems.

Self-healing data pipelines combine AI-powered monitoring with controlled automation to improve data reliability.

But AI doesn't replace data engineers.

It helps them spend less time on repetitive troubleshooting and more time solving complex engineering problems.

title: More of the New Code Around You Will Be Written in Memory Safe Languages
description:
For decades, a large part of the software the world runs on has been written in C and C++. Those languages are fast and flexible, and they let the programmer manage memory directly. They also make it easy to make mistakes, such as reading past the end of a buffer or using memory after it has been freed. Those mistakes are a major source of security vulnerabilities.

The numbers are striking. Microsoft and the Chromium project have each said that roughly seventy percent of their serious security bugs come from memory safety problems. Google has reported that as Android wrote more new code in memory safe languages, the share of its vulnerabilities caused by memory safety fell from about three quarters in 2019 to about a quarter in 2024.

Governments have noticed. In the United States, CISA and the FBI have published guidance telling software makers that products written in memory unsafe languages should have a published plan for reducing that risk, with January 2026 named as the date to have one. Other agencies around the world have issued similar advice.

The direction is clear. More new projects will be started in languages such as Rust, Go, Java, C sharp, Swift and Python, where the language or its runtime manages memory for you. Rust gets most of the attention because it offers memory safety without a garbage collector, which matters for operating systems, browsers and devices. It is already used in parts of the Linux kernel, Android and Windows.

What does that mean for you?

If you already write in a memory safe language, the most useful thing is to understand why it matters. Customers and security teams will increasingly ask about it, and you should be able to explain it in plain words.

If you work in C or C++, nobody is going to rewrite everything soon. Huge amounts of existing code will be maintained for many years. But new components may well be written differently, and the people who can work comfortably across the boundary between old and new code will be very valuable.

And if you are choosing what to learn next, a few weekends with Rust are a good investment. Even if you never use it at work, it changes how you think about who owns a piece of memory, and when.

– Asael Shinder

title: Will Your Photo Come Out Sideways? A Python EXIF Orientation Preflight Before You Pay for a Bama Bound Clip (Tested)
description:
Checked November 17, 2026 (15:19–15:21 CST, UTC+8). I build bamabound.app, an independent studio that turns one photo of one person into a vertical clip of them holding a red I'M BAMA BOUND banner. It is not the University of Alabama, and the clip is not an admission letter.

The photo rule on the FAQ and the photo guide is short: one JPEG, PNG or WebP of one person, up to 10 MB, with the face uncovered. There is no prompt. Resolution is the only extra setting. The site does not publish a required aspect ratio, and it does not mention EXIF Orientation.

That last gap is the one that bites people who write their own "is this photo okay?" check before they pay. A phone held upright often stores the pixels as a landscape rectangle and writes Orientation 6 or 8. A naive width, height = Image.open(path).size then reports 1280×720 for a picture that displays as 720×1280. If your script rejects "landscape" uploads on that number, you will fail a perfectly ordinary portrait. If it only looks at the stored size, it can also miss the opposite mistake.

I wrote a local preflight that never uploads anything. It reads the file, applies ImageOps.exif_transpose, and tells you whether a size check that ignored the tag would have lied. Then I built a small fixture set and ran it.

What the tag actually does

EXIF Orientation 1 means the stored pixels are already the right way up. Orientation 3 is a 180° rotation: the axes stay put, so a 720×1280 file is still 720×1280 after a compliant viewer rotates it. Orientation 6 and 8 are the 90° tags. Those do swap the axes. The fixtures that honour the usual phone convention store those two as 1280×720 and display them as 720×1280.

The preflight flags exif_orientation_would_fool_a_naive_size_read when the displayed picture is portrait and the stored pixels, read without the tag, look landscape (or the other way around).

The preflight


python

!/usr/bin/env python3

"""Preflight a still before you pay to upload it to a one-photo studio.

Checks: format, file size, pixel size, EXIF Orientation vs how Pillow opens
the file, and whether a naive dimension read (without applying Orientation)
would lie about portrait vs landscape.

This script never uploads anything. It only reads a local file.
"""
from future import annotations

import argparse
import json
import sys
from pathlib import Path

from PIL import Image, ImageOps, UnidentifiedImageError

ALLOWED = {"JPEG", "PNG", "WEBP"}
MAX_BYTES = 10 * 1024 * 1024
MIN_SHORT_SIDE = 256 # a practical floor, not a site rule

def exif_orientation(img: Image.Image) -> int | None:
try:
exif = img.getexif()
except Exception:
return None
if not exif:
return None
# 0x0112 is Orientation
value = exif.get(0x0112)
"format_allowed": False,
"mode": None,
"width_stored": None,
"height_stored": None,
"orientation": None,
"width_displayed": None,
"height_displayed": None,
"orientation_swaps_axes": False,
"looks_portrait_displayed": None,
"looks_portrait_if_you_ignore_exif": None,
"short_side": None,
"issues": [],
"ok_for_upload_shape": False,
}
if not rec["exists"]:
rec["issues"].append("missing_file")
return rec
rec["over_10mb"] = rec["bytes"] > MAX_BYTES
if rec["over_10mb"]:
rec["issues"].append("over_10mb")
try:
with Image.open(path) as img:
rec["format"] = img.format
rec["mode"] = img.mode
rec["width_stored"], rec["height_stored"] = img.size
rec["orientation"] = exif_orientation(img)
applied = ImageOps.exif_transpose(img)
rec["width_displayed"], rec["height_displayed"] = applied.size
except UnidentifiedImageError:
rec["issues"].append("unreadable_image")
return rec
except OSError as e:
rec["issues"].append(f"open_error:{e}")
return rec

rec["format_allowed"] = rec["format"] in ALLOWED
if not rec["format_allowed"]:
    rec["issues"].append("format_not_jpeg_png_webp")

rec["orientation_swaps_axes"] = (
    rec["width_stored"], rec["height_stored"]
) != (rec["width_displayed"], rec["height_displayed"])
rec["looks_portrait_displayed"] = rec["height_displayed"] >= rec["width_displayed"]
rec["looks_portrait_if_you_ignore_exif"] = rec["height_stored"] >= rec["width_stored"]
rec["short_side"] = min(rec["width_displayed"], rec["height_displayed"])
if rec["short_side"] < MIN_SHORT_SIDE:
    rec["issues"].append("short_side_under_256")
if rec["orientation"] in (5, 6, 7, 8) or rec["orientation_swaps_axes"]:
    if rec["looks_portrait_displayed"] != rec["looks_portrait_if_you_ignore_exif"]:
        rec["issues"].append("exif_orientation_would_fool_a_naive_size_read")
rec["ok_for_upload_shape"] = (
    rec["format_allowed"]
    and not rec["over_10mb"]
    and "unreadable_image" not in rec["issues"]
    and "short_side_under_256" not in rec["issues"]
)
return rec

def main() -> int:
p = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=doc)
p.add_argument("paths", nargs="+", type=Path)
p.add_argument("--json", action="store_true")
args = p.parse_args()
rows = [inspect(path) for path in args.paths]
if args.json:
json.dump(rows, sys.stdout, indent=2)
sys.stdout.write("
")
else:
for rec in rows:
flag = "OK " if rec["ok_for_upload_shape"] and not rec["issues"] else "SEE"
print(
f"{flag} {rec['path']}
"
f" {rec['bytes']} bytes format={rec['format']} "
f"stored={rec['width_stored']}x{rec['height_stored']} "
f"displayed={rec['width_displayed']}x{rec['height_displayed']} "
f"Orientation={rec['orientation']}
"
f" issues={rec['issues'] or ['none']}"
)
return 0

if name == "main":
raise SystemExit(main())


python

MIN_SHORT_SIDE = 256 is a practical floor I put in the script so a obviously tiny test file gets a warning. It is not a published site rule. The live FAQ and guide only state JPEG, PNG or WebP, up to 10 MB. A 200-pixel photo might still be accepted by the upload field; I would not use one, but I will not pretend the studio published a 256 px minimum.

A short fixture builder

A short fixture builder

The full fixture kit I used also writes a 73 MB JPEG so the 10 MB check has something to trip over. I am not shipping that file, and the script below does not create it. Point the oversize test at any JPEG larger than 10,485,760 bytes if you want that row. Everything else you need is here: the four orientation tags, a portrait and a landscape with no EXIF, PNG, WebP, a TIFF, and an 80×142 thumbnail.


python

!/usr/bin/env python3

"""Build a small set of orientation / format fixtures. Does not write an oversized JPEG."""
from future import annotations

from pathlib import Path

from PIL import Image, ImageDraw

OUT = Path("fixtures")
W, H = 720, 1280 # same frame as a 9:16 720p clip

def upright() -> Image.Image:
img = Image.new("RGB", (W, H), (236, 232, 224))
d = ImageDraw.Draw(img)
d.rectangle((0, 0, W, 80), fill=(20, 20, 20))
d.rectangle((0, H - 120, W, H), fill=(165, 20, 30))
d.text((24, 24), "TOP", fill=(255, 255, 255))
d.text((24, H - 80), "BOTTOM BANNER", fill=(255, 255, 255))
return img

def save_jpeg_with_orientation(img: Image.Image, path: Path, orientation: int) -> None:
# Store pixels without applying the tag. Compliant viewers rotate on open.
exif = Image.Exif()
exif[0x0112] = orientation
exif[0x0131] = "bama-exif-preflight-fixture"
img.save(path, format="JPEG", quality=92, exif=exif, subsampling=0)

def main() -> None:
OUT.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
base = upright()
# Inverse-transform so ImageOps.exif_transpose restores the upright picture.
# EXIF 6: stored as landscape (1280x720); displayed 720x1280.
# EXIF 8: the other 90° tag. EXIF 3 is 180° and does not swap axes.
inv = {
1: lambda im: im,
3: lambda im: im.transpose(Image.ROTATE_180),
6: lambda im: im.transpose(Image.ROTATE_270),
8: lambda im: im.transpose(Image.ROTATE_90),
}
for orient, fn in inv.items():
save_jpeg_with_orientation(fn(base), OUT / f"orient-{orient}.jpg", orient)
base.save(OUT / "no-exif-portrait.jpg", format="JPEG", quality=92)
land = Image.new("RGB", (1280, 720), (236, 232, 224))
ImageDraw.Draw(land).text((24, 24), "LANDSCAPE", fill=(20, 20, 20))
land.save(OUT / "no-exif-landscape.jpg", format="JPEG", quality=92)
base.save(OUT / "portrait.png", format="PNG")
base.save(OUT / "portrait.webp", format="WEBP", quality=90)
base.resize((80, 142)).save(OUT / "too-small.jpg", format="JPEG", quality=92)
base.save(OUT / "portrait.tif", format="TIFF")
print(f"wrote fixtures in {OUT}")
for p in sorted(OUT.iterdir()):
print(f" {p.name:28} {p.stat().st_size:9} bytes")

if name == "main":
main()


markdown

What I measured

I ran exif_preflight.py on the fixtures. Displayed size is after ImageOps.exif_transpose.

File Stored Displayed Orientation Issues
orient-1.jpg / orient-1-upright.jpg 720×1280 720×1280 1 none
orient-3.jpg 720×1280 720×1280 3 none (180°, axes not swapped)
orient-6.jpg 1280×720 720×1280 6 exif_orientation_would_fool_a_naive_size_read
orient-8.jpg 1280×720 720×1280 8 same issue
no-exif-portrait.jpg 720×1280 720×1280 None none
no-exif-landscape.jpg 1280×720 1280×720 None none
portrait.png / portrait.webp 720×1280 720×1280 None none
portrait.tif 720×1280 720×1280 None format_not_jpeg_png_webp (2,764,940 bytes, format TIFF)
too-small.jpg 80×142 80×142 None short_side_under_256
over-10mb.jpg 4000×6000 4000×6000 None over_10mb (73,278,492 bytes, 69.89 MiB)

A few things worth spelling out.

Orientation 3 is the easy one to over-think. The picture is upside down if you ignore the tag, but the stored size is already 720×1280, and the displayed size is the same. The script does not flag it as a naive-size lie, because a width/height check would not have been fooled. You still need exif_transpose (or a viewer that honours the tag) if you want the head at the top.

Orientation 6 and 8 are the ones that fool a size read. Stored 1280×720, displayed 720×1280. Both are allowed formats, both are under 10 MB, and both came back ok_for_upload_shape=true with that one issue noted. I would upload the transposed, upright JPEG if I were being careful, but the live pages do not require you to strip the tag first.

The landscape file with no EXIF is also not rejected. The script does not treat landscape as a failure, because the site asks for one person, not a required aspect. A group photo still does not create extra people in the clip; that is a different rule, on the FAQ, and this preflight does not try to detect it.

TIFF is rejected on format alone: format_not_jpeg_png_webp. The studio lists JPEG, PNG and WebP. A 2,764,940-byte TIFF of the same portrait does not become allowed just because it is under 10 MB.

The oversize fixture was 73,278,492 bytes, 4000×6000. The check is a raw byte count against 10 * 1024 * 1024, not a megapixel cap.

Flattening a copy, if you want to

If you prefer to upload a file whose stored size is already the displayed size, transpose and save a new JPEG with Orientation 1 (or with no Orientation tag):

from pathlib import Path
from PIL import Image, ImageOps

src = Path("phone-photo.jpg")
with Image.open(src) as im:
    upright = ImageOps.exif_transpose(im)
    upright.save(src.with_name(src.stem + "-upright.jpg"), format="JPEG", quality=92)

That is a local convenience, not a published requirement. The live FAQ and guide do not ask you to strip EXIF first. They ask for one JPEG, PNG or WebP, up to 10 MB, with the face uncovered.

How I would use it

Run it on the photo you are about to upload, locally:

python3 exif_preflight.py portrait.jpg
python3 exif_preflight.py --json fixtures/*.jpg fixtures/*.png fixtures/*.webp fixtures/*.tif

If you see exif_orientation_would_fool_a_naive_size_read, open the file in anything that honours EXIF (Preview, Photos, a browser, or Pillow with exif_transpose) and confirm the person is upright. Saving a flattened copy with Orientation 1 is a reasonable habit. It is not a published requirement.

If you see format_not_jpeg_png_webp or over_10mb, that does match the published rule. Convert or compress before you pay. The studio still does the real check at upload time; this script is only a preflight.

One photo, face uncovered, then choose a resolution if you want more than the 480p default. That part has not changed.

title: How to Solve AWS WAF in Python for Automated Testing
description:
The other three task types in this series all make you wait. You create a task, you get a taskId, and you poll until somebody else finishes the work. AWS WAF does not work that way. The call that creates the task is also the call that returns the token.

This walkthrough uses Kaptra's captcha API and the AntiAwsWafTask type. It covers the one required field, the optional triple you should not split, and what to do with a token that comes back on the same response.

One call, not two

Kaptra's own introduction names this type as the current exception. AntiAwsWafTask returns status=ready from /createTask. Every other type returns status=processing and a taskId, and you poll /getTaskResult every 1 to 2 seconds, at most 120 times.

So the client you copied from the Turnstile or reCAPTCHA v2 article will not port. There is no second request, and there is no taskId worth saving. If errorId is 0 and status is ready, read solution and move on.

HTTP status stays 200 either way. The result lives in errorId (0 or 1) and errorCode.

What the page needs from you

Required:

  • websiteURL: the public URL of the page that served the AWS WAF challenge.

Optional, and the minimal request sends none of these:

  • referrer. It defaults from websiteURL. Set it only when the challenge was issued by a different page than the one you are requesting.
  • awsKey, awsIv, and awsContext. These three travel together. Send all of them, or send none. One or two is a malformed request.

There is no proxy field. The Cloudflare challenge task needs your proxy because its cookies are issued for one IP. This task returns a token, so that binding does not apply.

What you attach on the retry

A successful response has solution.token, a string shaped like aws-waf-token=.... Split on the first =, and set a cookie named aws-waf-token to the value on the right. Then retry the same page.

The documented solution has no expiresInMs and no userAgent. Use the token on that retry. Do not print it and come back later.

Full Python example 

import requests
BASE_URL = "https://api.kaptra.ai"
API_KEY = "YOUR_KAPTRA_API_KEY"
def solve_aws_waf(website_url: str) -> dict:
    # synchronous: createTask returns the result, no polling
    resp = requests.post(
        f"{BASE_URL}/createTask",
        json={
            "clientKey": API_KEY,
            "task": {
                "type": "AntiAwsWafTask",
                "websiteURL": website_url,
            },
        },
    ).json()
    if resp.get("errorId"):
        raise RuntimeError(f"createTask failed: {resp.get('errorCode')}")
    if resp.get("status") != "ready":
        raise RuntimeError(f"unexpected status: {resp.get('status')}")
    return resp["solution"]  # {"token": "aws-waf-token=..."}
if __name__ == "__main__":
    page = "https://www.example.com/page"
    solution = solve_aws_waf(page)
    token = solution["token"]
    print(token)
    # retry the page with the token as a cookie
    value = token.split("=", 1)[1]
    session = requests.Session()
    session.cookies.set("aws-waf-token", value)
    page_resp = session.get(page)
    print(page_resp.status_code)

If status comes back as anything other than ready, stop. Do not invent a poll loop for a type the docs say is synchronous.

The other AWS WAF task is a grid

AwsWafClassification is a different type, for the visual grid where the page asks you to pick the tiles that show a target. That one is asynchronous. You send nine base64 tiles and a question such as aws:grid:bag, you poll getTaskResult, and the solution is objects: tile indices from 0 to 8, top-left first.

Supported targets on that type are bag, bed, bucket, chair, clock, curtain, and hat. A target outside that list fails with ERROR_CAPTCHA_UNSOLVABLE and is not billed. If your page is a 3 by 3 image grid, you are on the wrong guide.

Before you wire it into the suite

Start with the minimal body. websiteURL alone is the documented minimal request. Add awsKey, awsIv, and awsContext only when you already have all three. A partial set is how you get ERROR_BAD_REQUEST.

A failure is a reason to look, not to hammer retry. Average time on the pricing page is under 3 seconds. ERROR_CAPTCHA_UNSOLVABLE means the solve failed. The error dictionary says not to charge-retry blindly: check the page and the fields, then create a new task. Failed and timed-out tasks are not billed.

Price. $0.60 per 1,000 successful solves, the same rate as the grid type. No monthly fee, and top-up credit does not expire. A new account includes $10 in test credit, which is 16,666 solves at this rate.

Other codes. ERROR_TASK_NOT_SUPPORTED means the type string is wrong or the type is disabled. ERROR_ZERO_BALANCE means stop and top up. None of these change the HTTP status. It stays 200.

Where this sits next to the other three

Turnstile and reCAPTCHA v2 are widgets: a site key goes in, a token comes out, and you poll. The Cloudflare challenge page is a wall: your HTTP proxy goes in, cookies come out, and you poll. AWS WAF is the short one. A page URL goes in, aws-waf-token comes out, and the function returns.

  • Site: kaptra.ai
  • AntiAwsWafTask docs: kaptra.ai/docs
  • The polling widget this does not copy: How to solve Cloudflare Turnstile in Python
  • The proxy-and-cookies case: How to solve the Cloudflare 5-second challenge in Python
  • The other token that expires: How to solve reCAPTCHA v2 in Python

title: Oracle AI Database 26ai(23.26.4): Streaming Windowing Table Functions
description:
Analyzing time-based data is a common requirement in modern database applications. Oracle AI Database 26ai(RU 23.26.4) introduces four SQL streaming windowing table functions that simplify this type of analysis by dividing table rows into time-based windows.

These functions are:

  • TUMBLE: Divides rows into consecutive, non-overlapping time windows.
  • HOP: Creates sliding time windows that can overlap or have gaps.
  • CUMULATE: Creates expanding time windows with a common starting point.
  • SESSIONS: Groups rows into sessions based on the time interval between consecutive events.

Each function accepts a datetime column and interval parameters to determine how rows are assigned to windows. The returned result includes two additional columns, WINDOW_START and WINDOW_END, which identify the time boundaries of each window.

In this article, we will explore how these four functions work and demonstrate their practical applications using customer activity data.

1. How Streaming Windowing Functions Work

Before exploring the individual functions, it is useful to understand how Oracle assigns records to time windows.

A windowing function takes a table, a datetime column, and interval values to divide records into time periods.

The general syntax is:

function_name (
    table_name,
    COLUMNS (datetime_column),
    interval_arguments
)

The result contains the original columns from the input table, together with two additional columns:

WINDOW_START: The timestamp representing the beginning of the window.
WINDOW_END: The timestamp representing the end of the window.
These two columns allow us to identify the time range associated with each record.

For example, the following query creates one-hour windows using the event_time column:

SELECT *
FROM TUMBLE (
    sales,
    COLUMNS (event_time),
    INTERVAL '1' HOUR
);

In this example, Oracle uses the value of event_time to determine which one-hour period contains each sales record.

An important detail is how Oracle handles the beginning and ending points of a window. The starting time is included, but the ending time is not.

In other words:

WINDOW_START <= event_time < WINDOW_END

For example, with one-hour windows, a record timestamped at 11:00 belongs to the 11:00–12:00 window rather than the 10:00–11:00 window.

This boundary rule ensures that records occurring exactly between two consecutive windows are assigned consistently.

2. Four Different Approaches to Time-Based Analysis

Although the four functions share the same general purpose, their behavior can produce significantly different results.

Let’s examine each one and see how it can be used in real-world scenarios.

2.1. TUMBLE: Organizing Data into Fixed Time Periods

Sometimes we need to summarize information within predefined time intervals. For example, a business might want to know how many transactions occurred during every 10-minute period.

It divides the timeline into consecutive windows of equal duration. Each record with a non-null datetime value is assigned to one window, so records are not repeated across different windows.

Consider the following timeline:

10:00 - 10:10
10:10 - 10:20
10:20 - 10:30
10:30 - 10:40

Each interval represents an independent reporting period.

Practical implementation

In our example, we have a table called user_activities containing customer information, activity timestamps, and transaction amounts.

SQL> CREATE TABLE user_activities (
  2      activity_id NUMBER PRIMARY KEY,
  3      first_name  VARCHAR2(30),
  4      last_name   VARCHAR2(30),
  5      event_time  TIMESTAMP,
  6      amount      NUMBER(10,2)
  7  );
Table created


SQL> 
SQL> INSERT INTO user_activities VALUES
  2  (1, 'Vahid', 'Yousefzadeh',
  3   TIMESTAMP '2026-11-14 10:01:00', 120);
1 row inserted

SQL> 
SQL> INSERT INTO user_activities VALUES
  2  (2, 'Vahid', 'Yousefzadeh',
  3   TIMESTAMP '2026-11-14 10:04:00', 250);
1 row inserted

SQL> 
SQL> INSERT INTO user_activities VALUES
  2  (3, 'Masoud', 'Sori',
  3   TIMESTAMP '2026-11-14 10:06:00', 180);
1 row inserted

SQL> 
SQL> INSERT INTO user_activities VALUES
  2  (4, 'Vahid', 'Yousefzadeh',
  3   TIMESTAMP '2026-11-14 10:08:00', 300);
1 row inserted

SQL> 
SQL> INSERT INTO user_activities VALUES
  2  (5, 'Masoud', 'Sori',
  3   TIMESTAMP '2026-11-14 10:12:00', 200);
1 row inserted

SQL> 
SQL> INSERT INTO user_activities VALUES
  2  (6, 'Kourosh', 'Barmak',
  3   TIMESTAMP '2026-11-14 10:14:00', 150);
1 row inserted

SQL> 
SQL> INSERT INTO user_activities VALUES
  2  (7, 'Vahid', 'Yousefzadeh',
  3   TIMESTAMP '2026-11-14 10:25:00', 400);
1 row inserted

SQL> 
SQL> INSERT INTO user_activities VALUES
  2  (8, 'Masoud', 'Sori',
  3   TIMESTAMP '2026-11-14 10:22:00', 350);
1 row inserted

SQL> 
SQL> INSERT INTO user_activities VALUES
  2  (9, 'Vahid', 'Yousefzadeh',
  3   TIMESTAMP '2026-11-14 10:29:00', 220);
1 row inserted

SQL> 
SQL> INSERT INTO user_activities VALUES
  2  (10, 'Masoud', 'Sori',
  3   TIMESTAMP '2026-11-14 10:40:00', 500);
1 row inserted

SQL> COMMIT;
Commit complete

We want to calculate the number of transactions and their total value for every customer within each 10-minute period.

The following query demonstrates this approach:

SQL> SELECT
    first_name,
    last_name,
    window_start,
    window_end,
    COUNT(*) AS transaction_count,
    SUM(amount) AS total_amount
FROM TUMBLE (
    vahid.user_activities,
    COLUMNS (event_time),
    INTERVAL '10' MINUTE
)
     GROUP BY
    first_name,
    last_name,
    window_start,
    window_end
ORDER BY
    window_start,
    first_name; 

FIRST_NAME   LAST_NAME      WINDOW_START                   WINDOW_END                     TRANSACTION_COUNT TOTAL_AMOUNT
------------ -------------- ------------------------------ ------------------------------ ----------------- ------------
Masoud       Sori           14-NOV-26 10.00.00.000000 AM   14-NOV-26 10.10.00.000000 AM                   1          180
Vahid        Yousefzadeh    14-NOV-26 10.00.00.000000 AM   14-NOV-26 10.10.00.000000 AM                   3          670

Masoud       Sori           14-NOV-26 10.20.00.000000 AM   14-NOV-26 10.30.00.000000 AM                   1          350
Vahid        Yousefzadeh    14-NOV-26 10.20.00.000000 AM   14-NOV-26 10.30.00.000000 AM                   2          620
Masoud       Sori           14-NOV-26 10.40.00.000000 AM   14-NOV-26 10.50.00.000000 AM                   1          500

7 rows selected.

As the results demonstrate, Oracle groups transactions according to their timestamps. For example, Vahid has three transactions in the first 10-minute period, with a combined amount of 670.

2.2. HOP: Analyzing Data Across Overlapping Periods

There are situations where fixed reporting periods are not sufficient. We may want to evaluate recent activity more frequently while still considering a longer time range.

For these requirements, HOP provides a different approach.

Instead of moving from one completed window to the next without overlap, HOP creates windows at regular intervals. The starting point of each new window is determined by the slide parameter, while the size parameter controls its duration.

For example, consider a configuration with:

Window size: 10 minutes.
Slide interval: 5 minutes.
The resulting windows can look like this:

09:55 - 10:05
10:00 - 10:10
10:05 - 10:15
10:10 - 10:20
10:15 - 10:25

Because each new window starts before the previous one has finished, a record may participate in multiple windows.

Practical implementation

Using the same user_activities dataset, we can examine the transaction results produced by overlapping 10-minute windows.

The following results demonstrate how the same customer’s activities can appear in different windows.

SQL> SELECT
    first_name,
    last_name,
    window_start,
    window_end,
    COUNT(*) AS transaction_count,
    SUM(amount) AS total_amount
FROM HOP (
    vahid.user_activities,
    COLUMNS (event_time),
    INTERVAL '5' MINUTE,
    INTERVAL '10' MINUTE
)
GROUP BY
    first_name,
    last_name,
    window_start,
    window_end
    ORDER BY
    window_start,
    first_name;

FIRST_NAME   LAST_NAME      WINDOW_START                   WINDOW_END                     TRANSACTION_COUNT TOTAL_AMOUNT
------------ -------------- ------------------------------ ------------------------------ ----------------- ------------
Vahid        Yousefzadeh    14-NOV-26 09.55.00.000000 AM   14-NOV-26 10.05.00.000000 AM                   2          370
Masoud       Sori           14-NOV-26 10.00.00.000000 AM   14-NOV-26 10.10.00.000000 AM                   1          180
Vahid        Yousefzadeh    14-NOV-26 10.00.00.000000 AM   14-NOV-26 10.10.00.000000 AM                   3          670
Kourosh      Barmak         14-NOV-26 10.05.00.000000 AM   14-NOV-26 10.15.00.000000 AM                   1          150
Masoud       Sori           14-NOV-26 10.05.00.000000 AM   14-NOV-26 10.15.00.000000 AM                   2          380
Vahid        Yousefzadeh    14-NOV-26 10.05.00.000000 AM   14-NOV-26 10.15.00.000000 AM                   1          300
Kourosh      Barmak         14-NOV-26 10.10.00.000000 AM   14-NOV-26 10.20.00.000000 AM                   1          150
Masoud       Sori           14-NOV-26 10.10.00.000000 AM   14-NOV-26 10.20.00.000000 AM                   1          200
Masoud       Sori           14-NOV-26 10.15.00.000000 AM   14-NOV-26 10.25.00.000000 AM                   1          350
Masoud       Sori           14-NOV-26 10.20.00.000000 AM   14-NOV-26 10.30.00.000000 AM                   1          350
Vahid        Yousefzadeh    14-NOV-26 10.20.00.000000 AM   14-NOV-26 10.30.00.000000 AM                   2          620
Vahid        Yousefzadeh    14-NOV-26 10.25.00.000000 AM   14-NOV-26 10.35.00.000000 AM                   2          620
Masoud       Sori           14-NOV-26 10.35.00.000000 AM   14-NOV-26 10.45.00.000000 AM                   1          500
Masoud       Sori           14-NOV-26 10.40.00.000000 AM   14-NOV-26 10.50.00.000000 AM                   1          500

14 rows selected.

The output contains more rows than the TUMBLE example because the same activity can contribute to multiple overlapping time windows.

This behavior allows us to examine transaction activity from different time perspectives without changing the original dataset.

2.3. CUMULATE: Building Progressively Larger Time Windows
Another interesting requirement is comparing activity at different stages of a reporting period.

For example, we might want to examine transaction totals after 5 minutes, 10 minutes, and 15 minutes, while keeping the same starting point.

CUMULATE provides this capability.

It creates multiple windows that begin at the same timestamp. Each subsequent window extends the ending timestamp by a predefined step until the maximum configured duration is reached.

Consider a step of 5 minutes and a maximum duration of 15 minutes:

10:00 - 10:05
10:00 - 10:10
10:00 - 10:15

The next group of windows starts at the following 15-minute boundary:

10:15 - 10:20
10:15 - 10:25
10:15 - 10:30

This arrangement allows us to compare different stages of the same reporting interval.

Practical implementation

Using our customer activity table, the following query generates progressively expanding windows with a 5-minute step and a maximum size of 15 minutes.

SQL> SELECT
    first_name,
    last_name,
    window_start,
    window_end,
    COUNT(*) AS transaction_count,
    SUM(amount) AS total_amount
FROM CUMULATE (
    vahid.user_activities,
    COLUMNS (event_time),
    INTERVAL '5' MINUTE,
    INTERVAL '15' MINUTE
)
GROUP BY
    first_name,
    last_name,
    window_start,
    window_end
    ORDER BY
    window_start,
    window_end,
    first_name;

FIRST_NAME   LAST_NAME      WINDOW_START                   WINDOW_END                     TRANSACTION_COUNT TOTAL_AMOUNT
------------ -------------- ------------------------------ ------------------------------ ----------------- ------------
Vahid        Yousefzadeh    14-NOV-26 10.00.00.000000 AM   14-NOV-26 10.05.00.000000 AM                   2          370
Masoud       Sori           14-NOV-26 10.00.00.000000 AM   14-NOV-26 10.10.00.000000 AM                   1          180
Vahid        Yousefzadeh    14-NOV-26 10.00.00.000000 AM   14-NOV-26 10.10.00.000000 AM                   3          670
Kourosh      Barmak         14-NOV-26 10.00.00.000000 AM   14-NOV-26 10.15.00.000000 AM                   1          150
Masoud       Sori           14-NOV-26 10.00.00.000000 AM   14-NOV-26 10.15.00.000000 AM                   2          380
Vahid        Yousefzadeh    14-NOV-26 10.00.00.000000 AM   14-NOV-26 10.15.00.000000 AM                   3          670
Masoud       Sori           14-NOV-26 10.15.00.000000 AM   14-NOV-26 10.25.00.000000 AM                   1          350
Masoud       Sori           14-NOV-26 10.15.00.000000 AM   14-NOV-26 10.30.00.000000 AM                   1          350
Vahid        Yousefzadeh    14-NOV-26 10.15.00.000000 AM   14-NOV-26 10.30.00.000000 AM                   2          620
Masoud       Sori           14-NOV-26 10.30.00.000000 AM   14-NOV-26 10.45.00.000000 AM                   1          500

10 rows selected.

The results show how Oracle produces different window boundaries for the same starting period. This makes it possible to compare transaction activity over progressively longer durations.

An important configuration requirement is that the maximum window size must be an integer multiple of the step. For example, a 15-minute maximum size is compatible with a 5-minute step.

2.4. SESSIONS: Identifying Continuous Periods of Activity

The previous functions use predefined time intervals to organize records. However, some business requirements are based on user behavior rather than fixed clock periods.

Consider a website where a customer performs several actions. We may want to consider consecutive actions part of the same session as long as the customer does not remain inactive for too long.

This is where SESSIONS becomes useful.

Instead of relying on a fixed window size, it examines the timestamps of consecutive records. A configured inactivity gap determines whether a record continues an existing session or starts a new one.

For example, if the maximum gap is 10 minutes, activities separated by 3 or 5 minutes can remain in the same session. However, when the interval between consecutive activities exceeds 10 minutes, a new session begins.

Another useful feature is PARTITION BY. It allows us to separate records according to one or more column values before identifying sessions.

This is especially important when analyzing multiple customers because each customer should have an independent activity history.

Practical implementation

In our example, we use the customer’s first and last names as partitioning columns. This ensures that activities from different customers are evaluated separately.

The session gap is configured to 10 minutes.

SQL> SELECT
    first_name,
    last_name,
    window_start,
   window_end,
    COUNT(*) AS activity_count,
    SUM(amount) AS total_amount
FROM SESSIONS (
    Vahid.user_activities PARTITION BY (first_name, last_name),
    COLUMNS (event_time),
    INTERVAL '10' MINUTE
)
GROUP BY
    first_name,
   last_name,
    window_start,
    window_end
ORDER BY
    first_name,
    window_start; 

FIRST_NAME   LAST_NAME      WINDOW_START                   WINDOW_END                     ACTIVITY_COUNT TOTAL_AMOUNT
------------ -------------- ------------------------------ ------------------------------ -------------- ------------
Kourosh      Barmak         14-NOV-26 10.14.00.000000 AM   14-NOV-26 10.24.00.000000 AM                1          150
Masoud       Sori           14-NOV-26 10.06.00.000000 AM   14-NOV-26 10.32.00.000000 AM                3          730
Masoud       Sori           14-NOV-26 10.40.00.000000 AM   14-NOV-26 10.50.00.000000 AM                1          500
Vahid        Yousefzadeh    14-NOV-26 10.01.00.000000 AM   14-NOV-26 10.18.00.000000 AM                3          670
Vahid        Yousefzadeh    14-NOV-26 10.25.00.000000 AM   14-NOV-26 10.39.00.000000 AM                2          620

The output identifies separate activity sessions for each customer.

For example, Masoud has two sessions. His first session contains three activities, while the second contains one activity. Vahid also has two separate sessions because the inactivity between his activities exceeds the configured gap.

title: Six Test-Bench Mistakes That Make Good RF Parts Look Bad
description:
Six Test-Bench Mistakes That Make Good RF Parts Look Bad

Every few weeks someone sends us a switch or an attenuator with a note saying it measures worse than the datasheet. Most of the time the part is fine. The bench is not.

This is not a defence of our datasheets. It is a list of the six things that account for almost every "out of specification" RF component I have seen, in the order they usually turn out to be the cause.

1. The calibration plane is at the analyser, not at the part

You calibrate at the front panel because that is where the cal kit connects. Then you add two adapters, a cable, and a fixture, and measure the DUT. The analyser reports the loss of everything between the plane and the DUT, and calls it the DUT's insertion loss.

At 3 GHz the two adapters might be 0.1 dB. At 18 GHz the same pair can be 0.4 dB, and the mismatch term adds another 0.1 dB that changes sign with frequency. That is more than the specification you are arguing about.

Fix it with adapter removal, or calibrate at the DUT plane. If neither is practical, at least write the reference plane on the test record, so the next person knows what the number includes.

2. Nobody torqued anything

A hand-tight SMA is not a connection, it is a hope. The specification for a 3.5 mm connector is around 0.9 N·m; for SMA about 0.45 N·m. Under-torque gives you a gap in the dielectric and a reflection. Over-torque deforms the outer conductor and permanently degrades both connectors.

The practical symptom is measurement repeatability of 0.05 to 0.1 dB per re-mate, which people then attribute to the component drifting. Buy a torque wrench. It costs less than the argument.

3. The cables moved between calibration and measurement

A flexible cable is a mechanical device that happens to carry RF. Bend it and the impedance changes; the change is small but it is real, and at high frequency it appears as a phase shift and a small loss change.

Tape or clip the cables down before calibrating, and never use a cable as a handle again. If a measurement changes after someone reached across the bench, suspect the cable before the DUT.

4. The DUT is better than the test setup

Measuring a 0.3 dB component on a bench with 0.15 dB of uncertainty produces a number with a 50 % error bar. That is not a measurement, it is an opinion with decimals.

The four contributors, roughly: calibration standards, test port match, trace noise, connector repeatability. Averaging only addresses one of them, and it is usually the smallest. Fix the match and the connectors first — a 6 dB pad in front of the analyser often improves accuracy more than 1000 averages.

5. The unused ports were left open

A multi-throw switch measured with its unused ports open is not the switch you will install. An open port reflects, and the reflection couples back into the selected path. On a SP4T at X-band this can move the measured insertion loss by 0.1 dB and do strange things to the return loss.

Terminate every unused port with a load rated for the power present, and say in the test record which ports were terminated. This matters even more for a coaxial switch with more than four throws, where the geometry makes the coupling larger.

6. The part is at a different temperature than the calibration

A resistive film has a temperature coefficient. A connector has a different one. Twenty degrees of ambient difference between the factory and the receiving inspection is enough to move a 0.3 dB attenuator by 0.02 dB and a return loss by a couple of dB at the band edge.

This one is genuinely hard to eliminate, which is why the specification should be read as "typical at 25 °C" and not as a guarantee at whatever temperature the rack runs at.

What to do instead

A short, boring routine removes most of these:

  • Torque every connection, every time, with the same wrench.
  • Calibrate at the plane you will quote, and record it.
  • Keep a verification artefact — a short, a load, a stable fixed attenuator — and measure it at the start and end of a session.
  • Terminate unused ports.
  • Let the analyser and the DUT reach the same temperature before calibrating.
  • When comparing with a datasheet, check whether the figure is typical or maximum, and whether connectors are included.

None of that is exotic. It is just the difference between a measurement and a number.

The uncomfortable part

The uncomfortable part is that a vendor's specification and a customer's measurement are often both correct, and they are simply describing different things. A coaxial termination measured on a bench with 0.1 dB of adapter uncertainty, at 40 °C, with an open reference port, is a different object from the one on the datasheet.

Which means the useful question is rarely "is this part in specification" but "what exactly did each of us measure". Answering that takes ten minutes and saves a month.

Notes from the engineering team at DB Design / MeiXun (Wuxi) Communication Technology, who make coaxial switches, waveguide switches, loads and attenuators, and who have had this conversation more times than they can count.

title: Our thirty second timeout let one call to the customs portal run for forty minutes
description:
Every evening a Python worker submits our export declarations to our customs broker's API, one consignment at a time, so that the lorries leaving at six the next morning have their clearance. Years ago a hung partner call had taken down a service of ours, and since then every outbound client we own has a timeout. This one used requests with timeout=30. We read that as: no call can take longer than thirty seconds.

In October the broker's platform had a bad night. Their gateway stayed up, but responses came back a few kilobytes at a time. One submission returned a large validation report, and its call ran for forty one minutes without raising anything. The worker processes declarations in order, so the three hundred behind it waited. Ninety consignments missed the morning lorries.

The requests documentation is precise about this, and we had never read it. The timeout is not a limit on the whole response. It applies to connecting, and then to each wait for data on the socket: the exception is raised only if no bytes have arrived for thirty seconds. A server that sends something every twenty nine seconds can keep a call open for as long as it likes. A slow trickle never trips a timeout that only measures silence.

Our dashboard did not help either. We recorded the duration of calls that completed and the number that timed out. A call that never finished appeared in neither, so for forty minutes the graphs showed a quiet evening.

The worker now enforces a total deadline per call. It streams the response and checks the elapsed time on every chunk, abandoning the call at sixty seconds whatever the server is doing, and the submission goes to a retry queue instead of blocking the run. Declarations are submitted by four workers in parallel, so one stuck call delays a quarter of the run at worst. We also emit a metric for calls in flight with their age, and an alert fires when any outbound call has been open for longer than twice its deadline.

We audited the other clients and found the same assumption in eleven of them. The library's name for the setting and our idea of what it meant were the same word for two different things.

– Sergey Shinder
