title: What AI Agent Skills Are and How They Work
description:
AI Agent Skills: The Missing Piece of Procedural Knowledge

TL;DR

AI agents are great at reasoning and recalling facts, but they struggle with step‑by‑step workflows. Skills solve this by packaging procedural knowledge into lightweight, open‑standard Markdown files that agents load on demand. They’re fast, versionable, and portable across platforms—just watch out for security when installing third‑party skills.

What Are AI Agent Skills?

AI agents built on large language models (LLMs) can answer trivia, explain concepts, or describe architecture.

What they don’t do well is execute a specific multi‑step process—like generating a compliant financial report in 47 steps—without being told every single step.

A skill is the mechanism that injects that procedural knowledge into an agent. Think of it as a recipe that tells the agent what to do and when to do it.

The Anatomy of a Skill

A skill lives in its own folder and is centered around a single skill.md file.

---
name: PDF Builder
description: Use this when the user asks to extract a PDF.
author: Jane Doe
version: 1.0
---

## Goal
Extract text from a PDF and return a clean, searchable version.

## Steps
1. Receive the PDF file path.
2. Call the `pdf-extract` script.
3. Clean the extracted text.
4. Return the cleaned text to the user.

## Example
**Input:** `extract_pdf("report.pdf")`  
**Output:** `Cleaned text of report.pdf`

Mandatory Fields

Field Purpose
name Unique identifier for the skill.
description Trigger condition – tells the agent when to use the skill.

Optional Fields

  • author, version – for provenance.
  • scripts/ – executable JS/Python/bash files the agent can run.
  • references/ – extra docs the agent may load on demand.
  • assets/ – static resources like templates or data files.

How Skills Are Loaded: Progressive Disclosure

Loading every skill’s full content into the LLM’s context window would quickly exhaust the token budget.

Skills solve this with a three‑tier progressive disclosure strategy.

Tier What’s Loaded When
1 – Metadata name + description At agent startup
2 – Full Instructions Entire skill.md body When a request matches the description
3 – Resources scripts/, references/, assets/ Only when a specific task requires them

This keeps the agent lightweight, yet fully functional when a skill is needed.

Skills vs. Other Knowledge Injections

Knowledge Type What It Provides How It Works Limitations
MCP (Model Context Protocol) Tool access & API calls Agent calls external services No judgment on when to call
RAG (Retrieval‑Augmented Generation) Factual data from a knowledge base Pulls relevant chunks at runtime No procedural guidance
Fine‑Tuning Permanent knowledge baked into weights Model retrained on new data Expensive, inflexible to changes
Skills Procedural workflows Markdown + optional scripts Requires careful security review

Skills complement MCP, RAG, and fine‑tuning by adding judgment—the “when” and “how” to use other knowledge sources.

The Open‑Standard Edge

  • Format: skill.md + optional folders.
  • Spec: Published at agentskills.io under an Apache 2.0 license.
  • Portability: A skill built for Claude, Code, or OpenAI Codex works on any platform that supports the spec.

Security Considerations

Because skills can execute scripts with file‑system access, API keys, and environment variables, they’re a potential attack vector:

  • Prompt Injection – malicious prompts that manipulate the skill’s logic.
  • Tool Poisoning – tampering with external tools the skill calls.
  • Hidden Malware – scripts that perform unwanted actions.

Best practice: Treat skill installation like any other software dependency—review the code, understand its behavior, and audit before running it locally.

Key Takeaways

  • Procedural knowledge is the missing piece for AI agents; skills fill that gap.
  • A skill is a Markdown file (skill.md) that defines what the agent does and when to do it.
  • Progressive disclosure keeps agents efficient: metadata → instructions → resources.
  • Skills work alongside MCP, RAG, and fine‑tuning, adding judgment to the agent’s toolkit.
  • The open‑standard format ensures portability across AI platforms.
  • Security is paramount—review skills before executing them.

With skills, an agent that already knows the airspeed velocity of an unladen swallow can now learn to generate a compliant financial report—all by loading a few lines of Markdown. Happy skill‑building!

title: Seven checks to run on a T-12 before it goes into a model
description:
A T-12 (trailing twelve months) is a property's income and expense statement for its last 12 months, usually one column per month. In commercial real estate, buyers and lenders read it to see what a property actually earned and spent, as opposed to what an offering memorandum says it could earn. The net operating income (NOI) at the bottom drives the price and the loan size, so an error in the file moves both.

At a fixed cap rate, value is NOI divided by that rate, so a 5% error in NOI is a 5% error in price. And the file was not built for you to parse. It comes out of the seller's accounting system as an Excel export or, worse, a PDF.

Here are seven checks to run before the NOI goes into a model. The first four are in code at the end.

The shape of the data

One row per line item, 12 month columns, and a Total column. Section header rows (INCOME, OPERATING EXPENSES) carry no numbers. Subtotal rows (Total income, Total operating expenses, Net operating income) sit among the line items.

Things that break a parser: negatives in parentheses, a dash for zero, dollar signs and commas stored as text, merged header cells, and a PDF that has to become a spreadsheet first. Normalize the numbers, tag every row with its section, and mark the subtotals so you never add them in as if they were lines.

Check 1: do the rows tie to the Total column?

Add the 12 months of each line and compare the result with the Total column. Use a tolerance of a dollar for rounding.

A mismatch means a month was pasted over, a number was edited by hand, or the Total column came from a different export than the months. Any of those means you cannot trust the file until someone explains it.

Check 2: do the subtotals tie?

Three tests: total income against the income lines above it, total operating expenses against the expense lines, and stated NOI against income minus operating expenses.

A summary row that disagrees with its own detail usually means a line was added to one and not the other.

Check 3: one-month spikes

Compare each month of an expense line with that line's median month. An annual insurance premium booked in a single month, a roof repair, or a tax bill paid on a cash basis all show up as a month several times the median.

A spike is a question, not an error. It can be a one-off you should take out of the run rate, a recurring cost that happens to be lumpy, or timing. Flag it, then ask which. The same check works in reverse: a line that is blank for a month may be a bill that was never booked.

Check 4: missing lines

Look for taxes, insurance, property management and repairs. A statement with no management line may belong to an owner who runs the property personally, but a new owner will probably pay a fee. No taxes line, or a tax figure that predates the sale, matters because many places reassess after a sale. A missing line makes NOI higher than the property will deliver under new ownership.

Check 5: the trend

Set the T-12 beside two shorter windows: the last 3 months times 4 (T3 annualized) and the last month times 12 (T1 annualized). A gap between them means something changed. It might be new leases, burned-off concessions or a vacancy. Seasonality can also cause it, because utilities and turnover are not flat across the year, so read the three numbers together and ask.

Check 6: items that belong below the line

Debt service, capital expenditures and depreciation are not operating expenses. They come after NOI. If they are inside operating expenses, NOI is understated. The reverse also happens: a repair relabeled as a capital item lifts NOI. Ask for the capital ledger.

Replacement reserves are a judgment call. Some NOI figures deduct them and some do not, so two properties with the same cap rate can be on different bases. Write down which one you are using.

Check 7: sign and label hygiene

Vacancy and concessions should reduce income. When one arrives as a positive number, a naive sum adds it instead of subtracting it. Look for duplicated lines, and for one-time income, such as a lease termination fee or an insurance payout, sitting inside "Other income". Also ask whether the statement is cash or accrual. On a cash basis, one month can hold a year of a bill.

Checks 1 to 4 in pandas

Feed it a CSV with the line name first, then Jan to Dec, then Total. The header rows in the sheet (INCOME, OPERATING EXPENSES) set the section.

import sys
import pandas as pd

M = ["Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr", "May", "Jun", "Jul", "Aug", "Sep", "Oct", "Nov", "Dec"]

def num(x):
    s = str(x).replace("$", "").replace(",", "").strip()
    if s in ("", "-"):
        return 0.0
    return -float(s[1:-1]) if s.startswith("(") else float(s)

def load(path):
    raw = pd.read_csv(path, dtype=str).fillna("")
    raw.columns = ["line", *M, "total"]
    rows, section = [], ""
    for _, r in raw.iterrows():
        if not any(r[m] for m in M):              # header row such as INCOME
            section = r["line"].strip().lower()
        else:
            rows.append({"line": r["line"].strip(), "sec": section, "total": num(r["total"]),
                         **{m: num(r[m]) for m in M}})
    df = pd.DataFrame(rows)
    df["sum"] = df[M].sum(axis=1)
    return df

def checks(df, tol=1.0):
    out = []
    sub = df.line.str.lower().str.match(r"(total|net operating|noi)")
    inc = df[df.sec.str.startswith("income") & ~sub]
    exp = df[df.sec.str.startswith("operating") & ~sub]
    for _, r in df[(df["sum"] - df.total).abs() > tol].iterrows():            # check 1
        out.append(f"{r.line}: months add to {r['sum']:,.0f}, Total says {r.total:,.0f}")
    for pat, lines in [("total income", inc), ("total operating", exp)]:     # check 2
        s = df[df.line.str.lower().str.startswith(pat)]
        if len(s) and abs(s.iloc[0]["sum"] - lines["sum"].sum()) > tol:
            out.append(f"{pat}: lines add to {lines['sum'].sum():,.0f}, stated {s.iloc[0]['sum']:,.0f}")
    for _, r in exp.iterrows():                                              # check 3
        med = r[M].astype(float).median()
        out += [f"{r.line}, {m}: {r[m]:,.0f} against a median month of {med:,.0f}"
                for m in M if med > 0 and r[m] > 2.5 * med]
    for label, pat in {"taxes": "tax", "insurance": "insur", "management": "manage",
                       "repairs": "repair|maint"}.items():                   # check 4
        if not exp.line.str.contains(pat, case=False).any():
            out.append(f"No {label} line in operating expenses: NOI may be too high")
    return out

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("\n".join(checks(load(sys.argv[1]))) or "No flags.")

The 2.5 times the median threshold is my choice. Tune it to the property. A flag on a file with one bad month looks like this:

Other income: months add to 18,000, Total says 18,500
Repairs and maintenance, Aug: 9,500 against a median month of 1,800
No management line in operating expenses: NOI may be too high

What to ask the seller

Flag Question
Row does not tie to Total Which export is this, and can you send the original from the accounting system?
Spike in one month What was it, and does it recur? Is the statement cash or accrual?
Missing management fee Who manages the property, and what do they charge?
T3 or T1 far from T-12 What changed in the last quarter, and is it permanent?
Repairs looking low Can I see the capital ledger?

None of this uses market benchmarks. The script finds arithmetic and omissions, not opinions about what a property should cost to run. A flag is a question, not a verdict. After the arithmetic, tie rent to the rent roll, collections to bank statements and taxes to the tax bills.

Run the same checks without code

Pacific Software Ventures (PSV) publishes free CRE tools. PSV's T12 analyzer totals income, expenses and NOI, annualizes the last 3 months and the last month, and flags totals that do not add up, one-month spikes and missing lines. It runs in the browser and does not upload your numbers: T12 analyzer and guide.

Disclosure: PSV made that tool, and sells AI consulting and training to commercial real estate firms. This is general education, not investment, legal or tax advice.

title: Our logs put one order's email failure under another order's number because a pooled thread remembered it
description:
Our order service puts the order number into every log line through the logging context, the MDC, so that one search shows everything that happened to an order. A servlet filter puts the number in when a request arrives and clears it when the response goes out. On the request thread that works perfectly.

In September we moved label printing and customer emails off the request path into a Spring thread pool, so checkout would not wait for them. Two weeks later a customer complained that her confirmation email had never arrived. Support searched for her order number and found the checkout and nothing after it. Searching for email errors in that minute found a failure logged against a different order, belonging to a customer who had received his email without any trouble.

Logback keeps the MDC in a ThreadLocal. It belongs to the thread that set it, and a pool thread does not inherit it from the thread that submitted the work. So the async tasks started with an empty context and their lines carried no order number at all. That alone would have been merely unhelpful. The worse part came from the label task, which put the order number into the MDC itself and never removed it. Pool threads are reused, so the next email task on that thread logged under whatever order the last label had left behind. Some lines had no order number, some had the wrong one, and nothing in the line told you which.

For two weeks every search by order number had silently missed the async half of an order's life, and now and then shown someone else's.

The executor now has a TaskDecorator that copies the submitting thread's MDC into the task and clears it in a finally block when the task ends, whatever happened inside. Tasks may no longer call MDC.put themselves, and an architecture test in the build enforces that. Every log line also carries the thread name, and a dashboard counts log lines without an order number by logger, a number that should be zero outside startup.

A context that lives on a thread is only as accurate as the last piece of code that ran there.

– Sergey Shinder

title: We Cloned Our Purchasing Server to Test an Upgrade and Our Suppliers Received Every Order Twice
description:
Our purchasing server runs the jobs that turn the morning's replenishment into purchase orders and send them to suppliers, some by email and some as files to their own systems. In May we needed to test an upgrade to the purchasing software, and the quickest way to get a realistic test machine was to clone the production server.

An engineer made the copy on a Friday afternoon and attached it to our test network. Our test network can reach the internet, because testers need to download things and reach suppliers' test portals. He planned to start the upgrade on Monday.

At six on Saturday morning, the clone woke up and did exactly what the original did. It read the same purchasing database, built the same purchase orders and sent them to the same suppliers, from the same addresses and under the same order numbers. Every supplier on that morning's run received each order twice.

Most of their systems rejected the repeats or someone noticed. Three did not. On Monday we received a second lorry of cement, a double delivery of roof battens and twice the copper fittings we had asked for. Returning them cost us collection charges and an awkward call to each supplier.

Nothing about the clone was faulty. A copy of a server includes its scheduled jobs, its credentials and its idea of who it is. We had taken great care that test systems never touch production data, and none that a copy of production never behaves as production.

Clones are now created switched off and started on an isolated network with no route out. The engineer disables every scheduled job and checks the list with a colleague before the clone is moved anywhere it can reach a supplier, a customer or a mail server. Every job that sends anything outside the company first asks a central setting whether the server it runs on is the named production server, and stops if it is not. We also asked our twenty largest suppliers to reject a purchase order number they have already received, and most of them now do.

Automation does not know it has been copied. Make sure the copy can tell.

– Serguey Shinder

title: We moved our cut-off service to a scratch image and it started working in UTC
description:
Our delivery promise service is a small Go program that answers one question for the website: if this order is placed now, which day will it arrive. The answer depends on the depot's cut-off, five o'clock UK time. In June we moved it from a Debian based image to FROM scratch with a statically linked binary. The image went from ninety megabytes to eleven, and every package our scanner had been complaining about disappeared.

The service loads Europe/London at start with time.LoadLocation. Go looks for the time zone database in the operating system's zoneinfo directories, among a few other places, and a scratch image has no operating system. LoadLocation returned an error. Years earlier someone had written the obvious defensive code around that call: log a warning and fall back to UTC so the service can still start. It started, the health check passed, and the warning went into a log nobody read.

In June the UK is on British Summer Time, an hour ahead of UTC. Five o'clock in UTC is six o'clock in London. For three weeks, every order placed between five and six in the evening was promised next day delivery from a depot that had already closed for the day. Roughly four hundred customers a week were told tomorrow and received their parcel the day after. Customer service found the pattern before we did, because every complaint came from the same hour.

The fix inside the binary was one line. Importing the time/tzdata package, available since Go 1.15, embeds the time zone database in the program for a few hundred kilobytes. We also removed the fallback. A service whose whole job is local cut-off times now refuses to start if it cannot load its zone, because a crash on deploy is found in minutes and a wrong answer took three weeks. The cut-off tests now run inside the built image, with a fixed clock set once to a summer date and once to a winter date.

A minimal image is minimal about everything, including the files your code assumed every machine would have.

– Sergey Shinder

title: Open-source tooling and process enable migrating a large codebase from Node to Go in two weeks
description:
The Two-Week Sprint: Anatomy of an Improbable Migration

When an organization attempts to transition a massive production codebase from Node.js to Go in a compressed 14-day window, standard engineering methodologies collapse under their own weight. Under the guidance of a former Go core team member, this high-stakes sprint bypassed exploratory evaluation phases, leveraging deep domain patterns established during core runtime design to force rapid structural convergence.

The core technical friction stems from the fundamental divergence between Node's single-threaded, asynchronous event-loop paradigm and Go's synchronous, statically typed execution model. In a literal, line-by-line translation—the primary trap that triggers cascading memory leaks and concurrency race conditions—developers attempt to map callback queues directly onto goroutines without redesigning the underlying concurrency boundaries. This creates silent memory fragmentation and unhandled channel blocking:

  • Dynamic to Static Boundary Shock: Shifting from runtime type coercion to strict compile-time checks forces explicit memory allocation layout definitions, exposing hidden data mutation flaws that previously manifested as intermittent undefined-property errors.
  • Event-Loop Starvation: Naive asynchronous-to-synchronous wrapping traps CPU cycles inside blocking I/O calls, inflating thread contention and spiking latency percentiles before core queues can flush.
  • Scope Explosion: Attempting feature parity and optimization simultaneously breaks the 14-day window through analysis paralysis, necessitating a strict rule: if a feature does not protect the core API contract, defer it entirely to post-migration iterations.

To eliminate these failure modes, the migration utilized specialized open-source tools—Gatekeeper and Harness—acting as structural force multipliers. Rather than trusting manual code refactoring, automated gateway validation and testing harnesses enforced absolute API contract parity between the legacy Node monolith and the emerging Go microservices. This decoupled routing validation logic from application code, ensuring zero downtime and complete backward compatibility for active production clients during the cutover window.

By viewing the legacy codebase as a disposable translation artifact rather than a permanent monolith, the engineering team compressed decision latency, pruned redundant dependency graphs, and replaced bloated third-party packages with Go's lean standard library. The result is a predictable, high-performance backend transition driven by rigorous constraint management and architectural discipline.

Deconstructing the Legacy Monolith: Audit and Dependency Mapping

Migrating a large-scale codebase from Node.js to Go in a compressed two-week window requires bypassing standard exploratory evaluation phases. An expert-led approach treats the legacy Node monolith not as a permanent structure, but as a disposable translation artifact. This shift in perspective compresses decision latency and eliminates the analysis paralysis that typically plagues multi-month rewrites.

The primary architectural hazard during the initial audit is falling into the trap of a literal, line-by-line code translation. Node.js operates on a single-threaded, asynchronous event-loop model utilizing dynamic type coercion and callback queues. Blindly translating these patterns into Go's synchronous, statically typed execution model causes severe internal failures:

  • Concurrency Race Conditions: Direct mapping of asynchronous callback queues to goroutines without redesigning concurrency boundaries strips away single-threaded execution safety, triggering cascading memory leaks and hidden data mutation flaws.
  • Event-Loop Starvation: Naive asynchronous-to-synchronous wrapping traps CPU cycles inside blocking I/O calls, inflating thread contention and spiking tail latency percentiles across the infrastructure.
  • Boundary Shock: Shifting from runtime flexibility to compile-time checks forces explicit memory allocation layout definitions, exposing structural flaws in how payloads are parsed and stored.

To neutralize these risks, the audit phase must strictly enforce an architectural redesign suited to Go's execution primitives rather than forcing syntactic compatibility. The decision framework relies on a binary choice during dependency and scope mapping:

  • Option A (Feature Parity First): Attempting to rewrite every legacy microservice feature and third-party utility simultaneously within the two-week time-box. This consistently triggers scope explosion, exhausting memory resources and stalling CI/CD pipelines under a mountain of unvetted boilerplate.
  • Option B (Contract-First Pruning - Optimal): Pruning redundant dependency graphs entirely, replacing bloated third-party packages with Go's lean standard library, and deferring non-core API contract features to post-migration iterations.

Decision Rule: If an API route does not belong to the immediate core request path during the two-week window, defer it. Decoupling routing validation logic from application code via specialized open-source gateways (such as Gatekeeper and Harness) acts as a structural force multiplier. By offloading contract parity enforcement to automated gateways, engineering teams achieve absolute backward compatibility and zero downtime for active production clients, preventing the catastrophic latency spikes that break production during cutovers.

Leveraging Open-Source Accelerators and Automated Tooling

When compressing a massive backend migration from months into an unforgiving two-week window, manual code translation becomes an immediate vector for catastrophic failure. If engineering teams attempt a literal, line-by-line semantic mapping from an asynchronous Node.js event-loop model to Go's statically typed, synchronous execution runtime, the cognitive friction triggers severe analysis paralysis. Mechanically, mapping Node callback queues directly to goroutines without redesigning concurrency boundaries strips away single-threaded safety, driving memory leaks and concurrency race conditions where unmanaged data mutation corrupts state across threads.

To bypass this manual bottleneck, our architecture relied entirely on specialized open-source accelerators—specifically Gatekeeper and Harness—which function as structural force multipliers. Instead of letting application code handle raw protocol translation, these tools decouple API contract validation and route dispatching from the service core.

Evaluating our strategic options reveals a clear architectural divergence:
Approach Operational Mechanism & Failure Mode Verdict
Manual Line-by-Line Translation Direct translation of asynchronous callback queues to goroutines causes boundary shock. Shifting from runtime type coercion to compile-time checks forces explicit memory layout definitions, exposing hidden data mutation flaws and inflating thread contention via blocking I/O wrappers. Rejected: High defect rates and scope explosion cause systemic failure under compressed timelines.
Automated Gateway Decoupling (Gatekeeper & Harness) Externalizes routing validation and protocol translation. Gatekeeper enforces contract parity at the network boundary, while Harness automates regression testing and schema mapping, treating the legacy monolith as a disposable transient artifact. Optimal: Eliminates translation bottlenecks, guarantees zero downtime, and enforces absolute backward compatibility.

Decision Rule: If a legacy system exhibits deep event-loop entanglement and dynamic-to-static type boundary shocks, then prohibit manual code translation and enforce automated gateway decoupling via Gatekeeper and Harness to protect core execution threads from traffic spikes.

This automated gateway strategy has precise operational boundaries: it breaks down if the legacy API payloads lack rigorous structural schemas, as automated parsers cannot reliably map dynamic JSON objects to static Go structs without manual intervention. Nevertheless, by intercepting and mirroring traffic externally, the tools allowed us to prune redundant dependency graphs, strip software bloat, and lean entirely on Go's standard library while maintaining total operational continuity.

Execution, Safety Nets, and Continuous Testing Under Pressure

Migrating a massive production codebase in a compressed fourteen-day window leaves zero room for exploratory code rewrites. When engineering teams attempt a manual, line-by-line translation from an asynchronous Node.js event-loop model to Go's statically typed, synchronous runtime, the execution invariably shatters under concurrency pressure. Directly mapping Node callback queues to unmanaged goroutines strips away single-threaded execution safety, immediately triggering cascading memory leaks and severe race conditions as raw pointers collide across shared memory spaces.

To survive this transition without triggering production outages, execution must be governed by a strict optimization strategy: treating the legacy monolith as a disposable translation artifact rather than a permanent blueprint. Attempting full feature parity rewrites simultaneously induces immediate analysis paralysis and CI/CD pipeline stalls. Instead, engineering teams face a stark architectural choice during sprint execution:

  • Option A (Feature Parity First): Rewriting all business logic and API endpoints concurrently. This introduces high cognitive load, exhausts system resources, and inevitably traps CPU cycles inside blocking I/O calls, spiking tail latency percentiles.
  • Option B (Contract-First Pruning - Optimal): Deferring all non-core API contracts to post-migration iterations, pruning redundant third-party package graphs, and leaning exclusively on Go's lean standard library to eliminate software bloat and compile-time friction.

Decision Rule: If a legacy system exhibits deep event-loop entanglement and dynamic-to-static type boundary shocks, engineers must prohibit manual code translation and enforce automated gateway decoupling. Specialized open-source tools like Gatekeeper and Harness act as critical structural force multipliers. Gatekeeper enforces absolute API contract parity and route dispatching at the network boundary, while Harness automates regression testing and schema mapping against live traffic feeds.

However, this automated safety net possesses a hard operational boundary. The gateway strategy breaks down entirely if legacy API payloads lack rigorous structural schemas. Without strict typing at the edge, parsers cannot reliably map dynamic JSON objects to rigid Go structs, forcing manual intervention and bleeding precious hours from the two-week time-box. By decoupling routing validation from the core application logic via automated gateways, teams protect core execution threads from traffic spikes, maintaining absolute backward compatibility and achieving zero downtime during the cutover window.

Long-Term Performance Gains and Infrastructure ROI

When an engineering organization compresses a multi-month rewrite into a rigorous two-week sprint, the immediate performance aftermath exposes the deep mechanical divergence between Node.js and Go execution models. In a legacy Node environment, the single-threaded event loop relies on dynamic runtime type coercion and heap allocations for asynchronous callback queues. Under heavy throughput, this architecture creates garbage collection pressure and CPU cycle fragmentation as promises chain and block. Transitioning to Go replaces this dynamic paradigm with statically typed, compiled machine code running on an M:N scheduler utilizing lightweight goroutines and explicit memory layout definitions.

The causal chain of this architectural shift directly impacts latency percentiles. Because Go enforces compile-time memory allocations and eliminates V8 runtime overhead, tail latency spikes (p99) collapse. Execution threads no longer contend for event-loop time slots; instead, synchronous execution flows process requests with predictable CPU cache utilization. Organizations capturing this ROI bypass incremental optimization loops entirely, instantly shrinking their infrastructure footprint by eliminating the bloated third-party package graphs that typically plague asynchronous monoliths.

Resource Compression and Dependency Pruning

Infrastructure cost reductions in the wake of a rapid migration stem directly from aggressive dependency minimization. Standard enterprise Node applications accumulate massive codebases filled with redundant helper libraries that mask the lack of a robust standard library. During a compressed two-week window, teams face a strict decision rule: If a dependency is not strictly required for core API contract routing, it must be pruned. This forces a shift from Feature Parity First—which historically stalls pipelines through scope explosion—to Contract-First Pruning.

By stripping software bloat and relying on Go's lean standard library, the compiled binary becomes a fraction of the original container size. The mechanical effect on cloud infrastructure is immediate: memory footprints drop precipitously, allowing organizations to run identical workloads on a fraction of the compute instances. However, this optimization carries a strict operational boundary. If legacy API payloads lack rigorous structural schemas, automated parsers fail to map dynamic JSON objects to rigid Go structs, forcing fallback mechanisms that can temporarily inflate memory overhead during payload normalization.

Cultural Shifts and Cognitive Load Reduction

The cultural impact of an expert-led, two-week migration alters how engineering teams approach legacy debt. Traditional enterprise rewrites suffer from analysis paralysis because teams treat the old codebase as a sacred artifact that requires line-by-line archaeological auditing. By redefining the legacy monolith as a disposable translation artifact, cognitive load is compressed. Engineers stop trying to preserve historical idioms and instead focus strictly on network-boundary interface contracts.

This mindset shift eliminates decision fatigue. Shifting from runtime type coercion to compile-time checks exposes hidden data mutation flaws instantly during compilation rather than silently in production. The institutional velocity achieved through strict time-boxing acts as a cognitive filter: it strips away non-essential features, forces disciplined scope management, and anchors engineering output to absolute contract parity enforced by automated tooling rather than manual guesswork.

Industry-Wide Implications for Enterprise Architecture

What does a two-week transition from Node to Go mean for modern enterprise architecture? It shatters the myth that large-scale infrastructure migrations require multi-quarter roadmap allocations and risky, phased big-bang cutovers. The repeatable blueprint relies on automated gateway decoupling using specialized open-source tools like Gatekeeper and Harness to externalize routing validation and protocol translation away from the core application code.

The architectural rule emerging from these case studies is definitive: For systems exhibiting deep event-loop entanglement and dynamic-to-static type boundary shocks, manual code translation must be strictly prohibited in favor of automated network-boundary decoupling. Gatekeeper enforces absolute backward compatibility and zero downtime at the network edge, while Harness automates regression testing against live traffic feeds. Organizations adopting this decoupled, tool-driven methodology bypass the historical risks of technical debt, transforming legacy remediation from a multi-year engineering crisis into a rapid, highly predictable operational upgrade.

title: We Stopped a Cloud Server to Resize It and Nine Months of Supplier Messages on Its D Drive Were Gone
description:
Our larger suppliers send us order confirmations, delivery notices and invoices electronically, and we send them our purchase orders the same way. A translation package on a Windows server turns their formats into ours. In 2023 we moved that server from our own building into Azure, and the supplier of the package reinstalled it there.

On the old server, drive D was a data disk. On the new one, the package's engineer found a drive D with plenty of free space and pointed the outgoing queue and the message archive at it.

In Azure, drive D on most virtual machines is not a data disk. It is temporary storage on the physical host, meant for things like the page file. Its contents can disappear whenever the machine is moved to another host, including when it is stopped and deallocated. It even contains a file called DATALOSS_WARNING_README.txt. Nobody had opened it.

In August we stopped the server one Sunday to give it more memory for month end. When it started again, drive D held that readme and nothing else. Two hundred and sixty purchase orders waiting to be sent had gone, and so had nine months of archived messages.

The orders were easy, because our trading system could export them again, and they went out by Monday lunchtime. The archive was not. Our backup of the server had run every night and had never included drive D, because Azure's virtual machine backup does not protect temporary storage. Two weeks later a timber supplier disputed a price we had confirmed electronically in June, and we could not produce the message.

The package now writes only to a managed data disk, which is backed up with the rest of the server, and our build checklist for every cloud server includes listing which folders live on temporary storage. We found two more servers using drive D for something that mattered: a print spool and a folder of scanned delivery notes. Both have moved.

A migration copies the habits of the old building into the new one. Find out what each disk letter means on the platform you have moved to, before something important is written to it.

– Serguey Shinder

title: You Changed the Prompt and Your Score Went Up Four Points on Fifty Questions
description:
You had an evaluation set.

Fifty questions,
each with a correct answer.

The old prompt
scored seventy eight percent.

You rewrote the instructions
and the new one
scored eighty two.

Four points better.

You wrote it up,
shipped it,
and moved on.

Look at what four points means
on fifty questions.

Each question is worth two points.

Four points is two questions.

Two questions
out of fifty
went the other way.

That is not a result.

That is a coin
landing differently twice.

Here is the arithmetic.

At around eighty percent,
the standard error
on fifty questions
is close to six points.

A rough ninety five percent range
is plus or minus eleven.

Your true score
could be anywhere
from about seventy
to about ninety.

Both prompts
fit easily inside that.

And the model
is not perfectly repeatable either.

Run the old prompt again
and it may move
a question or two by itself.

Same prompt.

Same questions.

A different afternoon.

So do not compare totals.

Compare question by question.

How many did the new prompt fix?

How many did it break?

Fixed seven
and broke five
is not the same change
as fixed two
and broke none,
even though both
add up to plus two.

Read the five it broke.

They are often
the important ones.

Then make the set bigger.

To see a few points of difference
with any confidence,
you need hundreds of questions,
not dozens.

Run each version
more than once,
and look at how much
a version disagrees with itself
before you trust
how much it disagrees with another.

Keep a note of the noise.

If two runs of the same prompt
differ by three points,
a three point improvement
means nothing.

A score is a measurement.

Every measurement
comes with an error bar,
whether you draw it or not.

If you never draw it,
you will spend months
chasing changes
that were never there.

– Serguey Asael Shinder

title: Form error messages that actually help: tie them to the field, say what to do, and don't rely on red
description:
Most form errors I see on store sites are a red border and a word in small red text that appears somewhere near the field. Sighted mouse users usually figure it out. Everyone else gets a form that just refuses to submit and doesn't say why.

Good error handling isn't complicated. It's mostly HTML that's been around for years, plus a couple of decisions about timing. Here's the checklist I use when I review a form, whether it's a checkout, a contact form, or the "pick a size" step on a product page.

Tie the message to the field

The error text has to be connected to its input, not just placed near it visually.

<label for="phone">Phone number</label>
<input
  id="phone"
  name="phone"
  type="tel"
  autocomplete="tel"
  aria-invalid="true"
  aria-describedby="phone-hint phone-error"
>
<p id="phone-hint">We'll only call if there's a problem with delivery.</p>
<p id="phone-error" class="field-error">Enter a phone number with at least 9 digits.</p>
  • aria-describedby makes the screen reader read the error when the field gets focus. You can list several ids, so the hint and the error can both be attached.
  • aria-invalid="true" goes on only when the field actually has an error. Don't ship it as "false" hard-coded in a template and forget to flip it, and don't set it to "true" before the user has typed anything.
  • Keep the error element in the DOM and empty it, or add and remove it together with the aria-describedby reference. A reference to an id that doesn't exist is harmless but messy; an error that exists but isn't referenced is invisible to assistive tech.

Say what to do, not what went wrong

"Invalid input" is the classic. Compare:

  • "Invalid phone" → "Enter a phone number with at least 9 digits."
  • "Required" → "Choose a size before adding to cart."
  • "Invalid date" → "Enter the date as DD/MM/YYYY."

The second version is a little longer and a lot more useful. If there's a format, show it in the hint before the error happens, not only after.

Don't rely on red

A red border is fine as an extra signal. On its own it fails for people who don't see red well, and it fails in forced-colors / high-contrast mode, where your border color may be replaced entirely. Add an icon or the word "Error:" in the message, and make sure the text itself has enough contrast against the background. Pale red on white often doesn't.

When to validate

This is where most of the debate happens. What I've ended up with:

  • On submit: always. This is the one moment the user clearly asked "is this okay?"
  • On blur (leaving the field): fine for fields with a clear format, like email or phone, but only after the user has typed something. Tabbing through an empty form shouldn't light it up in red.
  • While typing: only to clear an error once it's fixed. Showing "too short" after the first character is just noise.

On submit, give a summary and move focus

If the form has more than two or three fields, a summary at the top saves people from hunting.

<div id="error-summary" tabindex="-1" role="alert">
  <h2>There are 2 problems with your details</h2>
  <ul>
    <li><a href="#phone">Enter a phone number with at least 9 digits</a></li>
    <li><a href="#city">Enter your city</a></li>
  </ul>
</div>

form.addEventListener('submit', (e) => {
  const errors = validate(form);
  if (errors.length === 0) return;

  e.preventDefault();
  renderSummary(errors);   // fills the list above
  markFields(errors);      // sets aria-invalid + message per field
  document.getElementById('error-summary').focus();
});

Each link jumps straight to the field. For a short form, skip the summary and move focus to the first invalid field instead. Either way, don't leave focus on the submit button with nothing announced.

Native validation: use it, or turn it off on purpose

The browser's built-in required / type="email" bubbles are better than nothing, but they look different in every browser, disappear after a few seconds, and can't be styled. If you build your own messages, add novalidate to the <form> so you don't get both at once. Keep required and the input types anyway; they still help with keyboards on mobile and with autofill.

Don't wipe the form

If submit fails on the server (stock changed, session expired, payment declined), keep what the person typed. Re-rendering an empty checkout after an error is the fastest way to lose someone. Password and card fields are the reasonable exceptions.

The non-form forms

Product pages have hidden forms too. The size or color picker on clothing is the common one. On things like work shirts, where you must pick a size before adding to cart, the same rules apply: the size group needs a label (a <fieldset> with a <legend> works well), and "Add to cart" without a size should produce a real message tied to that group and move focus to it, not just shake the button.

Five-minute test

  1. Submit the form empty with a screen reader on. Do you hear what's wrong and where?
  2. Fix one field. Does its error clear?
  3. Tab through without typing anything. Does anything turn red? (It shouldn't.)
  4. Turn on forced colors (Windows high contrast or the DevTools emulation). Can you still see which field is wrong?
  5. Trigger a server-side error. Is your input still there?

None of this needs a form library, although a good one will handle most of it for you. What's the error message pattern you've seen that annoyed you most? Mine is the password field that only tells you the rules after you've broken three of them.

title: Our order service built against a library snapshot someone had deployed from a feature branch
description:
Our pricing rules live in a shared Java library that four services depend on. Between releases its main branch publishes 2.3.0-SNAPSHOT to our Nexus repository, and the services' main branches depend on that snapshot so they pick up rule changes without waiting for a release. That arrangement had worked for three years.

In October an engineer working on a branch that changed how pallet surcharges round ran mvn deploy from his laptop, to try the change in a test environment. It published as 2.3.0-SNAPSHOT, because that is what the branch's pom said. Nexus accepted it, as it accepts every snapshot deploy from anyone with write access.

A snapshot version is not a build. It is a name for whichever timestamped build was deployed last. Maven resolves it by reading the version's maven-metadata.xml in the remote repository and taking the newest entry, and nothing in that file records which branch a build came from. The next morning the order service's main build resolved the branch build, passed its tests, because none of them covered surcharge rounding, and went to staging.

It was not even consistent. Maven's default update policy checks the remote for a newer snapshot once a day, and two of our six build agents still had the previous day's copy in their local repository. Services built on those agents that morning got the main branch code. The same commit of the same service behaved differently depending on which agent picked it up.

A tester noticed staging quotes a few pence away from production for a third of pallet orders. It took most of a day to trace, because every pom we opened said the same version.

Snapshots now publish only from the library's main branch, by the CI user. Developers lost deploy rights to the snapshot repository and test their branches with a version that carries the branch name. Builds run with -U, so every agent asks the repository rather than trusting a day old cache, and every service release runs the enforcer plugin's requireReleaseDeps rule, so nothing reaches production depending on a snapshot at all.

A version that anyone can overwrite tells you the name of the code, not which code it is.

– Sergey Shinder

title: Google TPUs Are Coming to Oracle Cloud. Does That Change the AI Lock-In Problem?
description:
Google’s partnership with Oracle could let enterprises use TPUs without moving to Google Cloud. But does having the same AI accelerator available on different clouds make applications easier to move between them?

Imagine a company that runs its business applications and databases on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI).

The company is building an AI assistant to help employees find information, answer business questions and complete routine tasks. Its existing AI workloads run on NVIDIA GPUs, but the technology team wants to evaluate other accelerators, including Google’s Tensor Processing Units (TPUs).

Until now, accessing Google’s cloud-based TPU services has generally meant using Google Cloud. For a company already committed to OCI, that could mean introducing another cloud environment simply to use a different type of AI processor.

The team would need to consider connectivity, data access, monitoring, security and operating costs across both environments.

What if the company could use Google TPUs directly within OCI instead?

On October 27, 2026, Oracle and Google announced plans to bring TPUs to Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, beginning in calendar year 2027.

That could give organizations another way to choose AI hardware without necessarily changing their primary cloud provider.

But it also raises a question that is more important than the announcement itself.

If the same AI accelerator becomes available through different cloud providers, does that reduce cloud lock-in, or simply change where the dependencies exist?

Why the Oracle agreement matters beyond another hardware option

In our earlier TechiesJournal article, Can Google TPUs Reduce AI’s Dependence on NVIDIA?, we examined how alternative accelerators and improving software support could reduce reliance on NVIDIA’s ecosystem.

That is one part of the infrastructure problem.

An organization may want access to different processors so it can compare performance, availability and operating costs. But choosing a different accelerator can also introduce dependencies on its software tools and supported cloud environments.

The Oracle agreement adds another dimension.

Google developed TPUs for machine-learning workloads and has offered cloud access to them through Google Cloud. The planned OCI deployment would make Oracle the first hyperscale cloud provider outside Google to offer these processors.

That changes the potential relationship between the company supplying the accelerator and the company operating the surrounding cloud infrastructure.

Google can extend the reach of its TPU systems beyond Google Cloud, while Oracle can add another accelerator architecture to its existing infrastructure portfolio.

For enterprise customers, the immediate significance is choice.

A company that already depends on OCI may eventually be able to evaluate Google’s specialized AI processors without establishing an entirely separate Google Cloud deployment solely for TPU compute.

However, the announcement establishes a future offering, not a finished customer deployment model.

Oracle and Google say TPU capacity will begin appearing in OCI in calendar year 2027, with expansion planned over multiple years. Oracle has also described an ambition to reach gigawatt-scale TPU deployment over that period.

As of November 16, 2026, the companies have not established publicly verifiable customer pricing, initial regions, provisioning details or complete service-level commitments for the planned offering.

Oracle’s own announcement includes a forward-looking statement warning that plans and expectations may change.

For architects, this distinction matters: an announced capability can influence a technology roadmap, but it cannot yet replace an available production service.

How Google TPUs would fit into Oracle’s infrastructure

The partnership is technically interesting because it brings together different parts of an AI computing system.

An accelerator does not work in isolation. It needs high-speed communication, data access, networking, cooling, power and software capable of coordinating computation across processors.

Google’s TPU systems include specialized technologies for communication between accelerators.

The Inter-Chip Interconnect (ICI) enables communication among TPU chips, while Optical Circuit Switching (OCS) helps manage communication paths in large TPU systems.

This becomes particularly important during the training of large AI models. Thousands of processors may need to exchange information repeatedly, and slow communication can leave expensive computing resources waiting for data.

Google’s technical explanation of the partnership describes how ICI and OCS form part of its system-level approach to accelerator communication and resilience.

Oracle provides the surrounding cloud infrastructure.

OCI will supply data-center power, cooling and networking, with Oracle Acceleron providing the network foundation that connects TPU capacity to other OCI resources.

Google specifically describes Acceleron’s SmartNIC-based isolation, High Performance Fabric and Zero Trust Packet Routing as technologies intended to support those connections.

These responsibilities operate at different levels.

Google’s TPU communication technologies connect and coordinate the accelerators within the TPU system. Oracle’s infrastructure connects that computing capacity to the wider cloud environment, including storage, databases and applications.

The result is not simply a Google processor installed in an ordinary server.

It is a planned integration of Google’s specialized AI computing systems with Oracle’s data-center and cloud networking infrastructure.

Even so, the companies have not published every detail an enterprise architect would need to deploy and operate the service.

The exact customer provisioning model, management interfaces, monitoring integrations and operational limitations will need to be evaluated when Oracle makes the offering available.

Following an enterprise AI request through the proposed architecture

Consider the fictional enterprise introduced earlier.

Its employees use an internal AI assistant to retrieve approved information from business databases.

The assistant must respond quickly, respect access permissions and avoid exposing confidential information.

Suppose the company eventually runs its AI inference workloads on Google TPUs hosted in OCI.

A request could follow this illustrative path.

First, the employee submits a question.

An application running on OCI receives the request, authenticates the employee and determines which business information the employee is permitted to access.

Next, the application retrieves relevant information.

The application queries the appropriate Oracle database or retrieval service using established access controls.

Only information that the employee is authorized to access should be made available to the AI workload.

The AI model then processes the request.

The application sends the relevant input to a model running on TPU compute. The TPU performs the numerical calculations required to generate the model’s response.

For a large model distributed across multiple TPU chips, Google’s TPU interconnect technologies may be involved in coordinating computation inside the accelerator system.

Oracle’s networking infrastructure provides connectivity between TPU capacity and the surrounding OCI services.

Finally, the application returns the answer.

The application processes the model output, applies any required validation or business rules, and returns a response to the employee.

This is an illustrative application architecture, not a published Oracle deployment specification. The exact networking, security and inference-service interfaces for OCI TPUs have not yet been confirmed.

The example nevertheless shows why the partnership could matter.

The business application, enterprise database and AI compute could potentially operate within the same cloud environment, rather than requiring a separate Google Cloud deployment to access TPU hardware.

That may simplify certain network designs and reduce some cross-cloud transfers.

But those benefits will depend on the actual deployment.

If the application and TPU capacity are in different regions, or if relevant data still resides outside OCI, network delays and transfer costs may remain significant.

Similarly, hosting components within one cloud does not automatically establish secure access. Identity, permissions, data isolation, logging and operational controls must still be designed and verified.

A useful architecture is not determined merely by where the accelerator is installed. It is determined by how the entire workload behaves.

Does having TPUs on two clouds make AI workloads portable?

This is where the distinction between more infrastructure choice and genuine portability becomes important.

An application can depend on three different layers of technology.

Dependency What it means What the OCI agreement changes
Accelerator hardware The processor architecture used to execute AI workloads TPUs are planned to become available through another hyperscaler
AI software Frameworks, compilers, libraries and model execution tools Existing TPU software support may help, but compatibility must still be verified
Cloud services Networking, identity, storage, deployment, monitoring and operations OCI becomes another hosting option, but its surrounding services remain distinct

These dependencies are related, but they are not interchangeable.

Consider the company’s AI assistant.

Its model may be developed using PyTorch, a widely used machine-learning framework. Google’s TorchTPU project aims to support TPU execution through familiar PyTorch workflows.

Google announced that TorchTPU is available as open-source software and describes an ecosystem that includes tools such as vLLM, SGLang and Ray.

The objective is to make TPU adoption easier for developers using established AI software.

That is meaningful progress.

However, three different claims must not be confused.

Model-code compatibility means developers can use familiar programming interfaces and potentially reuse substantial parts of their model code.

Performance portability means a workload continues to perform competitively when moved to different hardware. This may require tuning, alternative kernels, different memory-management approaches or changes to model execution.

Cloud deployment portability means the complete application can move between cloud environments while preserving its necessary security, networking, storage, monitoring and operational behavior.

TorchTPU can improve the first of these. Google presents broader portability as an intended benefit of its software ecosystem.

But neither open-source framework support nor the Oracle agreement proves that all three are achieved automatically.

For example, even if the enterprise runs the same model code on TPUs in Google Cloud and OCI, its surrounding application may still depend on OCI networking, Oracle databases, provider-specific access controls and deployment automation.

Moving the model is only one part of moving the application.

Therefore, the Oracle partnership can reduce one form of restriction, the need to use Google Cloud for access to cloud-hosted Google TPU capacity, without eliminating software or operational dependencies.

That is a useful improvement, but it is not the same as making AI infrastructure cloud-independent.

Why reduced lock-in is not always the right objective

Before deciding whether the agreement solves a dependency problem, enterprises should ask whether that dependency was creating a meaningful business problem in the first place.

Cloud portability has costs.

An organization might deliberately build applications around technology supported by several providers. That can make future migration easier, but it may also require additional engineering, testing and operational expertise.

Another organization may prefer services closely integrated with one cloud because they are easier to manage or better suited to its workloads.

Neither approach is automatically superior.

For the fictional OCI enterprise, adding a separate cloud platform solely to access another accelerator could increase operational complexity.

If TPUs become available within OCI, the organization may gain another hardware choice while retaining its existing cloud operating model.

It would still depend on Oracle for important infrastructure services and on Google’s TPU technology for accelerator execution.

That may be a reasonable trade-off.

For an organization with strict multicloud resilience requirements or a need to relocate workloads between providers, the same arrangement may not offer enough independence.

The goal is not to eliminate every specialized technology.

It is to understand whether the benefits justify the resulting dependencies and whether the organization can change direction when necessary.

Why Google and Oracle would pursue this arrangement

The technical partnership also reflects the commercial interests of both companies.

For Google, extending TPU availability beyond its own cloud could increase adoption of its accelerator architecture.

Organizations already committed to OCI may be more willing to evaluate TPUs if they can use them alongside their existing applications and data.

A broader installed base could also encourage software developers, framework maintainers and AI platform providers to improve TPU support.

These are plausible strategic benefits, not independently established business outcomes from the Oracle deployment.

For Oracle, the advantage is a broader range of compute options.

OCI already supports several computing architectures. Oracle’s October 2026 infrastructure strategy describes plans involving NVIDIA, AMD, Intel and additional specialized AI hardware.

Adding TPUs would allow Oracle to offer another option for training and inference workloads.

Different workloads may benefit from different accelerator architectures. A large training run, a low-latency chatbot and a batch inference process do not necessarily have the same priorities.

Providing multiple options could help customers select infrastructure based on their requirements rather than forcing every workload onto a single architecture.

However, the partnership does not establish that Google TPUs on OCI will be cheaper, faster or more reliable than competing alternatives.

Nor does it demonstrate that customers will reduce their NVIDIA spending.

To make those claims, enterprises would need comparable workloads running on available infrastructure, with measured performance and complete costs.

The business opportunity is credible. Its magnitude remains unproven.

What should an architect evaluate before making a decision?

Return to our enterprise AI assistant.

The organization wants reliable answers, acceptable response times, strong data protection and predictable operating costs.

Its decision should start with those requirements, not with the availability of a new processor.

When OCI TPUs become available, a useful evaluation would compare the complete application against its existing deployment.

Evaluation Question to answer
Model compatibility Does the model run correctly with its required software libraries and execution tools?
Performance Does it meet response-time and throughput targets under realistic demand?
Data access Can the workload access enterprise data securely without unnecessary transfers?
Operational support Can the organization deploy, monitor, scale and recover the service reliably?
Capacity Are suitable TPU configurations available in the required region and quantity?
Economics Is the total cost better than the existing practical alternative?
Future flexibility Which components would need to change if the organization later chose a different accelerator or cloud?

The comparison needs to include more than accelerator rental charges.

A deployment with lower compute pricing may still cost more when engineering effort, network charges, storage, operational support or application changes are included.

Similarly, an accelerator that produces faster results under one test may not deliver better economics under actual production demand.

A useful evaluation should therefore use the organization’s own workload and a credible alternative it could actually deploy.

Until Oracle publishes service details and customers can measure the resulting platform, several of these questions remain unanswered.

What should organizations do now, and what should wait?

The partnership does not require an immediate infrastructure change.

Organizations already running AI workloads successfully should continue improving and benchmarking their existing systems. They should not delay necessary deployments solely because another option is planned for 2027.

Companies evaluating TPU technology today can use currently available platforms to understand model compatibility, software requirements and the effort needed to operate their workloads.

For enterprises committed to OCI, the planned TPU service is worth including in future infrastructure evaluations, especially where AI workloads depend heavily on data already held in Oracle systems.

But organizations should wait for actual OCI service availability before assuming particular performance, prices, regions or operational capabilities.

A practical distinction is:

Decide now: Which workloads might benefit from alternative accelerators? What performance and cost measures matter? Which application dependencies would make a future change difficult?

Evaluate when available: OCI TPU pricing, supported hardware, software compatibility, regional capacity, network architecture, operational tooling and measured production performance.

Do not assume: That using TPUs on OCI automatically reduces total costs, eliminates cloud lock-in or makes existing Google Cloud TPU workloads portable without modification.

This approach keeps the organization prepared without committing to capabilities that have not yet been delivered.

More choice does not mean complete independence

Google’s decision to bring TPUs to Oracle Cloud is significant because it begins separating access to Google’s specialized AI hardware from the requirement to use Google’s own cloud infrastructure.

For enterprises already using OCI, that could remove an important obstacle to evaluating TPU-based workloads.

It may also create more competition among accelerator options within the same cloud environment.

But the infrastructure surrounding an AI processor remains important. Models still depend on software. Applications still depend on data, networking, identity and operational services. Businesses still need evidence that a different deployment delivers measurable value.

The Oracle partnership changes where Google TPUs may become available. It does not yet demonstrate that AI workloads can move freely between clouds.

For technology leaders, the useful question is not how to eliminate every dependency. It is which dependencies are worth accepting, which limit future choices, and what evidence would justify changing them.

That is the decision this partnership makes more interesting.

Go deeper

  1. Oracle: Oracle Brings Google TPUs to Oracle Cloud Infrastructure: October 27, 2026. The official announcement covering the planned OCI offering, timing, infrastructure responsibilities and intended AI workloads.
  2. Google Cloud: Bringing Google TPUs to Oracle Cloud Infrastructure: October 27, 2026. A technical explanation of TPU communication, the planned role of Oracle Acceleron, software ecosystem support and potential deployment benefits.
  3. Oracle: Building the Next Decade of Oracle Cloud Infrastructure: October 27, 2026. Oracle’s wider infrastructure strategy, its plans to support multiple specialized computing architectures and its plan to ramp TPU capacity to gigawatt scale over multiple years.
  4. TechiesJournal: Can Google TPUs Reduce AI’s Dependence on NVIDIA?: November 14, 2026. Related reading on AI accelerator competition, software dependencies and the practical considerations involved in choosing alternatives to NVIDIA.

Source review: November 16, 2026. The OCI TPU offering remains a future commitment. Product specifications, timing, availability and commercial terms should be rechecked against official documentation before any deployment decision.
