title: Oracle SQL Developer 26.2 Startup Failure on Windows: Fixing Netigso Errors and Recovering Database Connections
description:
Oracle SQL Developer 26.2 Fails To Start On Windows – Fixing Netigso Errors & Recovering Connections

A practical example of troubleshooting an Oracle SQL Developer error when launching the application. This includes checking the ZIP archive, Java libraries, user profile and moving connections.

Windows x64 Environment

Oracle SQL Developer 26.2.0.186.2220

Previous version SQL Developer 24.3

Date: 15th November 2026

Topic: Oracle Database tools & Windows Troubleshooting.

Introduction

Oracle SQL Developer is a tool used by DBAs and Developers to interact with Oracle databases. This allows SQL to be run, database objects managed and general administration tasks performed.

Although upgrading to a newer version of SQL Developer should be a simple task, sometimes the application can have issues launching.

Example

When attempting to install Oracle SQL Developer 26.2 on a Windows workstation.

Upon trying to launch the application there were errors relating to multiple software modules failing to be loaded.

The application raised an initial warning:


Warning - could not install some modules

There were also additional messages relating to Netigso and missing software bundles.

At first this appeared to indicate that there was an issue with the archive not being fully downloaded, or the application missing some files.

Further investigation showed that the downloaded archive had the correct checksum when compared to Oracle. The chosen Java libraries were also present.

The issue was resolved by backing up and refreshing the SQL Developer user profile.

This article covers how the issue was investigated, the commands used, the results and how DBAs should be cautious when dealing with similar errors.

  1. Understanding The Issue

The version of Oracle SQL Developer we had was:


26.2.0.186.2220

Installed on Windows using the ZIP archive.

ZIP Archive:


sqldeveloper-26.2.0.186.2220-x64.zip

Extracted application folder:


C:\oracle\SQLDeveloper26.2\sqldeveloper

Upon attempting to launch the application there were errors relating to several modules not being initialised.

Errors:


Warning - could not install some modules

org.netbeans.InvalidException: Netigso

Not found bundle: oracle.jewt_core

Not found bundle: oracle.external.jdbc

Not found bundle: oracle.ide.editor

Not found bundle: oracle.javatools_jdk

What Is Netigso?

Netigso is used by NetBeans to allow modules to be integrated into the application.

Oracle SQL Developer uses multiple modules.

If some modules are not loaded or initialised correctly then SQL Developer will raise warnings and fail to launch.

It is important to note that just because there is an error related to a missing bundle does not mean that the file is not present.

The module may be present however there may be another issue preventing it from loading.

It may not be best practice to replace the files.

  1. Checking The ZIP Archive

The first thing to do was check that the SQL Developer ZIP file had been downloaded correctly.

The issue with modules failing to load could be due to the archive being corrupt.

Oracle will provide checksums for their downloadable archives.

A checksum is used to help confirm that the file you have downloaded is the correct one.

Step 1 – Launch PowerShell

Open PowerShell on your Windows workstation.

Navigate to the folder containing the Oracle SQL Developer archive file, or enter the full path.

Step 2 – Get File Checksum

Run:


$zip = "C:\oracle\sqldeveloper-26.2.0.186.2220-x64.zip"

Get-FileHash -Path $zip -Algorithm SHA1

The SHA1 value for this example was:


6A1BCA6CD756B821C11E92B821DB73A6AEB67D02

Which matched the value provided on Oracle’s download page for the x64 Windows version.

What Does This Mean?

This confirms that the ZIP file was the same as the one provided by Oracle.

This makes it less likely that the issue was to do with the download being incomplete or modified.

Lesson learnt

Always check the software package has the correct checksum provided by the vendor. This will help to avoid having to reinstall, or download multiple times.

  1. Checking Application Libraries

Now we know that the ZIP has the correct checksum we can now check that some of the important .jar files are present.

.java Archive Files normally use the .jar extension.

There are many .jar files within SQL Developer.

Multiple errors were raised relating to modules and Java libraries.

Step 1 – Find Installation Folder

The application had been extracted to:


C:\oracle\SQLDeveloper26.2\sqldeveloper

Step 2 – Check 5 JAR Files

The below PowerShell script will check that 5 JAR files are present.


$base = "C:\oracle\SQLDeveloper26.2\sqldeveloper"

@(

"external\oracle.jewt-core.jar",

"external\oracle.external.jdbc.jar",

"external\oracle.external.woodstox.jar",

"ide\lib\annotations.jar",

"jdev\lib\jdkver.jar"

) | ForEach-Object {

[PSCustomObject]@{

File   = $_

Exists = Test-Path (Join-Path $base $_)

}

}

Results

Java Library | Present

--- | ---

oracle.jewt-core.jar | True

oracle.external.jdbc.jar | True

oracle.external.woodstox.jar | True

annotations.jar | True

jdkver.jar | True

All 5 JAR files were present.

What Does This Prove?

That all 5 JAR files are present.

Although it does not prove that they are all correct, or that the modules can all be loaded, when combined with the ZIP having the correct checksum it shows that there may be an issue with something else.

We do not need to copy random JAR files from another SQL Developer installation.

  1. Understanding SQL Developer User Settings On Windows

Oracle SQL Developer stores some user settings in a separate folder.

This may be your application settings, connections, UI settings etc.

The user settings on Windows are usually located in:


%APPDATA%\SQL Developer\

For the SQL Developer 26.2 version this was:


%APPDATA%\SQL Developer\system26.2.0.186.2220

This is important as even though the application files may be correct, the user settings may have an impact on the application launching.

The next controlled action we can take is to refresh the user profile for this version.

Why Backup?

The user settings folder may contain important settings.

Removing this folder straight away may make it difficult to get back to your previous settings.

It is better to rename the folder.

This will make it easier to revert.

  1. Fixing The Issue By Refreshing User Profile

Ensure SQL Developer is closed.

IMPORTANT! These commands will affect your chosen version user profile. Ensure you backup any settings or connections you need.

Step 1 – Close SQL Developer

Ensure that SQL Developer 26.2 is closed.

If you need to, ensure that no processes are running for the application before renaming the configuration folder.

Step 2 – Find User Profile Folder

Open PowerShell and run:


$profile = Join-Path $env:APPDATA `

"SQL Developer\system26.2.0.186.2220"

Test-Path -LiteralPath $profile

If the folder exists you will receive:


True

Ensure that this is the correct version of SQL Developer.

Step 3 – Rename User Profile

Rather than delete the folder, we will rename it with a timestamp.


$profile = Join-Path $env:APPDATA `

"SQL Developer\system26.2.0.186.2220"

if (Test-Path -LiteralPath $profile) {

$backupName = "system26.2.0.186.2220.backup-" +

(Get-Date -Format "yyyyMMddHHmmss")

Rename-Item -LiteralPath $profile `

-NewName $backupName

Write-Host "Profile backed up as:" $backupName

} else {

Write-Host "Profile folder not found."

}

Step 4 – Launch SQL Developer 26.2

Launch the application from the installation folder.

E.g:


C:\oracle\SQLDeveloper26.2\sqldeveloper\sqldeveloper.exe

You will be asked if you want to import settings from a previous installation. In this example we chose No to ensure we had a clean configuration.

A new user profile was created.

Step 5 – Confirm Application Launched Successfully

The application launched successfully.

The Welcome Page opened, and we could confirm that we had the correct version installed.


Help > About

The version shown was:


26.2.0.186.2220

What Was The Fix?

By renaming and replacing the user profile we were able to get the application to launch successfully.

Although we do need to be careful with our conclusions.

We were unable to confirm what the exact cause was of the Netigso error on launch.

We can confirm that the previous user profile had an impact on the issue however we cannot confirm what file in the configuration was causing the error.

  1. Confirm Previous Version Of SQL Developer Works

We also had Oracle SQL Developer 24.3 installed on the workstation.

Sometimes when upgrading an application you may worry that the new version will affect the previous working version.

In this case we were able to use SQL Developer 24.3 as the new installation was in a separate application folder, and we only renamed the user settings folder for version 26.2.

Best Practice

When testing a new version of SQL Developer:

Have a separate installation folder.

Keep the previous working version until you have confirmed the new version works.

Backup any user configuration folders.

Ensure that any critical connections are still working.

Only remove older versions once you have accepted the upgrade (based on your maintenance policy).

This means that if the new application does not meet your requirements you can go back to your previous tools.

  1. Moving Connections From 24.3 To 26.2

Once we had launched SQL Developer 26.2 we needed to ensure that we kept our connections.

SQL Developer allows you to export connections from one installation and import them.

This should only be done for authorised connection profiles.

Step 1 – Launch SQL Developer 24.3

Launch SQL Developer 24.3.

Navigate to the Connections panel.

Step 2 – Export Connections

Right click on the Connections node and select:


Export Connections

Select the connections you wish to move.

Complete the wizard and save the connections in a JSON file.

Store this file somewhere secure. Connection files may contain sensitive information.

Where possible ensure that you have password protection enabled.

Step 3 – Launch SQL Developer 26.2

Launch the recovered SQL Developer 26.2.

Navigate to the Connections panel.

Step 4 – Import Connections

Right click on the Connections node and select:


Import Connections

Select the connection file you wish to import and complete the wizard.

Your connections should now appear in the Connections navigator.

Step 5 – Confirm Connections

Check all important connections.

Ensure that the connection properties are correct. If authorised, check the connections work.

Pay particular attention to connections using:

TNS Aliases

Oracle Wallet files

SSH or network tunnels

External authentication

Custom JDBC properties

Connection settings for the environment.

Just because you have moved a connection profile does not mean that all external files, passwords, network access and authentication have been moved.

Other Things To Consider

There may be other things you want to keep from SQL Developer. This can include:

SQL History

Snippets

Reports

Templates

Preferences

These should be checked separately as the connection export is not intended to move all application user data.

Note: The original troubleshooting confirmed that SQL Developer 26.2 launched successfully and that SQL Developer 24.3 was still working. The export/import process is guidance to help you move your connections, it was not confirmed that all connections were tested.

  1. Summary Of Troubleshooting

Below is a summary of what we found.

Step | Findings | Outcome

--- | --- | ---

Launch SQL Developer 26.2 | Module installation warnings | Fail

Review Netigso messages | Multiple bundles not available | Error

Check ZIP | SHA1 matched Oracle | Pass

Check 5 JAR files | All 5 JAR files present | Pass

Backup old 26.2 profile | Renamed existing settings folder | Complete

Launch with fresh profile | Application launched | Success

Check Help > About | Version 26.2.0.186.2220 | Confirmed

Check previous version | SQL Developer 24.3 still works | Confirmed

The main thing we found was that by refreshing the user profile for version 26.2 we were able to use the application. Despite the warnings suggesting modules were not available.

This shows that it is important to investigate multiple factors when troubleshooting an application.

  1. Screenshots & Evidence

Including screenshots in a technical troubleshooting article helps to make it more useful. Below are the screenshots we should include from the original issue.

Screenshot 1 – Application Error

A screenshot of the initial warning. This should show that some modules couldn’t be installed.

Include Netigso messages if available.

Remove any personal details from your Windows account.

Screenshot 2 – Check ZIP

A screenshot of the Get-FileHash command in PowerShell. This should show that the checksum matches Oracle.

Screenshot 3 – Check JAR Files

A screenshot of the PowerShell output confirming that the 5 application libraries are present.

Screenshot 4 – Application Launched

A screenshot of the Welcome Page for SQL Developer 26.2.

Screenshot 5 – Application Version

A screenshot of the Help > About screen confirming the version.

Ensure that the screenshots are original, clear and relevant. Do not fake any screenshots showing a success. Do not include any connection details for your live databases.

  1. Lessons Learnt

We learnt a few lessons from this troubleshooting.

Missing Bundle Doesn’t Mean Missing File

The initial error suggested that the application couldn’t find the required modules. However by checking we confirmed that the chosen JAR files were present.

Always Check The Archive

Comparing the checksum is a great first step. Often you will be able to avoid downloading the package multiple times as it will match the published checksum.

Backup Before Refreshing

It is better to rename the user settings folder. This means that if you need to get back to your previous settings you can.

Keep Previous Working Application

By keeping SQL Developer 24.3 we were able to investigate the new version. This is useful when troubleshooting tools used for operational activities.

Document Troubleshooting

When troubleshooting an issue it is important to document what you have done. This will help other DBAs understand what was checked to resolve the issue. Avoid assuming anything without verifying it.

Application May Be Recovered But Not Root Cause

Whilst we were able to recover the application we were unable to prove what the exact root cause was. By creating a fresh profile we were able to resolve the issue. A deeper investigation would be required to determine what part of the profile was causing the Netigso error.

  1. Troubleshooting Checklist

When troubleshooting an Oracle SQL Developer launch error on Windows:

Check what version & package you have installed.

Check relevant Java requirements.

Compare download checksum to vendor.

Check application files have been extracted into the correct folder.

Check what error you are receiving.

Check relevant application libraries.

Backup version specific user profile.

Test application with fresh profile.

Do not overwrite previous working installation.

Confirm application launched & version.

Carefully restore required connection profiles.

Document & remove sensitive details.

Not all launch errors will have the same cause. Refreshing the profile may be one option.

Conclusion

Oracle SQL Developer launch errors can be tricky to troubleshoot. In this article we looked at an example of Oracle SQL Developer 26.2 on Windows. We had issues with the application not launching and had errors relating to Netigso modules.

We confirmed that the downloaded installation ZIP had the correct checksum from Oracle. We also confirmed that the 5 JAR files were present.

By renaming the version specific user profile and creating a fresh profile we were able to get the application to launch successfully. We also confirmed that the previous SQL Developer 24.3 installation was still working.

The main takeaway from this is by taking a methodical approach, being cautious when recovering the configuration and keeping the existing settings we can have a safer and more effective solution.

By documenting the steps taken this can be a useful reference for DBAs in the future.

References

Oracle SQL Developer Downloads

https://www.oracle.com/database/sqldeveloper/technologies/download/

Official installation packages, versions & download checksums.

Oracle SQL Developer 26.2 Installation Guide

https://docs.oracle.com/en/database/oracle/sql-developer/26.2/rptig/index.html

Installation requirements & guidance.

Migrating Information From Previous Releases

https://docs.oracle.com/en/database/oracle/sql-developer/26.2/rptig/migrating-information-previous-releases.html

Oracle guidance for keeping connections & information when moving between versions.

SQL Developer Concepts & Usage

https://docs.oracle.com/en/database/oracle/sql-developer/26.2/rptug/sql-developer-concepts-usage.html

Abdulrawof Totakhil

title: What Is XDBL and How Does Database-Independent Querying Work?
description:
Modern enterprise applications rarely operate with simple database requirements. They process financial transactions, manage customer records, coordinate business operations and generate analytical reports. As organizations grow, their applications may need to work with different database engines, support existing database infrastructure or separate transactional workloads from analytical processing.

However, supporting multiple databases introduces a technical challenge: each database engine has its own SQL dialect, data types, functions, sequence mechanisms and stored procedure implementations. An application written specifically for one database can require significant changes when deployed on another.

XDBL addresses this challenge by providing a unified, database-independent source for defining database structures, queries and procedural logic. Instead of maintaining separate database-specific implementations, developers define operations once and use a schema compiler to generate native SQL for supported database engines.

Understanding how this works requires looking at database independence, SQL dialect differences, schema compilation and the role of native SQL generation.

What Is XDBL?

XDBL is Airtool's XML-based, database-independent language for defining database operations and structures. It provides a unified format for expressing different aspects of database development without directly embedding the syntax of a particular database engine into application definitions.

Its scope includes four important database language categories:

  • DDL (Data Definition Language): Defines database structures such as tables, indexes and constraints.
  • DML (Data Manipulation Language): Defines operations for retrieving, inserting, updating and deleting data.
  • DCL (Data Control Language): Handles database permissions and access control statements.
  • SPL (Stored Procedure Language): Defines procedural database logic, including stored procedures and related database objects.

These definitions are maintained in a common source format. Airtool's schema compiler processes the XDBL definitions and generates SQL appropriate for the selected database engine.

The important distinction is that XDBL does not attempt to replace SQL inside database engines. It provides a higher-level source from which the compiler produces the SQL those engines actually execute.

Why Is Database-Independent Querying Important?

Different database engines implement SQL differently. Although SQL provides a common foundation for relational databases, individual vendors introduce their own syntax, functions, data types and procedural capabilities.

For example, a date calculation, string operation or sequence definition may require different SQL expressions depending on whether an application uses PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server or MySQL.

These differences create several challenges.

1. Database-Specific Code Increases Maintenance

When developers write queries directly for a particular database, the application becomes dependent on that database's syntax and behaviour. Supporting another database may require rewriting queries, procedures and schema definitions.

As the application grows, maintaining multiple versions of the same business logic becomes increasingly difficult.

2. Database Migration Becomes More Complicated

Organizations may change database platforms because of licensing decisions, infrastructure requirements, performance considerations or existing technology investments.

However, applications containing database-specific logic cannot always move easily between engines. Developers must identify incompatible statements, modify database objects and test the resulting application.

3. Different Workloads Require Different Database Engines

Transactional applications and analytical systems have different requirements.

Online Transaction Processing (OLTP) databases handle frequent business operations, such as sales orders, payments, inventory movements and employee records. Online Analytical Processing (OLAP) databases are designed for analytical queries involving large datasets, aggregations and reporting.

A business may need both types of database engines without wanting to maintain entirely separate application definitions.

Database-independent querying helps address these challenges by separating application definitions from database-specific SQL syntax.

How Does Database-Independent Querying Work?

Airtool uses XDBL and a schema compiler to translate unified database definitions into engine-native SQL.

The process can be understood through three main stages.

1. Define Database Operations in a Unified Format

Developers create database structures, queries and procedural logic using XDBL rather than writing separate SQL implementations for every supported database.

For example, a business application may need a table containing employee information, including employee IDs, names, departments and salary records.

Instead of manually creating different table definitions for each database, developers maintain one XDBL definition.

The same principle applies to queries, database functions, stored procedures and triggers.

2. Compile XDBL into Database-Specific SQL

The schema compiler interprets the XDBL definition and generates SQL according to the selected database engine.

This is where database-specific differences are handled.

The compiler accounts for variations in:

  • SQL syntax and dialects.
  • Data types and column definitions.
  • Date and time calculations.
  • String functions.
  • Sequence and identity handling.
  • Stored procedure structures.
  • Database-specific constraints and other capabilities.

Rather than requiring developers to maintain these differences manually, the compiler handles the translation.

3. Execute Native SQL on the Target Database

The generated SQL is executed using the target database engine's native capabilities.

This distinction matters because database independence does not have to mean restricting every application to the smallest set of SQL features shared by all supported databases.

Instead, the compiler can generate different SQL implementations for the same XDBL definition, allowing each database to use its own supported syntax and functionality.

The result is a common application source with database-specific SQL generated for execution.

Why Native SQL Generation Matters

Not all database-independent approaches work in the same way. Some rely on a common subset of SQL supported across multiple engines. Others use runtime drivers or abstraction layers to manage database communication and query differences.

These approaches can be useful, but they address different parts of the problem.

A database driver provides connectivity and communication with a database. An ORM (Object-Relational Mapper) maps application objects to database records and may generate queries from application-level expressions. A query builder provides an abstraction for constructing SQL statements.

These tools do not automatically provide a unified source for every database definition, stored procedure and trigger.

A lowest-common-denominator approach can also restrict developers to features available across all supported databases. This may prevent applications from using certain engine-specific capabilities.

Airtool's XDBL approach takes a different direction: maintain one database-independent definition while generating SQL that uses the capabilities of the target engine.

For example, database engines may use different approaches to handle date arithmetic, string aggregation, sequence generation and data types. The compiler can produce the appropriate native expression rather than forcing every engine to execute an identical SQL statement.

The database optimizer can then work with SQL expressed in its own dialect.

This does not automatically guarantee identical query performance across engines. Actual performance still depends on query design, indexing, data distribution, execution plans and the underlying infrastructure. However, native SQL generation avoids making portability depend solely on a restricted common SQL subset.

A Practical Example: Handling Date Calculations Across Databases

Date arithmetic is a useful example of why database independence matters.

Suppose an enterprise application needs to calculate the number of hours between two timestamps. This calculation may be required for employee working hours, project duration, service response times or transaction processing.

Although the business requirement is identical, different databases can express the calculation differently.

One database may support direct timestamp subtraction, while another returns an interval that needs additional processing. Other engines may require different date functions or conversions.

Without a database-independent approach, developers may need to maintain separate SQL expressions for each database.

With XDBL, the date calculation is defined once. Airtool's schema compiler generates the appropriate SQL for each supported engine.

Airtool's published technical example demonstrates this difference across ten database engines. The generated SQL varies significantly in length and structure. For example, the SQL Server implementation requires substantially less SQL than the Oracle implementation because Oracle's interval result requires additional calculations to reconstruct the total hours.

The important point is not that every generated query looks identical. It is that the underlying operation can be defined once while the compiler handles the database-specific implementation.

This approach is also useful for string functions, sequence handling, table definitions and other operations where SQL dialects differ.

Supporting Both OLTP and OLAP Database Engines

Database independence becomes particularly valuable when an enterprise application needs to support transactional and analytical workloads.

OLTP and OLAP databases serve different purposes, and organizations may choose different engines for each workload.

Airtool's data architecture supports seven OLTP engines:

  • PostgreSQL
  • Informix
  • Oracle
  • IBM DB2
  • Microsoft SQL Server
  • MySQL
  • SAP HANA

For analytical workloads, Airtool supports three OLAP engines:

  • Vertica
  • ClickHouse
  • Google BigQuery

The same application model can support these different database environments through the platform's compilation approach.

For example, an enterprise application may use PostgreSQL or Oracle for transactional operations while routing analytical workloads to ClickHouse, Vertica or BigQuery.

This separation allows organizations to select database engines according to their operational and analytical requirements without maintaining an entirely separate application definition for each database environment.

It is particularly relevant for businesses that need reliable transaction processing alongside large-scale reporting and analytics.

How Does Schema Compilation Simplify Database Maintenance?

Database independence is not limited to translating individual queries. Database structures and procedural objects also need to be managed consistently.

Airtool's schema compiler supports the import of existing customer database schemas into its metadata repository.

This includes objects such as:

  • Tables and columns.
  • Indexes and constraints.
  • Stored procedures.
  • Triggers.
  • Other supported database definitions.

Once imported, these objects can be managed through the platform's schema compilation process.

This is important for organizations with existing database investments. They do not necessarily need to approach database modernization as a complete rewrite of their existing data structures.

The compiler also processes different categories of database objects through its MODEL and CODE pipelines. MODEL handles table-related objects, while CODE processes stored procedure language objects in dependency order.

Dependency handling matters because database objects often rely on other objects being available first. A procedure, for example, may depend on a function or database structure that must be resolved before compilation.

By managing these relationships through a structured compilation process, the platform can support more consistent database deployment and maintenance.

What Does Database Independence Mean for Enterprise Development?

For developers, database independence reduces the need to maintain multiple versions of the same database logic.

For software architects, it provides greater flexibility when designing applications for different customer infrastructure environments.

For businesses, it helps reduce dependence on a single database engine and supports technology decisions based on operational requirements.

The practical advantages include:

Reduced Database-Specific Development: Developers maintain common definitions instead of repeatedly rewriting database structures and operations.

Simplified Database Migration: Changing the target database can become a recompile-and-migrate exercise rather than requiring the entire application to be rewritten. Migration still requires appropriate data conversion, validation and testing.

Greater Infrastructure Flexibility: Organizations can choose supported database engines according to existing investments, licensing arrangements and technical requirements.

Support for Different Workloads: Applications can use transactional and analytical database engines within the same broader platform architecture.

Consistent Application Logic: Business rules and database definitions remain centrally managed rather than being duplicated across separate database implementations.

XDBL and AI-Assisted Application Development

Database-independent development also has implications for AI-assisted software development.

AI coding agents often need to understand database structures, generate queries and interact with application data. When an agent must produce native SQL for every database engine, it needs to account for the differences between their dialects and capabilities.

XDBL provides a structured alternative.

Its grammar is described through an XML Schema Definition (XSD), allowing compatible AI development tools to work with a defined language structure.

An AI agent can generate XDBL definitions without independently implementing the SQL dialect of every supported database. The schema compiler then handles the translation into the appropriate native SQL.

This separates the AI agent's task of expressing database operations from the compiler's responsibility for handling database-specific syntax.

It can make AI-assisted development more consistent across supported database environments, although the generated definitions still need validation, appropriate permissions and testing.

Conclusion

Database independence is about more than connecting an application to different databases. It is about maintaining application logic without making every database-specific difference a development responsibility.

XDBL addresses this through a unified XML-based source format and a schema compiler that generates native SQL for supported database engines.

By supporting seven OLTP engines and three OLAP engines, Airtool provides a common application development approach across different transactional and analytical database environments.

For enterprise applications, this means greater database flexibility, reduced duplication of database-specific logic and a more consistent foundation for development and modernization.

The goal is straightforward: define database operations once, let the compiler handle engine-specific differences, and allow applications to work with the database technology that best fits the organization's requirements.

title: Debugging SQL Should Be Just Like Debugging Code
description:
Debugging SQL is still mostly guesswork

Suppose you run an 80-line SQL query and discover that one of the result columns contains incorrect numbers. What’s your first instinct? Run it again.

At this point, a programmer would open the debugger, set breakpoints, and step through the code. They could see exactly how each variable changes and what value it holds at every step. What about SQL developers? They can only stare at the final result and guess: Is the join condition wrong? Does a window function miss a partition? You want to see the result of an intermediate step? You can’t. You have to split the CTEs and even the nested queries, one by one, turn them into standalone SELECT statements, run them individually, and then piece everything back together.

This isn’t debugging – this is archeology.

SQL debugging is still stuck at “run it, then stare at the output and guess.”

You’d never accept this way of debugging when write code – so why do you put up with it when you write SQL?

A real-world scenario: finding a neighboring record by offset

That’s all abstract. Let’s look a concrete example.

A workshop scan log table records, in each row, the cardboard sheet number scanned at a certain moment on a certain production line. The requirement: group by production line and sort by time within each group. Then find the records whose number equals a given string (for example, spL1ml82N4o), together with the 2 records before and the 2 records after each one, and finally remove duplicates by id.

Written in traditional SQL (MySQL), it looks like this:

SELECT id,
  MAX(Cardboard_Number) AS Cardboard_Number,
  MAX(date_Time) AS date_Time,
  MAX(ProductionLine_Number) AS ProductionLine_Number,
  MAX(flag) AS flag,
  MAX(in_range) AS in_range
FROM (
  SELECT id, Cardboard_Number, date_Time, ProductionLine_Number, flag, in_range
  FROM (
    SELECT id, Cardboard_Number, date_Time, ProductionLine_Number,
      MAX(flag) OVER (
        PARTITION BY ProductionLine_Number
        ORDER BY ProductionLine_Number ASC, date_Time ASC
        ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND 2 FOLLOWING) AS in_range
    FROM (
      SELECT id, Cardboard_Number, date_Time, ProductionLine_Number,
        CASE WHEN Cardboard_Number = 'spL1ml82N4o' THEN 1 END AS flag
      FROM table1
    ) AS flagged
  ) AS marked
  WHERE in_range = 1
) AS filtered
GROUP BY id;.

We won’t explain this code line by line, only what it looks like: three layers of nested derived tables, with flagging, window frame, filtering, and distinct all crammed into one query. Every layer has to list the fields all over again, and to see an intermediate result, all you can do is keep breaking it apart from the inside.

The real problem isn’t that the SQL is hard to read. It’s that it’s hard to debug. The most fragile part of this SQL is the window frame: ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND 2 FOLLOWING. If you get the offsets wrong, it won’t throw an error. If you leave out a segmentation key, it won’t throw an error either. It will simply produce slightly incorrect results, silently. The output looks almost right, but not quite – the kind of result that makes your palms sweat just before deployment. And the intermediate flag columns and window-match indicator columns aren’t included in the final output at all. If you can’t see them, you can’t validate whether they’re correct.

SQLazy: Write step by step, debug one step at a time

What if we took a different approach? Instead of delivering a single SQL query as the final product, we break the logic into steps, each of which can be executed and its result inspected.

That’s exactly what SQLazy does. SQLazy is an intuitive, easy-to-understand language for structured data processing. It breaks logic into clear steps, produces deterministic output, and makes the entire process easy to audit. The same task takes just five steps in SQLazy:


It also has a dedicated debugging feature: single-step execution. Click once and it runs one step. and the result tables of the current step and all the steps before it are there for you to browse at any time. This is the same thing as the single-stepping you use when debugging Python or Java. The only difference is that SQLazy’s code structure is simpler, with no branches, loops or subroutines, so you don’t need breakpoints, step in and step out routine. Every statement is already one step.

Back to the task above, here’s what the debugging experience looks like:

  • Step 1: Sorting: click a group and check whether the order is right;

  • Step 2: Flag the target rows and check whether any have been missed.

  • Step 3: Retrieve the two preceding and two following rows. This is the most error-prone part of the entire query, where both the window frame and segmentation keys come into play. Step through the query to this point and inspect the in_range column. You can see at a glance which rows matched and which didn’t.

  • Step 4: Filter the rows.

  • Step 5: Remove duplicates. Just click each step to inspect its result.

In SQL, a mistake in the window frame leaves you guessing. In SQLazy, just step through to Step 3 and inspect the results.

If something goes wrong, just fix the step where the error occurs – there’s no need to rewrite the entire query from scratch. Once you’ve verified that the logic is correct, you can also execute all the steps with a single click, letting them run in sequence to produce the final result.

It’s a change in form, not just syntax

Someone might argue, “Can’t I just run a SELECT on each CTE in SQL to inspect the intermediate results?” Yes, you can. But that’s manual, makeshift step-by-step debugging. Every time the logic changes, you have to split the query again. Those steps aren’t saved for you. AI can’t fix this either. What AI writes for you is still one final SQL statement. If something goes wrong, you’re back to guessing from scratch.

AI writes the logic. A compiler writes the SQL.

In SQLazy, AI plans the business logic as a sequence of steps, and the compiler compiles these steps into native SQL. The steps are for human to read and debug, and the SQL is for machines to run. Each has its own job.

he compiled SQL is equivalent to what you’d write by hand. There’s no extra abstraction layer – j you can copy it and use it as is, and it isn’t tied to any particular database.

To be honest, for simple CRUD, just write the SQL directly. You don’t need SQLazy for that. What really deserves step-by-step debugging is logic where one wrong step spoils everything – things like grouping records to find the neighbor, condition-based resets, and segment-based alignment.

A different approach to debugging

Want to try the step-by-step execution? Visit https://www.sqlazy.com/?2Qkto run this example of searching for adjacent records by offset.

You can also visit our example library (https://github.com/SPLWare/SQLazy/tree/master/examples) to find more examples about sessionization, continuous interval, and dynamic grouped reports.

How do you usually find errors when you debug SQL? Break the CTEs apart and run them one by one, or stare at the output and think hard? Either way, it’s more tiring than clicking single-step execution.

title: Role of Python in Backend Web Development
description:
Introduction

Due to technological changes, websites and web applications are now getting very important for the development process, especially while dealing with the clients. Be it an e-commerce site, banking application, social networking site or the booking site; all should have a good backend for functioning effectively. As while the frontend is responsible for handling the front side of the product for the user, the backend is responsible for handling data, business logic, server, etc. Some of the languages used in the backend programming are Java, PHP, JavaScript and Python. Among all, Python has gained importance as one of the most loved programming language among the programmers.Python in Backend Web Development helps developers build secure, scalable, and efficient web applications with less complicated code.

What Is Backend Web Development?

"Backend Web Development" involves the development of a website or web application on the server-side. It takes care of all operations that occur in the background every time a user uses the website.
Server: The server receives requests from the users and processes them.
Application logic: This includes rules and operations necessary to carry out different operations.
Database: A place where information such as user details, products information, order and transactions are kept.

What Is Python?

It is one of the high-level programming languages. The features of the language are simplicity in syntax and readability. It can be used in various industries, including web development, software development, automation, artificial intelligence, machine learning, and data science. Some of the reasons why developers opt for Python language are its ability to produce clean code. In contrast with other programming languages, Python produces code that consists of fewer lines. Moreover, Python has a large library of tools for developing applications.

Role of Python in Backend Web Development

Python is useful for controlling the server side functionality of websites and applications. The programming language assists the developers in developing application logic, receiving requests from users, dealing with the databases, and connecting different services together.

  • Management of Server-Side Logic
    The most important task of backend development is related to management of the application logic performed at the server side.Using Python, developers can develop all the functions needed to perform different actions. These include user registration, log-in procedures, order processing, payment procedures, and form submission.For instance, if a user registers himself or herself on a website, then using Python developers can receive the input from users, validate it and store it in the database.

  • Database Management and Integration
    Each web application needs a database to store and manage data. Python helps developers easily connect backend applications to various database management systems.
    The database management systems supported by Python include:

  1. MySQL
  2. PostgreSQL
  3. SQLite
  4. MongoDB

Python provides libraries and utilities through which developers can perform database actions like adding, modifying, fetching, and deleting data.For instance, an online shopping website can utilize Python to fetch product data, modify availability of the products, and store order details.

  • API Development and Integration
    API stands for Application Programming Interface. It enables different software applications to interact and exchange data.Python is extensively employed for the development of APIs connecting websites to mobile applications, payment gateways, third-party applications, and various other software.For instance, an e-commerce site might use an API to connect with a payment gateway for facilitating payments through the internet.The Python frameworks like Flask, Django, and FastAPI are some of the popular choices when it comes to the development of APIs.

  • User Authentication and Security
    Security is an important aspect in backend web development. The websites need to ensure the security of the data of the users and prevent any unauthorized access to this data.Python can be used for several security-oriented processes, which include:

  1. User registration and login process.
  2. Hashing of passwords.
  3. Session management.
  4. Role-based access control.
  5. API authentication.

Frameworks like Django have inbuilt capabilities for the purposes of user authentication.However, developers should also adopt other security best practices.

  • Developing Scalable Web Applications The term scalability denotes the capability of an application to deal with more and more users, requests, and data without impairing its performance.There are several ways to develop scalable web applications with the help of Python, using such concepts as its frameworks, caching, database features, and background processing.A programmer can utilize such techniques as Redis, Celery, as well as cloud services together with Python in order to perform background processes and enhance application performance.For instance, an online shopping website may implement background processing to send confirmation emails regarding orders without hindering the checkout process.

Popular Python Frameworks Used in Backend Development

Python in Backend Web Development plays an important role in building modern websites and web applications. It helps developers manage server-side operations, handle databases, create APIs, and develop secure and scalable applications. With powerful frameworks such as Django, Flask, and FastAPI, Python makes backend development easier and faster. Its simple syntax and flexibility make it a popular choice for both beginners and professional developers.

  • Django Django is a high-level Python framework for developing web applications rapidly and in a highly secure and maintainable way.It uses Model Template View architecture and has many inbuilt features, which include:
  1. Authentication of users.
  2. Database management.
  3. Routing of URLs.
  4. Admin interface.
  5. Security.

Django can be used for developing content management systems, e-commerce sites, and social networking websites.

  • Flask Flask is a minimalistic Python web framework, which allows developers to have a certain degree of freedom.In contrast to Django, Flask does not have such an extensive list of features. The key features are as follows:
  • Simple application architecture.
  • Flexibility in the development process.
  • Routing for URLs.
  • Support for API development.
  • Database integration.

Flask is widely used for the development of small and medium-sized web applications, prototyping, and API development.

  • FastAPI FastAPI is a state-of-the-art Python framework primarily designed to build APIs fast and effectively.It incorporates asynchronous programming and automatic documentation, which makes it perfect for applications handling several requests at once. The following are the main characteristics of FastAPI:
  1. High-speed API development.
  2. Automated interactive documentation.
  3. Validation of data.
  4. Asynchronism.
  5. Python type hints.

FastAPI is highly suitable for the development of contemporary backend systems and API applications.

Benefits of Using Python for Backend Web Development

  • Ease of Learning
    The programming language uses simple and easy-to-understand syntax. Even beginners will easily grasp the basics without having to understand complex programming structures. Therefore, Python is a good starting point for learning backend programming.

  • Quicker Development
    Python comes with pre-built frameworks that contain libraries and components that make development much quicker and easier by allowing developers to reuse them.

  • Wide Array of Libraries
    Python possesses a wide array of libraries that cater to different software development needs. Developers can leverage these libraries for databases, APIs, authentication, testing, automation, and many other purposes.

  • Active Developer Community
    Python boasts of a huge developer community in different parts of the world. Both beginners and experienced developers will be able to find tutorials, documents, open source projects, and answers to programming issues.

  • Compatibility with Latest Technologies
    Python is compatible with technologies such as artificial intelligence, machine learning, data analytics, cloud computing, and automation.It enables developers to create applications that combine backend features and latest technologies.

Real-World Applications of Python in Backend Development

Python is used across different industries to develop and manage web applications.
E-commerce Websites: Managing customer accounts, product information, orders, and payments.
Social Media Platforms: Handling user profiles, content management, and notifications.
Banking Applications: Supporting backend operations, transaction processing, and data management.
Healthcare Applications: Managing appointments, patient information, and online services.
**Educational Platforms: **Supporting student registration, course management, and online learning systems.
These examples demonstrate how Python supports different types of backend operations across industries.

Skills Required to Become a Python Backend Developer

Being skilled only in Python programming is not sufficient to be a professional backend developer. It is necessary to have some knowledge of the technologies and concepts employed in developing applications in real world.
Python programming: Knowledge of variables, data types, functions, loops, object-oriented programming and exceptions handling.
Python frameworks: **Acquaintance with frameworks such as Django, Flask and FastAPI for developing backend applications.
**Database management: **Practical knowledge of databases such as MySQL, PostgreSQL and MongoDB.
**Frontend Technologies: Understanding of HTML and CSS – basic frontend technologies for building web pages.
API Development: **Familiarity with the concept of APIs and development of REST APIs.
**Version Control: Knowledge of Git and GitHub.
Testing and Debugging: Ability to find and fix errors.
Application Deployment: Understanding how to deploy applications using cloud services and web servers.
In addition, experience in projects is very important as it shows how different backend technologies work together.

Career Opportunities in Python Backend Development

With companies creating digital platforms and web applications, it is necessary to have qualified backend developers in various industries.Some career options one can pursue through learning Python and its backend frameworks include:

  1. Python Backend Developer
  2. Python Web Developer
  3. Django Developer
  4. Flask Developer
  5. API Developer
  6. Software Developer
  7. Full Stack Developer

These careers may require different skill sets according to the organizations’ needs and the project. Having hands-on experience with building projects and understanding databases, APIs, and frameworks will benefit one’s career.

Conclusion

This is a highly useful language in the field of backend web development in the contemporary world due to its ease, flexibility, and efficient development tools. This language can be applied for many different purposes in the field of backend web development including database management, API development, and more. Python in Backend Web Development can enable upcoming developers to develop a strong foundation in server-side programming. They gain those skills required for building web applications by learning how to use the frameworks of Python, which include Django, Flask, FastAPI, and database management as well as API integration. No matter if you are a beginner programmer starting your programming career or a new software developer in need of improving his/her technical skills, learning Python will be of great benefit to you.

title: I built a Node.js toolkit for India's DPDP Act, so compliance can't quietly drift
description:
If your app has Indian users and stores even a phone number, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 applies to you. The DPDP Rules, 2025 were notified on 13 November 2025, and most of their obligations start 18 months later, in May 2027: notices, security safeguards, breach reporting, erasure, and rights requests. The maximum penalty is ₹250 crore.

Most teams will handle this with a privacy policy page and a spreadsheet. Nothing in the code enforces either. Six months later someone adds an aadhaar_number column, nobody updates the spreadsheet, and the data is kept forever.

So I built dpdp-kit: an open-source, Node.js-native toolkit that builds the DPDP Act into your backend. Version 0.2.0 is out today.

npm i dpdp-kit

Not legal advice. dpdp-kit helps you put compliance into practice; it doesn't make an app compliant on its own. Every Section and Rule reference in it was checked against the official Gazette texts, but your lawyer still signs off.

What the law asks of your code

The law says Where dpdp-kit
Process data only for a stated purpose, with consent or a legitimate use Sections 4, 6, 7 Typed data map: every field lists its purposes
Prove a notice was given and consent was given Section 6(10) Hash-chained consent records with notice version and language
Notice in English or any Eighth Schedule language Sections 5(3), 6(3) All 22 languages built in
Erase when consent is withdrawn or the purpose ends, unless another law says keep it Section 8(7) Erasure plans + a runner, with legal holds
Keep data, traffic data and logs of processing for at least a year Rule 8(3) minimumRetention, enforced by the audit
Answer access, correction, erasure, grievance and nomination requests Sections 11–14 Rights requests with due dates
Answer grievances within 90 days Rule 14(3) Default due date, enforced by the audit
Tell processors to stop and erase Sections 6(6), 8(7)(b) Processor hooks

1. Declare your data, with types

Everything starts from one config file. Purposes are typed, so a typo in a field's purpose list is an error in your editor:

// dpdp.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from "dpdp-kit";

export default defineConfig({
  fiduciary: { name: "Acme Pvt Ltd", grievanceUrl: "https://acme.in/privacy/grievance" },
  purposes: {
    account:       { basis: "legitimate-use", retain: "while-active" },
    order_updates: { basis: "consent", retain: "while-active" },
    marketing_sms: { basis: "consent", retain: { afterWithdrawal: "0d" } },
  },
  data: {
    users: {
      table: "users",
      subject: "id",
      fields: {
        phone: { category: "contact", purposes: ["account", "order_updates", "marketing_sms"] },
        name:  { category: "identity", purposes: ["account"] },
      },
    },
    orders: {
      table: "orders",
      subject: "user_id",
      fields: { address: { category: "contact", purposes: ["account"] } },
      legalHold: { reason: "GST records", keep: "8y", then: "anonymise" },
    },
  },
  processors: { msg91: { purposes: ["order_updates", "marketing_sms"] } },
  minimumRetention: "1y", // Rule 8(3)
});

2. Catch schema drift in CI

This is the part I'm proudest of. A data map is only useful while it matches the database, so the audit reads your real Drizzle schema and checks both directions:


npx dpdp-kit audit --schema src/db/schema.ts

✖ error    schema.users.aadhaar_number
             Looks like personal data (identity, matched "aadhaar") but isn't in the data map.
✖ error    data.orders.fields.address
             Column "address" isn't in table "orders". Fix the name, or remove it if the column was dropped.
⚠ warning  schema.users.gender
             Looks like personal data (identity, matched "gender") but isn't in the data map.

It recognises phone and email columns, Aadhaar, PAN, passport and voter IDs, dates of birth, names, addresses and PIN codes, UPI, IFSC and bank details, IP addresses and device IDs, and health, biometric and location data. Clear cases are errors; maybe-personal ones like name or city are warnings. Columns that describe data rather than hold it, like email_verified_at or address_type, are left alone.

In GitHub Actions, each problem lands on the pull request as an annotation:

- run: npm ci
- uses: yogesh2902/dpdp-kit@main
  with:
    schema: src/db/schema.ts

3. Consent records that show tampering 

import { createDpdp } from "dpdp-kit";
import { drizzleData, drizzleStore } from "dpdp-kit/drizzle";

const dpdp = createDpdp({ config, store: drizzleStore(db), data: drizzleData(db, { schema }) });

await dpdp.consent.grant(userId, ["marketing_sms"], {
  noticeVersion: "2026-11",
  language: "hi",
  channel: "android",
});
await dpdp.consent.has(userId, "marketing_sms"); // true
await dpdp.consent.verify(userId);               // { ok: true, events: 1 }

Each person's grants and withdrawals form a SHA-256 hash chain. verify() catches an edited, deleted or reordered event, which matters because Section 6(10) puts the burden of proving consent on you.

4. Erasure that actually happens

Withdrawing consent schedules the erasure. A daily retention.run() carries it out:

await dpdp.consent.withdraw(userId, ["marketing_sms"]);
await dpdp.retention.run(); // from a daily cron
  • Processors are told to stop immediately (Section 6(6)), through hooks you provide.
  • Fields are erased only when none of their purposes remain. phone stays while account still needs it.
  • Rule 8(3)'s one-year minimum is respected. The data is restricted now and deleted after a year, which is what the Rule's own example asks ("even if X deletes her account").
  • Legal holds win. Invoices kept for GST wait 8 years, then get anonymised.
  • It's safe with several servers. Tasks are claimed atomically, retried on failure, and a processor without a hook becomes a manual task.

5. Rights requests on a clock 

const request = await dpdp.rights.open(userId, "grievance", { text: "Too many promo SMS" });
// due 90 days later (Rule 14(3))

await dpdp.rights.list({ overdue: true }); // your inbox of late answers
await dpdp.rights.summary(userId);         // Section 11: what you hold, why, and who you shared it with
await dpdp.rights.erase(userId, { keepFor: ["account"], requestId: request.id }); // Section 12(3)

Why Node-native

dpdp-kit is a library, not a service. It runs inside your Node process, writes to your own Postgres through the Drizzle setup you already have, and makes no network calls. There's no server to deploy, no API key, and personal data never leaves your infrastructure. It works with ESM, require() and TypeScript, with Express and Hono middleware included.

How it's tested

  • 85 tests, including full flows against real Postgres (PGlite): withdraw → processor stopped → column nulled a year later, account deletion with an 8-year GST hold, and three runners racing for the same tasks
  • CI on Node 20.19, 22 and 24, plus a job that runs the GitHub Action against a sample project
  • Legal references checked against the Act (Gazette, 11 August 2023), the Rules (G.S.R. 846(E)) and their corrigendum (G.S.R. 892(E))

What's next

Recording objections to a Section 7(a) use, React components for notices and a privacy centre, MySQL and SQLite data access, children's data and guardian consent (Section 9, Rule 10), and breach records with the 72-hour Board report (Rule 7).

Try it 

npm i dpdp-kit
  • GitHub: github.com/yogesh2902/dpdp-kit (MIT)
  • npm: npmjs.com/package/dpdp-kit

If you build for Indian users, I'd really like to hear what's missing. Issues and PRs are welcome, and a star helps other developers find it.

title: A Passing Balance Test Can Hide a Broken Invoice
description:
A brake shop charges $562.72 for a repair. The customer paid the $85 diagnostic fee at drop-off, and that payment belongs to the same invoice. The card reader at pickup should ask for $477.72.

Here’s a bug that survives an assertion on the balance alone. One implementation records a $562.72 sale and an $85 payment. Another quietly reduces the sale to $477.72 and records no payment. Both can display $477.72 due. Only the first one can explain the $85 receipt the customer is holding.

Reproduce it in a spreadsheet

In the sample workbook, row 19 charges $85 for diagnosing brake noise. The other lines cover labor, pads, rotors and supplies. They bring the subtotal to $544.00. With the sheet’s $18.72 example tax, cell E35 reads $562.72.

Leave the charge in row 19. Enter 85 in E36 (Amount paid). E37 (Balance due) uses =E35-E36 and changes to $477.72. E35 stays at $562.72. Here’s the sheet after that one edit.

Test the three numbers together

Here’s a small Node test you can run with node invoice-test.mjs. It follows the same invoice from drop-off through pickup. Amounts in the test are integer cents.

import assert from "node:assert/strict";

function summarize(total, payments) {
  const paid = payments.reduce((sum, payment) => sum + payment, 0);
  return { total, paid, due: total - paid };
}

// All amounts are integer cents.
const total = 56_272;
assert.deepEqual(summarize(total, []),
  { total: 56_272, paid: 0, due: 56_272 });
assert.deepEqual(summarize(total, [8_500]),
  { total: 56_272, paid: 8_500, due: 47_772 });
assert.deepEqual(summarize(total, [8_500, 47_772]),
  { total: 56_272, paid: 56_272, due: 0 });

That middle assertion is the one I'd keep if I could only keep one. An implementation that turns the payment into a discount can get due right. It still fails on total and paid. The last assertion catches the same mistake after the customer pays the remaining $477.72: the invoice should show $562.72 in payments and zero outstanding.

The example assumes one invoice and two payments. If the $85 was invoiced and settled separately, leave that charge and payment on their original invoice.

This article was written with AI. The three assertions were run in Node and the balance was checked against the workbook after entering the payment.

Download the Excel workbook used in this example.

title: I built a coupon search for AI assistants and Telegram: an MCP server, a bot, and posts that delete themselves
description:
Coupon sites have a reputation problem: half the codes are expired, the other half were never real. I wanted to build one that only shows what a store's affiliate program actually published, with end dates, and then make that data usable where people already are: in their AI assistant and in Telegram.

The result is Coupossum: a website, a public MCP server, a Telegram channel and a Telegram bot, all answering from the same PostgreSQL database. Right now that's about 35,000 codes and deals from about 5,000 stores, refreshed every two hours.

This post covers the parts that turned out to be interesting:

  1. One database, four front ends
  2. An MCP server that AI directories accept
  3. Telegram posts that disappear when the offer ends
  4. A Telegram bot without an AI model
  5. Links that are never opened by a machine

1. One database, four front ends

The data comes from Feedico's Partner API, which aggregates coupons and products from affiliate networks. Coupossum is my own product built on that data, not an official Feedico service.

A sync job pulls coupons every two hours, stores daily, products daily. Everything shown publicly goes through one file of read queries, so the visibility rules exist exactly once:

export const COUPON_VISIBLE = `
  c.is_active AND m.is_eligible AND NOT c.is_duplicate
  AND (c.ends_at IS NULL OR c.ends_at > now())
  AND (c.starts_at IS NULL OR c.starts_at <= now())
  AND (c.link_status IS NULL OR c.link_status NOT IN ${BAD_LINK})
  AND c.is_offer`;

Note ends_at > now() is checked at query time, not at sync time. An offer that ends at 14:00 disappears at 14:00, not at the next sync.

The website, the MCP server and the Telegram bot all import these queries. When I fix a ranking or filter bug, it's fixed everywhere.

Stack: Node 22, Fastify 5, PostgreSQL, the official MCP TypeScript SDK, node:test with PGlite (Postgres in WebAssembly) so the tests run against a real Postgres without Docker. pm2 and cron on a small VPS.

2. An MCP server that AI directories accept

The MCP server is public: https://coupossum.com/mcp, Streamable HTTP, no authentication, read-only. Four tools:

Tool What it does
search_coupons Codes and deals by keyword and/or store, optionally by country
get_store_offers One store's current offers
search_stores Stores by name or domain
search_products Products on sale, with max price and currency

Add it to Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor or VS Code as a remote MCP server and ask "any codes for Belleek?" or "running shoes under 80 euros on sale".

A few things I learned getting it into directories (Anthropic's connector directory, the official MCP Registry as com.coupossum/coupossum, Glama, LobeHub):

Tool descriptions must describe, not instruct. My first version had rules like "always show both links" inside the tool descriptions. Anthropic's directory policy doesn't allow that: tool descriptions are for what a tool does. The rules moved into the server's instructions, which every client receives on connect:

const server = new McpServer(
  { name: 'coupossum', version: '0.2.5', websiteUrl: SITE.origin },
  { instructions: INSTRUCTIONS },
);

Annotations matter. Every tool is marked readOnlyHint: true, destructiveHint: false, idempotentHint: true and openWorldHint: false, with a human-readable title. Reviewers and clients both use them.

Cap and say so. Every tool returns at most 10 results and tells the model when there are more, with a link to the full list. That keeps answers short and stops a model from paging through the whole database.

Rate limit in memory only. A fixed window per IP, kept in a Map for a few minutes and never written anywhere. Search terms are logged for statistics, IPs are not.

3. Telegram posts that disappear when the offer ends

The Telegram channel @coupossum posts one offer an hour during the day. Each post is a generated image plus a caption:

The images come from @napi-rs/canvas with the Inter font bundled from @fontsource/inter, so the server doesn't depend on system fonts. Store names are text only: no logos, no product photos.

The interesting part isn't posting. It's un-posting. A deals channel full of expired codes is exactly the reputation problem I wanted to avoid, so every post is stored with its message id, and every hour the job checks which posted offers are no longer visible:

for (const p of await endedPosts(db, chat)) {
  try {
    await tg.deleteMessage(chat, p.message_id);
    await setStatus(db, p.id, 'deleted');
    continue;
  } catch (err) {
    if (notFound(err)) { await setStatus(db, p.id, 'gone'); continue; }
  }
  // Telegram may refuse: replace the post instead
  await tg.editPhoto(chat, p.message_id, await endedImage(p), endedCaption(p.store_name));
  await setStatus(db, p.id, 'ended');
}

Why the fallback? The Bot API docs say a message "can only be deleted if it was sent less than 48 hours ago", and in the same list that a channel admin with the delete right "can delete any message there". It's not clear which wins for old channel posts, and most offers run longer than 48 hours. Editing has no such limit for a bot's own messages, so if deletion fails, the post becomes an "offer ended" card without the code. I'm running a test post past the 48-hour mark to find out which path Telegram actually takes.

This is also why Telegram is the first social channel and not Pinterest or WhatsApp. On Pinterest, deleting pins through the API needs an approved developer app, and free schedulers like Buffer can't delete published pins. WhatsApp Channels have no official API at all. A channel only gets added once its expired posts can be removed automatically.

4. A Telegram bot without an AI model

@coupossum_bot answers in private chats: send "homary" and you get that store's current codes; send "shoes 20% off" and you get a keyword search. It also works inline: type @coupossum_bot nike in any chat and pick an offer to share.

No LLM involved. A store name match is checked first, then a plain keyword search over the same queries as the website. It's instant, free to run, and it can't hallucinate a code.

The bot runs on a webhook inside the existing Fastify app, not a separate process. Telegram sends a secret token header with each request, which I derive from the bot token so there's no second secret to manage:

export const webhookSecret = (token) =>
  createHmac('sha256', token).update('coupossum-telegram-webhook').digest('base64url').slice(0, 48);

app.post('/telegram/webhook', async (req, reply) => {
  const got = Buffer.from(String(req.headers['x-telegram-bot-api-secret-token'] || ''));
  if (got.length !== expected.length || !timingSafeEqual(got, expected)) return reply.code(403).send('forbidden');
  // handle the update, always answer 200 so Telegram doesn't retry our own errors
});

Nothing about Telegram users is stored. Search terms are logged without user or chat ids; user ids live in memory for a minute for the rate limit.

5. Links that are never opened by a machine

Every store link is an affiliate link, and affiliate networks treat automated clicks as invalid traffic. That shaped more of the design than I expected:

  • Website: store links point to /go/<token> on my own domain (disallowed in robots.txt), and the actual partner URL is opened by JavaScript on a real click. I added this after a crawler that ignores robots.txt started following plain affiliate links.
  • MCP: the server instructions tell assistants to show links and never open them.
  • Telegram: the bot and channel only ever link to the offer's page on coupossum.com, and link previews are switched off, so Telegram's servers never fetch a link on their own.

If you build anything on affiliate data, design for "a human clicked this" from day one.

Try it

  • Website: coupossum.com
  • MCP server: https://coupossum.com/mcp (setup guide) or if you're using Claude you can add it from the directory https://claude.ai/directory/coupossum
  • Telegram: @coupossum (channel) and @coupossum_bot (search)

I'd love feedback on the MCP tool design in particular: what would you want a shopping tool to return that it doesn't?

Disclosure: Coupossum's store links are affiliate links; if you buy through one, I may earn a commission at no extra cost to you. Coupossum is independent: the stores don't run or endorse it. Offers come from the Feedico partner network; Coupossum is not an official Feedico product.

title: 10 Reasons Why Designers Are Switching Their Daily Driver from Figma to ExodeUI
description:
Designers are switching from Figma to ExodeUI at an unprecedented pace. Here are the top 10 reasons why:

  1. True Code Export: Output production React, Vue, Svelte, Solid, and Angular in one click.
  2. Physics-Based Springs: Damped second-order spring dynamics instead of stiff Bezier curves.
  3. Visual State Machines: Eliminates dozens of spaghetti prototype arrows.
  4. Liquid Glass Shaders: Hardware-accelerated refraction shaders for next-gen spatial interfaces.
