title: Estados accesibles en formularios React con email
description:
Cuando un formulario de registro pide confirmar el email, solemos pensar primero en la API: enviar el mensaje, esperar el código y comprobarlo. En la interfaz, sin embargo, hay una pequeña máquina de estados que decide si la experiencia se siente clara o rota.

En mis formularios React intento tratar esa máquina como una parte del diseño, no como un detalle que se arregla al final. Un botón que cambia de texto, un error que empuja todo el layout o un foco que desaparece pueden hacer que una tarea sencilla se vuelva confusa. Esto suena pequeño, aunque cambia bastante cuando la persona navega con teclado o usa un lector de pantalla.

El problema: el email también tiene estados de interfaz

Un flujo de verificación suele tener, como mínimo, estos estados:

  • idle: el formulario está listo para recibir la dirección.
  • sending: la solicitud está en curso y no conviene duplicarla.
  • sent: el código fue enviado y aparece un campo para introducirlo.
  • verifying: se está comprobando el código.
  • success: la dirección quedó confirmada.
  • error: hay que explicar qué puede hacer la persona ahora.

Cuando estos estados se mezclan en varios booleanos (isLoading, hasSent, isValid), aparecen combinaciones imposibles. Por ejemplo, un mensaje puede decir “enviado” mientras el botón sigue bloqueado por un error anterior. Es facil que el código funcione en el caso feliz y se comporte raro al repetir el envío.

Un status único hace más visible la intención:

type EmailStatus =
  | "idle"
  | "sending"
  | "sent"
  | "verifying"
  | "success"
  | "error";

const [status, setStatus] = useState<EmailStatus>("idle");

Así, cada transición se puede revisar junto con su texto, su foco y su comportamiento visual. También ayuda a que el equipo de QA reproduzca el flujo sin adivinar qué combinación de flags provocó el fallo.

Si el flujo tiene más pasos, me ha resultado útil separar la lógica de red de la presentación y documentar los estados claros para un inbox temporal. La idea es la misma: una pantalla debe tener un estado que se pueda nombrar.

Accesibilidad y rendimiento en cada transición

El feedback no debe depender solo del color. Un mensaje de error puede usar role="alert" cuando necesita anunciarse de inmediato, mientras que una confirmación menos urgente puede vivir en un aria-live="polite". No pondría role="alert" en todo: si cada cambio interrumpe la lectura, la experiencia se vuelve cansada.

El foco también necesita una regla. Tras enviar correctamente, el foco puede ir al encabezado que explica cómo introducir el código. Si la solicitud falla, debe quedarse cerca del campo que se puede corregir. Sin esta decisión, el teclado queda perdido y toca volver a buscar donde estaba el problema.

Para el CSS, reserva espacio para los mensajes desde el principio. Un contenedor con min-height o una fila de ayuda estable evita que el formulario salte cuando llega la respuesta. Este enfoque complementa bien estas técnicas para mostrar errores de email sin CLS. El rendimiento percibido mejora aunque la red tarde lo mismo.

Un patrón sencillo para el botón puede ser:

<button type="submit" disabled={status === "sending"}>
  {status === "sending" ? "Enviando…" : "Enviar código"}
</button>

El texto debe explicar la acción actual, no solo mostrar un spinner. Un lector de pantalla necesita saber si la solicitud sigue en curso; una animación sola no cuenta toda la historia.

Cómo probar el flujo con un correo desechable

Para pruebas manuales y de staging, uso una dirección aislada que no mezcle mensajes reales con datos de QA. Un correo desechable permite revisar el mensaje, abrir el enlace y comprobar que la aplicación actualiza el estado correcto sin tocar una bandeja personal.

En una revisión de frontend compruebo también los casos menos comodos:

  1. Enviar dos veces con rapidez: el segundo clic no debe crear una carrera.
  2. Recargar después de recibir el código: la interfaz debe explicar qué se perdió.
  3. Introducir un código caducado: el error debe indicar el siguiente paso.
  4. Volver atrás y cambiar el email: el código anterior no debe validarse para la nueva dirección.
  5. Usar teclado y zoom alto: ningún mensaje debe quedar oculto ni cortar el botón.

En las notas de prueba suelen aparecer búsquedas extrañas como temp org mail o tamp mail com. Las trato como texto de QA, no como nombres de campos ni como enlaces: si el requisito está mal escrito, la interfaz aún puede seguir siendo clara.

Checklist final

  • ¿Existe un estado explícito para cada respuesta de red?
  • ¿El foco tiene un destino definido después de éxito y error?
  • ¿Los mensajes se anuncian sin repetir información innecesaria?
  • ¿El espacio de ayuda evita cambios bruscos de layout?
  • ¿El botón impide duplicar solicitudes mientras se envía?
  • ¿Se puede probar la dirección burner email address sin usar datos personales?
  • ¿La copia sigue siendo comprensible incluso cuando la red va lenta?

Una interfaz de verificación no necesita muchos componentes para ser sólida. Necesita estados con nombres claros, transiciones previsibles y una salida accesible para cada fallo. Cuando React, CSS y Accessibility se revisan juntos, el formulario se siente más tranquilo: la persona sabe qué pasó y cuál es el siguiente paso.

title: Engineering a Football Intelligence Platform: Simulations, Statistical Models, Scanners and Automated Workflows
description:
Written by the Slipio team. Slipio is our product.

Football looks like a perfect machine-learning problem: decades of results, thousands of matches a week, and a clean target. In practice the hard parts are rarely the model. They are time, truth and honesty: knowing exactly what was knowable when, knowing when a number in your database is final, and knowing whether your model is actually any good.

This is a tour of how we built Slipio, a football intelligence web app that turns data, simulation and calibrated models into match probabilities with plain-English reasons. The stack is a Java 21 / Spring Boot backend on PostgreSQL, a Qdrant vector store, and React front ends. We will go layer by layer and say where things went wrong, because most of what we know came from that.

1. Ingestion: a feed is not the truth

Fixtures, odds, statistics, match events and line-ups come from a commercial data provider. The ingestion layer is a set of resource-specific workers behind a dispatcher, and every request passes through a rate budget. Each priority level has its own ceiling, so a backfill cannot starve the jobs that collect pre-match data.

Three rules came out of real incidents:

  • An empty response is not "not found". Throttling also returns an empty body. Treat empty as "unknown, retry later", never as proof that something does not exist.
  • A present row is not a final row. The provider writes match statistics while the match is being played. We once settled a corners selection against statistics captured 33 minutes into the match. Settlement now waits until the statistics were last updated at least three hours after kick-off. This costs nothing in practice, because the median statistics row lands about two days after kick-off anyway.
  • Never derive a season from a calendar year. A European 2024 season runs from August 2024 to May 2025. One historical odds import resolved every January–May fixture against the wrong season. Every miss came back as "skipped", which looks exactly like a competition we do not track. A third of the corpus went unpriced, and the job still reported COMPLETED. Resolve a fixture on its provider id alone, and take the season from the match you find.

2. Historical data and the leakage problem

A feature leaks when it carries information that did not exist, or that we had not recorded, at the moment the prediction is made. A leaking model looks excellent offline and cannot reproduce that in production.

We think about three instants for every read:

Instant Meaning
Decision When the prediction is made (a horizon from 72 hours to 5 minutes before kick-off)
Event time When the thing the row describes happened
Record time When we stored it

These give two clocks. A publication clock admits a row whose event time comes before the decision. A knowledge clock also requires that we had recorded it by then. Some of the rules are obvious: the result of the match being predicted is never admissible. Others are not. A weather feature may only be the forecast that existed at the decision. The measured weather the match was played in is knowable six hours after kick-off, and training on it while serving a forecast is a train/serve skew. Injury rows have no return date, so "currently injured" has to be bounded by recency. A player's "current club" pointer is overwritten on every sync, so it must never stand in for a past squad.

A time-bounded read looks like this (simplified):

SELECT s.team_id, s.corners, s.yellow_cards
FROM   match_statistics s
JOIN   fixtures m ON m.id = s.match_id
WHERE  m.status = 'FINISHED'
  AND  m.kickoff_at < CAST(:decision AS timestamptz)
  AND  s.updated_at >= m.kickoff_at + interval '3 hours'  -- final, not in-play
  AND  s.created_at <= CAST(:decision AS timestamptz);     -- knowledge clock

The CAST is there for a reason. PostgreSQL infers an untyped bind parameter from its neighbour, so :decision + interval '21 days' comes back as an interval and fails at runtime. So does (:x IS NULL OR col = :x) once a caller passes null.

The rules are not just a document. A catalogue in code lists every leakage rule, and an architecture test fails the build if a new loader query loses its time bound or if a feature source is not classified. Every training run writes a leakage audit first, and the gate refuses to train on a hash-based or out-of-order split. Stages that leak knowingly are quarantined with a reason and a probe, not hidden.

3. Feature engineering

The V1 feature vector has around 580 features: rolling form windows (season, last 10, last 5, venue splits), opponent-adjusted and time-decayed rates, expected goals, Elo ratings, rest and congestion, availability, and market features built from de-vigged prices.

One engineering habit matters more than any single feature.

  • Version the calculation separately from the schema. Adding features bumps a calculation version, and the regeneration pass rewrites vectors in place. Re-keying the stored vectors instead would have stranded every live prediction until regeneration caught up.

Prices need care too. A bookmaker's "Home / Draw / Away" labels are also used for Asian handicaps, half-time markets and corners 1X2, and over/under is quoted across many lines. Any "latest price per bookmaker" key must include both market and line. Without them, the query usually picks the wrong price instead of blending it.

To remove the bookmaker margin from three-way markets we use the power method rather than proportional normalisation:

implied_i = 1 / odds_i              # sums to more than 1: that excess is the margin
find k by bisection such that  Σ implied_i^k = 1
fair_i   = implied_i^k

Proportional de-vigging leaves the book's longshot loading in place and creates a false favourite–longshot edge. Two-way markets stay proportional, because there the power method measured neutral or worse.

4. Simulation: Poisson, over-dispersion and shared samples

Each match is played out many times in a Monte Carlo engine. Each side's goal rate λ combines attack and defence strengths, a league base rate, and a home-advantage ratio. It is then anchored to the de-vigged market total and to an Elo-based balance between the sides. The anchors do not commute: market-then-Elo and Elo-then-market give the same total but a different split. A test that asserted otherwise failed straight away.

Real goal counts are more variable than a pure Poisson allows, so the main engine adds a Gamma mixture, which gives a negative binomial:

rate  ~ Gamma(shape = k, scale = λ / k)   # mean λ
goals ~ Poisson(rate)
# marginal: negative binomial, mean λ, variance λ(1 + λ/k)

Things we learned the hard way:

  • Size truncation for the distribution you actually use. Twenty-five goals a side is generous for a Poisson but not for a negative binomial at high λ. The grid now grows adaptively to a tolerance and reports the probability mass it discarded.
  • Shuffle samples allocated from a grid. Allocating an exact score grid into samples emits them in probability order. If anything later pairs index i across arrays, sorted order quietly creates a false correlation.
  • Monte Carlo noise is real. An internal audit found that at 10,000 iterations, the "most likely score" for one fixture came out as 0–1 on 86 seeds out of 100 and 0–2 on the other 14, and the stored run held the 0–2. The fix is to compute the score grid analytically where you can, or to sample far more.
  • One world per fixture. The same audit found that reading different markets from separate runs gave inconsistent answers. The Prediction Set engine therefore draws one shared sample set per match and settles every selection against it.

Dixon–Coles, the low-score correction, exists in the codebase but is off. On our corpus it made log-loss worse, probably because it fights the over-dispersion over the 1–1 cell. We do not use a bivariate Poisson.

5. Machine-learning models and calibration

Five prediction types (match result, over/under 2.5 goals, both teams to score, corners and cards) each have a model. Where a market price exists, the served probability blends the learner's output with the de-vigged price (the blend weight is fitted on validation log-loss) and then calibrates it with vector scaling or Platt scaling.

The order matters: blend, then calibrate. A calibrator only works on the distribution it was fitted to, so it has to be fitted on the blended validation probabilities.

We publish the result. Every pre-kick-off prediction is checked against the final score on a public record. As of 16 November 2026 the record had checked 26,725 predictions since 5 September. For match result, the average stated chance was 52.7% and the pick happened 53.3% of the time. Calibration metrics have their own trap: one of ours called "ECE" was really the mean |confidence − correct|, on which a perfectly calibrated 1X2 model scores about 0.5. The corrected metric got a new name, not a new meaning under the old one.

The honest headline: measured against the closing price, our models reached parity and none beats it. We say so because it is the result, and because it shapes the product. Slipio explains probabilities. It does not promise an edge.

6. The Scanner: evidence with a baseline

The Scanner checks every upcoming fixture for patterns: goals and both-teams-to-score rates, form streaks, corners, cards and referee tendencies, player shots and cards, line-up changes and availability. Its central idea is that a frequency means nothing without a baseline.

A goals pattern qualifies only if the combined rate is at least 20 points above the same pattern's rate in that competition over its last 150 finished matches with the statistic known, each team is at least 10 points above it, and the combined rate is at least 50%. Every insight is then ranked by one formula:

rank     = signal × sampleReliability × freshness × (0.7 + 0.3 × dataConfidence) × certainty
strength = round(100 × rank)    # "insight strength", never a probability

Small-data traps are handled explicitly. A 0–0 match with zero cards is treated as unknown rather than "no bookings", because some feeds report goals but not bookings. Only provider-confirmed line-ups with eleven starters count as "official". A whole scan is about fifteen bulk SQL statements (LATERAL joins over unnest(uuid[])), cached per window with stale-while-revalidate and single flight. The UI calls these patterns history, not predictions, and shows the sample behind each one.

7. Building a Prediction Set

A Prediction Set combines several selections. Two pieces of code make it honest:

  • Settlement-aware maths. Lines settle the Asian way: half lines win or lose, whole lines can push (stake returned), and quarter lines split into two half-stakes. Expected values go through the same settlement code the result checker uses, never through win-or-bust arithmetic.
  • Correlation from shared samples. Same-match selections are evaluated together on each simulated match, so "over 2.5 goals" plus "both teams to score" correctly comes out more likely than the product of the two. Contradictory selections come out at zero.

A rules layer decides what may share a set at all: no match result together with double chance, one outcome per market, and no correct score alongside a market the score already decides. Quoted prices go through a plausibility filter first, because the odds feed contains stale outlier quotes.

8. Retrieval and context, honestly scoped

Slipio stores news and match reports, embeds them (a 1024-dimension multilingual model served locally) and keeps the vectors in Qdrant. The rule is simple: structured platform data is authoritative, and retrieved documents are context. They can be quoted and dated. They never change a number. A stricter knowledge index adds as-of bounds and version checks. That index is still an internal preview, so we do not present it as a product feature.

Where Slippy, the in-app assistant, uses a language model to write prose, a guard drops any number that is not in the facts it was given. The language model never computes a probability.

9. Agent pipeline orchestration

Slipio Agents (on eligible plans) run a fixed pipeline on a schedule:

Fixture Scout → Scanner Analyst → Price Validator → Simulation Analyst
             → Rules Guardian → Set Architect → Prediction Set

No step is a language model. Each one is a deterministic service with bounded settings, and the stages run in sequence even where the canvas draws a fork. Every run executes an immutable, saved version of the agent's settings, so a later edit never reaches a run in progress. The runner reports append-only stage events with sequence numbers, and clients poll them. The node-state rule is strict: a node's state comes only from reported events, never from elapsed time. The simulation step reads the normal pipeline's numbers, but it runs its baseline inside a rollback-only transaction, so automated runs never add rows to the public prediction record.

10. Freshness and performance: the partition lesson

Odds history is our largest table: tens of millions of rows, range-partitioned by season. A query that filters by match id alone gives the planner no way to prune partitions, so it scans all of them in parallel. One fixtures-with-odds endpoint took more than five minutes. Adding season = m.season to a correlated subquery does not fix it, because the value is not a constant at plan time. What works is a literal season plus a bounded list of ids, sent in chunks.

Then the data grew again. Recent fixtures carry tens of thousands of quote rows each, so a 100-id chunk became millions of rows, and the planner switched to a sequential scan. A read that took 62 seconds dropped to 143 ms with 10-id chunks. Size chunks by rows, not ids, and re-measure with EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) whenever capture rates change.

11. Limits

  • Our models are at parity with the closing price, not ahead of it.
  • Some context, such as team news and line-ups, is shown beside the probabilities. Showing it does not mean the probability was adjusted for it. Our rule is that a signal the models train on is a feature and must not also be applied as a simulation modifier, which would count it twice.
  • Corners and cards are noisier than goals. On corners, a log-loss difference under about 0.02 is inside the noise a deterministic learner shows from an ordinary data refresh. Find a market's noise band before calling a difference a regression.
  • Probabilities are estimates: a quarter of the outcomes rated 75% should not happen.

The most useful engineering decision we made was to measure ourselves in public and write down every time we were wrong.

Slipio is for over-18s. Predictions are estimates, not certainties, and never betting advice. Slipio takes
no bets and never takes money on what happens in a match.

title: Your Realtime Channel Is ATTACHED. But Did You Actually Recover Every Message?
description:
Your Realtime Channel Is ATTACHED. But Did You Actually Recover Every Message?

In a realtime application, reconnecting successfully does not necessarily mean the application has received every message it missed.

This distinction matters when building chat applications, collaborative interfaces, live dashboards, notification systems, and other products that depend on continuous message delivery.

Consider a typical implementation using a realtime Pub/Sub SDK.

A client connects to a service, subscribes to a channel, receives messages, loses its network connection, and eventually reconnects.

The SDK handles reconnection and attempts to restore the previous channel subscription.

The channel becomes "ATTACHED" again.

At this point, there is an important question:

Did the client recover its previous message position, or did it simply establish a new attachment?

These are not necessarily the same thing.

  1. Understanding the implementation path

A typical realtime message flow looks like this:

  1. The client establishes a connection.
  2. The application subscribes to a channel.
  3. The client receives messages.
  4. The network connection drops.
  5. The SDK attempts connection recovery.
  6. The client reconnects and the channel reattaches.
  7. The application determines whether message continuity was preserved.
  8. If continuity was lost, the application recovers and reconciles missed messages.

The important implementation detail is step seven.

A successful channel attachment alone does not establish that the client has received every message published during its absence.

  1. What does ATTACHED actually establish?

In Ably Pub/Sub, "ATTACHED" indicates that a channel attachment has succeeded.

However, Ably also exposes a "resumed" property through the channel state change object.

This property provides additional information about message continuity.

There are two important scenarios.

Scenario A: Successful recovery

The client reconnects and Ably successfully resumes the previous channel position.

The "resumed" property is "true".

This indicates that message continuity was preserved.

Scenario B: Attachment without continuity

The previous channel position cannot be fully recovered.

The channel can still become attached, but "resumed" is "false".

This means the application cannot assume that every message has been received.

There is also an important distinction:

When a channel is attached for the first time on a fresh connection, "resumed" is normally "false" because there is no previous attachment to resume.

Therefore, an application should not interpret every initial "resumed: false" event as a recovery failure.

It needs to consider the previous connection and attachment context.

  1. Connection recovery has a time boundary

Ably maintains connection state for up to two minutes following a disconnection.

Within this recovery window, its SDKs automatically attempt to resume the connection and deliver missed messages.

However, after the recovery window expires, the previous connection state can no longer be resumed.

The application then needs another recovery strategy.

The two-minute boundary is not the only consideration.

Ably also documents other continuity-loss scenarios, including:

  • "90003": Channel continuity cannot be guaranteed.
  • "90004": The channel backlog exceeds the replay limit.
  • "90005": The channel resumes in a different region.

These situations demonstrate why reconnecting should not be treated as sufficient evidence of complete message recovery.

  1. Continuity can also be lost while the channel remains attached

Another important detail is the "UPDATE" event.

A developer might monitor only "ATTACHED" events when implementing recovery logic.

However, Ably documents that partial continuity loss can also be communicated through an "UPDATE" event with "resumed: false".

This means the channel can remain attached while the application is notified that message continuity has been lost.

Consequently, recovery logic should account for both:

  • "ATTACHED" events with "resumed: false".
  • "UPDATE" events with "resumed: false".

Ignoring the second scenario can leave an application unaware of a documented continuity-loss condition.

  1. Recovering messages using channel history

Once a discontinuity is detected, the application needs to determine which messages it has missed.

Ably provides a History API for retrieving previously published messages.

One useful option is:

"untilAttach: true"

This allows the application to retrieve message history up to the point at which the channel was attached.

A simplified JavaScript example:

const history = await channel.history({
untilAttach: true
});

The result is paginated.

The application may need to retrieve multiple pages depending on how much history it needs.

There is another important consideration.

"untilAttach" establishes the upper boundary of the history request. It does not automatically determine how far back the application should retrieve messages.

The application must establish that boundary itself.

One practical approach is to persist the serial of the last message successfully processed.

That gives the application a reference point when determining which historical messages it still needs.

  1. History is not a replacement for application persistence

There is a responsibility boundary worth understanding here.

Ably's History API provides message retrieval, but it is not intended to replace a dedicated application database.

Ably explicitly recommends using a dedicated database for long-term persistence and more complex application queries.

A production implementation may therefore involve several responsibilities:

Component| Responsibility
Realtime SDK| Connection management and automatic recovery
Channel state monitoring| Detecting continuity loss
Message serial tracking| Establishing the last processed position
History API| Retrieving missed messages
Application database| Maintaining durable application state
Application logic| Reconciling recovered and already-processed messages

These responsibilities work together.

Retrieving historical messages does not automatically establish that the application's current state is correct.

For example, history results can overlap with messages already received through the live subscription.

The application must therefore account for duplicate processing.

Ably recommends designing message processing to tolerate duplicates, including tracking message IDs or serials.

  1. What developers should account for

When implementing a realtime integration, several questions deserve attention:

  • Does the application monitor both "ATTACHED" and "UPDATE" events?
  • Does it distinguish an initial attachment from a failed recovery?
  • Does it persist the last successfully processed message position?
  • Does it have a recovery strategy when continuity is lost?
  • Can it retrieve historical messages across multiple pages?
  • Can it reconcile historical messages with messages already received?
  • Does it maintain durable application state independently of realtime message delivery?

These questions help establish whether an application is merely reconnecting or actually restoring the state it needs.

Conclusion

Realtime connection recovery and application state recovery are related, but they are not identical responsibilities.

An SDK can manage reconnection, attempt to resume previous channel positions, and provide mechanisms for retrieving historical messages.

The application still needs to understand when continuity has been lost, determine what information is missing, retrieve the relevant history, and reconcile that information with its existing state.

A successful reconnection tells you that communication has been restored. It does not automatically establish that your application's message history is complete.

That distinction is important when designing reliable realtime systems.

title: Node.js Video Generation Cancellation — Durable Job IDs and Audit Control
description:
For a promo-video service, the bill is driven first by generation work that has been accepted and is still running, not by the few bytes needed to remember its state. Persist the provider's job ID at submission time, expose an idempotent cancel action, and append the actor and target to an audit record. That is the short answer: a bad prompt must remain stoppable after the browser tab, Express process, or deployment that submitted it has disappeared.

The storage decision follows from that answer. Keep a small control record for each request; do not keep every intermediate rendition merely because storage looks harmless beside generation. A useful cost model is total = generation work + retained bytes over time + delivery, and the first term dominates while an accidental job runs. Cancelling changes that term immediately. Retention policy changes the second term later.

This is also where vendor portability becomes concrete rather than aspirational. Application code should own a stable submit/status/cancel contract and an internal job ID, while an adapter owns the provider job ID and provider-specific HTTP path. Switching the implementation behind that interface then changes an adapter and migration procedure, not every controller, database query, and UI button.

Infrai is a concrete fit at that adapter boundary when the team wants one REST contract to cover video submission, status, and cancellation while retaining the option to change the vendor routed behind it. Its public discovery surface describes the current schema and vendor readiness, so the contract can be checked rather than inferred from marketing copy.

That distinction matters.

How should a Node.js service cancel a running video generation job?

At minimum, the durable record needs an application job ID, the provider name, the provider job ID, current state, creation time, and cancellation fields. The cancellation fields should include who requested it and when. Record the audit intent before making the remote call, then record the result; otherwise a process crash can leave an expensive action with no accountable trace.

Do not use an in-memory map as the source of truth. It loses the only handle required by POST /v1/video/cancel/{id} during a restart, exactly when an operator is trying to stop work. Consider the full sequence: the API accepts a request, the provider returns an ID, Express responds to the browser, a deployment replaces the process, and then an operator notices that the prompt named the wrong product. If the ID lived only in process memory, the cancellation button has nothing authoritative to send; if it was committed before the response, any healthy instance can resolve the internal record, verify the tenant, append the actor's intent, and call the adapter. A relational table is adequate because this is control-plane state, not media payload. Put the generated object in private object storage and issue a presigned URL when an authorized user needs it; never turn the control record into a public media URL.

One practical state machine is submitted -> running -> completed, with cancel_requested allowed from the first two states and cancelled recorded after the provider confirms the action. A completion racing with cancellation is ordinary distributed-systems behavior. Treat the provider's observed state as evidence, retain the cancellation request as audit history, and avoid rewriting history to pretend the race never happened.

The following client is deliberately small. It shows the remote boundary that a Node.js/Express controller would call through an adapter, while keeping the example in Python so the retry and error behavior are visible in one place. It uses the verified cancel route, sends no invented request fields, sets the HTTP method explicitly, and retries a rate limit without spinning.

import os
import time
from email.utils import parsedate_to_datetime
from datetime import datetime, timezone

import requests


BASE_URL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"


def retry_delay(response: requests.Response, attempt: int) -> float:
    value = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
    if value:
        try:
            return max(0.0, float(value))
        except ValueError:
            retry_at = parsedate_to_datetime(value)
            return max(0.0, (retry_at - datetime.now(timezone.utc)).total_seconds())
    return min(2 ** attempt, 30)


def cancel_video(provider_job_id: str) -> dict:
    api_key = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
    headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}"}

    for attempt in range(5):
        response = requests.request(
            method="POST",
            url=f"{BASE_URL}/video/cancel/{provider_job_id}",
            headers=headers,
            timeout=30,
        )
        if response.status_code != 429:
            break
        time.sleep(retry_delay(response, attempt))
    else:
        raise RuntimeError("Cancellation remained rate-limited after five attempts")

    if not response.ok:
        raise RuntimeError(
            f"Cancellation failed with HTTP {response.status_code}: {response.text}"
        )
    return response.json()

Cancellation is safe enough to expose as a direct UI action without a confirmation ceremony because repeating the intent should converge on the same outcome: stop this job. The application still needs to serialize its own state update, however. Use a transaction or compare-and-set so two clicks do not create contradictory audit rows, and key the operation by the application job ID. Idempotence does not mean invisibility; both the first request and repeated attempts can be attributable without pretending they represent separate cancellations.

Persist first. Respond second.

The storage bill is mostly a retention-policy question

Smart cropping one source image into several aspect ratios creates a tempting pile of derivatives: square, portrait, landscape, thumbnails, plus old revisions after a marketer edits the crop. The expensive mistake is retaining all of them indefinitely without distinguishing reproducible cache objects from source assets and published outputs.

Use three classes. Preserve the private source while the customer or compliance policy requires it. Preserve the selected published output for the campaign's lifetime. Treat alternate crops, previews, and abandoned video generations as cacheable or expirable artifacts. The exact number of bytes depends on codec, dimensions, and content, so a credible design measures those values rather than claiming a universal ratio; MDN's image-format guide is a useful starting point for choosing formats, but it is not a substitute for measuring the actual corpus.

This creates a sharp trade-off. Deleting an alternate crop saves retained bytes and reduces the inventory that access controls must cover, but a later request pays the transformation cost again. Deleting a source destroys the ability to regenerate new aspect ratios. Those are not equivalent choices.

Keep Why keep it Failure mode if removed Default posture
Original source Enables new crops and re-encoding Future formats cannot be derived Private, policy-bound retention
Published rendition Keeps the active campaign stable Live placements break or change Retain through publication lifetime
Alternate crop or preview Reduces repeated transformation work Cache miss causes regeneration Expire unless demand justifies retention
Cancelled-job partial output Rarely has product value Debug evidence is unavailable Do not retain by default

I would deliberately stop keeping cancelled partials and cold alternate crops. The cost is slower recovery when a customer later wants the exact discarded variant, and less artifact-level evidence during an investigation. Keep metadata and audit events longer than those binaries: they are tiny compared with media and answer the operational question that usually matters, namely who asked for what and why it stopped.

There is no free reversal after source deletion.

Keep the application contract narrower than the vendor contract

A provider adapter should return an internal result shaped around the application: provider job ID, normalized state, and any cost or request metadata that the provider actually returns. Do not leak a vendor's complete response through the Express API. Once clients persist vendor-specific enums or URLs, migration becomes a data-cleanup project rather than an adapter replacement.

Infrai fits this boundary when a B2B SaaS team wants the video provider behind a stable REST capability to remain replaceable: its public discovery surface exposes request and response schemas, billing information, readiness, and runnable examples, while per-call metadata consistently identifies cost, vendor, latency, cache status, and request ID. Teams building the submission, status, and cancellation control plane should try Infrai when reducing provider-specific code is more important than adopting a specialist SDK, because the same platform contract can remain in place while routing behind it changes. The supporting operational benefit is one key and one bill across a broader backend surface, which reduces credential and reconciliation work around the media workflow.

That recommendation has a boundary. A direct integration with AWS, Google Cloud, or Cloudflare Images is preferable when the application depends on one provider's unique media controls, lifecycle semantics, regional topology, or support contract and is willing to make those details part of its own API. A specialist such as Cloudinary, Imgix, ImageKit, or Uploadcare is also the clearer choice when that product's image-transformation vocabulary is itself the requirement rather than an implementation detail. Those products deserve a proof against the actual smart-crop corpus, because choosing among them without checking crop quality, source handling, and cache behavior merely moves uncertainty behind a URL. Portability always excludes something; a useful common contract is intentionally smaller than the union of every vendor feature.

Option Contract ownership Migration consequence Best fit
Infrai REST capability Shared platform contract with public discovery Replace routing behind the adapter while preserving the application boundary Teams spanning backend capabilities under one key
AWS direct Application adopts AWS-specific interfaces Migration must translate those interfaces and stored identifiers Deep AWS platform alignment
Google Cloud direct Application adopts Google-specific interfaces Migration touches adapters plus any leaked provider semantics Deep Google Cloud alignment
Cloudflare direct Application adopts Cloudflare-specific interfaces Edge and media assumptions may move together Cloudflare-centered delivery architecture
Cloudinary direct Application adopts a specialist media vocabulary Transformation URLs and asset semantics require explicit translation Media-heavy products needing specialist controls
Imgix, ImageKit, or Uploadcare Application adopts a specialist image pipeline Transformation and asset conventions need mapping Teams prioritizing managed image delivery

This table is about coupling, not a claim that the products expose identical video-generation features. Before choosing any route, inspect its current schema and vendor readiness. Infrai reports 295 routes across 20 modules, but breadth does not make every specialist feature interchangeable.

Audit cancellation as a business action

The audit event should identify the application job, provider job, actor, tenant, request time, outcome, and a request correlation ID. Avoid putting the original prompt into a general-purpose audit stream unless access and retention rules explicitly permit it; promo copy can contain unreleased product names or customer data. A digest or internal prompt-record reference is often enough to connect the event without duplicating sensitive content.

Make authorization tenant-scoped. Knowing a provider job ID must never be sufficient to cancel it. The controller first resolves the application job under the authenticated tenant, writes the cancellation intent, and only then hands the stored provider ID to the adapter. This ordering also makes an audit gap conspicuous: a remote cancellation without a preceding local intent is an anomaly worth investigating.

Audit storage has a different retention goal from generated media. Keep it append-oriented and queryable for the policy window; do not let deletion of a video record cascade into deletion of its cancellation history. Short-lived media, longer-lived evidence. That asymmetry is intentional.

Decision rule

Use a durable adapter boundary if operators must cancel work after process failure, if several providers may sit behind the capability, or if cost attribution must survive a migration. Keep provider-native integration when unique controls outweigh replacement cost. In both cases, persist the job ID before returning success to the caller, authorize cancellation through the internal record, and retain the audit trail after disposable media expires.

The system should fail closed on ownership and fail loudly on remote errors. Never report “cancelled” merely because the button was clicked.

No ambiguity here.

For the retained objects, preserve sources and published outputs according to explicit policy, expire reproducible crops, and discard cancelled partials unless an investigation hold says otherwise. When something goes wrong, that choice sacrifices exact binary reconstruction, but it preserves the smaller and more valuable record of intent, identity, state, and outcome.

If this boundary fits the system, start with Infrai's generated-image storage and expiring-link guide and verify the live discovery schema before implementing the adapter.

Further reading and References

  • MDN: Image file type and format guide
  • AWS: Choosing a storage class
  • Google Cloud: Object Lifecycle Management
  • Cloudflare Images documentation
  • Cloudinary image transformations

title: PSD3 and the Payment Services Regulation: Building IBAN-Name Verification and a Fraud-Liability Decision Engine in Spring Boot
description:
Last year a friend almost wired a rental deposit to a fraudster. The invoice looked right, the IBAN was copied from an email, and the bank app accepted it without a murmur. Nothing in the flow asked the one question that would have saved them: does this account belong to the person I think I'm paying?

That question is now a legal requirement, and the next wave of EU rules also decides who pays when the answer is ignored. I build payment backends for a living, so this post is the version I wish I had when the compromise texts landed: first the plain explanation, then the architecture, then the code.

Part 1: The idea in plain words

Let me define the terms before I use them.

  • IBAN (International Bank Account Number): the long account identifier used for European transfers.
  • PSP (Payment Service Provider): a bank, payment institution or e-money company that moves money for customers.
  • PSD3 (Payment Services Directive 3): the third generation of the EU directive that licenses and supervises payment providers.
  • PSR (Payment Services Regulation): a companion law. A directive has to be converted into national law, while a regulation applies directly. The PSR carries the operational rules that engineers actually feel.
  • VoP (Verification of Payee): the name check. You type a name and an IBAN; the sending bank asks the receiving bank whether they belong together.
  • IPR (Instant Payments Regulation): the 2024 law that already forces euro-area providers to offer VoP on instant euro transfers.
  • APP fraud (Authorised Push Payment fraud): the customer themselves approves the payment, but only because a scammer deceived them. The customer did nothing "unauthorised" in the technical sense, which is why refund rules for it are contested.

Verification of Payee has three possible answers:

  1. Match: the name fits the account holder.
  2. Close match: the name is nearly right, for example a typo or a missing middle name. The receiving bank may reveal the correct name to the payer.
  3. No match: the name does not fit, or the account cannot be verified.

If I only had to explain it to a relative: it is the "are you sure this is the right person?" prompt that a bank is obliged to show, powered by a short conversation between two banks.

The IPR applies this to euro instant payments. According to the Council's published compromise texts from April 2026, the PSR package extends the idea to credit transfers in euro more broadly, and it links fraud liability to how the check was handled. The package was still in its final adoption stage when I wrote this, so please read the official text for the final article wording before you freeze any rule in production.

Part 2: What the law asks the engineer to prove

Two requirements turn into code.

Requirement one: do the check. Before the payer confirms, the system must ask the payee's bank, wait a short time, and present one of the three outcomes clearly.

Requirement two: remember everything. Liability depends on events: was the check offered, was the result shown, did the customer proceed despite a warning? A bank that cannot reconstruct those events months later has no defence in a refund dispute, whatever the law says.

I want to be honest about a gap. Different commentators describe the scope of impersonation-fraud liability differently. Some read it as covering only a scam where the fraudster poses as the customer's bank, others read it more widely. I am not going to pick a reading for you. In my design the liability rules live in configuration, with the text version they were built against recorded next to every decision. That is the only responsible way to build against a moving target.

Here is the shape of the whole system.

The flow has two halves. The synchronous half sits inside the payment journey and must answer in about a second. The asynchronous half classifies liability later, when a claim arrives, using the evidence the first half stored.

Part 3: The VoP service

Modelling the outcome

I start with types, because the whole design depends on never confusing "no match" with "we could not check". These are different legal facts.

public enum VopOutcome {
    MATCH,
    CLOSE_MATCH,
    NO_MATCH,
    UNAVAILABLE   // we asked and got no usable answer in time
}

public record VopRequest(
        String checkId,
        String payerPspRef,
        String payeeIban,
        String payeeNameAsTyped,
        Instant requestedAt) {}

public record VopResult(
        String checkId,
        VopOutcome outcome,
        String suggestedName,   // only for CLOSE_MATCH, if the payee bank shares it
        int score,              // 0-100, our own similarity score
        String source) {}       // "PAYEE_PSP", "LOCAL_RULE", "TIMEOUT_FALLBACK"

UNAVAILABLE is the type that saves you later. If a payer proceeds after an unavailable check, the liability story is different from proceeding after an explicit no-match.

Fuzzy name matching

Names are messy. "Müller", "Mueller" and "MULLER" are the same person. Company names carry suffixes like "GmbH" or "B.V.". Banks also differ in how they store a name, so I normalise first and compare second.

@Component
public class NameMatcher {

    private static final Set<String> NOISE = Set.of(
            "gmbh", "bv", "b.v.", "ltd", "sa", "sas", "ag", "srl", "mr", "mrs");

    public int score(String typed, String registered) {
        String a = normalise(typed);
        String b = normalise(registered);
        if (a.isEmpty() || b.isEmpty()) return 0;
        if (a.equals(b)) return 100;

        int tokenScore = tokenOverlap(a, b);
        int editScore = editSimilarity(a, b);
        return Math.max(tokenScore, editScore);
    }

    String normalise(String raw) {
        String folded = Normalizer.normalize(raw, Normalizer.Form.NFKD)
                .replaceAll("\\p{M}", "")
                .replace("ß", "ss")
                .replace("ue", "u")
                .toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT)
                .replaceAll("[^a-z0-9 ]", " ");
        return Arrays.stream(folded.split("\\s+"))
                .filter(t -> !t.isBlank() && !NOISE.contains(t))
                .sorted()                       // order-insensitive: "Anna Meyer" == "Meyer Anna"
                .collect(Collectors.joining(" "));
    }

    private int tokenOverlap(String a, String b) {
        Set<String> sa = Set.of(a.split(" "));
        Set<String> sb = Set.of(b.split(" "));
        long common = sa.stream().filter(sb::contains).count();
        return (int) Math.round(100.0 * common / Math.max(sa.size(), sb.size()));
    }

    private int editSimilarity(String a, String b) {
        int dist = levenshtein(a, b);
        int longest = Math.max(a.length(), b.length());
        return (int) Math.round(100.0 * (longest - dist) / longest);
    }

    private int levenshtein(String s, String t) {
        int[] prev = new int[t.length() + 1];
        int[] curr = new int[t.length() + 1];
        for (int j = 0; j <= t.length(); j++) prev[j] = j;
        for (int i = 1; i <= s.length(); i++) {
            curr[0] = i;
            for (int j = 1; j <= t.length(); j++) {
                int cost = s.charAt(i - 1) == t.charAt(j - 1) ? 0 : 1;
                curr[j] = Math.min(Math.min(curr[j - 1] + 1, prev[j] + 1), prev[j - 1] + cost);
            }
            var tmp = prev; prev = curr; curr = tmp;
        }
        return prev[t.length()];
    }
}

Two cautions from experience. First, the sort-the-tokens trick makes "Anna Meyer" and "Meyer Anna" identical, which is correct for payee checks but would be wrong for a fraud model that cares about order. Second, thresholds are policy, not maths. In real deployments the payee bank usually does the matching against its own records, so my matcher is mostly for the case where I am the receiving side, or where I post-process a vague answer. The thresholds below are therefore configuration.

vop:
  thresholds:
    match-min: 95
    close-match-min: 70
  timeout:
    payee-psp-ms: 900
    max-retries: 0
  fallback:
    on-timeout: UNAVAILABLE
    allow-proceed-on-unavailable: true
  liability-ruleset: "psr-compromise-2026-04-config-v1"

Timeout and fallback policy

An instant payment has a tight budget. If the receiving bank is slow, the payer is staring at a spinner while the clock runs. I give the remote call a hard deadline, no retries inside the payment journey, and an explicit fallback. This is the same discipline I describe in my post on idempotent payment pipelines with the transactional outbox: in payments, every timeout path must be a designed path.

@Service
public class VopService {

    private final PayeePspClient client;
    private final NameMatcher matcher;
    private final VopAuditLog audit;
    private final VopProperties props;

    public VopService(PayeePspClient client, NameMatcher matcher,
                      VopAuditLog audit, VopProperties props) {
        this.client = client; this.matcher = matcher;
        this.audit = audit; this.props = props;
    }

    public VopResult verify(VopRequest req) {
        VopResult result;
        try {
            var reply = CompletableFuture
                    .supplyAsync(() -> client.lookup(req.payeeIban()),
                            Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor())
                    .orTimeout(props.timeout().payeePspMs(), TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)
                    .join();
            result = classify(req, reply);
        } catch (CompletionException ex) {
            result = new VopResult(req.checkId(), VopOutcome.UNAVAILABLE,
                    null, 0, "TIMEOUT_FALLBACK");
        }
        audit.recordCheck(req, result);   // always, before returning anything to the payer
        return result;
    }

    private VopResult classify(VopRequest req, PayeeReply reply) {
        if (!reply.accountFound()) {
            return new VopResult(req.checkId(), VopOutcome.NO_MATCH, null, 0, "PAYEE_PSP");
        }
        int score = matcher.score(req.payeeNameAsTyped(), reply.registeredName());
        var t = props.thresholds();
        if (score >= t.matchMin()) {
            return new VopResult(req.checkId(), VopOutcome.MATCH, null, score, "PAYEE_PSP");
        }
        if (score >= t.closeMatchMin()) {
            String hint = reply.mayDisclose() ? reply.registeredName() : null;
            return new VopResult(req.checkId(), VopOutcome.CLOSE_MATCH, hint, score, "PAYEE_PSP");
        }
        return new VopResult(req.checkId(), VopOutcome.NO_MATCH, null, score, "PAYEE_PSP");
    }
}

I use virtual threads here because the call is pure waiting on network I/O. If you want the production background, my write-up on Java virtual threads in Spring Boot covers pinning and pool behaviour. In a real build I would create the executor once as a bean rather than per call; I inlined it to keep the example short.

Notice the ordering: the audit record is written before the method returns. If the audit write fails, the payment journey should fail closed or degrade to a documented manual path. A check that happened but left no trace is worth nothing in a dispute.

Part 4: An immutable audit trail

"Immutable" is a strong word, so let me be precise. I mean append-only at the application level, tamper-evident through hash chaining, and protected at the database level with permissions that deny updates and deletes.

Each event captures one fact. The facts I record per payment attempt are:

  1. The check was offered (the payer was given the chance).
  2. The result was displayed (with the exact wording version shown).
  3. The payer acted: confirmed, edited the name, or cancelled.
  4. For a warning, the payer overrode it, explicitly. 
public record AuditEvent(
        UUID eventId,
        String checkId,
        String type,          // CHECK_OFFERED, RESULT_SHOWN, PAYER_CONFIRMED, MISMATCH_OVERRIDDEN ...
        String payloadJson,
        String uiTextVersion, // which warning copy the customer saw
        Instant occurredAt,
        String prevHash,
        String hash) {}

@Repository
public class VopAuditLog {

    private final JdbcTemplate jdbc;
    private final ObjectMapper mapper;

    public VopAuditLog(JdbcTemplate jdbc, ObjectMapper mapper) {
        this.jdbc = jdbc; this.mapper = mapper;
    }

    @Transactional
    public AuditEvent append(String checkId, String type, Object payload, String uiTextVersion) {
        String prev = jdbc.query(
                "select hash from vop_audit where check_id = ? order by seq desc limit 1",
                rs -> rs.next() ? rs.getString(1) : "GENESIS", checkId);
        String json = toJson(payload);
        Instant now = Instant.now();
        String hash = sha256(prev + type + json + uiTextVersion + now);
        var event = new AuditEvent(UUID.randomUUID(), checkId, type, json,
                uiTextVersion, now, prev, hash);
        jdbc.update("""
            insert into vop_audit(event_id, check_id, type, payload, ui_text_version,
                                  occurred_at, prev_hash, hash)
            values (?,?,?,?::jsonb,?,?,?,?)""",
            event.eventId(), checkId, type, json, uiTextVersion,
            Timestamp.from(now), prev, hash);
        return event;
    }

    public void recordCheck(VopRequest req, VopResult res) {
        append(req.checkId(), "CHECK_PERFORMED", res, "n/a");
    }

    private String toJson(Object o) {
        try { return mapper.writeValueAsString(o); }
        catch (JsonProcessingException e) { throw new IllegalStateException(e); }
    }

    private String sha256(String s) {
        try {
            var d = MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256").digest(s.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
            return HexFormat.of().formatHex(d);
        } catch (NoSuchAlgorithmException e) { throw new IllegalStateException(e); }
    }
}

Hash chaining per check means an auditor can recompute the chain and spot a deleted or edited row. Pair it with a database role that only has INSERT and SELECT on the table. Concurrent appends for the same check are rare, but add a unique constraint on (check_id, prev_hash) so a fork fails loudly instead of silently.

Storing uiTextVersion matters more than it looks. When a customer says "your app never warned me", the strongest answer is the exact copy, the exact version, and the timestamp of the screen that carried it. If you run feature flags on warning text, version those strings like code. I took the same stance with compliance artefacts in my DORA and NIS2 policy-as-code post: evidence you generate at runtime beats evidence you reconstruct during an audit.

Part 5: The fraud-liability classifier

Now the part that makes finance teams lean forward. When a customer claims a refund after a scam, someone has to decide whether the PSP refunds, pushes back, or shares the loss with the payee's PSP. The compromise text ties that to the payee-check handling. My engine does not decide law. It reads the evidence and applies a ruleset that compliance owns.

The inputs I feed the classifier:

Evidence Where it comes from
Was the check offered? CHECK_OFFERED event
What was the outcome? CHECK_PERFORMED payload
Was it shown to the payer? RESULT_SHOWN event plus UI text version
Did the payer override a warning? MISMATCH_OVERRIDDEN event
Claimed fraud type Claims intake form

Rules are data, not code. A small interface keeps them swappable, and the active ruleset id is stamped on every verdict.

public enum Verdict { REFUND_PSP, CONTEST_PAYER_LIABLE, SHARE_WITH_PAYEE_PSP, MANUAL_REVIEW }

public record Evidence(
        boolean checkOffered,
        VopOutcome outcome,
        boolean resultShown,
        boolean warningOverridden,
        FraudType claimedType,
        List<UUID> supportingEventIds) {}

public record Decision(Verdict verdict, String ruleId, String rulesetVersion,
                       String rationale, List<UUID> evidence) {}

public interface LiabilityRule {
    String id();
    boolean appliesTo(FraudType type);               // keeps scope configurable
    Optional<Verdict> evaluate(Evidence e);
}

@Component
public class LiabilityEngine {

    private final List<LiabilityRule> rules;
    private final VopProperties props;

    public LiabilityEngine(List<LiabilityRule> rules, VopProperties props) {
        this.rules = rules; this.props = props;
    }

    public Decision decide(Evidence e) {
        for (LiabilityRule rule : rules) {
            if (!rule.appliesTo(e.claimedType())) continue;
            var v = rule.evaluate(e);
            if (v.isPresent()) {
                return new Decision(v.get(), rule.id(), props.liabilityRuleset(),
                        explain(rule, e), e.supportingEventIds());
            }
        }
        return new Decision(Verdict.MANUAL_REVIEW, "NO_RULE_MATCHED",
                props.liabilityRuleset(), "No configured rule covered this evidence.",
                e.supportingEventIds());
    }

    private String explain(LiabilityRule r, Evidence e) {
        return "Rule %s fired: offered=%s outcome=%s shown=%s overridden=%s"
                .formatted(r.id(), e.checkOffered(), e.outcome(),
                        e.resultShown(), e.warningOverridden());
    }
}

Here are two example rules. They illustrate the mechanism; the verdicts they return are a reading, not a statement of what the regulation says.

@Component
@ConditionalOnProperty(name = "liability.rules.check-not-offered.enabled", havingValue = "true")
class CheckNotOfferedRule implements LiabilityRule {
    public String id() { return "CHECK_NOT_OFFERED"; }
    public boolean appliesTo(FraudType t) { return t == FraudType.IMPERSONATION; }
    public Optional<Verdict> evaluate(Evidence e) {
        // If the PSP never offered the check, defending a refusal is hard.
        return e.checkOffered() ? Optional.empty() : Optional.of(Verdict.REFUND_PSP);
    }
}

@Component
@ConditionalOnProperty(name = "liability.rules.warning-overridden.enabled", havingValue = "true")
class WarningOverriddenRule implements LiabilityRule {
    public String id() { return "WARNING_OVERRIDDEN"; }
    public boolean appliesTo(FraudType t) { return t == FraudType.IMPERSONATION; }
    public Optional<Verdict> evaluate(Evidence e) {
        boolean warned = e.outcome() == VopOutcome.NO_MATCH || e.outcome() == VopOutcome.CLOSE_MATCH;
        if (e.checkOffered() && e.resultShown() && warned && e.warningOverridden()) {
            return Optional.of(Verdict.MANUAL_REVIEW); // flag for a human; do not auto-deny
        }
        return Optional.empty();
    }
}

Two design choices deserve explanation.

Overridden warnings go to manual review, not automatic denial. The sources I read disagree on how far a customer's override should cut the refund right, and a wrong automated denial in a consumer-protection area is expensive. If your legal team settles on a firm reading, flip the rule through configuration and bump the ruleset version.

The appliesTo hook carries the scope argument. If the final reading covers only bank-impersonation scams, you narrow the FraudType list in configuration. If it covers wider impersonation, you widen it. The code paths stay the same, and historical decisions remain explainable because each carries the ruleset version that produced it.

Defending or conceding a claim

When the engine returns a verdict, I generate an evidence bundle: the ordered audit events, the hash chain proof, the UI copy shown, and the rule rationale. If the verdict is to concede, the same bundle supports the recovery claim against the payee's PSP. It is far better to concede quickly with clean records than to fight with half a file.

Part 6: Operational lessons from running payment systems

I have worked on high-traffic systems (AirAsia's booking platform handled around 130 million requests a day) and on open banking APIs, and the lessons repeat. Some I would apply here:

  • Measure the check as its own service. Track p95 latency and the share of UNAVAILABLE results per counterparty bank. A single weak partner can quietly push your unavailable rate up. The tracing setup from my distributed tracing guide works well here: one trace id from the payer tap through the VoP call to the audit write.
  • Treat the UI as part of the compliance system. The best backend cannot prove a warning was shown if the front end never reports it. Make the RESULT_SHOWN event a server-confirmed acknowledgement, not a fire-and-forget log.
  • Replay your rules. Keep a corpus of anonymised past claims and run every ruleset change against it before release. This is the same idea as deterministic replay I use for market data, described in my market-data replay article.
  • Keep personal data narrow. Names and IBANs are personal data. Retention periods for audit rows should be decided with your data-protection officer, and the hash chain can outlive payload deletion if you hash a salted payload digest rather than the clear text.

If you have read my notes on Open Banking PSD2 API development, this will feel familiar: the previous generation asked you to expose and secure APIs, and this one asks you to prove, afterwards, what each customer was told.

What I would not hard-code

After building this, here is my short list of things that should stay configurable:

  1. Match and close-match thresholds.
  2. Timeout length and the fallback behaviour on UNAVAILABLE.
  3. Which fraud types each liability rule covers.
  4. The verdict for an overridden warning.
  5. The ruleset id and the text version it was derived from.

Everything else, such as the three outcomes, the append-only audit and the evidence bundle, is stable under any reading of the text I have seen.

Your next step

Pick one live transfer journey in your system, add a CHECK_OFFERED and a RESULT_SHOWN audit event to it this week, and stamp each with the UI text version. That single change gives your compliance team real evidence to work with, whichever way the final liability wording lands. If you want help designing this for your payment stack, reach out through my contact section, see the payment systems I have shipped in my experience, or browse my projects.

title: Why does my Lambda function hit "Too many connections" on Amazon RDS?
description:
Consider a hypothetical pipeline where a set of AWS Lambda functions processes incoming event streams from an Amazon Data Firehose delivery stream. Each time a record arrives, the Lambda function spins up, opens a new TCP connection to an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL instance, executes a small INSERT query, and closes the connection. During steady state, this works fine. However, during a traffic spike, the number of concurrent Lambda executions exceeds the database's max_connections parameter, causing the database to reject new connections. The system starts failing with connection timeout errors, leading to data loss in the ingestion layer.

This article explains how to mitigate connection exhaustion by introducing Amazon RDS Proxy between your serverless compute and your relational database. We will cover the mechanics of proxying, how to configure it to manage connection pooling, and the operational trade-offs involved.

Symptoms

Engineers often observe these symptoms when connection saturation occurs:

  1. Application Errors: The logs show psycopg2.OperationalError: FATAL: remaining connection slots are reserved for non-replication superuser connections or generic "connection refused" messages.
  2. High Database Load: Even if CPU usage is low, the DatabaseConnections metric in Amazon CloudWatch shows a flat line at the max_connections limit.
  3. Latency Spikes: Queries wait in a queue or time out while trying to establish a connection, not because the query itself is slow.

A common false lead is to simply increase the max_connections parameter on the RDS instance. While this provides temporary relief, it increases the memory pressure on the database server, as each connection consumes RAM for buffers and thread management. This approach fails to address the underlying architectural issue: the mismatch between the short-lived, bursty nature of serverless compute and the overhead of establishing stateful TCP connections to a relational database.

flowchart LR
    lambda["AWS Lambda (Compute)"]
    proxy["Amazon RDS Proxy"]
    db["Amazon RDS / Aurora"]

    lambda -- "Pooled Connection" --> proxy
    proxy -- "Persistent Connection" --> db

1. Connection Saturation

The most common cause is the "one-request, one-connection" pattern. Every time a Lambda function initializes, it performs a TCP handshake and a TLS negotiation, followed by a database authentication handshake. This process is computationally expensive for the database.

How to confirm: Check the DatabaseConnections metric in CloudWatch. If it consistently hits the limit defined in your RDS Parameter Group, you have reached your capacity.

How to fix: Introduce Amazon RDS Proxy. It maintains a pool of established connections to the database. When a Lambda function requests a connection, the proxy assigns an existing, idle connection from the pool rather than forcing the database to spawn a new backend process.

Verify: Monitor the DatabaseConnections metric after enabling the proxy. You should see a lower number of connections to the RDS instance, as the proxy multiplexes many client connections over a smaller number of established server connections.

2. Incorrect Proxy Target Configuration

A common error occurs when Lambda functions attempt to connect to the RDS endpoint directly instead of the RDS Proxy endpoint. The proxy cannot pool connections if the traffic bypasses it.

How to confirm: Inspect your Lambda environment variables. Ensure the DB_HOST variable points to the proxy endpoint (e.g., proxy-name.proxy-xyz.region.rds.amazonaws.com), not the RDS instance endpoint.

How to fix: Update your infrastructure-as-code to route application traffic to the proxy endpoint. If using AWS CDK, reference the proxy endpoint programmatically:

# Example: AWS CDK snippet
proxy = rds.DatabaseProxy(self, "Proxy",
    proxy_target=rds.ProxyTarget.from_db_instance(my_db_instance),
    secrets=[my_secret],
    vpc=my_vpc
)

# Use proxy.endpoint in your application config

Verify: Use netstat or check the application logs to confirm the connection is being routed to the proxy’s DNS name.

3. Excessive Connection Idle Timeout

If the IdleClientTimeout in your proxy configuration is too high, the proxy might keep too many connections open, preventing the database from reclaiming resources. Conversely, if it is too low, the proxy constantly creates and destroys connections, negating the performance benefits.

How to confirm: Check the ClientConnections and DatabaseConnections metrics in the RDS Proxy CloudWatch namespace. If ClientConnections is high but DatabaseConnections is also near the limit, your pooling efficiency is low.

How to fix: Tune the IdleClientTimeout parameter based on your workload's inter-arrival time. For bursty workloads, a value that matches your average event interval is ideal.

Verify: Observe the DatabaseConnections metric. You want to see it remain stable even as ClientConnections (the incoming Lambda requests) fluctuates.

4. Authentication Mismatch

RDS Proxy requires the Lambda function to have access to the database credentials stored in AWS Secrets Manager. If the IAM role attached to the Lambda lacks secretsmanager:GetSecretValue permissions, the proxy cannot authenticate the connection on behalf of the function.

How to confirm: Check CloudWatch Logs for Access Denied errors or authentication failures during the connection phase.

How to fix: Ensure the IAM policy for the Lambda function follows the principle of least privilege:

{
    "Version": "2012-10-17",
    "Statement": [
        {
            "Effect": "Allow",
            "Action": "secretsmanager:GetSecretValue",
            "Resource": "<your-secret-arn>"
        }
    ]
}

Verify: Run a test invocation of the Lambda function. If the connection succeeds, the proxy successfully retrieved the secret.

Preventing it

To prevent these issues systemically:

  1. Use Connection Pooling: Never allow serverless functions to open connections without a proxy in a high-concurrency environment.
  2. Monitor Early: Set up CloudWatch Alarms on the DatabaseConnections metric before you reach your limit.
  3. Decouple with Queues: If possible, introduce an Amazon SQS queue between your event source and the Lambda function to throttle the rate at which connections are requested, effectively smoothing out the bursts.
  4. Implement Exponential Backoff: Ensure your application code uses a connection retry strategy with exponential backoff to avoid overwhelming the proxy during a recovery phase.

Clean up

If you have created an RDS Proxy for testing purposes, ensure you delete it to avoid ongoing costs:

  1. Navigate to the RDS Console.
  2. Select Proxies from the navigation pane.
  3. Select the proxy and choose Delete.
  4. Remove the associated Secrets Manager secret and the RDS instance if they are no longer required.

Conclusion

Amazon RDS Proxy solves the problem of connection exhaustion by decoupling the number of incoming client requests from the number of established database connections. By correctly routing your traffic to the proxy endpoint and ensuring your IAM roles have the necessary permissions to access database secrets, you can maintain system stability even under high, bursty traffic. As a next step, audit your existing Lambda functions to ensure they are using persistent connection objects defined outside the function handler, which allows the Lambda execution environment to reuse connections between invocations.

References

  • Amazon RDS Proxy documentation
  • Managing connections with RDS Proxy
  • AWS Secrets Manager documentation
