title: The 8.9% you publish: auditing a visibility gate that is statistically indistinguishable from random
description:
Every prediction platform grows a gate. Not the model — the filter after the model, the code deciding which predictions the public may see. Ours is one boolean, is_visible, on a table with 47,150 rows. 8.98% are visible; the other 91% are computed, stored, graded, and hidden.

A gate is a claim: the rows I publish are better than the rows I suppress. That claim is testable. Almost nobody tests it. This is the audit, run against production data — including the part where the gate fails.

The setup: six gate-related columns, three of them dead

ai_predictions holds one row per model per match. Columns that look like they participate in the publish decision:

is_visible          boolean   47,150 populated
rec_level           varchar   46,721 populated   (A/B/C/D)
bet_worthiness      smallint  21,002 populated   (1..8)
veto_reason         text      10,223 populated
gate_reason         text           0 populated
gate_want_visible   boolean        0 populated
direction_gate      varchar        0 populated

Three of six are NULL on every row. That is the first finding — gate_want_visible at 0% occupancy says the gate was refactored and the audit trail did not survive. veto_reason survives on 10,223 rows, which is a reason code we can work with.

Baseline: 47,150 rows, 46,996 settled, 46,877 graded, 26,773 hits (57.11%), 3,796 models, 16,898 matches.

Step 1 — the pooled comparison, and why it is nearly useless

Start with the obvious query — the one that will mislead you.

SELECT is_visible,
       count(*)                                              AS n,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE hit)                            AS hits,
       round(100.0 * count(*) FILTER (WHERE hit)
             / nullif(count(*) FILTER (WHERE hit IS NOT NULL), 0), 2) AS hit_pct
FROM ai_predictions
WHERE hit IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY 1;

is_visible | n     | hits  | hit_pct
false      | 42684 | 24360 | 57.07
true       |  4231 |  2413 | 57.53

A lift of +0.48pp. With 4,231 published rows against 42,684 suppressed, the standard error of that difference is 0.80pp, so z = 0.60. Wilson intervals: visible 56.05–59.04, hidden 56.60–57.54 — overlapping across almost their entire width.

The gate's output is not measurably different from its own reject pile. Publish a random 8.9% sample instead and you would land within noise of what the gate actually publishes.

Two caveats. The gate need not be useless to produce this number — only diffuse: 4,231 rows from 543 models, selected by a mechanism that varies per model, pool flat even if each local gate works. And the audit was possible only because 42,684 of 42,918 suppressed rows (99.45%) were graded. Stop grading what you hide and the gate becomes unfalsifiable.

Step 2 — stratify by model, and watch the sign flip

The pooled query collapsed 3,796 models into one number. Redo it per model, keeping only models that publish some and suppress some — else it degrades to "always shows" vs "never shows".

WITH per_model AS (
  SELECT model_id,
         count(*) FILTER (WHERE hit IS NOT NULL AND is_visible)    AS vis_graded,
         count(*) FILTER (WHERE hit AND is_visible)                 AS vis_hits,
         count(*) FILTER (WHERE hit IS NOT NULL AND NOT is_visible) AS hid_graded,
         count(*) FILTER (WHERE hit AND NOT is_visible)             AS hid_hits
  FROM ai_predictions
  GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT count(*)                                                   AS models_compared,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE hid_hits * 1.0 / hid_graded
                          > vis_hits * 1.0 / vis_graded)          AS gate_is_worse,
       round(avg((vis_hits * 1.0 / vis_graded
                - hid_hits * 1.0 / hid_graded) * 100), 2)         AS mean_lift_pp
FROM per_model
WHERE vis_graded >= 5 AND hid_graded >= 5;

models_compared | gate_is_worse | mean_lift_pp
218             | 146           | -7.92

On 146 of 218 models, the published rows are worse than the hidden ones. Mean per-model lift is −7.92pp. Across the 194 models publishing at least 5 graded rows, visible rows average 56.05% and their suppressed siblings average 63.15%.

This is Simpson's paradox, and it is why a pooled gate audit is worthless. The pooled number looks fine only because visible rows are unevenly distributed: 387 of the 675 models with ≥20 graded rows (57.3%) never publish a single row, contributing zero to the "visible" bucket. The pooled average is a weighted sum whose weights have nothing to do with the gate's competence.

Step 3 — the tier system does not rank what it claims to rank

rec_level is the human-facing grade: A strongest, D weakest. It is populated on 46,721 rows.

rec_level graded rows hit % 95% Wilson published share
A 1,052 52.95 49.93–55.95 15.97%
B 2,027 63.15 61.06–65.19 14.41%
C 15,859 57.66 56.91–58.41 9.46%
D 27,514 56.56 56.00–57.12 7.78%

A is the worst grade in the table — 3.61pp below D, z = −2.31, p ≈ 0.021. B is the best, 6.6pp over A. The ordering is B > C > D > A: rec_level does not encode "how likely this row is to be right", and 1,052 rows carry the strongest label while being the weakest cohort.

Now the gate's behaviour inside each tier:

tier published hit % suppressed hit % gate lift
A 58.33 (n=168) 51.92 (n=884) +6.41pp
B 62.33 (n=292) 63.29 (n=1,735) −0.96pp
C 57.50 (n=1,501) 57.68 (n=14,358) −0.18pp
D 56.14 (n=2,141) 56.60 (n=25,373) −0.46pp

Inside tier A the gate works. Inside B, C and D it does not. And the published mix is 168 A / 292 B / 1,501 C / 2,141 D — 86.86% of published rows come from the two lowest grades. The gate operates where it has no edge and stays quiet where it has one: an A row is barely more likely to surface than a D row (15.97% vs 7.78%), and that 2× ratio cannot rescue an inverted tier.

Step 4 — a confidence inversion visible in one table

If the gate were a confidence threshold, publication would rise with confidence. That column is an integer 1–10, not a percentage.

confidence graded published % hit %
3 8,212 4.46 53.64
4 8,978 7.03 60.16
5 11,780 12.57 56.04
6 9,534 12.48 55.07
7 4,329 8.45 60.04
8 2,041 4.26 65.51
9 549 1.09 73.77
10 58 0.00 56.90

Publication peaks at 5–6, where accuracy sits below average, and collapses to 1.09% at 9 — the most accurate bucket in the table at 73.77%. The 58 rows at 10 are never published.

So it is not a confidence filter. rec_reason says what it actually is:

"结构未知（样本不足或无此组合）"    12,932 rows
"结构B但非竞彩/北单(观察)"          7,490 rows
"低质结构 ROI-8.3% (n=222)"         3,043 rows
"低质结构 ROI-4.8% (n=31)"          2,399 rows
"低质结构 ROI-0.2% (n=493)"         2,075 rows

The gate keys off a structure bucket and labels it with a bucket-level return figure computed over n=31, n=222, n=493 prior rows. That is the failure mode in one line: a decision about a single match made by a statistic computed over a different set of matches. It also explains the negative per-model lift — bucket membership is a property of market shape, not of the evidence for that particular match.

Step 5 — two integrity failures that block any future audit

Published rows carrying a veto. veto_reason is populated on 10,223 rows; 803 of them sit where is_visible = true. 19.0% of the published set has a recorded reason for being rejected. Either the flag is written after publication, or the veto is advisory and not wired into the publish path. Both are unverifiable from outside, and both mean the gate has no single source of truth.

Partial slates. 4,232 published rows span 4,212 of 16,898 matches — 24.93% carry at least one published row, and exactly 4 matches are fully published. A reader is not seeing "this match has a published view" but "this match had one model whose row survived", with the model varying per match. Any comparison built on that surface compares different things under one label.

Step 6 — what an auditable gate looks like

None of this is fixable with a threshold. The gate has to become a decision with a recorded counterfactual and a published scorecard.

import math

def wilson(k, n, z=1.96):
    p = k / n
    d = 1 + z * z / n
    c = (p + z * z / (2 * n)) / d
    h = z * math.sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n + z * z / (4 * n * n)) / d
    return c - h, c + h

def audit_gate(vis_hits, vis_n, hid_hits, hid_n, min_lift_pp=3.0, z_crit=1.96):
    """PASS only if the gate beats its own reject pile by a margin
    that this sample can actually resolve."""
    pv, ph = vis_hits / vis_n, hid_hits / hid_n
    pooled = (vis_hits + hid_hits) / (vis_n + hid_n)
    se = math.sqrt(pooled * (1 - pooled) * (1 / vis_n + 1 / hid_n))
    lift_pp = (pv - ph) * 100
    lo, hi = wilson(vis_hits, vis_n)
    need_n = 2 * pooled * (1 - pooled) / (min_lift_pp / 100) ** 2
    return {
        "lift_pp": round(lift_pp, 2),
        "z": round((pv - ph) / se, 3),
        "vis_ci": (round(lo * 100, 2), round(hi * 100, 2)),
        "n_needed_per_arm": round(need_n),
        "verdict": "PASS" if (lift_pp >= min_lift_pp
                              and abs((pv - ph) / se) >= z_crit
                              and min(vis_n, hid_n) >= need_n) else "FAIL",
    }

print(audit_gate(2413, 4231, 24360, 42684))
# {'lift_pp': 0.46, 'z': 0.578, 'vis_ci': (56.05, 59.01),
#  'n_needed_per_arm': 544, 'verdict': 'FAIL'}

The n_needed_per_arm term matters: at a 57% base rate, resolving a 3pp lift takes ~544 graded rows per arm. Both arms clear that bar, so the effect is genuinely absent — which blocks the usual answer ("we need more data").

Four changes follow: publish the gate's own scorecard, not only its output; keep grading suppressed rows, since 99.45% coverage is what made this audit possible; wire up the dead columns or delete them; and make the decision and the label one event, since 803 published rows with a veto reason mean the publish and skip paths can disagree.

The uncomfortable summary

A gate publishing 8.9% of 47,150 graded rows, with a pooled lift of +0.48pp (z = 0.60), a per-model lift of −7.92pp across 218 models where it fails on 146, an A-tier 3.6pp below its own D-tier, a confidence curve that publishes most where accuracy is lowest, and 19% of its output carrying a veto reason.

That is not a tuning failure. It is what happens when a publication decision is made by a bucket statistic and never scored against its own counterfactual. The fix is not a better threshold — it is making the gate answerable to the rows it threw away, which requires having graded them.

Analytics and research content. Not betting advice. 18+

本内容仅供数据分析与研究参考，不构成任何决策建议。

title: PostgreSQL Transactions & Basic Indexing: Understanding Atomicity, Consistency and Query Performance
description:
PostgreSQL Transactions & Basic Indexing: Understanding Atomicity, Consistency and Query Performance

Introduction

PostgreSQL is a powerful relational database management system that provides features to manage data safely and efficiently.

Two important concepts in PostgreSQL are Transactions and Indexing.

Transactions help maintain data integrity by ensuring that database operations are completed successfully as a single unit. Indexing improves query performance by helping PostgreSQL locate records efficiently.

In this blog, we will explore transaction commands, different types of indexes, EXPLAIN basics, and how Atomicity and Consistency work in real-world applications.

1. Understanding Transactions in PostgreSQL

A transaction is a group of SQL operations treated as one logical unit of work.

Consider an e-commerce application where a customer purchases a product. The application needs to:

  • Create a new order.
  • Insert order details.
  • Update product stock.

All these operations should succeed together. If one operation fails, the database should undo the changes.

PostgreSQL provides three important transaction commands.

BEGIN

BEGIN starts a new transaction.

BEGIN;

After executing BEGIN, PostgreSQL groups subsequent SQL operations into the current transaction.

COMMIT

COMMIT saves all successful changes permanently.

BEGIN;

INSERT INTO users (full_name, email)
VALUES ('Swaroop', 'swaroop@example.com');

COMMIT;

Once COMMIT executes successfully, the inserted user is saved.

ROLLBACK

ROLLBACK cancels changes made in the current transaction that have not yet been committed.

BEGIN;

INSERT INTO users (full_name, email)
VALUES ('Ravi', 'ravi@example.com');

ROLLBACK;

The inserted record will not be saved.

Real-world example: Bank transfer

Imagine Ravi transfers ₹1,000 to Swaroop.

Initially:

Person Balance
Ravi ₹5,000
Swaroop ₹2,000 
BEGIN;

UPDATE accounts
SET balance = balance - 1000
WHERE account_id = 1;

UPDATE accounts
SET balance = balance + 1000
WHERE account_id = 2;

COMMIT;

After successful execution:

Person Balance
Ravi ₹4,000
Swaroop ₹3,000

If the second operation fails, the application should execute ROLLBACK so the first deduction is also undone.

This prevents incomplete financial transactions.

2. Understanding Indexing in PostgreSQL

An index is a database structure that helps PostgreSQL find records faster.

Think of a textbook. Instead of searching every page for a topic, you can use the index at the back to locate the required page.

Database indexes work similarly.

PostgreSQL supports different types of indexes.

Primary Key Index

A primary key uniquely identifies each row in a table.

CREATE TABLE students (
    student_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    student_name VARCHAR(100),
    email VARCHAR(100)
);

Here, student_id uniquely identifies every student.

PostgreSQL automatically creates a unique B-tree index for a primary key.

Unique Index

A unique index prevents duplicate values in an indexed column.

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_students_email
ON students(email);

Now two students cannot have the same email address.

A unique index enforces uniqueness, while a primary key also identifies the row and does not allow NULL values.

Composite Index

A composite index is created using two or more columns.

CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_status
ON orders(user_id, order_status);

This index can help PostgreSQL execute queries such as:

SELECT *
FROM orders
WHERE user_id = 1
AND order_status = 'PAID';

Column order matters in a composite index. An index on (user_id, order_status) is generally most useful for queries that filter using the leading user_id column.

Comparison of indexes

Index type Purpose
Primary Key Index Uniquely identifies rows
Unique Index Prevents duplicate indexed values
Composite Index Indexes multiple columns together

Indexes improve read performance, but they also require storage and add work to INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE operations. Therefore, indexes should be created based on actual query requirements.

3. Understanding EXPLAIN in PostgreSQL

EXPLAIN is used to understand how PostgreSQL plans to execute a SQL query.

It displays the query execution plan, including the operations PostgreSQL expects to perform.

Example:

EXPLAIN
SELECT *
FROM users
WHERE user_id = 1;

PostgreSQL may display:

Index Scan using users_pkey on users
  Index Cond: (user_id = 1)

This indicates that PostgreSQL plans to use the primary key index to find the requested user.

Sequential Scan

A Sequential Scan means PostgreSQL reads rows from the table one by one.

EXPLAIN
SELECT *
FROM users
WHERE full_name = 'Swaroop';

If no suitable index exists, PostgreSQL may choose a sequential scan.

Index Scan

An Index Scan means PostgreSQL uses an index to locate matching records.

CREATE INDEX idx_users_name
ON users(full_name);

EXPLAIN
SELECT *
FROM users
WHERE full_name = 'Swaroop';

PostgreSQL may use the newly created index.

EXPLAIN ANALYZE

EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the query and displays actual execution measurements.

EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT *
FROM users
WHERE user_id = 1;

Difference:

  • EXPLAIN displays the planned execution.
  • EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the query and displays actual execution statistics.

A sequential scan is not always inefficient. For small tables or queries that return many rows, it may be faster than using an index.

4. Atomicity in Practice

Atomicity is one of the ACID properties of database transactions.

It means all operations in a transaction succeed together, or none of them are applied.

Consider an e-commerce order placement process:

  1. Create an order.
  2. Insert order items.
  3. Reduce product stock.

If stock updating fails, the order and its items should also be rolled back.

Example:

BEGIN;

INSERT INTO orders (
    user_id,
    order_status,
    shipping_name,
    shipping_line1,
    shipping_city,
    shipping_postal_code
)
VALUES (
    1,
    'PENDING',
    'Asha Rao',
    '12 Lake Road',
    'Bengaluru',
    '560001'
);

UPDATE products
SET stock_qty = stock_qty - 1
WHERE product_id = 1
AND stock_qty >= 1;

COMMIT;

In a real application, we must check whether the stock update affected exactly one row. If it affected zero rows, we should execute ROLLBACK instead of COMMIT.

This ensures that an incomplete order is not saved.

5. Consistency in Practice

Consistency ensures that every committed transaction maintains the database's rules and constraints.

For example, product stock should never become negative.

We can enforce this using a CHECK constraint.

CREATE TABLE products_demo (
    product_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    product_name VARCHAR(100),
    stock_qty INT CHECK (stock_qty >= 0)
);

Valid insertion:

INSERT INTO products_demo
VALUES (1, 'Keyboard', 10);

Invalid insertion:

INSERT INTO products_demo
VALUES (2, 'Mouse', -5);

PostgreSQL rejects the second insertion because the stock quantity cannot be negative.

Other examples of consistency rules include:

  • Primary keys prevent duplicate row identifiers.
  • Foreign keys maintain valid relationships between tables.
  • Unique constraints prevent duplicate email addresses.
  • CHECK constraints validate prices and quantities.
  • Order status must belong to the permitted values.

These rules help maintain reliable and valid database records.

6. Practical Importance in Real-world Applications

Transactions and indexing are important in applications such as:

  • E-commerce: Maintaining reliable order placement and stock updates.
  • Banking: Ensuring correct money transfers.
  • Booking systems: Preventing multiple customers from purchasing the same last available seat.
  • User management: Efficiently searching users by email or ID.
  • Reporting systems: Improving query performance on frequently filtered columns.

Conclusion

PostgreSQL transactions and indexing play an important role in building reliable and efficient database applications.

Transactions use BEGIN, COMMIT and ROLLBACK to manage groups of SQL operations safely. Indexes improve data retrieval, while EXPLAIN helps developers understand query execution plans.

Atomicity ensures all-or-nothing execution, and Consistency ensures database constraints remain valid.

Understanding these concepts provides a strong foundation for developing database-driven applications that are both reliable and performant.

title: 💀 I Deleted My Kubernetes Pod… And Lost My Database Data! Understanding Kubernetes Storage
description:
Your Pod gets deleted. Kubernetes creates a replacement. Your application starts again. But where did your data go?

Imagine deploying a database on Kubernetes.

Everything works perfectly.

You create a database, insert 10,000 records, and verify that everything is running.

Then someone deletes the Pod.

kubectl delete pod mysql-pod

Kubernetes creates a replacement Pod.

You connect to the database.

And suddenly...

Database is empty.
No records found.

😭 What just happened?

You assumed Kubernetes would automatically preserve your database data.

But here's the problem:

Containers are designed to be replaceable. Your data needs a storage strategy of its own.

Let's understand Kubernetes storage, PersistentVolumes, PersistentVolumeClaims, StorageClasses, and how to protect application data.

🧠 1. Why Kubernetes Needs Persistent Storage

Containers are generally designed to be disposable.

When a container is removed, its writable container filesystem does not automatically survive as persistent application storage.

Consider this:

        Kubernetes Pod
              |
              v
        Application
              |
              v
       Container Filesystem
              |
              v
        Container Deleted
              |
              v
      Writable Data Lost

This creates a problem for stateful applications such as:

  • PostgreSQL
  • MySQL
  • MongoDB
  • Redis with persistence enabled
  • Applications that store uploaded files

These applications often need data to survive container restarts and Pod replacement.

That's where Kubernetes storage resources become important.

💾 2. What Is a PersistentVolume (PV)?

A PersistentVolume is a cluster resource representing storage available for use by workloads.

Think of it as storage that exists independently of an individual Pod.

Examples of possible storage backends include:

  • AWS EBS
  • Google Persistent Disk
  • Azure Disk
  • NFS
  • Local storage
  • CSI-compatible storage systems

A simplified architecture:

       Kubernetes Cluster
               |
               v
        PersistentVolume
               |
               v
        External Storage
               |
               v
          Application

A PersistentVolume describes the storage resource, including its capacity, access modes, and storage configuration.

Example:

apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolume
metadata:
  name: demo-pv
spec:
  capacity:
    storage: 2Gi

  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce

  persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy: Retain

  hostPath:
    path: /mnt/data
    type: DirectoryOrCreate

Save it as pv.yaml.

Apply it:

kubectl apply -f pv.yaml

Check:

kubectl get pv

Important This hostPath example is intended for local learning. It is not a production storage design. The data is tied to the node's filesystem and does not provide reliable cluster-wide storage.

🔗 3. What Is a PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC)?

Here's an important question.

Should every application developer need to understand the details of the underlying storage infrastructure?

Not necessarily.

That's why Kubernetes provides PersistentVolumeClaims.

A PVC is a request for storage.

The application requests storage, and Kubernetes attempts to find or provision suitable storage.

Think of it like this:

       Application
            |
            v
    PersistentVolumeClaim
            |
            v
     PersistentVolume
            |
            v
      Storage Backend

Example:

apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: demo-pvc
spec:
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce

  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 1Gi

Save it as pvc.yaml.

Apply:

kubectl apply -f pvc.yaml

Check:

kubectl get pvc

A PVC can remain Pending if no suitable PV exists and no compatible dynamic provisioner is available.

This is one of the most common Kubernetes storage troubleshooting scenarios.

🔥 4. Connect Persistent Storage to a Pod

Now let's use the PVC inside a Pod.

Create pod.yaml:

apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: storage-test
spec:
  containers:
    - name: nginx
      image: nginx:1.27

      volumeMounts:
        - name: storage
          mountPath: /usr/share/nginx/html

  volumes:
    - name: storage
      persistentVolumeClaim:
        claimName: demo-pvc

Apply:

kubectl apply -f pod.yaml

Check:

kubectl get pods

Now create a test file inside the mounted volume:

kubectl exec storage-test -- sh -c \
  'echo "Kubernetes Persistent Storage Works!" > /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html'

Read the file:

kubectl exec storage-test -- cat /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html

You should see:

Kubernetes Persistent Storage Works!

Now delete the Pod:

kubectl delete pod storage-test

Create it again:

kubectl apply -f pod.yaml

Read the file again:

kubectl exec storage-test -- cat /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html

If the PVC remains bound to storage that survives Pod replacement, the file should still be present.

That's the purpose of persistent storage.

The Pod can be replaced without automatically destroying the separately managed storage.

⚙️ 5. What Is a StorageClass?

Imagine you manage hundreds of applications.

Manually creating PersistentVolumes for every application would be difficult.

Kubernetes supports dynamic volume provisioning through StorageClasses.

A StorageClass describes how storage should be provisioned.

For example, a cloud provider may offer different storage classes for different performance or cost requirements.

A PVC can request a StorageClass:

apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: database-pvc
spec:
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce

  storageClassName: standard

  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 10Gi

When a compatible StorageClass and provisioner are configured, Kubernetes can dynamically provision storage for this claim.

Check available StorageClasses:

kubectl get storageclass

Inspect one:

kubectl describe storageclass <storage-class-name>

Remember that standard is only an example name. Your cluster may use a different StorageClass or may not have a default provisioner configured.

🆚 6. PV vs PVC vs StorageClass

This is an important comparison to remember.

Resource Meaning
PersistentVolume Represents available storage
PersistentVolumeClaim Requests storage
StorageClass Defines dynamic storage provisioning
VolumeMount Mounts storage into a container

A simple way to remember:

  • PV = Storage resource
  • PVC = Storage request
  • StorageClass = Storage provisioning mechanism

The relationship looks like this:

       StorageClass
            |
            v
     Dynamic Provisioning
            |
            v
    PersistentVolume
            |
            v
    PersistentVolumeClaim
            |
            v
          Pod
            |
            v
       Container

🚨 7. What Happens When You Delete a PVC?

This is where things become particularly important.

Deleting a PVC does not have one universal outcome for the underlying storage.

The result depends on the PersistentVolume's reclaim policy and the storage provisioner.

Two important reclaim policies are:

Retain

The underlying storage is retained after the claim is released. An administrator may need to handle the volume manually before it can be reused.

Delete

The provisioner may delete the underlying storage asset when the claim is released.

Check the reclaim policy:

kubectl get pv

Example:

NAME      CAPACITY   ACCESS MODES   RECLAIM POLICY
demo-pv   2Gi        RWO            Retain

For important workloads, understand your storage backend's behavior and configure backups independently.

A PersistentVolume is not a backup.

If someone deletes the storage or the underlying infrastructure fails, persistent storage alone may not protect your data.

☸️ 8. StatefulSet vs Deployment: Which One Should You Use?

Another important Kubernetes concept is the difference between Deployments and StatefulSets.

A Deployment is commonly used for stateless applications.

A StatefulSet is designed for applications that need stable identities and associated storage.

Feature Deployment StatefulSet
Pod identity Generally interchangeable Stable ordinal identity
Pod names Generated names Predictable names
Storage Can use PVCs Supports stable per-Pod PVCs
Typical use Web applications Stateful workloads
Scaling Replica-based Ordered scaling behavior

For example, a StatefulSet might create:

mysql-0
mysql-1
mysql-2

Each Pod can have its own persistent storage claim.

Example StatefulSet:

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: database
spec:
  serviceName: database
  replicas: 2

  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: database

  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: database

    spec:
      containers:
        - name: database
          image: mysql:8.4

          volumeMounts:
            - name: database-storage
              mountPath: /var/lib/mysql

  volumeClaimTemplates:
    - metadata:
        name: database-storage

      spec:
        accessModes:
          - ReadWriteOnce

        resources:
          requests:
            storage: 5Gi

This example demonstrates the storage pattern, not a complete production MySQL configuration. A real deployment needs secure credentials, appropriate database configuration, backup procedures, and a properly configured storage backend.

🛠️ 9. Kubernetes Storage Troubleshooting Commands

When storage stops working, these commands are extremely useful.

List PersistentVolumes:

kubectl get pv

List PersistentVolumeClaims:

kubectl get pvc

Describe a PVC:

kubectl describe pvc <pvc-name>

List StorageClasses:

kubectl get storageclass

Inspect Pod volume configuration:

kubectl describe pod <pod-name>

Check namespace events:

kubectl get events --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp

Common problems include:

  • PVC stuck in Pending.
  • No matching PersistentVolume.
  • StorageClass not found.
  • Provisioning failures.
  • Volume attachment problems.
  • Permission errors when mounting storage.
  • Node or CSI driver issues.

A simple troubleshooting flow 

PVC Not Working
      |
      v
Is PVC Bound?
      |
   No | Yes
      |   |
      v   v
Check PV  Check Pod
and SC    Events
      |   |
      v   v
Check     Check Volume
Provisioner Mount
      |
      v
Investigate Storage Backend

Follow the evidence instead of randomly deleting storage resources.

🧪 10. Your Weekend Challenge: Build a Kubernetes Storage Lab

Want to become confident with Kubernetes storage?

Build this project in Minikube or another local Kubernetes environment.

Project: Kubernetes Persistent Storage Lab

Your tasks:

  1. Create a PersistentVolume.
  2. Create a PersistentVolumeClaim.
  3. Mount the PVC into a Pod.
  4. Write a file into the mounted directory.
  5. Delete and recreate the Pod.
  6. Verify that the data remains.
  7. Test what happens when a PVC cannot be bound.
  8. Explore Retain and Delete reclaim policies in a disposable test environment.
  9. Create a StatefulSet with volumeClaimTemplates.

Suggested repository structure:

kubernetes-storage-lab/
│
├── pv/
│   └── pv.yaml
│
├── pvc/
│   └── pvc.yaml
│
├── pods/
│   └── storage-test.yaml
│
├── statefulset/
│   └── database.yaml
│
└── README.md

Document your commands, screenshots, errors, and solutions.

This project will help you understand storage concepts much more deeply than simply reading definitions.

🎯 Final Thoughts

Kubernetes makes it easy to replace failed Pods and maintain application availability.

But your application data needs a different level of protection.

Understanding PersistentVolumes, PersistentVolumeClaims, StorageClasses, and StatefulSets is essential when working with stateful applications.

And remember these three lessons:

  1. Containers are replaceable.
  2. Persistent storage must be managed separately.
  3. Persistent storage is not a substitute for backups.

A successful Kubernetes deployment isn't just about getting Pods into the Running state. It's about ensuring your applications and their data behave correctly when failures happen.

👇 Let's discuss!

Have you ever lost application data because of an incorrect Kubernetes storage configuration?

Which topic do you find most confusing?

  • PersistentVolumes and PVCs
  • StorageClasses
  • StatefulSets
  • Reclaim policies
  • CSI drivers

Share your experience in the comments!

☸️ Get the CKA Complete Study Guide

Build your Kubernetes foundation, strengthen your understanding of important concepts, and prepare with a structured learning resource.

Don't just memorize commands. Understand Kubernetes deeply. Practice consistently. Become confident.

title: The Complete 2026 Guide to Self-Hosting Private n8n + Local LLMs on Cloud VPS: Full Production Architecture & Cost Breakdown
description:
Published by PixelBrain Engineering Lab · Updated November 2026

Canonical URL: https://pixelbrain-tools.blogspot.com/2026/11/self-hosting-n8n-local-llm-cloud-vps.html

Executive Summary: The $500/Month SaaS Trap vs. The $18/Month Private Cloud

In 2026, autonomous workflow automation and local Large Language Model (LLM) agents have shifted from experimental curiosity to table-stakes infrastructure for engineering teams, digital agencies, and一人公司 (one-person unicorn companies).

However, teams scaling on hosted cloud solutions quickly hit an aggressive pricing wall:

  1. Per-Execution Cloud Tax: Mainstream hosted iPaaS platforms charge between $0.01 and $0.05 per task execution beyond their modest base tiers. A multi-step autonomous agent running scheduled scrapers, CRM updates, and webhook reconciliations easily burns through 150,000 tasks/month—translating to a $600–$1,200 monthly invoice.
  2. Token Leakage & Data Governance: Piping internal database records, customer support transcripts, and sensitive intellectual property into public commercial LLM APIs introduces compliance nightmares (GDPR, SOC2, HIPAA) and variable API billing spikes.
  3. Vendor Lock-in & Rate Limits: Relying entirely on multi-tenant cloud runners subjects your mission-critical operations to unannounced latency spikes, concurrency caps, and sudden API deprecations.

This production guide details the architectural blueprint for deploying a fully private, unlimited-execution automation fortress combining self-hosted n8n, containerized local LLMs (via Ollama & vLLM), PostgreSQL 16 with pgvector, Redis-backed BullMQ execution, and automated TLS reverse proxying on a low-cost, high-performance Cloud Virtual Private Server (VPS).

For under $20 per month in raw compute, this stack delivers zero per-execution fees, total data sovereignty, sub-millisecond local network latency, and complete enterprise auditability.

+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                                  THE 2026 PRIVATE AUTOMATION STACK                                |
+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                                                                                                   |
|  [ Inbound Webhooks & UI Traffic ]                                                                |
|                 |                                                                                 |
|                 v                                                                                 |
|  +---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+  |
|  | Caddy / Traefik Ingress Controller (Automatic Let's Encrypt TLS / Reverse Proxy)             |  |
|  +---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+  |
|         |                                              |                                          |
|         | Port 5678 (HTTPS Basic / OAuth2)             | Port 11434 (Internal Docker Bridge)      |
|         v                                              v                                          |
|  +-------------------------------------+      +------------------------------------------------+  |
|  | n8n Workflow Automation Engine      |      | Local LLM Inference Engine                     |  |
|  | (Queue Mode / BullMQ Executor)      |<---->| (Ollama / vLLM OpenAI-Compatible API)          |  |
|  +-------------------------------------+      | Models: Qwen 2.5 Coder 14B / DeepSeek-R1-14B   |  |
|         |                      |              +------------------------------------------------+  |
|         v                      v                               |                                  |
|  +--------------+      +---------------------------+           |                                  |
|  | Redis Queue  |      | PostgreSQL 16 + pgvector  |<----------+ (Embeddings / Long-term RAG)     |
|  | (Cache/Locks)|      | (State Storage / Vectors) |                                              |
|  +--------------+      +---------------------------+                                              |
|                                                                                                   |
+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

1. Cloud VPS Hardware Sizing & Provider Benchmarks (2026)

The secret to hosting local LLMs without thousand-dollar enterprise GPU instances lies in modern quantized weights (GGUF Q4_K_M / Q8_0) coupled with high-frequency DDR5 memory and AVX-512 CPU offloading.

For automated agents running deterministic tasks (data transformation, routing, webhook handling, code formatting, and summarization), a 14B parameter dense model (such as Qwen 2.5 Coder 14B or DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B) running on 4–8 modern CPU cores delivers 14–22 tokens per second—more than adequate for asynchronous background jobs.

Memory & VRAM Mathematics for 14B Models

Before purchasing server capacity, calculate exact memory consumption using the standard quantization formula:

$$\text{RAM Requirements (GB)} \approx \left(\frac{\text{Parameters} \times \text{Bits per Weight}}{8}\right) \times 1.25 + \text{KV Cache Footprint}$$

For a 14.7 billion parameter model:

  • FP16 (Unquantized): $14.7 \times 2 = 29.4\text{ GB}$ (Exceeds standard VPS tiers; requires expensive GPU instances).
  • GGUF Q8_0 (8-bit Quantization): $14.7 \times 1.05 = 15.4\text{ GB}$ (Near-zero quality loss, requires 24GB VPS).
  • GGUF Q4_K_M (4-bit Medium Quantization): $14.7 \times 0.58 = 8.5\text{ GB}$ (Industry standard sweet spot; 98.7% MMLU retention, comfortably fits inside an affordable 16GB VPS).
  • KV Cache for 8,192 Context Window: Consumes approximately $1.2\text{ GB}$ of additional RAM.
  • n8n + PostgreSQL + Redis Footprint: Allocates approximately $2.5\text{ GB}$ of baseline system memory.
  • Total Recommended Server RAM: 16 GB to 24 GB.

Tested VPS Configurations & Real-World Latency

Tier Target Workload Recommended Specs Monthly Cost Tested Providers
Starter Stack n8n + Webhooks + Fast Embedding Search + 7B Model 4 vCPU, 8 GB RAM, 100 GB NVMe $6.50 – $9.50/mo Hostinger KVM 2 / Hetzner CPX31 / Contabo Cloud VPS S
Production Matrix (Recommended) n8n Queue Mode + 14B Model (Q4_K_M) + PostgreSQL pgvector 6–8 vCPU, 16–24 GB RAM, 200 GB NVMe $14.00 – $19.00/mo Hostinger KVM 4 / Hetzner CPX41 / OVHcloud VPS Comfort
Heavy Inference Multi-Agent Swarms + 32B Model + Local Whisper Audio 8 vCPU + Dedicated Nvidia RTX 4060 (16GB) $45.00 – $65.00/mo Vast.ai / RunPod Community / OVH Cloud GPU

Pro Tip on Storage Performance: Workflow state management and vector searches require high Random I/O operations per second (IOPS). Always choose NVMe PCIe 4.0 storage over standard SSD block storage to avoid transaction locking when running concurrent n8n webhooks.

2. Production Docker Compose Architecture

Below is the verified, single-command production deployment file. It configures:

  • Caddy v2: Lightweight reverse proxy with zero-config automatic HTTPS (Let's Encrypt).
  • n8n (v1.65+): Configured for high-concurrency production with PostgreSQL backend.
  • PostgreSQL 16: Bundled with the official pgvector extension for native vector embedding storage.
  • Redis 7 (Alpine): Providing atomic lock management and BullMQ execution queuing.
  • Ollama: Serving local quantized LLMs with hardware acceleration.
  • Internal Docker Network: Ensuring the LLM and database ports are never exposed to the public internet. 
version: '3.8'

services:
  caddy:
    image: caddy:2-alpine
    container_name: production_caddy
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports:
      - "80:80"
      - "443:443"
    volumes:
      - ./caddy/Caddyfile:/etc/caddy/Caddyfile:ro
      - caddy_data:/data
      - caddy_config:/config
    networks:
      - automation_net
    depends_on:
      - n8n

  redis:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    container_name: production_redis
    restart: unless-stopped
    command: redis-server --appendonly yes --requirepass ${REDIS_PASSWORD:-ChangeMeSecureRedis2026!}
    volumes:
      - redis_data:/data
    networks:
      - automation_net
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "redis-cli", "-a", "${REDIS_PASSWORD:-ChangeMeSecureRedis2026!}", "ping"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 5

  postgres:
    image: pgvector/pgvector:pg16
    container_name: production_postgres
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: ${POSTGRES_USER:-n8n_admin}
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:-ChangeMeSecurePassword2026!}
      POSTGRES_DB: ${POSTGRES_DB:-n8n_production}
    volumes:
      - postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    networks:
      - automation_net
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U ${POSTGRES_USER:-n8n_admin} -d ${POSTGRES_DB:-n8n_production}"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 5

  ollama:
    image: ollama/ollama:latest
    container_name: production_ollama
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      - OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE=24h
      - OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL=4
    volumes:
      - ollama_models:/root/.ollama
    networks:
      - automation_net
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          memory: 14G

  n8n:
    image: n8nio/n8n:latest
    container_name: production_n8n
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      - N8N_HOST=${SUBDOMAIN}.${DOMAIN_NAME}
      - N8N_PORT=5678
      - N8N_PROTOCOL=https
      - NODE_ENV=production
      - WEBHOOK_URL=https://${SUBDOMAIN}.${DOMAIN_NAME}/
      - GENERIC_TIMEZONE=UTC
      - DB_TYPE=postgresdb
      - DB_POSTGRESDB_HOST=postgres
      - DB_POSTGRESDB_PORT=5432
      - DB_POSTGRESDB_DATABASE=${POSTGRES_DB:-n8n_production}
      - DB_POSTGRESDB_USER=${POSTGRES_USER:-n8n_admin}
      - DB_POSTGRESDB_PASSWORD=${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:-ChangeMeSecurePassword2026!}
      - EXECUTIONS_MODE=regular
      - QUEUE_BULL_REDIS_HOST=redis
      - QUEUE_BULL_REDIS_PORT=6379
      - QUEUE_BULL_REDIS_PASSWORD=${REDIS_PASSWORD:-ChangeMeSecureRedis2026!}
      - EXECUTIONS_DATA_PRUNE=true
      - EXECUTIONS_DATA_MAX_AGE=168
      - EXECUTIONS_DATA_PRUNE_MAX_COUNT=50000
    volumes:
      - n8n_data:/home/node/.n8n
    networks:
      - automation_net
    depends_on:
      postgres:
        condition: service_healthy
      redis:
        condition: service_healthy

volumes:
  caddy_data:
  caddy_config:
  postgres_data:
  redis_data:
  ollama_models:
  n8n_data:

networks:
  automation_net:
    driver: bridge

The Caddyfile Configuration (./caddy/Caddyfile) 

automation.yourdomain.com {
    reverse_proxy n8n:5678 {
        header_up X-Forwarded-For {remote_host}
        header_up X-Forwarded-Proto {scheme}
    }

    # Security Headers
    header {
        Strict-Transport-Security "max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains; preload"
        X-Content-Type-Options "nosniff"
        X-Frame-Options "DENY"
        Referrer-Policy "strict-origin-when-cross-origin"
    }

    log {
        output file /data/access.log {
            roll_size 10mb
            roll_keep 5
        }
    }
}

3. Step-by-Step Server Hardening & Zero-Downtime Deployment

Step 1: Base VPS Setup & Docker Engine Installation

Connect to your Ubuntu 24.04 LTS VPS instance via SSH:

# Update repository index and apply critical security patches
sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y
sudo apt install -y curl git ufw fail2ban jq htop libssl-dev

# Configure Uncomplicated Firewall (UFW)
sudo ufw default deny incoming
sudo ufw default allow outgoing
sudo ufw allow 22/tcp comment 'SSH Port'
sudo ufw allow 80/tcp comment 'HTTP Let’s Encrypt Challenge'
sudo ufw allow 443/tcp comment 'HTTPS Encrypted Ingress'
sudo ufw --force enable

# Install official Docker engine & Compose plugin
curl -fsSL https://get.docker.com | sudo sh
sudo usermod -aG docker $USER

Step 2: Fail2ban Protection Against Brute-Force Attacks

Create an automated jail configuration for SSH and HTTP authentication:

sudo cat <<EOF > /etc/fail2ban/jail.local
[DEFAULT]
bantime = 1h
findtime = 10m
maxretry = 5

[sshd]
enabled = true
port = 22
mode = aggressive
EOF

sudo systemctl restart fail2ban

Step 3: Directory Layout and Cryptographic Secret Generation 

mkdir -p ~/automation-stack/caddy
cd ~/automation-stack

# Generate hardened environment file with random 32-byte credentials
cat <<EOF > .env
DOMAIN_NAME=yourdomain.com
SUBDOMAIN=automation
POSTGRES_USER=n8n_master_$(openssl rand -hex 4)
POSTGRES_PASSWORD=$(openssl rand -base64 32 | tr -d '/+=')
POSTGRES_DB=n8n_production
REDIS_PASSWORD=$(openssl rand -base64 32 | tr -d '/+=')
EOF

chmod 600 .env

Step 4: Pulling the Highest-ROI Local Models

Once docker compose up -d completes container initialization, pull the verified open weights directly into the containerized Ollama instance:

# 1. Pull the 2026 Sovereign Workhorse: Qwen 2.5 Coder 14B (Instruct)
# Remarkable performance on JSON extraction, API calling, and logic validation
docker exec -it production_ollama ollama pull qwen2.5-coder:14b-instruct-q4_K_M

# 2. Pull the Advanced Reasoning Model: DeepSeek-R1 Distilled 14B
# Outstanding at chain-of-thought analysis, fraud detection, and complex routing
docker exec -it production_ollama ollama pull deepseek-r1:14b

# 3. Pull Fast Multilingual Embedding Model (for RAG & Vector Search in Postgres)
docker exec -it production_ollama ollama pull bge-m3:latest

4. Advanced Vector DB Tuning: PostgreSQL 16 + pgvector

By default, standard relational databases perform sequential scans on text queries. To enable true semantic retrieval across hundreds of thousands of customer support records, PDF manuals, and transaction receipts, configure HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) indexing inside PostgreSQL.

Connecting to PostgreSQL and Enabling Extension 

docker exec -it production_postgres psql -U n8n_admin -d n8n_production

Execute the vector setup commands:

-- Enable the vector extension
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector;

-- Create an enterprise document embeddings table
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS enterprise_knowledge_base (
    id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    document_id VARCHAR(128) NOT NULL,
    chunk_index INT NOT NULL,
    content TEXT NOT NULL,
    metadata JSONB DEFAULT '{}'::jsonb,
    embedding vector(1024), -- Matches bge-m3 dimension
    created_at TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);

-- Build high-speed HNSW Index for cosine similarity search
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_hnsw_kb_embedding 
ON enterprise_knowledge_base 
USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops)
WITH (m = 16, ef_construction = 64);

Querying Vectors with Sub-10ms Latency 

-- Semantic search query retrieving top 5 most relevant documentation chunks
SELECT id, document_id, content, metadata,
       1 - (embedding <=> '[0.012, -0.043, ...]'::vector) AS cosine_similarity
FROM enterprise_knowledge_base
WHERE metadata @> '{"department": "engineering"}'
ORDER BY embedding <=> '[0.012, -0.043, ...]'::vector
LIMIT 5;

5. Connecting n8n to Local LLM Agents (Zero-Cost Inference)

Inside the n8n interface at https://automation.yourdomain.com:

  1. Go to Credentials -> New Credential -> Select OpenAI API.
  2. Configure custom Base URL:
    • Credential Name: Local Ollama Internal Gateway
    • API Key: Enter any placeholder string (e.g. ollama-local-bearer).
    • Base URL: Set to http://ollama:11434/v1.
  3. In any n8n Workflow, insert the AI Agent node:
    • Connect the OpenAI Chat Model sub-node.
    • Set Model Name to: qwen2.5-coder:14b-instruct-q4_K_M or deepseek-r1:14b.
    • Set Temperature to: 0.1 (for deterministic schema validation & SQL synthesis) or 0.6 (for narrative drafting).
  4. Connect the Vector Store sub-node:
    • Select Postgres Vector Store.
    • Host: postgres, Port: 5432, Database: n8n_production.
    • Table: enterprise_knowledge_base.
    • Connect Embeddings OpenAI node pointed to bge-m3:latest on http://ollama:11434/v1.

You now possess an enterprise-grade Autonomous Agent capable of processing millions of records without a single external API call or token surcharge.

6. Enterprise Queue Mode & Scaling Beyond 500,000 Executions/Month

When running massive batch jobs or high-frequency webhook listeners, single-process n8n can bottleneck on Node.js event-loop CPU starvation. The enterprise solution is Queue Mode.

In Queue Mode, n8n decouples the user interface from execution runners:

  1. Webhook Process: Listens for inbound HTTP payloads, immediately returns an HTTP 200/202 acknowledgment, and enqueues job parameters into Redis.
  2. Worker Processes: Autonomous Node.js containers that dequeue jobs from Redis, execute the nodes, communicate with PostgreSQL/Ollama, and log the state.

Adding Dynamic Workers in Docker Compose

To scale up worker capacity during flash campaigns or month-end reconciliations, append a worker definition to your docker-compose.yml:

  n8n-worker:
    image: n8nio/n8n:latest
    restart: unless-stopped
    command: worker
    environment:
      - NODE_ENV=production
      - DB_TYPE=postgresdb
      - DB_POSTGRESDB_HOST=postgres
      - DB_POSTGRESDB_PORT=5432
      - DB_POSTGRESDB_DATABASE=${POSTGRES_DB:-n8n_production}
      - DB_POSTGRESDB_USER=${POSTGRES_USER:-n8n_admin}
      - DB_POSTGRESDB_PASSWORD=${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}
      - EXECUTIONS_MODE=queue
      - QUEUE_BULL_REDIS_HOST=redis
      - QUEUE_BULL_REDIS_PORT=6379
      - QUEUE_BULL_REDIS_PASSWORD=${REDIS_PASSWORD}
    networks:
      - automation_net
    depends_on:
      - redis
      - postgres

Scale instantly from the CLI without taking down the web interface:

# Spin up 3 parallel workers for high concurrency
docker compose up -d --scale n8n-worker=3

7. Automated Disaster Recovery & Remote S3 Backup Pipeline

Never rely solely on local disks. A production system must automate database dumps, workflow JSON exports, and model configuration backups to off-site cloud object storage (AWS S3, Cloudflare R2, or Backblaze B2).

The Automated Backup Script (/opt/scripts/backup_automation.sh) 

#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail

BACKUP_DIR="/var/backups/automation"
TIMESTAMP=$(date +"%Y%m%d_%H%M%S")
RETENTION_DAYS=14

mkdir -p "${BACKUP_DIR}"

echo "[${TIMESTAMP}] Initiating PostgreSQL atomic backup..."
docker exec production_postgres pg_dump -U n8n_admin n8n_production | gzip > "${BACKUP_DIR}/n8n_db_${TIMESTAMP}.sql.gz"

echo "[${TIMESTAMP}] Exporting active n8n workflows..."
docker exec -u node production_n8n n8n export:workflow --all --output=/tmp/workflows.json
docker cp production_n8n:/tmp/workflows.json "${BACKUP_DIR}/workflows_${TIMESTAMP}.json"

# Prune local backups older than retention window
find "${BACKUP_DIR}" -type f -mtime +${RETENTION_DAYS} -delete

echo "[${TIMESTAMP}] Syncing encrypted archives to remote Cloudflare R2 / S3..."
# rclone copy "${BACKUP_DIR}" r2:my-company-backups/automation/
echo "[${TIMESTAMP}] Backup completed successfully."

Make executable and register with system crontab:

chmod +x /opt/scripts/backup_automation.sh
(crontab -l 2>/dev/null; echo "0 3 * * * /opt/scripts/backup_automation.sh >> /var/log/automation_backup.log 2>&1") | crontab -

8. Financial ROI Comparison: Hosted SaaS vs. Private Cloud VPS

Let us examine the concrete economics of running 200,000 monthly automation tasks with an average of 450 tokens generated per task:

Metric Hosted SaaS Stack (Make.com Enterprise + OpenAI Tier 4) Private Cloud VPS Stack (Self-Hosted n8n + Ollama 14B)
Monthly Executions 200,000 tasks/month 200,000+ tasks/month (Uncapped)
Compute / Base Platform Fee $299.00 / month $16.50 / month (Cloud VPS 6-core 16GB)
LLM Inference Tokens Cost $180.00 / month ($2.00/1M tokens) $0.00 / month (Local hardware inference)
Data Privacy & Compliance Multi-tenant shared cloud; external logging 100% Private Isolated VPS; zero data egress
Custom Extension Freedom Restricted to pre-built marketplace apps Full Node.js/Python npm package support
Total Annual Cost $5,748.00 / year $198.00 / year
Net Annual Cashflow Savings — $5,550.00 (96.5% Immediate Reduction)

9. Production Troubleshooting & Deep Kernel Optimizations

When deploying autonomous agents in production environments, standard Linux defaults can cause memory thrashing, unexpected OOM (Out-of-Memory) kills, or unbounded log growth that exhausts VPS storage. Implement these battle-tested kernel and Docker tuning parameters.

9.1 Mitigating Kernel OOM Killer on Memory-Constrained VPS

Linux kernels aggressively terminate processes when memory runs tight. Because Ollama and n8n allocate large contiguous blocks of virtual memory, you must configure swap space and lower kernel swappiness to prevent sudden service crashes:

# Create an 8GB high-speed NVMe swapfile
sudo fallocate -l 8G /swapfile
sudo chmod 600 /swapfile
sudo mkswap /swapfile
sudo swapon /swapfile

# Ensure persistence across server reboots
echo '/swapfile none swap sw 0 0' | sudo tee -a /etc/fstab

# Tune Virtual Memory Subsystem
sudo cat <<EOF >> /etc/sysctl.conf
# Reduce aggressive swapping while preserving emergency buffer
vm.swappiness = 10
vm.vfs_cache_pressure = 50
vm.overcommit_memory = 1
EOF

sudo sysctl -p

9.2 Docker Global Daemon Log Rotation

By default, Docker preserves container standard output logs indefinitely. An automated agent logging thousands of JSON payloads per hour will fill a 100GB NVMe drive within weeks. Configure global log rotation in /etc/docker/daemon.json:

{
  "log-driver": "json-file",
  "log-opts": {
    "max-size": "25m",
    "max-file": "4"
  },
  "default-ulimits": {
    "nofile": {
      "Name": "nofile",
      "Hard": 65536,
      "Soft": 65536
    }
  }
}

Reload the Docker daemon:

sudo systemctl restart docker

9.3 GPU Passthrough Setup (Optional: Dedicated Cloud GPU VPS)

If you deploy on a cloud VPS equipped with an NVIDIA GPU (such as an RTX 4060, A4000, or T4), enable zero-overhead container passthrough via the official NVIDIA Container Toolkit:

# Add NVIDIA package repository
curl -fsSL https://nvidia.github.io/libnvidia-container/gpgkey | sudo gpg --dearmor -o /usr/share/keyrings/nvidia-container-toolkit-keyring.gpg
curl -s -L https://nvidia.github.io/libnvidia-container/stable/deb/nvidia-container-toolkit.list | \
  sed 's#deb https://#deb [signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/nvidia-container-toolkit-keyring.gpg] https://#g' | \
  sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/nvidia-container-toolkit.list

sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y nvidia-container-toolkit
sudo nvidia-ctk runtime configure --runtime=docker
sudo systemctl restart docker

Then simply update the ollama block in docker-compose.yml to request all available GPUs:

    deploy:
      resources:
        reservations:
          devices:
            - driver: nvidia
              count: all
              capabilities: [gpu]

10. Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)

Can I run this stack on a 4GB RAM VPS?

While n8n and PostgreSQL will run smoothly on 4GB of RAM, local LLM inference requires a minimum of 8GB to 16GB of memory to load 7B or 14B quantized models without severe thrashing. For 4GB instances, we recommend offloading inference to hybrid endpoints while maintaining self-hosted n8n and Postgres.

How does this stack compare to cloud-hosted n8n Cloud?

n8n Cloud is an exceptional managed platform for rapid prototyping. However, self-hosting unlocks unrestricted execution volume, custom npm dependencies, direct LAN access to local databases and Ollama instances, and eliminates the per-workflow execution pricing cap.

Is Ollama fast enough on pure CPU without a discrete GPU?

Yes. On modern AMD EPYC or Intel Xeon processors with AVX-512 extensions, GGUF 4-bit quantized 14B models achieve 14 to 22 tokens per second. Because background automation agents operate asynchronously (processing emails, webhooks, and tickets in queues), sub-second conversational latency is unnecessary—throughput and reliability take precedence.

What happens if the server reboots?

Every service in our Docker Compose blueprint utilizes restart: unless-stopped. Upon server restart, Caddy automatically rebinds TLS certificates, PostgreSQL performs atomic write-ahead log recovery, and n8n resumes listening on all webhook endpoints without manual intervention.

Need Enterprise Implementation & Hardened Deployment?

Building high-throughput autonomous agent infrastructure requires strict security baselines, reverse proxy hardening, and customized pgvector indexing. If your team is seeking bespoke enterprise AI deployment, custom multi-agent orchestration, or dedicated VPS migration:

title: Replacing Access & Excel Macro Apps With a Web App
description:
Many profitable businesses still run a critical process on a Microsoft Access database or an Excel workbook full of VBA macros. It started as a smart shortcut. Years later it holds the pricing logic, the customer history and the month-end report, it lives on one shared drive, and only one person really understands it. Replacing it is not a rewrite of screens. It is a migration of data, hidden business rules and daily habits, and that is where most projects fail.

At Loop Origin I build custom web applications on Laravel, Vue, Nuxt and PostgreSQL, and as a Principal Software Engineer I have moved several of these spreadsheet-era systems to the browser. I wrote this with help from AI tools and checked every command and code sample myself. This is the playbook I use.

How do you replace an Access or Excel macro app with a web app?

Direct answer: Inventory every table, form, query, macro and report first. Extract the data with scripted, repeatable imports, and capture each business rule as a test before rewriting it. Build the web app in small modules, run it in parallel with the old file, reconcile outputs daily, then cut over one team at a time and freeze the legacy file as read-only.

Signs it is time to move

You do not need to migrate just because Access is old. Move when the risk is real:

  • More than a few people need to edit at once, and you see locking errors or "who has the file open?" messages.
  • The file is corrupted or restored from backup more than once a year.
  • Remote staff or branches need access, and you are passing copies by email or VPN.
  • An auditor or customer asks who changed a value, and you cannot answer.
  • The one person who knows the VBA is leaving, or already left.
  • Integrations (accounting, e-commerce, couriers) are done by copy-paste.

Your options compared

Option Best for Main strengths Main risks Ongoing cost drivers
Keep Access, move tables to SQL Server or PostgreSQL Small teams on one office network Fast, little retraining Front end still on desktops; VBA knowledge risk stays Desktop licences, one maintainer
Low-code (Power Apps, AppSheet and similar) Simple forms and approvals inside one vendor's ecosystem Quick to build, built-in hosting Per-user licensing, limits on complex logic, lock-in to the platform Licences grow with every user
Off-the-shelf SaaS The process is standard (CRM, helpdesk, basic inventory) No build, vendor maintains it Your special rules may not fit; data export limits Subscription per seat or tier
Custom web app (Laravel/PostgreSQL + Vue or Nuxt) Core processes with unique rules and integrations You own the code and data; fits the real workflow; any device Needs a disciplined migration and a maintainer Hosting, maintenance retainer

I usually recommend custom only when the logic is the business's edge or the integrations are complex. If a standard SaaS covers the process, buy it.

Step 1: Inventory the legacy app

Treat the Access file or workbook as a system with parts, not a document. For Access, the open-source mdbtools package reads .mdb and .accdb files on Linux:

# List tables, dump the schema, export each table to CSV
mdb-tables -1 legacy.accdb
mdb-schema legacy.accdb postgres > schema_from_access.sql
for t in $(mdb-tables -1 legacy.accdb); do
  mdb-export legacy.accdb "$t" > "export/${t}.csv"
done
# Saved queries (newer mdbtools versions)
mdb-queries -L legacy.accdb

Forms, reports and VBA modules do not come out cleanly this way. Open the file in Access, use the Database Documenter, and export each VBA module to text from the editor. For Excel, list every sheet, named range, formula-heavy column, pivot and macro.

Record the results in an inventory sheet:

Item Type Used by How often Business rule inside? Keep, change or drop
tblOrders Table Sales, Finance Daily No Keep
qryMonthEndCommission Query Finance Monthly Yes: commission tiers Keep, test first
frmQuickQuote Form + VBA Sales Daily Yes: discount caps Change
rptOldBranchSummary Report Nobody since 2023 Never No Drop

Expect to drop a real share of the old reports. Ask who opened each one in the last year.

Step 2: Turn hidden rules into tests

The dangerous logic hides in VBA event handlers, query expressions and cell formulas: discount caps, rounding, tax, commission tiers, status changes. Before rewriting any of it, write down known inputs and outputs from the legacy system and turn them into tests. These are characterization tests: they pin down what the old system does today, bugs included, so you can choose which behavior to keep. I wrote about the technique in Characterization Tests Before You Refactor AI-Written Code.

// tests/Unit/CommissionTest.php (Pest)
// Each row: [monthly sales, expected commission] taken from the legacy query's output
dataset('legacy_commission', [
    [0, 0.00],
    [49999, 1499.97],
    [50000, 2500.00],
    [120000, 7200.00],
]);

it('matches the legacy month-end commission', function (int $sales, float $expected) {
    expect(app(\App\Services\Commission::class)->for($sales))->toBe($expected);
})->with('legacy_commission');

Take the expected values from real runs of the legacy file, not from someone's memory of the rules.


AI-generated image.

Step 3: Design the new data model, then import repeatably

Access schemas often carry years of drift: text columns holding dates, duplicate customers, "Yes/No" stored three ways, and no foreign keys. Do not copy that into PostgreSQL. Design a clean schema, then write an import that maps and cleans the legacy data, and run it again and again until it is boring.

// app/Console/Commands/ImportLegacyOrders.php (excerpt)
public function handle(): int
{
    $rows = SimpleExcelReader::create(storage_path('legacy/tblOrders.csv'))->getRows();
    $bad = 0;

    DB::transaction(function () use ($rows, &$bad) {
        foreach ($rows as $r) {
            $date = Carbon::createFromFormat('m/d/y H:i:s', $r['OrderDate'], 'Asia/Karachi');
            $customer = Customer::firstWhere('legacy_id', $r['CustomerID']);
            if (! $date || ! $customer) { $bad++; Log::warning('skip', $r); continue; }

            Order::updateOrCreate(
                ['legacy_id' => $r['OrderID']],
                ['customer_id' => $customer->id, 'ordered_at' => $date,
                 'total' => round((float) $r['Total'], 2)]
            );
        }
    });

    $this->info("Imported with {$bad} rejected rows");
    return self::SUCCESS;
}

Two habits matter. Keep a legacy_id on every migrated row so you can trace any record back. And make the import idempotent with updateOrCreate, so you can rerun it on fresh exports during the parallel run. Check the date format against your own export, because mdb-export output depends on version and options.

Step 4: Build in modules, not one big bang

Pick the module that hurts most, often order entry or approvals, and ship that first while the rest stays in the old file. Add the things a shared file never had: proper roles and permissions per team and branch, and a record of who changed what. I covered both in Laravel RBAC for Multi-Organization Portals and Immutable Audit Trails in Postgres for SaaS.

Keep the screens familiar at first. Users who spent ten years on one Access form will accept a cleaner web form with the same field order far faster than a redesign.

Step 5: Parallel run and reconcile

For two to four weeks, both systems run. Import fresh legacy data every night, and compare the outputs that matter: order totals by day, invoice counts, commission per salesperson, stock on hand.

-- Daily reconciliation: new system vs nightly legacy import
SELECT d.day,
       l.total AS legacy_total,
       n.total AS new_total,
       n.total - l.total AS diff
FROM generate_series(current_date - 30, current_date, '1 day') AS d(day)
LEFT JOIN legacy_daily_totals l ON l.day = d.day
LEFT JOIN (
  SELECT ordered_at::date AS day, SUM(total) AS total FROM orders GROUP BY 1
) n ON n.day = d.day
WHERE COALESCE(n.total, 0) <> COALESCE(l.total, 0);

Every difference is either a bug in the new app, a bug in the old one, or a data-entry mistake. Decide each one with the business owner and write the decision down.

Step 6: Cut over and freeze

Move one team or branch at a time. On cutover day, run the final import, set the legacy file to read-only, and keep it archived with its exports. Do not delete it for at least one audit cycle.

Failure modes I see most

Failure What causes it Prevention
Totals differ by small amounts Different rounding between VBA, Excel and PHP Test rounding rules explicitly; store money as integers or fixed decimals
Dates shift by a day Time zones and text dates in the legacy file Parse with an explicit format and time zone; reconcile by day
Users keep the old file "just in case" No read-only freeze, no trust in the new numbers Freeze on cutover; share reconciliation results
A forgotten monthly report breaks finance Inventory skipped rarely-used items Ask finance and management to sign off the inventory
Scope doubles mid-project Every wish list item added "while we are at it" Phase 1 replaces what exists; improvements come after cutover

Migration checklist

  1. Inventory every table, query, form, report, macro and integration, with an owner for each.
  2. Mark each item keep, change or drop, signed off by the business.
  3. Write characterization tests from real legacy outputs for every business rule.
  4. Design a clean schema; map every legacy column to it or to "dropped".
  5. Build an idempotent import with legacy_id traceability and a rejected-row log.
  6. Ship the highest-pain module first, with roles and an audit trail.
  7. Run in parallel with nightly imports and a daily reconciliation report.
  8. Cut over team by team, then freeze and archive the legacy file.
  9. Train users on the screens they use, not on the whole system.
  10. Agree on a maintenance owner before go-live.

FAQs

How long does an Access to web app migration take?

It depends on the number of forms, rules and integrations, not file size. A focused single-process app can move in weeks; a database running several departments is a phased project. The inventory in Step 1 is the only honest basis for an estimate.

Can we keep using Excel for reporting?

Yes. Many teams are happiest when the web app is the source of truth and exports clean Excel files or a read-only reporting connection. Just stop editing master data in spreadsheets.

What happens to the VBA code?

It becomes requirements and tests, not code you port line by line. Read it to find the rules, capture them as tests, then implement them cleanly in the new app.

Is moving Access tables to SQL Server enough?

Sometimes, for a small team on one network. It fixes storage and multi-user locking but not remote access, audit history or the single-maintainer risk in the forms and VBA.

Should we choose low-code instead of custom?

If the process is simple and you already pay for that vendor's ecosystem, low-code can be the right choice. Choose custom when the rules are complex, the integrations matter, or per-user licences will grow with your team.

How do we avoid losing data during cutover?

Run the import many times before cutover, keep a rejected-row log at zero or explained, reconcile daily during the parallel run, and archive the final legacy file read-only.

The short version

Treat the Access file or macro workbook as a real system. Inventory it, test its hidden rules, import its data repeatably, build in modules, prove the numbers with a parallel run, then cut over and freeze. The screens are the easy part; the rules and the data are the project.

Follow & Connect
