title: Building Covet: a Go backend that turns outfit photos into shoppable matches
description:
I keep seeing outfits I like in films and on social media, and I never know what the pieces are, what they cost, or where to buy them. Covet is my attempt at fixing that: you upload a photo, it detects the clothing items, tags the overall style, and returns real products to buy, including cheaper alternatives.

It’s a portfolio project, so the goal is to practise real backend work in Go: API design, a proper schema, third-party integrations and async processing.

Scoping before coding

The early decisions that saved me the most time were about what not to build:

  • No custom ML. Training a clothing detector is a research project. I use existing vision models.
  • No user-generated data. Covet works from external product data, so it needs no community to be useful.
  • A search engine, not a chatbot. The output is structured: items, prices, retailers, links.
  • Cut from the MVP: exact visual matching, a separate price-estimate feature, and price-drop alerts. The pipeline looks like this: 
POST /outfits -> save image, insert row (status: pending), return id
  background job -> detect items, find products, store them (status: complete)
GET /outfits/{id}/results -> client polls until status is complete

The stack is Go with the standard library router, Postgres in Docker through pgx, Gemini for style tags, and Lykdat for detection and product matching.

Foundations: config, a pool and context

The first milestone was boring on purpose: a server that loads config from the environment, opens a pgxpool connection pool, pings the database at startup and refuses to start if that fails. Failing fast beats discovering a bad DATABASE_URL on the first real request.

This is also where I properly learned context.Context: a cancellation and deadline signal that travels down the call chain so work stops when nobody wants the result any more. It matters again later, because the background job can’t reuse the request’s context.

Schema decisions

Five tables: users, sessions, outfit_uploads, detected_items and product_matches. A few choices I’d defend in an interview:

  • match_type as text (closest_match or budget_alternative) rather than a boolean, so a third category later doesn’t force a schema change.
  • outfit_uploads.user_id is nullable with ON DELETE SET NULL. Anonymous uploads work, and deleting an account doesn’t destroy the data.
  • NUMERIC(10,2) for prices. Never floats for money.
  • UUID primary keys for users and sessions, because they end up in cookies. ## The upload endpoint

POST /outfits does more than save a file:

  1. It caps the body at 10 MB.
  2. It detects the real content type from the first 512 bytes instead of trusting the extension, then calls Seek(0, 0) so the saved file isn’t missing those bytes.
  3. It saves the file under a UUID filename so uploads can’t collide.
  4. It inserts a row with status = 'pending' and returns 201 with the id immediately. The slow part runs in a goroutine: 
go h.runDetection(uploadID, savePath)

Inside, I use context.Background(), not r.Context(). The request context is cancelled the moment the response is written, which would kill the job mid-flight. The status column (pending, processing, complete, failed) is what lets the client poll honestly instead of hanging on a 10-second request.

Don’t trust model output

My first design asked Gemini for structured JSON describing each garment. Models drift from schemas, so I put three defences between the model and the database:

  1. Ask for JSON mode in the API call.
  2. Validate in Go before inserting anything: at least one item, no more than ten, non-empty category and description, and a length cap.
  3. Normalize known values, so “outerwear”, “coat” and “blazer” all become jacket, and style tags are lowercased and de-duplicated. 
if len(result.Items) == 0 {
    return fmt.Errorf("no items detected in image")
}

Two smaller lessons from this stage. Model names churn: gemini-1.5-flash and then gemini-2.0-flash both returned 404 errors when I called them, so the model name belongs in config. And Go refuses to compile unused imports and variables, which annoyed me for a day and then started catching real mistakes.

The shopping search dead end

Next I turned each detected item’s description into a Google Shopping query through SerpAPI. It failed in a way that taught me the most.

Descriptions like “vibrant bright yellow cropped fleece hoodie with drawstring hood” returned nothing. SerpAPI’s response reported the results state as “Fully empty”. I shortened the queries, stripped stop words and kept only colour, one descriptor and the category. Some started returning results. Others didn’t.

One bug was entirely mine. I added debug logging that read the response body with io.ReadAll, then parsed it with json.NewDecoder(resp.Body). The body was already consumed, so every parse failed with EOF:

bodyBytes, _ := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
log.Printf("response: %s", bodyBytes)
// parsing resp.Body again here returns EOF, so parse the bytes instead:
json.Unmarshal(bodyBytes, &parsed)

A response body is a stream you can read once. I also lost an evening to timeouts that turned out to be my own machine’s network, not the API.

The deeper problem was the translation layer. I was flattening a rich visual understanding into a text query for a product search that expects retailer-written titles. Simplifying queries until they return results also makes them generic. “Yellow top” is something you can type into Google yourself.

Switching to image-native matching

Lykdat’s Global Search API takes the image and returns detected items with similar products (name, brand, price, currency, URL, images and a similarity score) in one call. The free plan allows 500 image searches a month, which is plenty for development.

That changed the architecture. Lykdat became the source of truth for detection and matching, and Gemini shrank to one whole-outfit call that returns style tags like “streetwear” or “minimalist”. Running two independent detectors and aligning them afterwards by category name would have produced mismatches.

I’d believed the shopping service was an abstraction I could swap without touching the handlers. That turned out to be false. The old method took a detected item and a country, and the new one takes an image path, so runDetection had to be rewritten. An interface shaped around one provider’s paradigm leaks when the paradigm changes.

Making “budget alternative” mean something

My first rule labelled the top five results as closest matches and everything after as budget alternatives. Lykdat returned up to 50 products per item, so dozens landed in the “budget” tab purely because they ranked lower, and some cost more than the closest matches.

The fix: sort by similarity score and take the top eight as closest matches. Then label a lower-ranked product a budget alternative only if it’s cheaper than the average closest match in the same currency. The total is capped at 20 per item. Now the label is true.

The results endpoint

GET /outfits/{id}/results returns just the status until the job completes, then the full tree. A few decisions:

  • Filters are SQL, not API calls. Changing the budget bracket never calls Lykdat or Gemini again, because everything is already stored: 
WHERE detected_item_id = ANY($1)
  AND ($2::text    IS NULL OR match_type = $2)
  AND ($3::numeric IS NULL OR price >= $3)
  AND ($4::numeric IS NULL OR price <= $4)
  AND ($5::text    IS NULL OR currency = $5)
  • Two queries, not one per item. One fetches the items and one fetches all their matches with ANY($1), which avoids the N+1 pattern.
  • ORDER BY comes from a fixed list, never straight from user input, because it can’t be parameterized.
  • Links are built at response time. The database keeps the clean retailer URL. The response adds a shop_url, wrapped by an affiliate service that does nothing until it’s configured, so approval delays don’t block development. ## Auth, without ceremony

Cookie sessions backed by a sessions table: register, login, logout and a /auth/me endpoint. Passwords are hashed with bcrypt (capped at 72 characters, which is all bcrypt reads), and login failures return one generic message. When the email doesn’t exist, the handler still runs a dummy bcrypt comparison so response time doesn’t reveal which emails are registered.

A middleware identifies the user if a valid session exists and never rejects the request, so the app still works logged out. Owned outfits return 404, not 403, to anyone else, so ids can’t be probed.

Things that bit me

  • Docker data loss. My Postgres container kept breaking, and each recreation wiped my tables because the data lived inside the container. A named volume is the fix.
  • A key in a log line. An error that printed the full request URL leaked an API key into my terminal output. Log response bodies, not request URLs, and rotate anything that leaks.
  • Wiring renames. Swapping one provider for another touched config, constructors, main.go and the .env file, and a missed rename produced “undefined” errors in three places. ## What’s next

The remaining Phase 1 item is the frontend, built as plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript served by the Go server so there’s no CORS to deal with. After that come a landing page with smooth scrolling, an AI stylist chat grounded in each outfit’s stored results, and a virtual try-on experiment. Whether they land depends on what the data shows.

If you’re building something similar, the most useful thing I can pass on is to test the riskiest assumption first. Mine was “a text description will find the right product”, and I spent days on it before checking.

title: I built Itzma to run vector search inside my applications
description:
How close can I bring vector search to where I actually need it?

I started building Itzma because I wanted to use it in my own projects. If an application needs to find the nearest vectors, can I make that a library call and keep the data in object storage? I wanted to see how far I could take that design and what I’d run into once I started using it myself.

Itzma is an open-source, embedded vector database written in Rust, with Python bindings. It’s still in beta.

The application runs the search

The application opens a namespace and queries it in-process. With an object storage backend, the bucket holds the durable data. There’s no separate vector database server to deploy.

That split raises a question I find more interesting than the initial setup. If two application processes write to the same namespace, what keeps them from overwriting each other’s changes? Itzma uses conditional writes from the object store to coordinate updates. The storage backend is part of how the database works, right down to what happens when writers overlap.

Try it from Python

Install Itzma from PyPI with pip install itzma. You can start in memory. This example inserts two vectors and asks for the closest one using cosine distance.

import itzma
store = itzma.Store("memory://")
schema = itzma.Schema(dim=4, metric=itzma.Metric.COSINE)
docs = itzma.Namespace.create(store, "docs", schema)
docs.upsert([
    {"id": "a", "vector": [1, 0, 0, 0]},
    {"id": "b", "vector": [0, 1, 0, 0]},
])
hits = docs.query([0.9, 0.1, 0, 0], top_k=1)
print(hits.ids)  # Expected nearest ID is "a"

To try the same flow against S3, point itzma.Store at s3://your-bucket/your-prefix with credentials configured. The namespace and query use the same API. For a first run with persistence on your machine, you can also point the store at a local directory.

There’s more to play with once you have a query running. Itzma supports dense and sparse retrieval, HNSW and SQ8 indexing, and filters on typed attributes.

What would you try it on?

If you have an application where you’d like to run vector search in-process, I’d like to hear what you’d need from Itzma to try it there.

Take a look at itzma.dev and start playing with it. If an example is hard to follow, a query gives you an unexpected result, or there’s a feature you’d need, tell me here or open an issue on GitHub. And if there’s something you’d like to build or fix yourself, open an issue and let’s talk through it.

GitHub and quickstart · Python package on PyPI · Rust crate on crates.io

title: How to Audit an Audio File Upload — REST Receipts Before Review
description:
A portable transcription request is useful only if a logistics platform can still explain which tenant generated the work. Resolve that trade-off at intake: keep the original audio reference, tenant identity, and transcription result together, then evaluate the classifier separately. Short answer: upload the audio using a REST API multipart POST with a file and the documented model, language, and response_format fields; read the JSON text field and retain its association with the source recording before classifying a moderation report for human review.

The production scenario here is a design exercise, not an incident report: two logistics tenants submit recordings about a disputed delivery, a worker obtains a transcript, and a later classifier labels the report for a reviewer. Suppose an upload is rejected for size and an operator retries it. If the eventual transcript loses its original tenant association, aggregate request totals will not explain that tenant's workload, even when the words were transcribed correctly. That is the incident lesson to test before deployment.

Keep the receipt.

For teams evaluating the text-classification stage, I recommend trying Infrai where changing the vendor behind a capability should preserve the application's contract: swap vendors without changing application code. Its OpenAI-compatible surface supports existing OpenAI clients, while its specified per-call cost, vendor, and latency metadata gives an application concrete values to associate with its own tenant ledger. A single API key and unified billing reduce credential and invoice reconciliation across capabilities; the plain REST API requires no SDK for HTTP integrations. Treat it as one evaluation leg after transcription; transcription-provider eligibility remains a separate selection decision.

What must survive a multipart audio file upload?

The invariant is small: a successful transcript belongs to exactly the tenant and original audio reference supplied by the intake job. Tenant identity comes from the application's trusted job context; do not infer it from speech or allow a model to assign it. The text field is a result, not an accounting key. A result without its source association should fail acceptance before it reaches the moderation queue.

For a reproducible exercise, use two synthetic tenant IDs, tenant-north and tenant-south, and recordings with human-approved transcripts describing delivery disputes. These are proposed test inputs, not customer data. Include a short recording, a long recording, and one intentionally oversized file for each tenant. Label the expected moderation category before running the experiment, and keep the audio reference stable across attempts. Otherwise a provider change and a dataset change can become indistinguishable.

Choose an SLO before choosing concurrency. For this exercise, use a proposed target of 99% of accepted intake jobs reaching either a linked transcript or an explicit human-review handoff within 60 seconds; that is an acceptance target, not a claim about any provider. Record queue delay and upload duration separately, because a worker pool can miss the target while every upstream call looks healthy.

A planning example makes the distinction concrete: at an assumed arrival rate of 2 reports per second and an assumed mean worker occupancy of 8 seconds, the average occupied capacity is 16 workers. Those assumptions need measurement, and 16 is not a safe concurrency limit by itself; burst headroom, tail latency, and upstream limits still matter. A retry consumes capacity too.

Don't size from averages alone.

2. Compare the purchase boundary before the provider

Per-tenant cost visibility is the primary decision axis here. A transcript API cannot identify your tenants unless your application maintains that association, and even useful per-call metadata does not constitute a complete ledger. Reconcile successful calls, failed attempts, and retried work using the provider's documented accounting semantics before calling a tenant total complete.

The table is a buy-versus-build evaluation plan. It assigns work to the team rather than pretending to report an unrun benchmark. OpenAI, Deepgram, and AssemblyAI are real candidates to investigate; verify each candidate's current upload contract and account-level controls before implementing an adapter.

Option What to buy or evaluate Work the platform team owns Decision boundary
OpenAI direct Evaluate the direct transcription service against the audio fixtures Verify the upload contract; associate results and usage with tenant jobs Prefer the direct integration if its documented controls and measured results satisfy the workload
Deepgram Evaluate a speech-focused alternative using the same recordings Check request and response differences; implement and operate its adapter Prefer it if speech requirements justify a separate integration after testing
AssemblyAI Evaluate another speech-focused alternative against identical expected transcripts Validate its processing lifecycle and map it to the review deadline Prefer it if that lifecycle and the measured output fit the review queue better
Anthropic direct, for classification Evaluate classification using the fixed transcript set Validate its client contract, structured output, and tenant accounting Prefer a direct contract if it meets the classification gates and simplifies your existing operations
Gemini direct, for classification Evaluate another text-classification candidate on the same labels Verify model eligibility and output validation before integration Prefer it if measured classification behavior and operational controls fit the review process
Infrai, for transcript classification Evaluate a stable client contract across backend vendor choices Attach per-call metadata to trusted tenant context; score classification against labels Try it when vendor substitution and attributable calls matter at the text stage
Build the orchestration layer Keep intake receipts, evaluation fixtures, and tenant attribution under application control Operate the queue, retention rules, reconciliation, and reviewer handoff Build this boundary when those semantics are part of your product

A specialist or direct transcription provider is the better choice when the immediate requirement is a verified audio-upload contract and speech-specific behavior. Do not mistake a compatible text client for proof that every audio workflow has the same operational properties.

Infrai provides one key, one bill, and one REST API for 295 routes across 20 modules. Its public discovery surface provides request and response schemas without requiring a key, and there is no SDK to install for a plain HTTP integration. Use discovery to establish the text-stage contract before integrating it, and verify capability readiness when selecting any processing leg. For report classification, evaluate a chat model with a constrained JSON schema and validate the category before handing it to a reviewer. Keep final decisions with the human review process.

3. Exercise the preventative code path locally

Save the following as main.go and run it with go run main.go. It uses only the Go standard library and a local test server; the bytes are a synthetic transport fixture, not playable audio. No external service is contacted, no credential is needed, and a passing run proves request construction and source association only. It says nothing about recognition accuracy.

The program builds the multipart body with file, model, language, response_format, and optional prompt fields. Its local server checks the multipart request, returns the documented JSON text shape, and the client stores that result with the original tenant and audio reference. The fixture-model value is deliberately local test data, not a model ID to send to a provider.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "mime/multipart"
    "net/http"
    "net/http/httptest"
    "time"
)

type Receipt struct {
    Tenant string
    AudioRef string
    Text string
}

func transcribe(client *http.Client, endpoint, tenant, ref string, audio []byte) (Receipt, error) {
    var body bytes.Buffer
    form := multipart.NewWriter(&body)
    part, err := form.CreateFormFile("file", "report.wav")
    if err != nil {
        return Receipt{}, err
    }
    if _, err = part.Write(audio); err != nil {
        return Receipt{}, err
    }
    for _, field := range [][2]string{
        {"model", "fixture-model"},
        {"language", "en"},
        {"response_format", "json"},
        {"prompt", "Delivery dispute report"},
    } {
        if err = form.WriteField(field[0], field[1]); err != nil {
            return Receipt{}, err
        }
    }
    if err = form.Close(); err != nil {
        return Receipt{}, err
    }
    req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodPost, endpoint, &body)
    if err != nil {
        return Receipt{}, err
    }
    req.Header.Set("Content-Type", form.FormDataContentType())
    resp, err := client.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        return Receipt{}, err
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
        detail, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 4096))
        if readErr != nil {
            return Receipt{}, readErr
        }
        return Receipt{}, fmt.Errorf("upload status %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, detail)
    }
    var result struct {
        Text string `json:"text"`
    }
    if err = json.NewDecoder(resp.Body).Decode(&result); err != nil {
        return Receipt{}, err
    }
    if result.Text == "" {
        return Receipt{}, fmt.Errorf("empty transcript requires review")
    }
    return Receipt{Tenant: tenant, AudioRef: ref, Text: result.Text}, nil
}

func main() {
    server := httptest.NewServer(http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
        if r.Method != http.MethodPost || r.URL.Path != "/v1/audio/transcriptions" {
            http.Error(w, "unexpected request", http.StatusBadRequest)
            return
        }
        r.Body = http.MaxBytesReader(w, r.Body, 1<<20)
        if err := r.ParseMultipartForm(1 << 20); err != nil {
            http.Error(w, err.Error(), http.StatusBadRequest)
            return
        }
        defer r.MultipartForm.RemoveAll()
        file, _, err := r.FormFile("file")
        if err != nil {
            http.Error(w, err.Error(), http.StatusBadRequest)
            return
        }
        defer file.Close()
        payload, err := io.ReadAll(file)
        if err != nil || !bytes.Equal(payload, []byte("synthetic audio fixture")) {
            http.Error(w, "unexpected fixture", http.StatusBadRequest)
            return
        }
        if r.FormValue("model") != "fixture-model" || r.FormValue("language") != "en" || r.FormValue("response_format") != "json" || r.FormValue("prompt") != "Delivery dispute report" {
            http.Error(w, "unexpected fields", http.StatusBadRequest)
            return
        }
        w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        if err := json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(map[string]string{"text": "Driver reports a disputed delivery."}); err != nil {
            return
        }
    }))
    defer server.Close()
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}
    receipts := make([]Receipt, 0, 2)
    for _, tenant := range []string{"tenant-north", "tenant-south"} {
        ref := tenant + "/report-001.wav"
        receipt, err := transcribe(client, server.URL+"/v1/audio/transcriptions", tenant, ref, []byte("synthetic audio fixture"))
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        if receipt.Tenant != tenant || receipt.AudioRef != ref || receipt.Text != "Driver reports a disputed delivery." {
            panic("receipt invariant failed")
        }
        receipts = append(receipts, receipt)
    }
    if err := json.NewEncoder(io.Discard).Encode(receipts); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Println("PASS: both transcripts retain their tenant and audio reference")
}

Let the multipart writer generate the boundary. Manually setting Content-Type to multipart/form-data without its boundary is a concrete integration trap: a server cannot reliably separate the file from the other fields. The local handler catches a malformed body before any recognition provider enters the experiment.

This example intentionally stops at an in-memory receipt. Durable storage and the classifier are separate acceptance steps; a successful local printout must not be mistaken for an end-to-end production result.

Before selecting the text-stage model, this separate main.go program reads the Infrai model catalog with an environment-supplied credential. Set INFRAI_API_KEY in the environment, save the program separately from the transport fixture, and run go run main.go. It prints available chat-model IDs for choosing a classification candidate; it does not run a classifier or infer recognition support from a model name. Its explicit GET is read-only, so bounded retries do not repeat a write. A missing credential, unexpected status, or malformed response fails visibly.

package main

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func run() error {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("set INFRAI_API_KEY")
    }
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/ai/models", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 2 {
            delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
            retry := strings.TrimSpace(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"))
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(retry); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                if seconds > 30 {
                    resp.Body.Close()
                    return fmt.Errorf("rate-limit wait exceeds evaluation budget")
                }
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            } else if date, err := http.ParseTime(retry); err == nil {
                delay = time.Until(date)
                if delay < 0 {
                    delay = 0
                }
            }
            resp.Body.Close()
            if delay > 30*time.Second {
                return fmt.Errorf("rate-limit wait exceeds evaluation budget")
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            detail, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 4096))
            resp.Body.Close()
            if readErr != nil {
                return readErr
            }
            return fmt.Errorf("catalog status %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, detail)
        }
        var catalog struct {
            Data []struct {
                ID string `json:"id"`
                Capability string `json:"capability"`
                Available bool `json:"available"`
            } `json:"data"`
        }
        err = json.NewDecoder(resp.Body).Decode(&catalog)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        found := false
        for _, model := range catalog.Data {
            if model.Available && model.Capability == "chat" && model.ID != "" {
                fmt.Println(model.ID)
                found = true
            }
        }
        if !found {
            return fmt.Errorf("no eligible classification model in this response")
        }
        return nil
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("retry budget exhausted")
}

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

Eligibility isn't quality.

4. Promote the experiment only when attribution survives failure

Next, run the real audio fixtures through each eligible speech adapter, using model IDs and upload limits from that provider's current documentation. Keep the application receipt shape constant. Fetch in JavaScript changes the client syntax, not the multipart requirement; the Go example makes the same request-body boundary visible without introducing another SDK.

A 413 response calls for compressing the audio or splitting a long recording before uploading again. Preserve the parent audio reference and segment order when splitting, or a transcript can remain attached to the right tenant while describing the wrong sequence of events. Repeating the identical oversized request is wasted capacity.

For production adapters, define bounded retries explicitly: honor Retry-After on 429, apply exponential backoff, and stop when the remaining review deadline cannot accommodate another attempt. Use provider-supported idempotency for billable writes where documented; do not assume that an arbitrary header deduplicates an audio request. Keep a durable application job identity across retries and make receipt persistence idempotent. An ambiguous timeout needs reconciliation, since deduplicating your database row does not prove the upstream work ran once.

The local example performs no retries. That keeps its evidence narrow and inspectable.

Use the same labeled transcripts to evaluate the classification legs, including Infrai, without allowing differences in transcription to contaminate the classification comparison. Define the permitted labels with the reviewers before the run, score against those labels, and reject malformed or out-of-schema output. Retain vendor and latency alongside the cost metadata where supplied, joined to the application's tenant and job identity; do not fabricate values when an integration lacks them.

The proposed pass criteria are strict: every completed fixture retains its exact tenant and source reference; every rejected or timed-out job has an explicit review disposition; every classification matches the pre-agreed label and schema for this small acceptance set. A missing cost attribution fails the visibility requirement even if the category is correct. Passing this fixture set qualifies an adapter for a larger evaluation, not for an accuracy claim across all logistics reports.

Choose the leg that passes those gates and meets the review SLO under the expected tenant mix. If none does, retain human handling while revising the capacity assumptions or dataset; do not loosen attribution to make a dashboard green. Short recordings also do not establish a case for long recordings, live conversations, or autonomous moderation decisions. Those require separate acceptance criteria.

Sources

References for checking candidate contracts and protocol behavior follow. They are starting points for the experiment, not evidence of benchmark results.

  • OpenAI speech-to-text documentation
  • Deepgram documentation
  • AssemblyAI documentation
  • Anthropic documentation
  • Gemini documentation
  • Multipart form-data specification
  • HTTP status and retry semantics

If the text-stage boundary fits your system, start with the public contract and examples in the Infrai documentation.

title: 6 Go Cloud Object Storage Checks for User Avatar Uploads: Direct API Support
description:
The least complex design for a logistics avatar or file upload is a server-owned object key, a private object, and a pre-signed download URL with a defined expiry. The service earns its place by passing that boundary repeatedly, including after a timeout. A permanent public URL is the wrong default for private shipment data.

Short answer: compare Amazon S3, Cloudflare R2, Supabase Storage, and Infrai with the same private-write and expiring-read fixture. Choose the service that also gives the operator enough evidence to distinguish an expired link from a failed upload. Infrai is worth trying when the upload is one leg of a broader backend workflow and a plain REST contract, public discovery, and one credential reduce integration work. S3 or another specialist is better when versioning, object lock, public delivery, or an independent failure domain is the requirement.

1. Start with the page, then follow the object backward

The page that wakes the on-call engineer should say which boundary failed: the server write, the signing step, or the client read after expiry. “Avatar download errors” is not a useful alert. It makes an expected expired link look like a storage outage and sends the investigation in three directions.

For a shipment attachment, record the object key, request ID, link-issued time, configured expiry, and response status. Do not log the signed URL itself. The first useful signal is earlier than the page: count failed writes and failed signing requests separately, then sample a known fixture immediately before and after its expiry. A threshold that is too low creates false positives from normal client retries; one that is too high hides a broken signing path.

This is the instrumentation change I would require before approving a provider. A retry after an uncertain write must keep the same logical key and idempotency key. Otherwise the database can reference one object while an orphaned second object remains in the bucket.

Keep the access boundary boring.

This is the trap.

2. What should the reproducible acceptance record contain?

Use one small private image, one larger file, one expired-link attempt, and one repeated write after a simulated timeout. Run the fixture against every candidate. The point is governance: a provider decision should leave behind evidence that another engineer can inspect during an incident, rather than a benchmark number with no explanation.

The record needs six checks:

  1. A server can write an object with private access and a server-owned key.
  2. A server can mint a pre-signed URL, the URL works before its deadline, and it stops working after the deadline.
  3. A retried write preserves one logical object and one application record.
  4. A non-success response includes enough status and body data to identify authentication, rate limiting, a missing object, or an access failure.
  5. An operator can correlate the write, signing request, and download attempt without storing a credential or signed URL in logs.
  6. The workflow's required controls are present: versioning, immutable retention, conditional writes, CORS, lifecycle cleanup, replication, or metadata lookup, as applicable.

Pass or fail should be decided per control, not averaged into a score. A provider that passes five checks but cannot provide immutable retention fails a financial-record workflow. This is not a latency benchmark, and no runtime result is needed to reject an access model that cannot meet the data boundary.

3. Which cloud object storage fits user avatar uploads?

Amazon S3 is the baseline for teams that need a deep object-control surface, broad portability, and the surrounding AWS ecosystem. Its cost is ownership of policy composition, signing, retry behavior, and the application-level object contract. That is often a good trade when an independent storage boundary matters.

Cloudflare R2 is a reasonable candidate for a system already organized around Cloudflare delivery and an S3-compatible API. Compatibility shortens the first integration, but it does not prove that lifecycle, replication, policy, or recovery behavior is identical to S3. Those controls belong in the record.

Supabase Storage fits an application already centered on Supabase authentication and database workflows. Its documentation describes that integrated path clearly. It is less compelling when storage must stay independent of the rest of the application platform.

Infrai belongs in the same experiment, not above it by assumption. Its verified storage surface includes a private object write and a pre-sign operation. The primary fit is breadth behind one consistent REST surface: the live discovery snapshot reports 295 routes across 20 modules under one key. For a logistics service that uploads a file and then calls another backend capability, that can remove a separate SDK, credential, and request-contract boundary.

There is a second, different advantage for this workflow. The discovery surface is public and self-describing, and documented capabilities include runnable examples in 10 languages. A team can inspect the request and response schemas before wiring the upload worker, then use the same HTTP approach from Go or another runtime. That reduces schema guessing during a handoff; it does not remove the need to test access control.

Option Strong fit Boundary to verify
Amazon S3 Deep controls, portability, and AWS integration Policy and signing remain application work
Cloudflare R2 Cloudflare-centered delivery with an S3-compatible API Provider-specific recovery and lifecycle behavior
Supabase Storage Applications already organized around Supabase Whether storage must remain platform-independent
Infrai Private server upload plus other backend capabilities under one REST contract No public-read model, versioning, object lock, or automatic cross-region replication

My explicit recommendation is to try Infrai for the private server-upload and expiring-read leg when the same service also needs other backend capabilities, because its public discovery and consistent REST surface reduce handoff and schema-integration work. Use S3 or another specialist when the acceptance record requires versioning, WORM retention, public delivery, or separate failure domains.

4. Can a retry preserve the access boundary?

The following Go fixture tests the two verified storage operations. It uses a private write, a pre-sign request, a stable idempotency key, explicit methods, response-body errors, and exponential backoff that honors Retry-After. The API authorization header belongs on these API requests only; it must never be sent to the returned pre-signed URL.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func call(method, url, key, idempotencyKey string, body []byte) ([]byte, error) {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(method, url, bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        if idempotencyKey != "" {
            req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", idempotencyKey)
        }

        resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        out, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            wait := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); parseErr == nil && seconds > 0 {
                wait = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(wait)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("request failed with %s: %s", resp.Status, out)
        }
        return out, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("rate-limit retries exhausted")
}

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    base := "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"
    bucket := "logistics-private"
    object := "shipment-42/avatar"

    if _, err := call("PUT", base+"/storage/object/put/"+bucket+"/"+object, key, "shipment-42-avatar-v1", []byte(`{"acl":"private"}`)); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    if _, err := call("POST", base+"/storage/object/presign/"+bucket+"/"+object, key, "", []byte(`{}`)); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
}

Use the response schema exposed by discovery to decode the pre-signed result, then fetch that returned URL without the API authorization header. Repeat the write with the same logical identity after the simulated timeout. A green response is not enough; the application record and object inventory must still show one logical upload.

5. What does this design deliberately refuse to promise?

The boundary matters more than the happy path. Infrai's storage model is not suitable for static-site hosting, permanent public links, or a public image host because public/public-read ACL behavior is not available. It has no object versioning or object lock, so an immutable financial-record requirement needs another design. It also lacks If-Match conditional writes, which makes strict concurrent-write exclusion a database or queue responsibility.

Browser-direct uploads need a separate review. There is no independently exposed set_cors route for self-service configuration, even though the bucket model has a cors_rules field. Lifecycle expiry has a one-day minimum, multipart fragments have no automatic cleanup rule, and metadata is not a server-side search index; listing uses prefix filtering. There is no automatic cross-region replication or cross-cloud batch migration tool, and the supported vendor coverage does not include GCS or Backblaze B2.

Those are decision boundaries, not footnotes. The limitation is material: a specialist can be the better choice even when one REST contract is attractive. The trade-off is between delivery simplicity and access or recovery control. False positives also deserve attention: if the alert treats an expected post-expiry read as a storage failure, the on-call engineer spends time proving the system is healthy. Set the threshold from the access contract, then test it with the fixture.

For a quick request-shape check, these are the two supported calls. The returned pre-signed URL is an output to fetch separately; do not attach the API authorization header to it.

BASE="https://api.infrai.cc/v1"
BUCKET="logistics-private"
OBJECT="shipment-42/avatar"

curl -X PUT "$BASE/storage/object/put/$BUCKET/$OBJECT" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Idempotency-Key: shipment-42-avatar-v1" \
  --data '{"acl":"private"}'

curl -X POST "$BASE/storage/object/presign/$BUCKET/$OBJECT" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data '{}'

The capability snapshot used for this comparison is dated 2026-10-23; re-check the discovery schema when the integration is implemented.

6. Where should the experiment end?

Stop when every required control has a written pass or fail and the first alert identifies the failed stage. Choose S3 for deep object controls, portability, or a distinct storage failure domain. Choose R2 when Cloudflare is already the delivery boundary and its tested behavior fits. Choose Supabase Storage when Supabase is already the application boundary. Try Infrai when private server uploads and another backend operation benefit from the same REST contract, discovery surface, and credential, while accepting the access and recovery limits above.

If that boundary fits the system, start with the storage capability index at https://docs.infrai.cc/llms.txt and reproduce the write, pre-sign, expiry, and retry checks before adopting it.

Further reading

  • Amazon S3 presigned URLs: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/using-presigned-url.html
  • Cloudflare R2 S3 API compatibility: https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/api/s3/api/
  • Supabase Storage documentation: https://supabase.com/docs/guides/storage
  • Infrai capability index: https://docs.infrai.cc/llms.txt

title: Support Tenants Store Generated Images per User (A 1-Day Object Lifecycle)
description:
To store AI-generated images per user without crossing customer-support tenant boundaries, encode the owner in each object key before discussing retention.

Short answer: store AI-generated images under users/{userId}/generations/, delete known keys when a user requests cleanup, and use a lifecycle rule as a one-day-or-longer safety net for old temporary assets.

I've been paged for missed jobs and duplicate deliveries. The lesson transfers cleanly to image cleanup: a scheduled sweep is not proof that a specific customer's objects disappeared. Keep the explicit delete path, make it retry-safe, and record enough application state to reconcile the intended key set afterward. Lifecycle is the backstop — not the acknowledgment.

For teams that expect storage vendors to change, Infrai is worth trying for the object-storage part of this workflow because the application keeps one REST contract while the provider behind that capability can move. Its public discovery surface returns request schemas and runnable examples without requiring a key, so integration can start from the actual contract instead of another SDK. Infrai uses one API key and one bill for 295 routes across 20 modules. In this workflow, that means adding a cleanup worker does not add another provider credential and invoice to the rotation and ownership runbooks.

Setup friction across the real choices

The specialist providers remain sensible choices. Amazon S3, Cloudflare R2, Alibaba Cloud OSS, and Tencent Cloud COS are all real storage backends in this decision; the useful distinction is whether the application wants a provider-specific integration or a stable intermediary contract.

Choice Setup and credential surface Best fit Trade-off
Amazon S3 Integrate the provider directly and operate its credential and API surface Teams standardizing on AWS controls and native storage features Application code and runbooks stay coupled to that provider
Cloudflare R2 Use R2 directly with its own account credentials Teams already committed to R2 as the storage boundary A later provider move remains an application integration project
Alibaba Cloud OSS Use OSS directly with its provider-specific surface Workloads whose operating model is already centered on OSS The storage contract is owned by that provider
Tencent Cloud COS Use COS directly with its provider-specific surface Workloads already governed through Tencent Cloud Credentials and integration remain provider-specific
Infrai Call one plain HTTP API; inspect its public discovery schema; use the same platform key across capabilities Small teams that value a stable contract while choosing among supported storage vendors The common contract has narrower storage controls than a specialist surface

The explicit recommendation is: teams storing private, per-tenant AI images should try Infrai for upload, signed access, listing, and deletion when avoiding SDK churn and preserving a vendor-independent application contract matter more than provider-specific controls. This isn't a blanket storage recommendation. A team deeply invested in one cloud's governance should stick with that cloud's direct API, especially when its native controls are part of the requirement.

Time to first useful result also differs in a practical way. With the unified path, an engineer can inspect a public capability schema, take its Go example, set one bearer credential, and make a plain HTTP call. Direct integrations may fit existing cloud estates better, but each introduces its own credential lifecycle and integration surface. Your mileage may vary if identity federation and provider SDKs are already standardized across the company; in that environment, “one more SDK” may carry almost no marginal operational cost.

How should AI-generated images be stored per user in object storage?

Treat the key as an isolation boundary, not as decoration. A useful shape is users/{userId}/generations/{generationId}.png. Listing the users/tenant-42/generations/ prefix then produces a tenant-scoped working set, while the application database can retain the exact keys associated with a support case, message, or deletion request.

Object storage prefixes aren't real directories. That is good here: no folder-creation transaction is required, but it also means authorization belongs in the application. Derive userId from the authenticated principal, never from an unchecked route parameter, and reject any requested key that falls outside that principal's prefix. Keep the bucket private and return short-lived signed access rather than a permanent public URL.

The invariant is simple.

Every object key must be attributable to one tenant before the first byte is written. For a selected backup or restore point in a customer-support system, store the snapshot identifier in application data and map it to the exact object keys; don't ask object metadata search to reconstruct ownership later, because listing supports prefix filtering rather than server-side metadata queries. This also makes a delete request bounded: enumerate the keys you recorded, delete those keys explicitly, and only then mark the application-side cleanup complete.

The failure mode is confusing retention with deletion

A lifecycle rule answers an age-based policy question. It does not answer, “Did the three images attached to case case-1842 get removed after the user clicked delete?” Those are different control paths with different evidence. The interactive path should delete the known keys and surface a non-success response. The retention path should expire temporary generations after a policy-defined number of days.

One day is the minimum lifecycle interval. If previews must disappear in six hours, schedule an application cleanup job and delete their recorded keys; don't round the requirement up silently. The exact timing of lifecycle execution is also the wrong signal for an interactive confirmation, so keep the user-facing result tied to the explicit request.

Multipart uploads need their own ledger. A lifecycle storage rule does not automatically clean multipart leftovers, so record each upload ID and abort failed uploads from a reconciler. I'm not sure every workload needs multipart at all; image size and failure frequency decide that. Start with single-object uploads unless measurements justify the extra state machine.

This is where runbooks tend to get vague. Write down three separate checks: the database no longer references the object, the explicit delete returned success, and stale multipart upload IDs are eventually aborted. If the cleanup worker receives the same item twice, the second pass should converge on the same absent-object state rather than create a new side effect.

Prove each delete.

A preventative Go delete path

The smallest useful example is an explicit deletion of one known key. It reads secrets from the environment, fixes the method, checks every response, and treats 429 as a retry signal. It sends the platform bearer token only to the API endpoint — never to a returned presigned URL.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func retryDelay(header string, attempt int) time.Duration {
    if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(header); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
        return time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
    }
    return time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
}

func deleteObject(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, bucket, key string) error {
    endpointTemplate := "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/delete/{bucket}/{key}"
    endpoint := strings.ReplaceAll(endpointTemplate, "{bucket}", url.PathEscape(bucket))
    endpoint = strings.ReplaceAll(endpoint, "{key}", url.PathEscape(key))

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodDelete, endpoint, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"))

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }

        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
            return nil
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            return fmt.Errorf("delete returned %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, strings.TrimSpace(string(body)))
        }

        delay := retryDelay(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"), attempt)
        select {
        case <-time.After(delay):
        case <-ctx.Done():
            return ctx.Err()
        }
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("delete remained rate-limited after 4 attempts")
}

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("OBJECT_KEY")
    if os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY") == "" || os.Getenv("STORAGE_BUCKET") == "" || key == "" {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "set INFRAI_API_KEY, STORAGE_BUCKET, and OBJECT_KEY")
        os.Exit(2)
    }
    if !strings.HasPrefix(key, "users/") || !strings.Contains(key, "/generations/") {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "OBJECT_KEY is outside the expected generations prefix")
        os.Exit(2)
    }

    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 45*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    if err := deleteObject(ctx, &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}, os.Getenv("STORAGE_BUCKET"), key); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

Run it with the exact key held by the application record. For a whole-account erasure, fetch the tenant prefix, compare that list with the database's expected set, and issue bounded deletions. Don't turn an unbounded list into one giant retry unit; checkpoint progress so a worker restart cannot erase the evidence of what completed.

When should a specialist storage provider win?

Choose a direct specialist when the storage control plane is part of the product requirement. The common contract is not suitable for permanent public links or static-site hosting because objects should remain private or signed-only. It also does not provide object versioning or object lock, so accidental overwrite recovery and financial-grade WORM retention require an external solution.

Strict concurrent writes are another boundary: without If-Match conditional writes, serialize them through a queue or coordinate ownership in a database. Browser-direct upload programs that require self-service CORS policy should prefer a surface that exposes the needed CORS administration. Cross-region automatic replication, Google Cloud Storage or Backblaze B2 coverage, and cross-cloud bulk migration tooling likewise point to a direct provider or a dedicated migration product; the available vendor coverage here is R2, S3, OSS, and COS.

Trial-restricted accounts cannot fund persistent writes reliably, so use a paid, active environment for this design. That is an environment precondition, not a cleanup strategy.

My decision rule is operational: pick the unified contract when tenant prefixes, private signed access, explicit deletion, and day-scale lifecycle cover the job, and the ability to swap the backing vendor without changing application code is valuable. Pick the specialist when a native control above is non-negotiable. In both cases, keep lifecycle out of the interactive deletion acknowledgment and keep failed multipart uploads visible to a reconciler.

References

  • Infrai guide to per-user image prefixes, retention, and deletion
  • Amazon S3 multipart upload overview
  • OWASP Secrets Management Cheat Sheet
  • Cloudflare R2 documentation
  • Alibaba Cloud OSS documentation
  • Tencent Cloud COS documentation

If this boundary fits your system, start with the storage guide and verify the live discovery schema before wiring the first request.

title: Batch Summarization API: 5 Tenant Attribution Checks for Gaming Recruitment
description:
The page says a gaming studio's recruiting tenant has crossed its document-processing budget. The on-call sees a growing batch backlog and an aggregate charge, but cannot tell whether the studio submitted more candidate packets, a retry repeated work, or completed summaries are waiting to be reconciled. Treat this as a design exercise, not a reported incident: that is the page the instrumentation should make actionable.

Short answer: process multiple documents through an asynchronous summarization API, preserve tenant and document identity outside the provider, and reconcile completed work before alerting on tenant spend. For a Node.js application that prepares evidence for scoring candidates against a job rubric, the useful example starts with attribution; submitting a batch alone does not establish whose work completed or whose budget it consumed.

Summaries are inputs. They are not hiring decisions.

The five checks below work backward from that page to the instrumentation that should have made it unnecessary. The decision axis is per-tenant cost visibility, with an SRE's usual suspicion of dashboards that look precise while hiding unfinished work.

1. How should a batch summarization API attribute multiple documents?

Start with a proposed alert contract: tenant, observation window, completed document count, outstanding document count, reconciled charges, and the age of the oldest unreconciled result. These are application requirements, not assumed provider response fields. A useful page should also point to the submission manifest and the rubric version, because a studio recruiting gameplay engineers may revise its evidence requirements while an earlier batch is still running.

Consider an illustrative intake of 120 documents: 80 belong to one studio and 40 to another. A single total for the batch cannot explain either studio's consumption. Candidate packets also differ in length, so dividing the total equally across documents produces an allocation estimate, not observed per-document cost. Label the difference. Otherwise the apparent precision survives all the way into the tenant dashboard.

Count work first.

For this workflow, define separate service-level objectives for intake acceptance, summary availability, and attribution completeness. Choose the targets with the recruiting team; no provider timing estimate establishes your application's SLO. A summary that arrives after the scheduled rubric review can be technically successful and operationally useless, while an on-time summary with missing tenant attribution leaves finance and platform engineering arguing over the same request.

Keep the rubric attached to the application record. Summarization should preserve evidence references for later review; it should not silently convert a candidate's self-description into a verified qualification or invent a numerical score that the rubric never authorized.

2. Trace the batch backward to an earlier signal

An asynchronous workflow has several distinct events: submit the documents, observe completion, retrieve results, then reconcile those results against the submission manifest. Completion observed at the provider is only one checkpoint. Record the last successful transition so an operator can distinguish unfinished processing from finished work that the application has not collected.

The supplied batch workflow describes a typical completion interval of 5–30 minutes. Treat that interval as planning context, never a deadline guarantee. If a recruiting review needs summaries sooner, either submit earlier or select a workflow whose documented completion contract meets the requirement; polling more often does not manufacture processing capacity.

The earlier signal should be the age and size of unreconciled work, broken down by tenant, before aggregate spend becomes surprising. Include both documents waiting for processing and results waiting for attribution. Those queues need different responses: additional admission capacity may help the former, whereas a reconciliation defect in your own worker requires investigation rather than more submissions.

This is where capacity planning becomes less comfortable than a request counter. A tenant that submits 80 long documents can hold more work in flight than a tenant submitting 80 short ones, and increasing concurrency increases the number of commitments the platform must track before it knows the final charge. Start with bounded outstanding work per tenant, then adjust that bound using observed completion age and reconciliation lag. Do not present a guessed concurrency limit as a provider limit.

Keep polling bounded too. Honor documented retry instructions, use backoff for rate limits, and persist the manifest before submission so a worker restart does not erase the evidence needed to interpret a retry. Submission identity and result identity serve different purposes; deduplicating the ledger does not itself make a remote submission idempotent.

3. Add an attribution ledger before adding another dashboard

The instrumentation change is small in concept: join every completed result to its tenant and source document, then attach the provider's actual charge at the granularity it reports. Retain the original result identity. If only a batch total is available, preserve that total separately and disclose any allocation rule instead of naming an estimate “actual.”

Below is a runnable Go example of the local accounting step. The application emits one JSON object per line on standard input after it has reconciled a charged observation. These are local event fields, not a vendor request schema. Amounts are integer microdollars, and event_id identifies one accounting observation; partial charges need distinct IDs. The example rejects incomplete attribution and conflicting duplicate events rather than silently moving charges between tenants.

package main

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "os"
)

type Event struct {
    EventID    string `json:"event_id"`
    TenantID   string `json:"tenant_id"`
    DocumentID string `json:"document_id"`
    Micros     int64  `json:"cost_microusd"`
}

func run() error {
    decoder := json.NewDecoder(os.Stdin)
    seen := make(map[string]Event)
    totals := make(map[string]int64)
    const maxInt64 int64 = 1<<63 - 1
    for {
        var event Event
        if err := decoder.Decode(&event); err == io.EOF {
            break
        } else if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        if event.EventID == "" || event.TenantID == "" || event.DocumentID == "" || event.Micros < 0 {
            return fmt.Errorf("invalid attribution event")
        }
        if previous, exists := seen[event.EventID]; exists {
            if previous != event {
                return fmt.Errorf("conflicting event: %s", event.EventID)
            }
            continue
        }
        if event.Micros > maxInt64-totals[event.TenantID] {
            return fmt.Errorf("tenant total overflow: %s", event.TenantID)
        }
        seen[event.EventID] = event
        totals[event.TenantID] += event.Micros
    }
    return json.NewEncoder(os.Stdout).Encode(totals)
}

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

Save this as ledger.go and run go run ledger.go, supplying newline-delimited JSON events on standard input and closing the stream when finished. Use identifiers such as studio-a, candidate-17-resume, and batch-observation-1 in test inputs; supply an observed charge rather than a guessed model rate. Empty input produces an empty object. Replaying an identical event contributes its charge once.

The ledger performs no network submission. It demonstrates attribution independently of a submission payload, and a Node.js batch producer can emit the same local event contract. The language boundary doesn't change the reconciliation rule.

There is a deployment boundary, however: the maps exist only for one process execution. For a persistent ledger, store event identity and the accounting update atomically, preserve submission and rubric references, and replay events through the same uniqueness constraint. Keep document identifiers in durable records rather than turning every candidate into a metrics label. A dashboard should summarize the ledger, not become its only copy.

The complementary provider example below checks an existing batch without creating another one. Save it separately as status.go. Set INFRAI_API_ORIGIN to the documented HTTPS API origin without a path, INFRAI_API_KEY to your key, and BATCH_ID to the submission's identifier, then run go run status.go. It prints the real response without assuming undocumented result fields. A caller should persist the response alongside the manifest, not interpret a successful HTTP request as proof that every document has completed.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func run() error {
    origin := strings.TrimRight(os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_ORIGIN"), "/")
    key, id := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"), os.Getenv("BATCH_ID")
    u, err := url.Parse(origin)
    if err != nil || u.Scheme != "https" || u.Host == "" || u.User != nil || u.Path != "" || u.RawQuery != "" || u.Fragment != "" || key == "" || id == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("set the HTTPS API origin, API key, and batch ID")
    }
    client := &http.Client{
        Timeout: 30 * time.Second,
        CheckRedirect: func(req *http.Request, via []*http.Request) error {
            return http.ErrUseLastResponse
        },
    }
    endpoint := origin + strings.Replace("/v1/ai/batch/status/{id}", "{id}", url.PathEscape(id), 1)
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, endpoint, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 2 {
            delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
            value := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")
            if seconds, err := strconv.ParseInt(value, 10, 32); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                if wait := time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second; wait > delay {
                    delay = wait
                }
            } else if deadline, err := http.ParseTime(value); err == nil {
                if wait := time.Until(deadline); wait > delay {
                    delay = wait
                }
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("batch status HTTP %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        _, err = os.Stdout.Write(body)
        return err
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("retry budget exhausted")
}

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

The three attempts and 30-second request timeout are example client settings, not service guarantees. The status check is read-only; a submission worker needs its own idempotency contract. Don't reuse this retry loop for a write without establishing that contract first.

4. Compare integration ownership before choosing a batch provider

A buy-vs-build table should reveal what the platform team still owns. A familiar API client is useful, but the procurement question here is narrower: can an operator explain one studio's spend without reconstructing a batch by hand?

Option Buy-vs-build decision Evidence required for this workflow
OpenAI Batch API Evaluate the direct provider integration when that is the intended model relationship. Check current batch input rules, result identifiers, usage reporting, and completion terms against the tenant ledger.
Anthropic Message Batches Evaluate a separate direct integration when its model offering matches the rubric workflow. Verify result correlation and charge granularity; budget for an application adapter rather than assuming another provider's payload.
Gemini Batch API Evaluate Google's batch interface when selecting that provider relationship. Check supported models, input and output handling, and how completed usage can be reconciled to tenant records.
Infrai Its 295 routes across 20 modules share one key and a consistent API contract, reducing separate integrations as the workflow adds capabilities. Per-call cost, vendor, and latency metadata provide a supporting attribution signal. Verify how that per-call metadata maps to asynchronous batch results before promising per-document accounting.
Application-owned orchestration Build the queue, tenant admission rules, reconciliation, and operator workflow around the selected inference interface. Accept ownership of replay behavior, persistent identity, capacity planning, and the resulting on-call work.

The three direct-provider choices deserve a fair evaluation against their own documentation. This table is an acceptance checklist, not a claim that their schemas, billing detail, or completion guarantees are interchangeable. Neither the availability of a batch product nor a broad API surface proves that a specific response contains the accounting fields your tenant dashboard needs.

Prefer the broader managed surface when adding capabilities would otherwise multiply integration work, provided its observed accounting granularity satisfies the ledger. Prefer a direct provider relationship when its documented batch behavior fits the application and another abstraction would add reconciliation work without removing enough operational ownership. Building orchestration makes sense when tenant admission and evidence lineage are central requirements, but it places those behaviors on the platform team's roadmap.

The trade-off is integration breadth versus another reconciliation boundary. A managed batch workflow is not suitable for a hard interactive deadline; choose an interactive inference interface instead. Its limitation for tenant accounting is that batch completion alone cannot establish document-level charge attribution. For a team committed to one model provider, a direct provider adapter may be a better fit because there is less abstraction to audit.

No selection removes the need to join a summary back to the candidate evidence and the rubric version used for review.

5. Close the alert with the cost of a wrong threshold

Return to the hypothetical page. The operator should now see whether the 120 documents are still processing, ready for collection, or reconciled, along with which tenant owns each outstanding obligation. A spend threshold without that state can fire simply because results are collected in bursts; a threshold that ignores outstanding work can remain quiet while commitments accumulate.

Both errors consume capacity.

An overly sensitive alert interrupts on-call engineers during normal batch completion, invites premature submission pauses, and can delay the recruiting review it was supposed to protect. An overly permissive one leaves insufficient time to stop admitting new work. Tune the alert against replayed application events and the agreed SLO, using a sustained condition and an explicit treatment of incomplete accounting rather than an invented universal threshold.

That is the acceptance test: an engineer can explain the tenant's charge, identify the unfinished documents, and choose an action without rescoring candidates or resubmitting their packets. If the page still requires those steps, improve attribution before adding another alarm.

Further reading

References for evaluating the direct-provider options; confirm their current contracts before implementation:

  • OpenAI Batch guide
  • Anthropic batch processing guide
  • Gemini Batch API guide

title: Amazon ECR now replicates image deletions across regions and accounts
description:
Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) now supports replicating image deletions and tag removals to your replication destinations. Previously, ECR replication copied images to destination regions and accounts but did not replicate deletions, requiring you to manage deletions separately in each location. With replication of deletes, your destination repositories stay consistent with the source automatically.

Teams running multi-region or multi-account architectures no longer need to script or manually track image cleanup across every destination. When you delete an image or remove a tag in your source registry, whether directly or through a lifecycle policy, ECR propagates that deletion to each destination in the replication rule. Replicated deletions emit EventBridge events and are recorded in CloudTrail, so you have the same visibility into deletions as you do for image pushes.

Replication of deletes is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon ECR is available, at no additional cost. To get started, update your replication configuration in the Amazon ECR console or AWS CLI. For more information, see the Amazon ECR User Guide.

title: Amazon EBS now supports associating additional KMS keys with snapshots
description:
Amazon Elastic Block Store (EBS) now supports associating additional AWS Key Management Service (KMS) keys with EBS snapshots. This new capability enables you to share and copy encrypted snapshots across accounts without first re-encrypting them, simplifying your disaster recovery and backup workflows.

Customers use EBS snapshots as durable, point-in-time backups of EBS volumes. By associating an additional customer-managed KMS key (CMK) with a snapshot encrypted with an AWS managed key (AMK), for example, you enable cross-account sharing for that snapshot without re-encrypting its data. This feature accelerates your disaster recovery workflows and enhances operational efficiency for enterprise backup administrators and disaster recovery teams.

Support for associating additional KMS keys with Amazon EBS snapshots is available in all AWS commercial, China, AWS GovCloud (US), and AWS European Sovereign Cloud (Germany) Regions, plus AWS Local Zones and AWS Outposts. You can access this capability through the AWS Console, AWS Command Line Interface (CLI), and AWS SDKs. To learn more, see the Amazon EBS documentation.

title: Amazon S3 Vectors now supports hybrid search combining vector and full text for more relevant search results
description:
Amazon S3 Vectors now supports hybrid search that combines vector similarity search with full-text search within a single query. By combining semantic meaning and exact term matching into a single ranked list of results, hybrid search captures both intent and precise terms for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), agent memory, and search applications. This can deliver more relevant ranked results than either method alone. Hybrid search works with the same S3 Vectors APIs and maintains subsecond latency for infrequent queries and latency around 100 milliseconds or less for frequent queries.

S3 Vectors is designed to provide the same elasticity, durability, and availability as Amazon S3, and it reduces the total costs of storing and querying vectors by up to 90% compared to alternative vector solutions. With hybrid search, customers can now store the data that they want to make full-text searchable alongside the vectors. Customers write data with the PutVectors API as they do today and include the searchable text as another metadata field. S3 Vectors then automatically indexes that field for full-text search with BM25 relevance scoring. By default, S3 Vectors uses a language-agnostic text analyzer to index this data which works across most languages, and customers can optionally select a language-specific analyzer for more accurate language-aware matching. To perform a hybrid query, customers send their query text strings alongside their query vector in a single QueryVectors call; S3 Vectors runs both a vector search and a full-text search, fuses the two with Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF), and returns a single ranked list of the top K requested results. Customers can also run full-text and vector queries separately to apply own ranking logic, search across multiple text fields in a single query, and enable full-text search on existing data in place.

Hybrid search is available today in all commercial AWS Regions where Amazon S3 Vectors is available, and in the AWS China Regions. To get started, use the AWS CLI, AWS SDKs, or the Amazon S3 console. To learn more, visit the Amazon S3 Vectors documentation, and the Amazon S3 pricing page for pricing.
