title: Amazon Connect Health medical coding is now available in public preview
description:
Today, AWS announces the public preview of medical coding in Amazon Connect Health, a HIPAA-eligible AI service that works alongside healthcare teams across patient engagement and point-of-care workflows. Medical coding uses existing clinical documentation to suggest ICD-10-CM and CPT codes, including E&M levels and modifiers, for a provider or coder to review and approve before submission. You can integrate medical coding into your EHR or billing application through the Amazon Connect Health SDK, or use it with Amazon Connect Health ambient documentation.

Each code links to the evidence that supports it and carries a confidence score, so reviewers can confirm a code before a claim goes out. In this public preview, you can choose to upload your organization's previously coded encounters, and the service builds a coding reference set specific to your organization. The corrections coders make feed that reference set and improve future coding suggestions.

Medical coding is available in public preview in the US East (N. Virginia) and US West (Oregon) AWS Regions. To learn more, see medical coding in the Amazon Connect Health user guide.

title: Amazon Connect Customer agent assist now supports interactive responses
description:
Amazon Connect Customer agent assist now supports interactive components, including cards, carousels, buttons, and input fields. The AI agent analyzes conversation context in real time, recommends actions, retrieves information, and executes tasks on behalf of contact center agents using MCP tools in Connect Customer or third-party services. Interactive responses let agents review information, provide details, select options, and confirm actions without manually typing a separate request for each action. The AI agent can also recommend step-by-step guides, cases, customer profiles, and third-party applications that agents can open with one click.

For example, when a customer calls to dispute a charge, the AI agent can dynamically generate an interactive list of the customer’s recent transactions. The agent can select the disputed transaction, provide or confirm the required details, and approve the action. The AI agent can then use a connected tool to create the dispute request and display confirmation in the agent workspace.

This feature is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon Connect Customer agent assist is available. To learn more and get started, see Agent Assist in the Amazon Connect Administrator Guide.

title: Scheduling the removal of the kube-proxy IPVS backend
description:
The ipvs backend for kube-proxy was an experiment in providing a service proxy implementation with better performance than the iptables backend. While it succeeded in that goal, the kernel IPVS API has turned out to be a bad match for the Kubernetes Services API, and the ipvs backend was never able to implement all of the edge cases of Kubernetes Service functionality correctly.

In Kubernetes 1.29, the project introduced the nftables backend for kube-proxy, which became GA in 1.33. Part of the plan behind adding the nftables backend was the idea that it would eventually replace both the iptables and ipvs backends. Because the ipvs backend in particular is complex, not 100% feature complete, and architecturally quite different from the other two backends (and thus more work to maintain), Kubernetes SIG Network decided to officially deprecate it as of Kubernetes 1.35. Although it currently remains available in kube-proxy (with a warning about its deprecation), we (Kubernetes SIG Network) now plan to remove it in Kubernetes 1.40. All ipvs users should therefore be planning to migrate to either the nftables or iptables backends.

Why was the ipvs backend written?

The ipvs backend was originally designed to fix two different kinds of performance problems in the iptables backend:

  • First, iptables had problems with data plane latency (the speed at which clients could establish new connections to services), because kube-proxy would write a separate iptables rule to match each service IP, so every new connection would need to be matched against a long series of rules that was O(n) in the number of services in the cluster.

  • Second, it had an even larger problem with control plane latency (the speed at which kube-proxy could process changes to services and endpoints and update the data plane rules), because kube-proxy would rewrite the entire iptables ruleset every time any service or endpoint changed. While the list of rules itself was only O(n) in the total number of endpoints, the amount of time, RAM, and CPU that it took to process the updated ruleset grew faster than that. In very large clusters, kube-proxy would use 100% of one CPU all the time just to process iptables updates. (In fact, the control plane scaling problem was bad enough that for most users it was not even possible to grow the cluster to the size where the data plane scaling problem became noticeable.)

The ipvs backend solved both of these scaling problems. The data plane problem was solved mostly automatically, because the kernel IPVS subsystem uses hash tables rather than linear lookup. The control-plane problem was solved by not rewriting the entire ruleset on every update. (The kernel IPVS API doesn’t have a way of doing batch updates anyway, so this was essentially forced.)

Why is the ipvs backend now being deprecated?

Almost from the start, the ipvs backend also had problems.

The first version didn’t have 100% compatibility with the iptables backend, but it was assumed that this would be fixed over time. Unfortunately, the original authors moved on to other things outside the Kubernetes ecosystem (as inevitably sometimes happens in open source), and it took a while to find new people interested in maintaining the code.

Meanwhile, as people began using the ipvs backend in larger and larger clusters, its own scaling problems started to emerge. In particular, the lack of batch update operations in the IPVS API meant that while the ipvs backend was faster than iptables when making a few small changes, it was potentially slower when making a large number of changes at once. And because the IPVS API is fairly limited in what it can do, kube-proxy's ipvs backend needed to fall back to using iptables to implement various features of Kubernetes Services beyond basic "load balancing", making it run into some of the same scaling problems the iptables backend has. While the ipvs backend tried to mitigate this by using ipset for some of its rules, this again ran into the problem of not having a batch update API. Additionally, the fact that the ipvs backend uses iptables means that it has the same long-term support problem as the iptables backend: Red Hat's plan to remove the iptables API entirely from Red Hat Enterprise Linux means the ipvs kube-proxy backend will also no longer be available to Kubernetes users on RHEL.

What about IPVS schedulers?

Beyond performance, the other reason some users were excited about the ipvs backend was the ability to pick from among various IPVS "schedulers" for distributing traffic to endpoints, rather than relying on the simple random selection used by iptables (and nftables).

Unfortunately, the way IPVS is used by kube-proxy prevents it from being able to use most of the IPVS schedulers in a useful way. The problem is that kube-proxy is a distributed service that runs on all nodes in the cluster, but the kube-proxy processes on different nodes do not share their IPVS scheduler state, so each node picks endpoints without knowing what is happening with clients on any other node. Even the schedulers that are designed to work in a distributed way generally don't work better than random selection in the context of kube-proxy. For example, the mh scheduler uses Maglev Hashing to select endpoints, which theoretically allows for extremely efficient distributed load balancing. But that efficiency is only in the context of a specific sort of two-layer load-balancer design, and kube-proxy does not have the right architecture to be able to act as either of the two layers in that design.

Switching away from ipvs

Switching to nftables

If you are running Kubernetes 1.36 or later, and your nodes are running a Linux distribution with kernel 5.13 or later, and you use the ipvs proxy mode, then Kubernetes recommends switching to the nftables mode of kube-proxy. (Although the nftables backend is GA —and fully usable—as of Kubernetes 1.33, there have been some performance- and scaling-related fixes since then that that weren't backported to releases earlier than 1.36.)

The nftables backend is fully supported, feature-complete, and even has very slightly better performance than ipvs:

(Taller bars represent longer latency. The "p50" group is the average connection establishment latency. Note that even the largest numbers in this graph are quite tiny; the point is not to claim that nftables is (noticeably) faster than ipvs, just to show that, unlike iptables, it's not slower.)

Switching is as easy as changing the kube-proxy configuration and restarting kube-proxy. For example, in clusters deployed via kubeadm, change mode: ipvs to mode: nftables in the kube-proxy ConfigMap and then restart the kube-proxy pods, as described in the documentation on reconfiguring a kubeadm cluster. (If you are overriding other ipvs-specific kube-proxy configuration, you will also need to change those options to the corresponding nftables ones.)

Switching to iptables: "It's Not As Slow As You Think!"

If you can't switch to nftables, either because you are on an older version of Kubernetes, or because your cluster runs on an older Linux distribution that isn't new enough to support the nftables backend, you may be able to just switch to the iptables backend, which has improved greatly since the original creation of the ipvs backend in 2017:

  • The generated ruleset has been optimized to remove redundant and irrelevant rules (#57461, #60306, #96959, #108251), reducing data plane latency.

  • The code that generates the ruleset has been optimized to do fewer allocations, and to avoid unnecessarily recomputing the same information multiple times (#65755, #65902, #67948, #85617, #90103, #97238), reducing CPU and memory usage when resyncing.

  • Rather than doing “check the current state of the rules, then update them to the new state”, iptables kube-proxy now does “assume the current state is correct, update to the new state based on that assumption, and only explicitly check the current state if that update fails”. This greatly improves the resyncing speed, because it turns out that even reading the iptables ruleset is extremely slow in large clusters (#81517, #110334, #114181).

  • To the extent possible within the constraints of the iptables APIs, kube-proxy’s iptables backend now only updates iptables rules for services/endpoints that have changed since the last sync, rather than rewriting the entire ruleset every time (#110268 / KEP-3453).

The net result of this is that the iptables backend of 2026, while still not as good as the ipvs backend, is at least much better than the iptables backend of 2017 was, and many people who found iptables unusable in the past would not have problems with it now.

As with switching to nftables, switching to iptables is mostly just a matter of updating your kube-proxy configuration, although for technical reasons, in this case we recommend that you reboot each node after changing the kube-proxy configuration, rather than merely restarting kube-proxy.

Learn more

  • KEP-5495 gives the full timeline and plan for kube-proxy IPVS deprecation.

  • The blog post "NFTables mode for kube-proxy" has more information about nftables mode and its performance relative to ipvs and iptables.

title: AWS KMS now supports key sharing with AWS Resource Access Manager
description:
AWS Key Management Service (KMS) now integrates with AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM), giving you a simpler and more consistent way to share KMS keys across your AWS accounts, within your organization in AWS Organizations, and with specific IAM roles and users. You can now let trusted parties define the access they need through reusable managed permissions in RAM, while keeping full control of your keys and key policies. To share a key, create a resource share by selecting the keys to share, choosing a managed permission, and specifying the principals. You can use AWS managed permissions for common scenarios, or customer managed permissions (CMPs) authored by you or by trusted parties such as SaaS providers and central security teams.

Sharing KMS keys through RAM makes enabling cross-account access faster to set up and safer to maintain. The trusted parties who need access to your keys can publish the policy once as a CMP, without the need for you to modify the key policies by hand. You simply fill in the values that scope it to your environment and attach it to the resource share. Your existing key policy is untouched, so you are always in control of your key as your environment grows. When a new policy version is available via an updated CMP, you decide when to apply it to your resource shares.

This enhancement is built on new AWS RAM capabilities that are available for every resource type RAM supports. CMPs now support multiple policy statements and additional IAM condition operators, including StringNotEquals, BoolIfExists, and ArnLike, along with the ForAnyValue and ForAllValues prefixes, so you can express precise, least-privilege access. The parameterized managed permissions lets you place a temporary placeholder in CMPs that allows each resource share owner to customize and scope down CMPs to their environment, enabling CMPs to be reused and serve many accounts. CMPs can now be published and shared across accounts, so the authors can maintain one permission, manage its versions centrally, and see every resource share that uses it, while other accounts can use it directly without keeping their own copy.

KMS key sharing with RAM is available in all AWS Regions where both services are available, except the Middle East (UAE) and Middle East (Bahrain). For more information, see Sharing KMS keys with AWS RAM in the AWS KMS Developer Guide and Working with shared AWS resources in the AWS RAM Developer Guide.

title: AWS Marketplace Metering Service now supports decimal usage quantities
description:
AWS Marketplace Metering Service now supports decimal usage quantities in the MeterUsage and BatchMeterUsage APIs. Previously, AWS Marketplace sellers reported usage to both APIs in whole numbers, and now they can report usage with up to six decimal places.

Sellers can price and meter in the units that match how customers consume their product, for example reporting 1.5 terabytes (TB) of storage instead of 1 or 2 TB. To report decimal quantities, sellers use the new UsageQuantityAsDecimal parameter in MeterUsage and QuantityAsDecimal parameter in BatchMeterUsage, and existing integrations that report whole numbers continue to work without changes. Usage allocations, which split reported usage into buckets by tags, also support decimal quantities with the new AllocatedUsageQuantityAsDecimal parameter.

This new feature is available in all AWS Regions where AWS Marketplace Metering Service is available. To learn more, see MeterUsage and BatchMeterUsage in the AWS Marketplace API Reference.

title: AWS Secrets Manager adds managed external secrets support for Auth0, Okta, and Palo Alto Networks
description:
AWS Secrets Manager now supports managed external secrets for Auth0, Okta, and Palo Alto Networks. Long-lived credentials that are not rotated increase the risk of unauthorized access if exposed. Rotating a third-party credential requires coordinated updates to the external service and every application that uses it. You set a rotation schedule from the AWS Management Console or API. Secrets Manager rotates the credential and stores the current value without a custom rotation Lambda function.

Secrets Manager offers self-rotation and administrator-assisted rotation for Auth0 credentials. With self-rotation, the target application replaces its own secret. With administrator-assisted rotation, a separate Auth0 application with Management API permissions replaces the target application's secret. For Okta, Secrets Manager offers administrator-assisted rotation with a separate administrator JSON Web Token (JWT) key and validates the replacement before deactivating the old secret. For Palo Alto Networks, Secrets Manager offers self-rotation, in which the current API key authorizes its replacement.

Applications that already retrieve credentials from Secrets Manager receive the rotated value without a code change or deployment.

These integrations join existing managed external secrets support for BigID, Cisco Security Platform, Confluent Cloud, Databricks, Datadog, GitLab, Jenkins, MongoDB Atlas, Netskope, Paddle, Salesforce, Snowflake, SonarQube, and Twilio.

Auth0, Okta, and Palo Alto Networks managed external secrets are available in all AWS Regions where AWS Secrets Manager managed external secrets is supported. To learn more, visit the  AWS Secrets Manager managed external secrets documentation .

title: IAM Identity Center now supports VPC endpoints and network access controls
description:
AWS IAM Identity Center now supports interface VPC endpoints powered by AWS PrivateLink and network access controls, enabling you to keep IAM Identity Center traffic private and restrict which networks can reach your IAM Identity Center services.

Previously, IAM Identity Center rejected traffic arriving through VPC endpoints, requiring all sign-in and API traffic to use public endpoints. With this launch, you can create interface VPC endpoints for AWS access portal and service APIs to route traffic over the AWS private network. IAM Identity Center sign-in traffic flows through the AWS Sign-in VPC endpoint. You can attach VPC endpoint policies to each endpoint to scope which AWS organizations, accounts and resources are reachable through your private connection.

Network access controls add a second layer of enforcement at the IAM Identity Center instance level. When enabled, you can require that all access arrive through a VPC endpoint, allow specific IP address ranges or VPCs as trusted sources, and exclude individual applications from enforcement to accommodate services that connect from outside your VPC. SCIM provisioning traffic from your external identity provider can be independently restricted to known IP address ranges. Network access controls are configured through the IAM Identity Center API and are disabled by default.

This capability is available in all commercial AWS Regions and the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions at no additional cost. To learn more, see Interface VPC endpoints in the IAM Identity Center User Guide. For more information, visit the IAM Identity Center product page.

title: Amazon SageMaker AI now supports KV cache-aware routing for real-time inference endpoints
description:
Amazon SageMaker AI now supports KV cache-aware routing for real-time inference endpoints, enabling you to reduce time to first token for LLM workloads with long or repeated prompts. Serving engines such as vLLM store the computed key-value (KV) cache for repeated prompt starts such as shared system prompts, documents, and conversation history, to skip repeated work. Across several instances, a request that lands where the cache is missing recomputes it. Under high load, instances also evict cached blocks to free GPU memory, including shared prompts and earlier conversation turns.

KV cache-aware routing sends each request to the instance that holds the longest matching part of its prompt in cache. The vLLM container reports the cache blocks it stores and evicts, and SageMaker routes with that live view. If the lookup is slow or finds no match, the endpoint falls back to load-aware routing, so the request is still served. Prefix-aware routing suits stable shared prompts, short prompts, or moderate load. KV cache-aware routing suits long prompts, high load, and limited GPU memory.

Customers can now enable this feature by setting `RoutingStrategy` to `KV_AWARE` on a production variant and adding one environment variable so the container reports cache events. Customer can invoke the endpoint with the same APIs and OpenAI-compatible payloads. It supports single-model endpoints and inference components, including LoRA adapters, on GPU instances. It requires the AWS vLLM Deep Learning Container version 0.33.0 or later with at least two instances or inference component copies. Detailed observability metrics show KV cache hit rate. There is no additional charge for KV cache-aware routing.

KV cache-aware routing is available today in all AWS Regions where Amazon SageMaker AI is available. To get started, update to the latest AWS SDK or CLI. To learn more, visit the Amazon SageMaker AI inference page and see the API documentation.

title: AWS announces Networking Flexible Cost Allocation for Amazon VPC
description:
Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) now supports Networking Flexible Cost Allocation (FCA), which splits shared networking costs by the resources that actually drive them, so you can see what each team or application used. Until now, AWS Cost and Usage Report (CUR), including CUR 2.0 in AWS Data Exports, showed networking usage as a single item, and most customers split it across teams with custom scripts and manual estimates. FCA splits this line item by the resources that generated it. It supports NAT gateway data processing and data transfer, including traffic to the internet, and in-Region Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) and VPC peering data transfer.

Today, when several teams share a resource such as a NAT gateway, the account that owns it pays the full cost and can't see which team or application drove it. To work around this, some customers built custom scripts to analyze VPC Flow Logs, which takes ongoing engineering effort. Others used fixed-percentage splits, which overcharge some teams and undercharge others. FCA breaks down usage based on traffic sources, helping you accurately track financial metrics based on applications and teams. To get started, attach a cost allocation policy to a NAT gateway, VPC peering connection, or Amazon EC2 instance, then select Networking flexible cost allocation under split cost allocation data in the AWS Billing and Cost Management console. Allocated line items appear in your CUR within 24 hours. FCA changes only how costs are shown in your reports. Your bill and total charges stay the same.

FCA is available at no additional charge. It's supported in all AWS commercial Regions except Middle East (Bahrain) and Middle East (UAE). It's also available in the China Regions. It is not available in the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions. To learn more, visit the Networking FCA product page.

title: AWS IAM Identity Center now supports ForceAuthn in SAML requests
description:
AWS IAM Identity Center now gives you the option to require workforce users to re-authenticate with your external identity provider (IdP) each time their user interactive session expires. By default, when a user's session expires, IAM Identity Center renews it through the user's existing IdP session, and the user isn't prompted to sign in again. For organizations with strict security or compliance requirements that mandate explicit user verification at regular intervals, this automatic renewal may not meet policy requirements.

When you set user re-authentication to Required and a user's user interactive session expires, IAM Identity Center prompts the user to re-authenticate with your external IdP. This helps you enforce stronger sign-in controls for regulated workloads. IAM Identity Center implements this by adding the SAML 2.0 ForceAuthn attribute to the SAML request sent to your IdP.

You can configure user re-authentication for any IAM Identity Center instance (organization or account) that's connected to an external IdP as its identity source. The setting applies only to service provider initiated sign-ins, where users sign in through your AWS access portal URL. Changes to the user re-authentication setting are logged in AWS CloudTrail, so you can audit when it was turned on or off.

User re-authentication is available in all AWS Regions where IAM Identity Center is available at no additional cost. To learn more, see Require user re-authentication in the AWS IAM Identity Center User Guide.
